text:
Democrats scored major victories in Tuesday’s midterm election, taking control of the U.S. House and Senate, including Senate wins in Republican strongholds like South Carolina and Texas.

In Michigan, the party maintained control of the governor’s office and state Senate, while also taking the Michigan House majority — a trifecta that could enable Democrats to protect the state’s clean energy law and advance other environmental protections.

The Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot initiative to ban political contributions by utilities and major government contractors passed with 81% of the vote, according to the Secretary of State. The state’s constitutional convention ballot measure, which environmental advocates warned could endanger environmental safeguards, failed with 74% of voters opposed, state data shows.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s victory over Republican Mike Rogers, a former Congressman, for Michigan’s open U.S. Senate seat was among the most closely watched contests in the country. It may prove consequential to efforts to federally regulate data centers.

El-Sayed released “terms of engagement” for data centers in January that he said will protect other utility ratepayers from data center costs, ensure community engagement and community benefits, protect energy reliability, safeguard water resources, and require projects to comply with clean energy laws.

Data centers face intense opposition in many Michigan communities, and many candidates called for moratoriums and guardrails to prevent impacts to the environment or utility ratepayers.

Rogers initially expressed support for streamlining data center development before saying in August that he supports a statewide, one-year data center moratorium.

El-Sayed voiced his support for Medicare for All throughout the campaign.

He criticized DTE Energy’s political spending, which he said helped the company gain fast-tracked approval for its Oracle and OpenAI data center contracts in Saline Township.

El-Sayed said during the Senate primary that he was the only candidate in the race who received no donations from corporate political action committees, including those funded by DTE.

Savit says he will continue Nessel’s ratepayer work

Utility accountability emerged as an issue in the Michigan attorney general contest. The winner of the race, Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, said he would continue outgoing Attorney General Dana Nessel’s work of intervening on behalf of ratepayers in cases before the Michigan Public Service Commission.

During her eight-year tenure, Nessel intervened in many gas and electric rate cases, calling on regulators to sharply reduce rate hikes requested by DTE, Consumers Energy, and other investor-owned utilities. Nessel intervened in the regulatory filings for DTE’s contracts for the Oracle and OpenAI data center in Saline Township and Google data center in Van Buren Township, and filed appeals after contracts were approved for both facilities.

Savit told Planet Detroit in September that utility rates “should be geared toward ensuring reliability and should be no more than is necessary to do that.”

He also challenged utilities’ returns on equity, or the profit passed on to shareholders, and the inclusion of expenses like travel and lobbying in rate cases.

Savit’s opponent, Eaton County Prosecutor Doug Lloyd, a Republican, expressed concern about ratepayer affordability in an April interview with the WDIV-TV program “Flashpoint.” He emphasized the attorney general’s law enforcement responsibilities in media appearances, telling WDIV that “one main focus of government should be public safety.”

Democratic sweep may safeguard clean energy legislation

Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson’s victory over U.S. Rep. John James (R-Shelby Township) in the governor’s race, and Democratic control of the Michigan Legislature, could pave the way for further action on climate and energy prices, environmental advocates say.

Courtney Brady, with the environmental group Evergreen Action, said in a statement that voters chose leaders who will bring down energy costs, with clean energy as part of the solution.

“Michigan has an opportunity to protect families from rising data center costs, hold utilities accountable, and accelerate the deployment of affordable clean energy,” Brady said.

In 2023, a Democratically controlled Michigan legislature passed the Clean Energy and Jobs Act, which looks to achieve 100% clean energy generation by 2040.

In March, Republicans introduced legislation entitled “Project Lighthouse” that would repeal the state’s clean energy mandates. State Rep. Pauline Wendzel, R-Watervliet, called the requirements “arbitrary” and said they benefit investor-owned utilities at ratepayers’ expense.

Analysis by 5 Lakes Energy and Evergreen Action said that Project Lighthouse would increase residential utility bills in the long term. Ben Poulson, state government affairs director at the Michigan League of Conservation Voters, told Planet Detroit in June that the legislation would repeal programs used to lower energy waste and hold utilities accountable.

Utility money initiative wins; public power comes up short

Proposal 2, the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot initiative, to bar political spending by utilities and contractors doing significant business with state, succeeded Tuesday after receiving support from Democrats running for statewide office and over 80 organizations.

Christy McGillivray, co-chair of the MMOP steering committee, said in August that anger over DTE and Consumers‘ proposed rate hikes could drive support for the ballot initiative.

“Michiganders are fed up with this pay-to-play system and overwhelmingly agree that our government should work for people, not powerful corporations,” she said.

The Mackinac Center for Public Policy conservative think tank filed a federal lawsuit Tuesday against Benson and Nessel alleging that Proposal 2 violates free speech protections, The Detroit News reported.

Representatives for utilities and Blue Cross Blue Shield of Michigan challenged the ballot initiative, saying it would silence their employees who look to engage in the political process.

Another challenge to DTE Energy fell short Tuesday. Ann Arbor’s Proposition E lost 52% to 48%. This citizen-led ballot initiative would have created a municipal energy utility board that could have eventually replaced DTE Energy in the city.

Backers of the Ann Arbor for Public Power ballot initiative argued it was the best way to improve energy affordability and reliability in the city, and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.

Opponents said the effort would have been extremely expensive and set back Ann Arbor’s efforts to deliver clean energy and other city services.

title: As Washington Shifts, Manufacturers Keep Working Across the Aisle - NAM
description:
One potential solution already has bipartisan backing: permitting reform.
Timmons drew a parallel to Sen. Whitehouse’s leadership on permitting reform, praising his efforts to expand energy infrastructure and create opportunities for American manufacturers.
He also pointed to the NAM’s “America on Hold” report, which found that permitting delays cost manufacturers nearly $8 billion annually.
The Laborers’ International Union of North America also called for permitting reform in an op-ed in The Hill.
Sen. Whitehouse highlighted the roundtable on X, amplified by Timmons, as well as in a press release.
text:
Democrats swept control of the House and Senate in Tuesday’s elections, intensifying the focus in Washington on addressing the economic pressures facing Americans. One potential solution already has bipartisan backing: permitting reform.

The big picture: Voters sent a clear message Tuesday: They are frustrated with the persistently high cost of living (The Wall Street Journal, subscription). For manufacturers and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, permitting reform offers a bipartisan path to meet soaring demand for energy, unlock new energy supplies and bring down costs for families and businesses all while supercharging manufacturing in America.

A bipartisan push: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) today acknowledged the ongoing negotiations, saying, “We have a bipartisan group working on permitting, permitting reform and hopefully they’ll come up with a good deal on that.”

But the election has also raised questions about whether lawmakers will advance the existing agreement during the lame-duck session or revisit negotiations in the new Congress.

Building momentum: Just ahead of the election, NAM President and CEO Jay Timmons and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and key architect of the permitting reform legislation introduced in the Senate, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, convened a permitting reform roundtable that followed a facility tour at manufacturer Cooley Group in Pawtucket, Rhode Island.

The NAM-hosted event brought together leaders from manufacturing, organized labor and the business community to build support for the bipartisan agreement, negotiated by Sens. Whitehouse, Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Martin Heinrich (D-NM) and Mike Lee (R-UT).

Participants included Cooley Group President and CEO and NAM Executive Committee member Dan Dwight; Partnership for Rhode Island Executive Director Liz Catucci; Rhode Island Manufacturers Association President and CEO Melissa Travis; Greater Providence Chamber of Commerce President Laurie White; Laborers’ International Union of North America General Secretary-Treasurer Mike Sabitoni; and Rhode Island AFL-CIO President Pat Crowley.

Policy, not politics: Timmons emphasized that the agreement reflects shared priorities that transcend party lines: lower costs, more jobs, greater investment and responsible environmental stewardship.

“This bill is not about politics; it’s about the success of manufacturers here in the United States,” Timmons said, praising the four Senate negotiators for putting country over party.

“It’s a good thing when we have a stronger economy with more jobs and lower costs and a cleaner environment, all at the same time,” said Sen. Whitehouse. “So that’s what our intention is to deliver here. And I appreciate the terrific work that was done in the Senate to pull this together. … This was a good example of solid bipartisan work. It took a ton of time and a ton of effort.”

A historic connection: Timmons highlighted a personal connection between Sen. Whitehouse and the NAM that dates back more than 130 years. Thomas Dolan, the NAM’s first president in 1895 and Sen. Whitehouse’s great-great-grandfather-in-law, was a woolen manufacturer who later entered the energy business, helping develop the nation’s emerging electrical grid.

Timmons drew a parallel to Sen. Whitehouse’s leadership on permitting reform, praising his efforts to expand energy infrastructure and create opportunities for American manufacturers.

Calling Cooley Group an “American success story,” Timmons praised the century-old manufacturer and its 300 employees for driving innovation and creating jobs in Rhode Island.

“We want to make sure companies like Cooley have every tool that they need to make the next 100 years even more competitive than the last,” Timmons said. He also pointed to the NAM’s “America on Hold” report, which found that permitting delays cost manufacturers nearly $8 billion annually.

Sen. Whitehouse’s warning: During the roundtable, Sen. Whitehouse pushed back on the idea that Democrats should wait until the new Congress to negotiate a different deal if they made significant electoral gains.

“I vehemently disagree with that strategy,” Sen. Whitehouse said, arguing that delaying action could jeopardize an agreement that has a path to passage in both chambers and a presidential signature.

“Don’t sacrifice now for later,” he urged, emphasizing the importance of securing the benefits of the current agreement rather than restarting negotiations.

“This [isn’t] over, but I think we’re in a good place, assuming that the administration does what it has said it will do with respect to making its regulatory posture for clean energy fair,” he concluded.

Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM), a lead negotiator who is poised to chair the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee next year, echoed that urgency. “It doesn’t necessarily get easier just because of who the chair is,” Sen. Heinrich told Punchbowl News today. “This is the closest we have come to actually finding something that can get signed into law, and I’m not going to wait.”

Cooley Group says: Dwight emphasized why permitting reform matters so much to companies like his.

“Permitting is an important protection that does not need to come at the expense of growth,” he said. “Companies like Cooley Group will be able to continue our investments to decrease our environmental footprint without compromising business growth.”

“As manufacturers, we know what happens when reviews are duplicative and unpredictable. Investments are delayed, costs rise and opportunities to expand good jobs [disappear],” Dwight said. “Faster, more predictable permitting would bring infrastructure projects online sooner and unlock business growth for manufacturers of every size.”

Business and labor agree: The roundtable also highlighted the costs that permitting uncertainty imposes on employers and workers alike.

Dwight explained that faster permitting could help manufacturers expand domestic sourcing and reduce dependence on foreign suppliers.

Sabitoni stressed that “when business and labor and then government get on the same page, that’s usually when good things happen,” underscoring the importance of collaboration to advance the legislation, while Crowley emphasized the need to build new energy infrastructure to create jobs and achieve environmental goals.

Catucci pointed to the importance of regulatory certainty in attracting businesses and investment to Rhode Island, noting that delays cost money and jobs.

Travis praised Sen. Whitehouse’s “tenacity and determination” in building bipartisan support for legislation critical to Rhode Island’s nearly 1,800 manufacturers employing approximately 75,000 people.

More labor groups join the push: On Tuesday, four more unions joined the three unions who already endorsed the bipartisan legislation: Iron Workers, Sheet Metal Workers, Boilermakers and Teamsters joined Engineers, Laborers and Plumbers in a letter first reported by Politico. The NAM highlighted labor’s support on X.

The Laborers’ International Union of North America also called for permitting reform in an op-ed in The Hill.

In the news: The NAM’s roundtable was scooped by Punchbowl News in its Friday Midday newsletter as well as by reporter Josh Seigel on X. Punchbowl also covered it in its Monday AM newsletter, which Siegel amplified on X. In addition, the event was covered by Providence Business First (subscription), whose reporter, Mary Serreze, attended the event. Sen. Whitehouse highlighted the roundtable on X, amplified by Timmons, as well as in a press release.

A united message: Timmons and Sen. Whitehouse also joined forces in a video highlighting the bipartisan push for permitting reform and the importance of getting a deal across the finish line.

The bottom line: As Congress returns to Washington following the election, the coalition is focused on converting the support into legislative action—and addressing one of the cost drivers holding back American investment, job creation and economic growth.

text:
Data centres were on the ballot in the US midterm elections, with Democratic candidates who pledged to halt development claiming victory on Tuesday night.

The states of Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, which have become magnets for firms wanting to build out data centres to power artificial intelligence, voted for Democratic candidates who have vowed to crack down on the technology.

More than half of Americans are more fearful than excited about AI, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center poll.

They are also concerned about data centres, which use massive amounts of energy, make a lot of noise and cause pollution, and require a lot of land. At least 45 data centre projects were disrupted in the second half of 2026 due to local opposition, according to Data Center Watch, a research project run by the company 10a Labs.

US President Donald Trump has championed the build-out of data centres and in September, called a pushback against them and AI safety concerns “all a hoax,” adding that “data centres are great, and they make people wealthy, and they make states wealthy”.

More than 50% of respondents said AI and data centres were a “crucial or a major factor” in their decision to vote in the midterm elections, according to an NBC exit poll.

"Data centres weren’t the reason most people voted, but they gave the affordability argument a local, visible target and clearly drove votes," said Heather West, geotechnology practice head at consultancy firm Eurasia Group.

"Voters oppose data centres in their own communities by wide margins, and that opposition crosses party lines, as we see in data centre ballot measures," she told Euronews Next.

What does the vote mean for data centres now?

Texas has lured in the tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Oracle, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon with tax breaks and promises of land and energy.

Republican governor Greg Abbott tried to make the state an AI “epicentre” in September, but he later shifted course and paused permits for new data centres pending an audit.

The U-turn followed his Democratic opponent Gina Hinojosa pledged to temporarily halt all new data centre construction until there were legal safeguards.

"Multiple states - most importantly Texas, Ohio, and Georgia - now have governors who are vocally sceptical of data centres, and those states host nearly half of the US AI data centre buildout," said West.

But she said despite Hinojosa's pledge to maintain a moratorium, her power to go beyond Abbott’s temporary, grid-driven pause is "limited".

This will add "friction," as "it doesn’t stop the buildout," West said.

"Projects already permitted or under construction will largely proceed. The friction hits the next wave: local fights, slower permitting, and pressure to make data centers pay for their own power.

"That changes where companies build and what it costs them, but we don’t expect them to turn away from these projects.”

Elon Musk, who pumped $474 million (€420 million) into the Republicans for the midterms and has been building his "Colossus" - a massive cluster of AI-native data centres and supercomputers in Memphis - wrote on X “data centres in space looking pretty appealing right now,” following Tuesday’s election result.

In Ohio, voters fiercely rejected data centres, with 15 municipalities passing bans or implementing other restrictions.

Meta has planned to spend $1 billion (€890m) to construct a data centre in Ohio, and Amazon Web Services has also planned to spend $2 billion (€1.78bn) in the state.

description:

Data centers were one major issue on the ballot.
With rising power demand for data centers and rising energy costs, this election was also about the future of energy.

text:
On Tuesday, Americans voted for a change in direction – including on the environment.

Data centers were one major issue on the ballot. On Tuesday, data center bans or restrictions passed in at least 38 jurisdictions and counting across the country. In the states where the buildout is happening fastest, including Georgia, Ohio, and Texas, governors’ races turned on voter recognition of the need for stronger guardrails and robust community protections.

With rising power demand for data centers and rising energy costs, this election was also about the future of energy. Voters angry about growing energy bills focused attention on races for seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, the body that regulates utilities in that state. Similar dynamics were seen in races for two seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission, another utility regulator, and one seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the oil and gas industry.

These are small agencies with tremendous power. With these seats, there is an opportunity to usher in clean energy for people who are struggling with soaring energy costs. These were the opposite of sleepy races: Voters are understanding the connection between data centers, utility rates, and regulatory bodies.

And, in the midst of a rush to drill more oil and gas and entrench our fossil fuel dependence, voters rejected a ballot measure to establish a constitutional “right to gas” in Colorado, a major oil-and-gas-producing state. The oil and gas industry presented voters with a false choice between prosperity and policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Voters know better.

Among the most important debates in the country is how to build the infrastructure we need faster without running over people and wrecking the things we can’t afford to lose. For example, clean water and clean air. This “abundance” debate has its origins in the California housing crisis, and it has come to stand for the proposition that deregulation is the answer to our country’s problems. As data centers show what speed without guardrails looks like, the debate came full circle in California, with voters rejecting Prop 45, a sloppy effort to kill environmental review in the permitting process for even the most consequential projects.

This election is a thrilling reminder and a profound challenge: We can move forward together in this country if we are willing to throw in together, believe in our ambition for real change, and act on it.

Over the last two years, too many people have underestimated American voters and their ability to care about all the things that matter at once. This election was about the cost of living and an economy that must work infinitely better for everyone. It was also about our health, our health care, and the health of the communities where we live and work. It was about justice and the rights that Americans are not going to give up, no matter how much money is spent and how much power is abused to create division and drive despair.

People across this country did the real work to organize and vote. A whole bunch of courageous, good people stepped up to lead this work. The hope that millions of Americans felt on election night is a call to the most ambitious action. Let’s get to work!

title: Midterm Election Results in Divided Government for the 120th Congress
description:

Positioning for the 120th Congress The transition period between the 2026 midterm elections and the start of the 120th Congress is decisive.
text:
Voters have spoken, and the result is that Washington is entering a two-year period of divided government that will be marked by a new congressional policy agenda. Energy, environment and natural resources will be at the center of policymaking debates as the new Democratic majority in the U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate confront constituent demands to address energy affordability, strengthen domestic supply chains, accelerate the clean energy transition, protect resources, address tariffs, and reign in data center development. It will clash with the Administration through aggressive congressional oversight, dynamic budget and appropriations negotiations, slower confirmation of executive nominations and competing efforts to set the national policy agenda.

With control of both chambers, Democrats will have an easier path to pass legislation through Congress, but enactment still requires presidential approval or veto-proof majorities. Unless Senate rules change, major legislation is likely to face Senate procedural constraints. The most consequential results are expected to come through annual appropriations, targeted bipartisan bills, nominations, oversight, and the interaction among Congress, agencies, states, and the courts rather than through legislation passed by Congress and enacted by the President.

What Changes Immediately

On January 3rd the new Congress will be sworn in. At that time, the Democratic Majority in the Senate and House will have:

Congressional agenda control. Democratic leaders will set hearing calendars, committee priorities, floor schedules, and investigative agendas in both chambers.

Oversight intensity. Committees will scrutinize regulatory rollbacks, grants and loans, staffing and scientific integrity, enforcement, leasing and permitting, and compliance with enacted spending directives. Congressional oversight can proceed through hearings, document requests, subpoenas, reporting requirements, support-agency reviews, authorizations, and appropriations.

Appropriations leverage. Annual funding measures are expected to become the principal forum for negotiation over agency budgets, program direction, policy riders, and implementation deadlines. The President retains veto power, creating pressure for cross-party agreements.

Senate advice and consent. The Democratic Senate can slow, condition, or reject nominees for departments, independent commissions, and the federal judiciary, while using confirmation hearings to press for policy commitments.

Greater policy uncertainty, but also openings for deals. Conflict is likely to be substantial, yet growing electricity demand, grid reliability, infrastructure needs, permitting backlogs, domestic manufacturing, community impacts of data centers and large loads, wildfire and disaster risks, and conservation funding also can create opportunities for those stakeholders engaging in bipartisan negotiations.

Implications

Organizations should plan for simultaneous legislative, regulatory, oversight, and litigation tracks. A position that succeeds with one branch may be challenged by another. Effective engagement will require credible relationships across parties; a clear factual record; an understanding of committee, agency, and state processes; and policy solutions that can survive changes in political control.

The Congress-Administration Relationship

The central dynamic among federal branches of government will be institutional competition, not legislative paralysis. Congress is expected to seek to redirect, constrain, or expose Administration policy. While the White House is likely to exercise veto authority, executive management, rulemaking, enforcement discretion, and public messaging to preserve its agenda, courts will continue to review agency actions and disputes over statutory authority, procedure, funding, and access to information.

Oversight and investigations

Likely targets include executive orders and agency directives affecting energy development and environmental protections; the use, withholding, rescission, or redirection of appropriated funds; permitting and leasing decisions; enforcement priorities; advisory committees and scientific processes; and the implementation of statutes governing air, water, public lands, wildlife, and energy markets. Such oversight is fundamental to determining whether laws are working as intended and are administered effectively, efficiently, and economically.

For regulated entities and funding recipients, oversight can create both risk and opportunity. Companies, trade associations, project sponsors, states, tribes, local governments, and non-governmental organizations may be asked to provide information, testify, or help committees understand real-world consequences. Preparation should include document discipline, consistent messaging, privilege and confidentiality analysis, and coordination among legal, policy, technical, and communications teams.

Funding, shutdown risk, and negotiated outcomes

Democratic appropriators are expected to propose stronger funding for environmental review, enforcement, conservation, climate and resilience programs, clean energy deployment, and agency science, while seeking limitations on selected Administration initiatives. The White House is likely to press for its own spending priorities and policy conditions. Continuing resolutions, omnibus or minibus packages, rescission disputes, and shutdown deadlines will dominate the calendar.

Because annual appropriations recur and must ultimately become law, they may also provide the most reliable venue for negotiated outcomes. Those seeking to engage should distinguish between symbolic provisions, one-year directives, report language, and durable statutory changes. They should also monitor whether implementation instructions are matched with adequate funding and realistic timelines.

Nominations and independent agencies

Senate control gives Democrats substantial influence over the composition and policy direction of executive departments, independent commissions, and the judiciary. Vacancies or delayed confirmations may affect agencies such as the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Environmental Protection Agency, Department of the Interior, Department of Energy, and related boards and councils. The practical effects will vary by agency structure, quorum requirements, existing terms, and the nominations the President chooses to submit.

Where bipartisan action remains possible

Permitting improvements that preserve meaningful review while improving coordination, schedules, data quality, and certainty.

Electric reliability, transmission, interregional planning, grid security, and supply-chain resilience.

Advanced nuclear, geothermal, hydropower, carbon management, hydrogen, critical minerals, and other technologies with regional or industrial constituencies.

Wildfire risk reduction, forest and watershed restoration, drought response, coastal resilience, abandoned mine remediation, and disaster recovery.

Federal support for infrastructure, research, demonstration projects, and domestic manufacturing, especially where projects create local benefits across party lines.

Bipartisan negotiations are most likely to be specific, implementation-focused, and supported by diverse regional and sectoral interests. Broad packages may still emerge, but they will require careful design with strong and diverse stakeholder support, with trade offs extending beyond traditional partisan positions.

Anticipated Policy Issues in the 120th Congress

Highlighted below are public policy matters likely to be discussed, debated, and pursued during the next Congress, on which Van Ness Feldman has demonstrated experience supporting client objectives.

Energy affordability, reliability, and infrastructure

Electricity demand and system adequacy will remain a defining issue. The U.S. Energy Information Administration’s 2026 outlook identifies data-center server use as a major factor in projected electricity-consumption growth and emphasizes that capacity decisions depend on policy, regulation, resource availability, and market conditions. Congress is likely to examine generation adequacy, transmission build-out, interconnection, utility and customer costs, and the federal role in siting and permitting.

Democrat-led committees are positioned to seek to protect or restore clean-energy incentives and federal support that the Administration has narrowed, delayed, or redirected, while increasing scrutiny of fossil-fuel leasing, LNG policy, pipeline approvals, and emissions. The Administration likely will emphasize production, exports, affordability, reliability, and deregulation. Nuclear energy, hydropower, geothermal, carbon capture, storage, and certain critical-mineral initiatives are expected to attract cross-party support, though program design and funding will remain contested.

Environmental regulation and enforcement

Expect sustained conflict over Clean Air Act (CAA), Clean Water Act (CWA), Endangered Species Act (ESA), and National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) implementation, greenhouse-gas standards, environmental justice, chemical and waste regulation, methane, vehicle policy, and the scope of federal enforcement. Democratic leaders are expected to use hearings and the appropriations process to test whether agencies followed statutory procedures, considered scientific evidence, and implemented congressional directives. The Administration is likely to defend its interpretation of governing statutes and its regulatory priorities. Stakeholders should anticipate overlapping rulemakings, legislative proposals, state actions, and judicial review.

Permitting and project delivery

Both parties are likely to face pressure to accelerate infrastructure and resource projects, but they will differ over standards, judicial review, community engagement, mitigation, and the allocation of federal and state authority. Negotiations are expected to encompass NEPA processes, federal land authorizations, water permits, species consultation, transmission siting, pipeline and export infrastructure, and coordination among agencies. The most viable reforms will pair speed and accountability with clearer decision points, better interagency coordination, early stakeholder engagement, and predictable mitigation obligations.

Public lands, offshore resources, and critical minerals

The Democratic led 120th Congress is expected to challenge expanded leasing or reduced protections on federal lands and waters, while promoting conservation, recreation, habitat restoration, and tribal consultation. The Administration will continue to prioritize domestic resource production and streamlined approvals. Critical minerals may bridge the divide where proposals combine domestic supply, processing, recycling, community safeguards, and strategic security objectives.

Wildlife, species, forests, and water

ESA implementation is likely to become a major oversight and appropriations issue, including listing and critical-habitat decisions, consultation, recovery planning, mitigation, and agency resources. Forest management debates are expected to focus on wildfire, hazardous fuels, timber, restoration, and community protection. Water policy will continue to focus on drought, western infrastructure, drinking water, wastewater, watershed restoration, flood resilience, and the federal role in project finance and technical assistance.

Strategic considerations for stakeholders

Build a two-branch strategy. Treat Congress and the Administration as separate decision centers, with courts, states, and communities as additional centers of influence.

Lead with implementation facts. Quantify effects on reliability, cost, jobs, timelines, emissions, conservation outcomes, and local communities. Identify workable statutory or administrative language

Prepare for oversight before receiving an inquiry. Align records, witnesses, technical experts, and public statements. Understand committee jurisdiction and the legislative purpose of requests.

Pursue bipartisan durability. Policies supported only by one party are more vulnerable to reversal. Regional alliances and unusual coalitions can create staying power.

Engage early. Committee agendas, appropriations requests, nominations, and rulemaking records take shape well before public votes or final agency action.

Why Van Ness Feldman

For those preparing to navigate an era of divided government, the challenge is not choosing between Congress and the Administration or between Democratic and Republican decisionmakers. It is developing an integrated strategy that can operate credibly across institutions, parties, and policy cycles.

Van Ness Feldman enters its 50th year in 2027 as a nationally recognized law and lobbying firm focused on energy, environment, natural resources, and infrastructure, among other areas of expertise. The firm’s government advocacy and public policy practice is expressly bipartisan and combines substantive knowledge, strategic guidance, and legislative advocacy on complex matters that will be at the forefront of debates during the next Congress and during the next two years of the Administration.

Nearly five decades of experience enables the firm to help clients translate technical, commercial, legal, and operational realities into solutions that policymakers can use. Van Ness Feldman’s model integrates legal analysis, congressional strategy, agency engagement, project and permitting experience, coalition development, and strategic communications. That combination is particularly valuable during divided government, when objectives may move through several forums at once and when durable outcomes depend on trust with officials holding different perspectives.

How we help

Executive branch and regulatory engagement. Navigate rulemakings, permits, grants, enforcement, policy directives, and interagency processes with a clear understanding of statutory authority and administrative procedure.

Coalitions and communications. Build bipartisan or nonpartisan alliances, align diverse stakeholders, develop credible messages, and communicate effectively with policymakers, communities, and the public.

Positioning for the 120th Congress

The transition period between the 2026 midterm elections and the start of the 120th Congress is decisive. Organizations should identify priority outcomes, map decision-makers in both chambers and the Administration, assess exposure to investigations or funding disruption, and develop strategies that can command support beyond a single party. They should also preserve flexibility, as the same issue may require a legislative solution, an agency record, a state partnership, and a litigation strategy.

Van Ness Feldman is positioned to help clients anticipate these intersections and act with discipline. Our bipartisan approach does not depend on a particular election result. It reflects a longstanding commitment to substantive credibility, practical problem-solving, and representation that remains effective as political control changes.

Prepare now

text:
LG Energy Solution announced on Thursday a joint venture with Toyota Tsusho called Green Metals Battery Innovations LLC, focused on battery recycling. The venture will operate a pre-processing facility in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

Why it matters

The venture gives Winston-Salem a dedicated battery recycling operation tied to the electric vehicle supply chain. It also sets up a closed loop in which recovered lithium, cobalt, and nickel can return to new battery production.

The announcement describes a planned pre-processing facility in Winston-Salem, North Carolina, but no capacity, timeline, or cost figures were disclosed. The extraction did not include quantitative metrics for recovered material volumes.

The players

LG Energy Solution

A South Korean battery manufacturer and a major supplier of lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles, with a significant U.S. production presence.

Toyota Tsusho

The trading and logistics arm of the Toyota Group, which handles sourcing, logistics, and recycling operations across multiple regions.

The details

The facility will safely disassemble and crush used batteries and production scraps, including scraps from batteries produced for Toyota at LG Energy Solution's U.S. plant. Toyota Tsusho will collect used batteries and scrap materials across North America, and the recovered lithium, cobalt, and nickel will undergo post-processing before being reused in cathode materials and new batteries for Toyota's electric vehicles.

title: China weathered the Hormuz shock. Clean energy can make that resilience last.
description:
Crude oil imports fell sharply, while oil prices and shipping risks increased.
Around 34% of China’s clean power growth from 2020 to2025 happened in those fuel-importing provinces themselves.
Between March and August 2026, domestic coal production plus coal imports fell by 3.4% year-on-year.
In the power sector, gas power generation fell by 4% year-on-year, around 7 TWh, in the first six months after the Hormuz crisis.
China’s net coal imports rose year-on-year in the six months following the Hormuz disruption.
text:
By Qi Qin, China Analyst; Danny Hartono, Data Scientist; Lauri Myllyvirta, Lead Analyst; with contributions from Luke Wickenden, Energy Analyst

The disruption to oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz severely tested China’s energy security. Crude oil imports fell sharply, while oil prices and shipping risks increased. Yet, the import reduction did not produce the economic and social disruption in China one might normally expect from a shock of this scale, according to a CREA analysis. In fact, growth in non-fossil generation protected the country from economic costs more than any other in the world.

Key findings

Temporary adjustments cushioned the oil-import shock. Reduced crude oil stockpiling accounted for 47% of the year-on-year drop in imports between March and August 2026.

Clean power and transport electrification provided a structural buffer. Electric vehicles (EVs) displaced 38 million tonnes of oil equivalent in March-August 2026, equivalent to around 13% of China’s crude oil imports in the same period of 2025.

Growth in non-fossil generation reduced coal and gas requirements, saving an estimated USD 9.1 billion in fossil fuel imports since 2020, more than any other country.

Lower oil and gas imports were not accompanied by a broad-based acceleration in coal use. Coal supply contracted by 3.4% and steam coal consumption fell sharply in Q3. Contrary to some expectations, growth from coal chemicals slowed after the crisis began.

Further clean-power growth and electrification can meet rising demand while reducing exposure to fuel-supply risks. By 2030, non-fossil power could reach 54% of the generation, or 58% if it also offsets an annualised coal-supply shortfall like that seen in March-August 2026, both exceeding China’s 50% target.

Additionally, deploying an additional 40 million EVs could save 45 million tonnes of oil annually, while cleaner petrochemical feedstocks could further reduce dependence on oil.

Temporary relief and structural change

China’s immediate adjustment combined changes in inventories, refinery operations, and trade. Changes in implied crude stock balance accounted for around 47% of the year-on-year decline in net crude imports during the first six months of the crisis (between March and August 2026). At the same time, refinery throughput fell by about 9.6%. Lower exports offset roughly 29% of the decline in domestic production of petrol, diesel, and jet fuel. These measures redistributed the shock; they did not necessarily remove the underlying demand for oil.

Accelerated transport electrification provided a structural buffer. In the first six months after the Hormuz crisis, China’s EV fleet displaced an estimated 38 million tonnes of oil equivalent, 52% more than the same period of 2025. This was equivalent to around 13% of China’s crude oil imports in March-August 2025. Clean power provided a complementary buffer. Growth in non-fossil generation since 2020 avoided an estimated USD 9.1 billion in fossil fuel import costs over the same period — the largest savings of any country — primarily by reducing coal and gas requirements. As transport electrification expands, continued clean-power growth can meet more of the additional electricity demand without increasing reliance on fossil fuels.

Figure 1 — EVs displacement of oil consumption in China after the Hormuz shock

China’s seaborne coal and gas imports for power generation mostly go to coastal demand centres such as the Yangtze River Delta, Guangdong, Fujian, Hebei, and Shandong. Around 34% of China’s clean power growth from 2020 to2025 happened in those fuel-importing provinces themselves. Including clean power delivered from the north-west via long-distance transmission, the share rises to 38%. The increase in clean power supply to fuel-importing provinces reached 730 TWh — 1.5 times China’s LNG imports if all that gas had been used for power generation.

Figure 2 — Fossil fuel import costs avoided by clean power growth since 2020, top 10 countries, March to August 2026

Coal demand growth slows despite the oil and gas shock

China’s existing coal-based energy and industrial infrastructure offers some protection against disruptions to imported oil and natural gas. But this is different from turning to coal in response to the crisis.

China’s coal supply contracted in the six months after the crisis began. Between March and August 2026, domestic coal production plus coal imports fell by 3.4% year-on-year. On the consumption side, steam-coal consumption growth slowed from 4% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026 to 2.1% in the second, before falling by 2% in July.

In the power sector, gas power generation fell by 4% year-on-year, around 7 TWh, in the first six months after the Hormuz crisis. Over the same period, hydro, nuclear, wind and solar generation rose by 139 TWh, far more than the gas shortfall, while coal power generation remained broadly flat. Additionally, according to the China Electricity Council, large-scale coal power plants used 0.4% less coal and generated 1.6% less electricity in the first nine months of 2026.

Figure 3 — China’s clean power growth far exceeded the decline in gas generation

Coal consumption in the chemical sector increased 11.6% between March and July 2026, although growth slowed from 18.9% in the first quarter to 8.5% in the second. Coal use in the sector was still rising, but it did not clearly accelerate after the oil shock. Company disclosures suggest that higher chemical output partly reflected earlier developments rather than a new response to the crisis. Chinese coal mining giant China Coal Energy’s first-half polyolefin output rose 14.5%, but the comparison was affected by scheduled maintenance a year earlier. Baofeng, China’s largest coal-to-chemicals producer, reported that feedstock disruptions and rising costs reduced petrochemical operating rates, while coal-based plants maintained high operating rates–a contrast that does not show increased coal-based output to offset the shortfall. Some producers nevertheless adjusted operations. Shenhua, China’s largest state-owned coal mining enterprise and the world’s largest coal producer, attributed higher chemical sales partly to changes in market demand and prices, as well as unusually low sales in 2025.

Some factories may also have used coal instead of natural gas to produce steam and heat for manufacturing. Coal consumption for the heating sector rose 4.6% in the second quarter. Meanwhile, the National Energy Administration reported that industrial gas consumption declined in the first half as some price-sensitive demand was substituted or priced out of the market.

Making energy resilience last to 2030 and beyond

China’s long-term goal is to meet growing energy needs with less exposure to imported fuels. Clean electricity, transport electrification, and cleaner alternatives to fossil-based chemical feedstocks offer complementary ways to achieve this.

China would need around 2,600 TWh of additional annual clean electricity supply by 2030, relative to 2025, to meet the IEA’s projected demand growth without increasing fossil-fuelled electricity supply. This would raise the non-fossil share of electricity generation to approximately 54%, up from 42% in 2025 and above the 50% target set out in China’s 15th Five-Year energy plan.

China’s net coal imports rose year-on-year in the six months following the Hormuz disruption. Higher imports helped compensate for domestic output losses, including those caused by mine closures and tighter safety inspections following the Shanxi mining disaster in May. Between March and August 2026, domestic coal output fell by around 98 million tonnes, while net imports increased by 9 million tonnes, leaving combined supply 89 million tonnes lower than a year earlier. If the same average daily supply shortfall persisted throughout an entire year and were absorbed entirely by the power sector, approximately 420 TWh of clean electricity would be needed annually to replace the associated coal power. This raises the requirement to around 3,030 TWh of additional annual clean electricity supply in 2030 relative to 2025, bringing the non-fossil share of electricity generation to 58%.

Further transport electrification could help keep oil consumption lower as economic activity recovers. Before the crisis, the IEA expected China’s total oil demand in 2030 to remain broadly at its 2025 level, as declining transport fuel demand was offset by growth in petrochemical feedstocks and other sectors. Faster electrification could bring consumption below this pre-crisis trajectory as the economy recovers. To match the March-September 2026 decline of about 0.9 million barrels of oil per day, around 40 million additional EVs are needed to deliver roughly 45 million tonnes of annual oil savings. This would mean an extra 8 million EVs per year, equivalent to nearly two-thirds of the 12.6 million EVs added in 2025. This would provide lasting fuel savings beyond those already included in the baseline.

text:
Howard’s family operation, Texas Solar Sheep, grew into a business managing more than 8,000 animals and employing 26 people, according to reporting published in January 2025. His experience illustrates how solar grazing can help farmers gain access to agricultural land while offering solar operators an alternative way to manage vegetation. The approach is gaining attention across the United States, although its economic and environmental benefits depend on local conditions.

Why Texas solar farms are turning to sheep

Large solar installations require substantial areas of land. Beneath and between the panels, grass and other vegetation continue to grow, creating an ongoing maintenance challenge for operators.

If left unmanaged, vegetation can interfere with access to equipment, complicate maintenance, and potentially create fire hazards when dry plant material accumulates. Traditionally, companies have relied on mowing equipment or other vegetation-control methods.

But there is another possibility: letting sheep do some of the work.

This practice, known as solar grazing, allows livestock to feed on vegetation growing within solar installations. It forms part of a broader agricultural approach called agrivoltaics, in which land is used simultaneously for solar energy production and agricultural activities.

Sheep are particularly well suited to many solar farms because they are relatively small, can move between panel supports, and generally graze without reaching the height of the solar modules.

Unlike cattle, which are heavier and may damage infrastructure, sheep can often move safely through appropriately designed solar installations. Their grazing also reduces the need for some mechanical vegetation management.

According to the American Solar Grazing Association (ASGA), Texas has become an important center for this activity. Its Texas Solar Shepherds initiative highlights ranchers who use photovoltaic installations as productive grazing land.

The association reports that more than 70,000 acres of solar sites in the state are being grazed by sheep. That represents approximately 28,300 hectares of land where renewable energy production and livestock farming can coexist.

One rancher turned a small operation into a business with 8,000 sheep

For JR Howard, the opportunity emerged in 2021, when he and his family began contracting with solar companies to manage vegetation using their flock.

Howard founded Texas Solar Sheep, a business built around providing grazing services to solar operators. What began as a relatively small family enterprise expanded rapidly as more solar facilities sought alternative vegetation-management solutions.

By January 2025, the company was managing more than 8,000 sheep and employing 26 people, according to reporting by the Associated Press.

Rather than depending exclusively on access to conventional pastureland, Howard could use land within solar installations. This arrangement provided grazing opportunities while allowing energy companies to maintain their sites.

The business model differs from traditional livestock farming in an important way. Ranchers may receive payments from solar operators for maintaining vegetation, in addition to earning income from their livestock operations.

That does not mean solar grazing is automatically profitable. Transportation, fencing, water supplies, labor, animal health, and the design of solar facilities all influence operating costs.

For Howard, however, the growth demonstrated that commercial solar grazing could become a substantial agricultural activity rather than a small experimental project.

At one Texas solar farm, 3,000 sheep maintain thousands of acres

The scale of solar grazing becomes particularly clear at a large installation in Milam County, northeast of Austin.

In a January 2025 report, the Associated Press described an SB Energy solar project covering approximately 4,000 acres and having a generating capacity of 900 megawatts.

At the site, around 3,000 sheep were used to manage vegetation among the solar panels.

The animals graze grass and other suitable plants, reducing the amount of vegetation that must be removed by machinery. They can also reach some spaces around equipment that are difficult for larger mowing vehicles to access.

However, solar grazing does not necessarily eliminate mechanical mowing. Some plants remain too tall, woody, or otherwise unsuitable for sheep, while site designs can make certain areas inaccessible.

A combination of grazing and mowing is therefore common. The ASGA’s national survey found that approximately two-thirds of active solar graziers who responded were also responsible for vegetation-management activities beyond grazing.

Sheep can also provide an agricultural use for land that might otherwise be managed exclusively as an energy facility. This offers one way to address concerns about the expansion of solar infrastructure onto productive rural land.

Solar grazing is spreading across the United States

Texas is not the only state experimenting with sheep beneath photovoltaic panels.

The American Solar Grazing Association’s 2024 national census, published in May 2025 in partnership with the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, documented approximately 113,050 sheep grazing 129,261 acres of solar sites across 506 installations in 30 states.

The findings showed that solar grazing was already taking place at both smaller photovoltaic facilities and large utility-scale solar farms.

Texas accounted for approximately 68,626 acres and 36,237 sheep in the census, making it one of the country’s largest concentrations of solar grazing activity.

The difference between this census figure and the more than 70,000 acres highlighted by the Texas Solar Shepherds initiative reflects figures reported in different publications and periods. Neither should be interpreted as an independently verified total for November 2026.

The national survey also identified several practical factors influencing the success of grazing operations:

Site design: Panel height, spacing, wiring, and access routes affect how easily sheep and workers can move through an installation.

Water availability: Livestock require reliable access to drinking water, particularly during hot Texas summers.

Fencing: Suitable barriers help contain the animals and protect them from predators.

Vegetation and climate: The amount and type of forage determine appropriate flock sizes and grazing schedules.

Labor and logistics: Transporting sheep between installations and monitoring their health can create significant costs.

These conditions help explain why grazing is more straightforward at some solar farms than others.

Can combining sheep and solar panels benefit the environment?

The potential environmental advantages are one reason solar grazing has attracted growing attention.

Replacing some fossil-fuel-powered mowing with grazing may reduce fuel consumption and associated emissions. Grazing can also help manage vegetation without relying entirely on mechanical equipment.

There may be additional benefits for soil management and plant communities, particularly when grazing intensity is carefully controlled.

However, these outcomes are not guaranteed. Excessive grazing can reduce vegetation cover, increase soil disturbance, and harm plant diversity. Livestock also require water, transportation, veterinary care, and infrastructure.

Researchers are still investigating the long-term effects of combining photovoltaic installations with grazing, including changes in soil health, animal productivity, biodiversity, and land management costs.

Well-designed systems may create complementary benefits, but their overall environmental performance must be evaluated against realistic alternatives.

A new opportunity for ranchers facing shrinking access to land

For many American sheep producers, access to affordable pasture is a major challenge. Land competition, development pressures, and operating costs can make it difficult for smaller ranching businesses to expand.

Solar grazing offers a potential solution by opening access to land that remains vegetated beneath renewable energy installations.

The American Solar Grazing Association’s Texas Solar Shepherds project highlights several ranchers and businesses involved in this developing sector, including JR Howard of Texas Solar Sheep, Ely Valdez of Solar Farm Services, Reid Redden of Premier Solar Sheep, and the Hodges family.

The initiative emphasizes that solar sites can create new opportunities for agricultural businesses while continuing to produce electricity.

Yet long-term success will depend on fair contracts, reliable site access, appropriate infrastructure, and the ability of ranchers to maintain healthy and productive flocks.

Texas illustrates how two industries sometimes viewed as competitors for land can work together. Solar companies need to maintain vegetation, while sheep ranchers need places for their animals to graze.

By bringing those needs together, solar grazing offers a practical example of how renewable energy production and traditional agriculture can share the same landscape.

text:
The top story from Tuesday’s elections is clear: Democrats won big-time on the national level, dominating U.S. Senate and House races across the country. And on the state level, clean energy could get a jolt from Democratic wins for state offices and utility commissions and new approved ballot measures. Here’s a roundup of top results.

Democratic trifectas

The blue wave overtook several state legislatures and governor’s mansions last night. Come January, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and likely Arizona will all have Democratic trifectas — control of both houses of the legislature and the governor’s office. And some of the states are highly likely to use that power to further climate and clean energy action.

Take Michigan, where Democrats gained control of the legislature and governor’s seat in 2022 and then used that power to enact a target of 100% clean energy by 2040. That goal is still in place despite the Republican-controlled House’s attempt to repeal it earlier this year. Now, Democratic leaders may use their restored power to pass additional ambitious measures.

Minnesota’s Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party passed a similar clean energy mandate with the blue trifecta it won in 2022, and has the opportunity to further similar goals now that the DFL has regained control of the House.

Next door, in Wisconsin, clean energy advocates suggest the Democrats use their new trifecta to end policies that keep old, polluting power plants running and instead build more solar and batteries.

Total Democratic control is a fresh phenomenon in Pennsylvania, which hasn’t seen a blue trifecta in more than 30 years. Prior to the election, advocates told Inside Climate News that Democrats should use their power to pass several long-delayed bills that would allow Pennsylvanians to subscribe to local solar arrays, pave the way for more grid battery storage, and bar municipalities from installing blanket bans on renewable energy projects.

It’s only been a few years since Democrats had a trifecta in Nevada, but it’s been 60 since they controlled the Arizona legislature. Both states are among the top developers of solar power, and Arizona is rising in the ranks for battery storage. Now, they could lean even harder into clean energy.

Public utility commissions

Georgia’s Democratic sweep extended to its Public Service Commission, as voters elected two Democrats to the utility oversight board. Shelia Edwards is a new addition to the PSC, while Peter Hubbard was reelected after winning a special election last year for an abbreviated term. Democrats now have a 3–2 majority on the commission — a victory for the Solar Energy Industries Association, which spent to promote those candidates. The PSC is now controlled by Democrats for the first time in decades, making Georgia the only state that elects its utility commissioners with a Democratic majority.

Texas also voted blue when picking a new member of its all-Republican Railroad Commission, which oversees the state’s oil and gas industry. Democrat Jon Rosenthal beat GOP candidate Bo French, who had faced blowback for his racist comments.

Alabama’s Public Service Commission stayed in GOP hands as the two open seats went to Republicans. But the Republicans’ power will soon be diluted, as a recent law expands the three-seat commission to seven seats come January, with new members at first appointed by the governor and then gradually affirmed or replaced in elections over the next several years. Gov. Kay Ivey (R) has already named her four appointees, two of whom were nominated by Democrats.

Voters in Louisiana, Nebraska, North Dakota, Oklahoma, and South Dakota maintained Republican majorities on their utility boards. Utility commission races in Arizona and Montana still have not been called as of Wednesday afternoon.

Ballot measures

Voters approved ballot proposals in three states that will promote clean energy and utility accountability. In Eugene, Oregon, residents handily OK’d a new tax on corporations to fund clean energy and climate projects. In Michigan, voters resoundingly approved a proposal that would bar investor-owned utilities and other corporations from sidestepping current campaign-finance rules by donating to political action committees. And results so far indicate that a Colorado group’s attempt to enshrine a right to natural gas in the state constitution will fail.

Residents of Ann Arbor, Michigan, voted against creating a municipal utility board that could eventually have led to replacing investor-owned DTE Energy with a public utility in the city. But clean energy is still moving forward in Ann Arbor, which recently launched its own separate Sustainable Energy Utility and is building an innovative housing project powered by geothermal energy and piloting virtual-power-plant technology.

Results have been slow to come in for California’s Proposition 45, which would speed up environmental reviews for certain infrastructure projects, but early results suggest that voters will reject the revision to the state’s Environmental Quality Act. Some clean energy developers and utilities support Prop. 45, while environmental groups are largely opposing it.

text:
Press Contact:

Emily Freese

515-322-0435

IRFA Executive Director Monte Shaw Testifies at EPA Public Hearing in Support of Full Reallocation into 2026 and 2027

WEST DES MOINES, IA – Today, Iowa Renewable Fuels Association (IRFA) Executive Director Monte Shaw testified at a U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) public hearing on the agency’s proposed rule to reallocate additional 2025 Refinery Exemptions (SREs) under the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS).

IRFA supports EPA’s proposal to reallocate 100% of the volumes exempted through additional SREs into the 2026 and 2027 compliance years. Full reallocation ensures that exempted gallons do not reduce the overall renewable fuel blending obligations, helping protect demand for biofuels and uphold the integrity of the RFS.

In remarks at the hearing, IRFA Executive Director Monte Shaw stated:

“I want to start by thanking the EPA for proposing the full reallocation of the unexpected, additional SREs that were recently granted. It is difficult for us to understand, at a time of record profits in the petroleum industry, how companies can claim economic hardship and receive a nearly record number of SREs for 2025.

“I would simply ask that the EPA review Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird’s letter documenting the discrepancies between what some of these companies are telling the EPA and the Department of Energy (DOE) versus what they are reporting to the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and their shareholders. We are not aware of any response to that detailed documentation. We believe there needs to be a change to the SRE system, and that is something the EPA can address even as we hope Congress takes action as well.

“We support full reallocation, with 50% of the SRE volumes allocated to 2026 and the remaining 50% allocated to 2027. It is important to note that under the RFS, any obligated party can roll forward up to 100% of its obligation into the following year. So, if the EPA were to put all of these volumes into 2027, they could simply be carried into 2028. We believe it is very important that some of these volumes be allocated to 2026 and some to 2027.

“When the RFS blending levels were set earlier this year, we had plants in Iowa that were shut down and employees who were laid off. Today, those plants are running and running at full capacity. The robust RFS that the Trump Administration and EPA established earlier this year has done what it was intended to do. We do not want to see that progress reversed.”

Maintaining renewable fuel obligations for 2026 and 2027 is important to providing market certainty for renewable fuels producers, supporting Iowa farmers and strengthening the rural communities that depend on a strong domestic biofuels industry.

text:
I’ll admit that when the polling first came in, I didn’t believe it.

A few months ago, my editor showed me the newest result from the Heatmap Pro poll that we run with Embold Research. For more than a year, we had been asking Americans whether they would support a data center planned near their home; since then, we had been watching the “support” number steadily tick down.

But the newest result beggared belief: 75% of Americans now said they would oppose a data center in their town. Most would strongly oppose it. When was the last time, I thought, that 75% of Americans agreed about anything? Was this real?

Sure looks like it. As Michigan’s newest senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed said earlier this year: People really effing hate data centers. And they apparently really hate Donald Trump, too, and the Iran War, and higher gas prices.

On Tuesday night, Democrats … well, pick your synonym. They routed Republicans. Annihilated them. Crushed them, broke them, and heard the lamentations of their donors. Democrats captured at least 54 seats in the Senate and could take more than 260 seats in the House. The national House vote snapped more than 15 points in their favor, and key demographic groups whose preferences have defined the Trump era — such as Hispanics, young men, and white voters without a college degree — all swung in the double digits to Democrats.

For millennials like me, the wave elections par excellence have been 2006, when liberals took back Congress from a desperately unpopular George W. Bush, and 2010, when the Tea Party caroused against Barack Obama. This election was bigger than either, on par with the anti-Watergate tsunami of 1974 that shaped the Democratic Party for a generation and put a new class of professional-minded reformers at its helm. Unlike in 1974, though, the new Democratic majority will not rely on an old guard of state’s rights conservatives. The South turned indigo on Tuesday night, it’s true, but that was thanks to the normal politics of booming American cities and suburbs, not century-old polarization left over from the Civil War. This is a new kind of Democratic mega-majority.

It will usher in a new kind of energy and climate politics. From the moment he rode down the escalator 11 years ago, Donald Trump has defined himself by his climate change denial. His antipathy for decarbonization and clean energy reached new heights in his second term, as his administration waged a war on renewables and dismantled the government’s already-weak ability to regulate greenhouse gas pollution. At the same time, it embraced the artificial intelligence boom and gave some of the world’s wealthiest companies a blank check to pollute.

Now that is all over. Although Trump still has two years left in the White House, he will limp to 2029 without a pliant Congress, a supportive public, or an aura of invincibility. We should, to be sure, expect at least a few Cabinet resignations in the next few weeks, so the expiring GOP Senate can confirm their replacements; and federal agencies will still roll their regulatory agendas uphill in case the GOP wins the White House in 2028. Some Trump policies — like his nuclear plan — may even meet with Democratic approval. But the administration’s fossil fuel revolution is over. And everything that Trump has done on climate and energy since taking office, especially his family’s penetration of favored mining firms, will soon face scrutiny in the new year.

That will all be good for the fight against climate change. And yet it would be wrong to presume that this new era will look like the last one — or that these new congressional Democrats will be Green New Dealers or even ardent environmentalists. “We cannot change anything unless we accept it,” Jung wrote, and Democrats have finally overturned Trumpism in part by accepting its real force in American politics. I don’t mean their willingness to accept Trump’s conduct, to be clear: The No Kings rallies and the Minneapolis rebellion saw to that. But since Kamala Harris lost, Democrats have for the first time treated Trump as a normal Republican opponent — and their fight against him not as a “battle for the soul of the nation,” as President Biden liked to put it, but as a simple verdict on a powerful establishment politician.

That has meant learning from Trump, and from his energy and affordability politics in particular. Chief among those lessons: Voters really, really care about low prices; they especially really, really care about cheap energy; and they will reward politicians who share their concerns. Zohran Mamdani, Mikie Sherill, and Abigail Spanberger pioneered these appeals last year, playing down their respective climate goals and (in Sherill’s case) running on cheaper power bills. State and congressional Democrats in 2026 picked up that strategy and ran with it.

They had help. Inexplicably, Trump undercut his promises to start no new foreign wars and cut energy bills in half by launching a new Iran war that nearly doubled some energy prices. By one estimate, Americans have paid more than $100 billion in higher fuel costs since March. Trump’s compact with voters broke in that moment. Tuesday is the result.

Democrats know it. Look at Annie Andrews, for instance, the new Democratic senator from South Carolina (!). She wants to “suspend the gas tax, unleash American energy, and get gas prices down” — in other words, she seeks to cut taxes on fossil fuels. But Andrews also wants to restore the solar and wind tax credits and increase public transit spending. And she devotes an entire paragraph of her policy brochure to the need for bipartisan permitting reform.

What distinguishes Andrews isn’t her toughness on fossil fuels, but her opposition to data centers. She wants a two-year nationwide moratorium on the facilities, to end their tax breaks, and force them to stop passing on higher electricity costs to ratepayers. Almost every single Senate Democrat who won on Tuesday, in fact, promised to make data centers pay for their full cost of electricity service — it might be the caucus’s most unifying policy. (The bipartisan permitting bill, whose fate remains uncertain as of writing, would mandate it.)

Much like Andrews, this new class of congressional Democrats sought to embrace every kind of energy source except for coal. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat of Texas — get used to saying that — promised voters that “we can add to our hundreds of thousands of oil, gas, wind, solar, and battery jobs by creating new jobs” in geothermal and hydrogen. Mary Peltola, who seems likely to clinch her Alaska Senate race, argued for oil and gas’s ongoing importance, too. Adam Hamilton of Kansas, Scott Colom of Mississippi, and Andrews of South Carolina all spoke of their “all of the above” energy policy. None of these candidates are climate deniers — they all want to restore the wind and solar tax credits, and many spoke of increasing climate resilience funding — but they all have vowed to grow the energy system, not revolutionize it. Even Abdul El-Sayed, who wrote a 2019 Guardian op-ed advocating for the Green New Deal, disavowed that policy and opposed a government EV mandate.

The new state-level Democrats will push the party even further in this direction. Had Talarico alone won in Texas, he might have been able to walk a careful line on fossil fuels, recognizing oil and gas as the status quo without seeking to expand their reach. But Gina Hinojosa will also be the state’s next governor, with a much more direct role in managing the Permian Basin. To keep her job, she will have to accept that Texans' livelihoods depend on oil and gas, in the same way that Mamdani has had to recognize the reality of Wall Street's centrality to the economy of New York City. Democrats will face tough trade-offs.

They also won’t be any more radical about the 10% of U.S. emissions that come from American agriculture. If the Democrat Scott Colom holds out and wins Mississippi’s senate seat, it will be in no small part thanks to a viral commercial chiding the Republican incumbent for telling voters to choose a cheaper protein than beef. “Pick another protein?” an everyman griller asked the camera. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”

This is one reason why Tuesday’s victory might feel a smidge bittersweet for some climate defenders. Democrats have finally trounced Trumpism at the ballot box. Progressives like El-Sayed have shown they can win in battleground states, provided a favorable national environment, and moderates have stormed the heart of MAGA America.

But doing so required everyone, liberals and progressives alike, to articulate more moderate views on energy and climate policy. As recently as 2020, belief in the climate crisis unified the Biden coalition. Now, Democrats have tacitly accepted — as a price of winning big majorities — some cognitive dissonance between what they think the science says (that climate change is an urgent and worsening problem) and what domestic politics demands (that voters still care more about cheap energy).

In other words, more than just the Trump era ended on Tuesday. The old Obama dream finally died too. In the wake of the 2012 election, Democrats imagined a permanent progressive majority shorn of right-leaning white voters. That fantasy never materialized, and chasing it may have even led the party astray. Now they have built a new congressional coalition with energy moderates at its core.

Which is not to say that Democrats will give up on decarbonizing the economy. We can expect this new congressional class to expand clean energy, push for more transmission lines, and revive electric vehicle subsidies as a solution to high gas prices. Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who won one of the night’s most convincing victories, repeatedly mentioned microplastics and “forever chemicals” in his speeches, linking the contamination of human bodies to the corruption of the body politic. The fight against conventional air and water pollution, I suspect, will come back big.

The next era of American climate politics, in other words, will look different from the last one. Fossil fuel companies have long been climate advocates’ primary foil. At the national level, data centers and Big Tech could eclipse them. At least one former climate activist won on Tuesday by running against data centers and large-scale solar. Artificial intelligence, after all, is the country’s fastest growing form of industrial energy use, and it creates far fewer jobs than a chip fab or steel mill. For these reasons, you can imagine a kind of reformed normie environmentalism with anti-AI characteristics taking root in the next administration. Perhaps it already has.

Decarbonizing the economy is steady and long-term work, “a slow boring of hard boards,” to quote the political thinker Max Weber, and the politicians who next turn the screws hardest may not sit on Capitol Hill. The historic size of Tuesday’s swell means Democrats won key state offices that they haven’t held in a generation — on public utility commissions, fossil fuel regulators, and in state legislatures. They will be eager to wield their powers. With its new Democratic trifecta, for instance, Pennsylvania could allow community solar, mandate battery storage, and restrict utility profits. Decades of low-hanging climate policy will soon be plucked.

Amid all of this excitement, Democrats should keep failure in mind — the president’s and their own. Since 2020, Democrats have tried to revolutionize the energy system, reindustrialize the country, and overhaul the economy without recognizing the existence of any trade-offs between those goals. They failed, and voters hated it. President Trump and Republicans tried to reinthrone fossil fuels, give birth to a “superior intelligence,” and otherwise bring back a gloomy spoof of the midcentury American economy — without accepting any trade-offs. They failed too, and as we learned last night, voters hated them even more than they hated Biden.

The United States really does need to get better at commercializing batteries and making electric vehicles; it really must cut pollution, lower energy prices, and significantly boost its electricity generation. Both parties have failed to make progress on those goals so far. Democrats have shown they can learn from Donald Trump’s mistakes. Now we’ll see if they can learn from their own, too.
