description:
October gave the auto industry a sales increase, although the numbers suggest shoppers are still watching their wallets.
Retail sales increased 3.1 percent to about 1.1 million, while fleet deliveries climbed 9 percent and accounted for roughly 17 percent of the market.
F-Series sales increased 8.2 percent, and Maverick gained 3.4 percent, while Ranger fell 27 percent.
Honda-brand deliveries increased 9.1 percent, while Acura declined 2.5 percent.
The company’s electrified vehicle sales, consisting mostly of hybrids, increased 11 percent to 33,760.
text:
October gave the auto industry a sales increase, although the numbers suggest shoppers are still watching their wallets. Hybrids, crossovers and fleet purchases helped keep business moving, while affordability concerns, borrowing costs and softer electric vehicle demand continued to weigh on the market.

According to preliminary estimates released Nov. 4 by GlobalData put October U.S. new car and light-truck sales at approximately 1.3 million, up 4 percent from a year earlier. Retail sales increased 3.1 percent to about 1.1 million, while fleet deliveries climbed 9 percent and accounted for roughly 17 percent of the market.

Those fleet purchases remain an important support. Through October, fleet volume was up 5.4 percent for the year, while retail deliveries were down 2.9 percent. Total industry sales were off 1.5 percent, showing that a better October did not erase the challenges facing the business.

The monthly increase also came with some help from the calendar and an easier comparison. October had an additional selling day, and last year’s market had slowed after shoppers rushed to buy EVs before federal tax credits expired.

The underlying sales pace was less encouraging. October’s seasonally adjusted annual rate, which adjusts monthly results for seasonal patterns, was 15.6 million. That was the first reading below 16 million since February. GlobalData trimmed its full-year forecast by 40,000 vehicles to approximately 16.1 million, which would represent a 1.3 percent decline from 2025.

Hybrids continued to attract buyers. J.D. Power and GlobalData projected that gasoline-electric hybrids would account for 18.6 percent of October retail sales, up 4 percentage points from a year earlier. EVs were expected to represent 6.9 percent, down slightly. Consumers still want better fuel economy, and hybrids continue to give them a way to get it without changing their refueling routine.

Toyota Motor North America posted a 6.5 percent increase, with the Toyota division up 5.7 percent and Lexus ahead 12 percent. The RAV4 returned to growth with a modest 0.6 percent increase, while Sienna sales jumped 29 percent, Corolla Cross gained 21 percent and Grand Highlander increased 12 percent. Combined Toyota and Lexus electrified sales rose 35 percent to 126,054, representing 57 percent of total volume. That category includes more than hybrids alone.

Ford Motor Co. slipped 0.4 percent, although its biggest pickup delivered a solid performance. F-Series sales increased 8.2 percent, and Maverick gained 3.4 percent, while Ranger fell 27 percent. Ford’s hybrid deliveries dropped 21 percent, with the discontinued Escape and Lincoln Corsair continuing to affect results.

American Honda sold 119,953 vehicles, up 8 percent. Honda-brand deliveries increased 9.1 percent, while Acura declined 2.5 percent. CR-V sales rose 9.8 percent, and both the Accord and HR-V gained 11 percent. The company’s electrified vehicle sales, consisting mostly of hybrids, increased 11 percent to 33,760.

Hyundai and Kia both set October sales records. Hyundai increased 4.8 percent to 73,452 vehicles, while Kia jumped 16 percent to 80,008, outselling its larger corporate sibling for the third month this year.

Hyundai’s hybrid sales climbed 20 percent and accounted for 29 percent of its October business. Kia reported a 114 percent surge in hybrid deliveries, with strong increases for the Sorento, Carnival and Sportage hybrids. Kia also recorded substantial gains for its electric EV9 and EV6, a reminder that a softer overall EV market does not mean every electric model is struggling.

Elsewhere, Subaru increased 6 percent, led by a 26 percent gain for Forester, while Mazda jumped 25 percent. Genesis declined as GV80 and G70 sales weakened.

October’s message was fairly clear: Buyers are still purchasing vehicles, but value matters. Hybrids and practical crossovers continue to draw customers, fleet orders are helping the totals, and the industry is heading toward year-end with some momentum—and plenty of work left to do.

text:
San Pedro Sula, Honduras, October 29, 2026 - The International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, announced $130 million in financing for Banpaís, one of Honduras’s leading banks, to expand access to credit for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), promote sustainable investments, and boost job creation in the country.

Structured by IFC, the financing includes $60 million from IFC, comprising a $25 million senior tranche and a $35 million subordinated tranche, the latter currently being structured and approved. It also includes $50 million from Deutsche Investitions- und Entwicklungsgesellschaft (DEG) and $20 million from the Norwegian Investment Fund for Developing Countries (Norfund), both participating as parallel lenders. Of the total financing, 70 percent will be allocated to SMEs, with a focus on women-led businesses, and 30 percent to renewable energy projects, primarily distributed solar generation and biomass.

According to María del Rosario Selman-Housein, Executive President of Banpaís, “The trust placed in our institution through this financing is as valuable as the impact it will have on Honduran SMEs, helping them grow, strengthen their competitiveness, create jobs, and contribute actively to the country’s economic development.”

“We are pleased to strengthen IFC’s partnership with Banpaís to foster more productive and resilient businesses that can create more and better jobs in Honduras,” said Sanaa Abouzaid, IFC Regional Director for Mexico, Central America and the Dominican Republic. With the support of DEG and Norfund, the project is expected to contribute to the creation of 8,900 direct and indirect jobs over the next five years.

According to Gudrun Busch, Global Head of Financial Institutions at DEG, the transaction demonstrates how development finance institutions can join forces to achieve impact at scale. “Together with Banpaís, IFC and Norfund, we are supporting Honduran SMEs and strengthening the conditions for sustainable growth and job creation,” she said.

“In a country where inequality remains high and three out of four workers are employed in the informal economy, expanding opportunities for businesses and their workers is essential to achieving more inclusive growth. Through this investment in Banpaís, Norfund aims to help close the SME financing gap and support the creation of formal jobs, which can provide families with greater economic stability and access to social protection and health services. This helps reduce their vulnerability and strengthen their ability to withstand economic and climate-related crises and other shocks. In this way, the investment seeks to promote more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable growth in Honduras,” said María Esther Boquín, Norfund Investment Manager for Latin America.

The transaction seeks to address two challenges that constrain the growth of Honduran businesses: access to finance and a reliable, competitive energy supply. The SME financing gap, which disproportionately affects women, is equivalent to approximately 22 percent of GDP. At the same time, financing for renewable energy solutions can help businesses reduce costs and disruptions and improve efficiency, in line with Honduras’s goal of generating 70 percent of its electricity from renewable sources by 2035.

IFC’s relationship with Banpaís began in 2009, when the Honduran bank joined IFC’s Global Trade Finance Program (GTFP). In 2022, IFC provided Banpaís with a $60 million loan to support SMEs affected by the COVID-19 pandemic, and in 2024 it provided $50 million in financing to expand lending to women-led medium-sized enterprises.

About Banpaís

Banpaís is a universal bank and Honduras’s fourth-largest bank by loan portfolio, with a presence in every department of the country through a network of 184 branches, 255 ATMs, and 4,032 banking correspondents. It has a 13.7 percent market share in net lending. As of December 2025, the bank had $2.8 billion in deposits, a net loan portfolio of $3.4 billion, and total assets of $4.6 billion. In 2007, Banco Industrial, S.A. (BI), Guatemala’s largest bank, acquired 91 percent of Banpaís’s shares through Bi Capital Corporation (Bi Corp); the remaining 9 percent is held by 400 minority shareholders. BI is the principal subsidiary of Bi Corp, the holding company of BI Capital Group. Banpaís is headquartered in San Pedro Sula and has more than 2,850 employees. More information: www.banpais.hn.

About DEG

For more than 60 years, DEG has financed and advised private companies operating in emerging and developing countries. We are one of the largest development finance institutions for the private sector, with a portfolio of €11.7 billion. As an impact and climate financier, we support companies that want to address transformation and seize the opportunities it presents. Our clients receive not only tailored financing and advisory solutions, but also benefit from our market knowledge, impact and climate expertise, and international network. In this way, DEG, a subsidiary of the KfW Group, contributes to creating more skilled jobs and local income and to strengthening local value creation, in line with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). More information: www.deginvest-americalatina.com

About Norfund

Norfund, the Norwegian Investment Fund for Developing Countries, is the Norwegian Government’s development finance institution. Established in 1997, its mission is to create jobs and improve lives by investing in businesses that drive sustainable development. Norfund invests equity, debt, and other instruments across four areas: financial inclusion, renewable energy, scalable enterprises, and green infrastructure. In addition to its development mandate, Norfund manages Norway’s Climate Investment Fund, which supports the transition to clean energy in developing countries. As of December 2025, its committed portfolio totaled $5 billion. Companies in which Norfund invests employed 788,000 people, while financial institutions in its portfolio provided services to 158 million customers. For more information, visit www.norfund.no.

title: Tesla Cybercabs join Waymo in Detroit robotaxi testing | Jefferson City News Tribune
description:
A fleet of gold, butterfly-door Tesla Cybercabs has joined Waymo driverless vehicles in Detroit, expanding the competitive playing field from Austin, Texas, to Michigan's more complicated, multi-season environment.
The Cybercab's appearance in Metro Detroit this fall comes a year after Waymo LLC's rideshare service began testing in the region.
Waymo Product Communications Manager Chris Bonelli said there is still no timeline for the so-called Waymo Driver service deployment in Detroit.
Significantly, the Cybercabs operate with cameras only, while the Waymo vehicles operate with a combination of Lidar, radar and cameras.
In cities where Robotaxi and Waymo rideshare services operate, they work similarly through an Uber app for ride-hailing.
text:
SOUTHFIELD, Michigan -- The autonomous rideshare wars are heating up just in time for the cold Michigan winter.

A fleet of gold, butterfly-door Tesla Cybercabs has joined Waymo driverless vehicles in Detroit, expanding the competitive playing field from Austin, Texas, to Michigan's more complicated, multi-season environment. Two dozen Cybercabs are operating out of Tesla Inc.'s Southfield collision repair facility on 12 Mile and have been seen on major roads, including I-696, M-10, Telegraph and Eight Mile.

The distinctive, electric Cybercabs have test drivers using temporary steering wheels. The two-seat Cybercab is designed to have no steering wheel once the service becomes fully operational.

Cybercab is part of Tesla's larger Robotaxi ridesharing service that also uses Model Y electric vehicles. Cybercab is currently only accessible to the public in Austin; the Robotaxi service operates with Model Ys in Tampa and Miami in Florida and Austin, Dallas and Houston in Texas, with plans to expand. Cybercabs have been spotted at Miami International Airport and outside Philadelphia, according to teslarati.com.

The Cybercab's appearance in Metro Detroit this fall comes a year after Waymo LLC's rideshare service began testing in the region. Alphabet Inc.-owned Waymo began fully autonomous testing this October without human specialists driving its powder blue, Chinese-made Zeekr Ojai EVs as the rideshare company inches closer to public service.

Waymo Product Communications Manager Chris Bonelli said there is still no timeline for the so-called Waymo Driver service deployment in Detroit. Tesla, which has no public relations staff, could not be reached for comment on its timeline for public deployment.

"The expansion of autonomous rideshare testing in different weather situations in different cities is important for developing the technology," said Stephanie Brinley, associate director for automotive intelligence for Mobility Global. "Tesla has not officially said that they're testing here, so it's hard to say what they're specifically doing."

Waymo is the leader in the autonomous rideshare space, with 270 million miles logged in cities from San Francisco to Phoenix to Atlanta. In addition to Detroit, it is preparing to expand to snowbelt cities Denver, Minneapolis, Chicago and Montreal. Tesla's website says its Robotaxi service has logged more than 4 million miles.

Significantly, the Cybercabs operate with cameras only, while the Waymo vehicles operate with a combination of Lidar, radar and cameras. Tesla's solution is expected to be cheaper to operate as the competing services scale across North America. Tesla advertises on its website that "if you are interested in purchasing a fleet or an individual Cybercab vehicle for commercial purposes, fill out the form and a representative will contact you."

The Cybercab is built at Gigafactory Texas in Austin, Texas. Waymo buys Zeekr Ojai electric minivans from Zeekr in China, then outfits them with Waymo hardware and software in its Mesa, Arizona, facility.

Waymo does not disclose its Detroit operations. Tesla test drivers are under a non-disclosure agreement.

The Cybercab looks like a Model Y married a Model 3 with its Y-like, horizontal LED light arching across the fascia and its low, 3-like sedan body style. But with room inside for just two passengers and their luggage, it is noticeably smaller than either of Tesla's best-selling retail models. Its length is 11 inches shorter than a Model 3, and about 4 inches narrower.

"Detroit is important symbolically to these companies; it is a big area, and there's opportunity here, but it is not as important as in terms of potential use as at New York or Chicago or some of the other cities," Brinley said. "The weather plays an important role."

Specs are different, too, with a 48 kWh battery that is nearly half the size of the one in the Model Y, which contributes to the Cybercab's lighter 3,000-pound weight. Range is just shy of 300 miles on a charge. New York yellow cabs inspired the Cybercab's appearance, with gold seen as a premium upgrade.

Come up on the Cybercab in traffic and its narrow stance reminds one of a hybrid 2000 Honda Insight. The gold coupe's roof tapers to the rear tail, with no rear window. The side view is equally dramatic -- even before the butterfly doors open on exit -- with staggered gold aero wheels measuring 18 inches up front and 21 inches in the rear.

In cities where Robotaxi and Waymo rideshare services operate, they work similarly through an Uber app for ride-hailing.

title: Experts react: Democrats just swept the US midterms. Here's what it means for the world.
description:
Trump may double down on energy policy With Democrats having gained control of Congress, Trump is likely to lean more heavily on his substantial executive and foreign policy authority.
The tension will be particularly apparent in energy policy, where foreign policy ambitions, domestic industrial priorities, and consumer affordability do not always align.
Beyond foreign policy and diplomatic ambitions, the president has considerably more latitude to advance his domestic energy agenda without the cooperation of foreign governments or Congress.
Despite this already strong bipartisan support for NATO, Democratic control of Congress will still have a recalibrating effect on transatlantic security.
While Trump maintains broad executive privileges in the foreign policy arena, Democrats will start paving the way for a new approach to working with US allies.
text:
The midterm losses could delay, but not prevent, another Iran escalation

Trump’s policies toward the Middle East undoubtedly contributed to Republicans’ midterm defeats, and he appears to recognize that. Trump has already publicly acknowledged that his war with Iran contributed to his loss. Moreover, his surprising announcement early on Election Day that he would end US financial support to Israel’s military in two months suggests that he sees that issue as a pressing political problem on the right and left. In Israel, Trump’s statement was seized upon by Gadi Eisenkot who will likely get the first chance to form a new government in the wake of last week’s elections. The growing threat to the bilateral relationship will be a top priority for the next Israeli prime minister.

The Iranian regime will undoubtedly see the results as another example of their form of “regime change” in Washington. If they make this view public, they risk encouraging a Trump decision to escalate. Before the elections, Trump had already reviewed war plans and ordered additional military forces to the region. Thus far, encouragingly, statements from Iran about the US election results have generally been de-escalatory.

That respite may prove temporary. Iran has a relatively consistent track record of miscalculation and overplaying its hand, and while a Democratic Congress has the power to stymie Trump’s domestic legislative agenda, it doesn’t have much ability to stop a president from exercising his powers as commander in chief.

Trump may eventually surmise that a diplomatic agreement along the lines of the previous Memorandum of Understanding would only reinforce perceptions that his war was an unmitigated disaster that damaged US national security, the Republican Party’s electoral prospects, and his personal legacy. The only way out, Trump may therefore conclude, is to win the war. That could lead to a decision to restart major combat operations, if not immediately, then in the months to come.

Trump may double down on energy policy

With Democrats having gained control of Congress, Trump is likely to lean more heavily on his substantial executive and foreign policy authority. Despite mounting legislative headwinds, the president faces a narrowing window to translate his priorities into durable policy and investment decisions before the 2028 presidential race takes hold.

Affordability dominated the run-up to yesterday’s elections, with a Reuters/Ipsos poll finding that 48 percent of registered voters identified the cost of living as their top voting issue. Retail gasoline and diesel prices have also risen sharply this year, reinforcing the political pressure on the administration. But with the midterms behind him, Trump may increasingly weigh near-term consumer-price concerns against longer-term strategic objectives. The tension will be particularly apparent in energy policy, where foreign policy ambitions, domestic industrial priorities, and consumer affordability do not always align.

That starts with Iran, where Trump may place greater weight on his long-term objective of preventing a nuclear-armed Iran than on short-term electoral considerations. His behavior before the 2025 and 2026 strikes demonstrates that diplomatic rhetoric and military escalation can coexist. Sustained economic pressure remains a likely course, with renewed military escalation a viable alternative, even at the expense of regional stability and energy prices.

Presidential power has its limits, however. Trump may seek an energy-centered resolution to the war in Ukraine in negotiations with Moscow, but achieving one is another matter. Bipartisan congressional resistance to sanctions relief on this side of the Atlantic and Europe’s determination to eliminate its dependence on Russian gas—backed by a legally mandated phaseout through 2027—present formidable obstacles. And this doesn’t even account for the fact that restoring Russian energy flows to Europe would undercut US liquefied natural gas export interests and Trump’s broader energy dominance agenda.

Beyond foreign policy and diplomatic ambitions, the president has considerably more latitude to advance his domestic energy agenda without the cooperation of foreign governments or Congress. Expect a renewed push to expand conventional energy production, export capacity, and the infrastructure needed to power the United States’ artificial intelligence (AI) and manufacturing ambitions. These priorities may offer limited near-term consumer-price relief, but they present the administration with an opportunity to translate executive authority into long-term infrastructure investment and commercial commitments that will be harder for future administrations to unwind.

Markets are unsure what to make of the Democratic sweep

Two years ago, as Trump was reelected to the presidency, bond yields shot up—as markets expected higher tariffs and more deficit spending. They were right. Two years later, as Democrats swept Congress, bond markets initially reacted in the opposite direction—on the belief that AI-related infrastructure spending would have to slow down and gridlock would mean fewer spending deals. This time, the markets may be mistaken.

The Democrats are planning a hundred-hour legislative blitz in January on a range of their priorities, including rolling back tariffs—which, based on exit polls, were among the least popular policies of Trump’s second term—and restoring cuts from Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act. All of that would increase the deficit.

The markets assume Trump will veto the full package. But it’s not so simple.

The strength of the Democrats’ majorities in both the House and Senate means they will enter two major fiscal fights in a strong negotiating position. First up will be federal government appropriations, as current funding only runs through December 11. The lame-duck Congress may pass a continuing resolution, but in 2027 a budget fight will almost certainly take place. It could happen at the same time that the US hits the debt ceiling—the $41 trillion limit is projected to be breached sometime in the first half of the year. The Democrats will insist on their spending priorities as a condition of reaching an agreement. Don’t be surprised to see some deals in the coming year—ones where both sides get their spending priorities met and the debt continues to pile up.

Tariffs, meanwhile, are not likely to change. Voters delivered a clear message about how they felt about Trump’s trade policies and the impact they have on prices. But Trump will reject any attempt to limit the use of his favorite tool. The Democrats’ legislation will be important because it will show where the party wants to head on trade in 2028 and beyond. But for those countries looking for a break on tariff rates after the midterms, the wait will be at least a little longer.

The one exception may be China. Trump’s trade détente with Beijing was driven in part by the series of summits the two leaders had this year (with two more expected before year-end). Once those pass, Trump may refocus in his final two years on what has been the core animating economic idea since he first ran for president—China’s unfair trading practices. On that issue, he may find a rare area of bipartisan consensus.

The power of the purse will be the route to shaping US NATO policy

As long as Trump is in office, questions and concerns about US engagement in NATO will remain. It was not Congress, but rather the president, who created a transatlantic crisis by repeatedly threatening to annex Greenland, make Canada the fifty-first state, and withhold protection from NATO allies that do not spend enough on defense. It was also the administration, not Congress, that bypassed all efforts to build European support for (or even awareness of) its war with Iran. The administration took not only Europeans but also Congress by surprise when it canceled troop deployments to Europe earlier this year. Now that Democrats control the legislative branch, many on both sides of the Atlantic will be looking to see if the party can wrestle some degree of control away from the executive branch in foreign and security policy.

Democrats who favor a robust US presence in Europe and a strong commitment to NATO are starting from a solid foundation. Despite the administration’s unwieldy approach toward allies, support for NATO in Congress already crosses party lines—and to meaningful effect. In the fiscal year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), Republican majorities passed multiyear security assistance for Ukraine, as well as limits on the administration’s ability to enact troop cuts in Europe, and required the US military commander of European Command to retain the supreme allied commander Europe role in NATO.

Despite this already strong bipartisan support for NATO, Democratic control of Congress will still have a recalibrating effect on transatlantic security. Come January 2027, Democrats will chair every committee and subcommittee in the House and Senate, including the appropriations committees and those important for European security and foreign policy (the Senate Armed Services Committee, Senate Foreign Relations Committee, House Armed Services Committee, and House Foreign Affairs Committee). Democrats will decide which bills get hearings, control investigations, and oversee about two-thirds of committee staff and budgets. We will see the effects of this shift in the 2027 NDAA negotiations and hearings regarding US force posture in Europe. While Trump maintains broad executive privileges in the foreign policy arena, Democrats will start paving the way for a new approach to working with US allies.

Public trust is driving politics—and perhaps now policy—on AI

For the United States to compete effectively in the age of AI, the country must address the significant trust deficit the American public has toward the technology. This was a key finding of the Atlantic Council’s Commission on AI earlier this year, which brought together bipartisan members of Congress, industry leaders, and civil society experts.

The deep anxiety Americans feel about the technology and skepticism of the titans building it were on full display throughout the midterm elections and in the results. For example, an NBC News exit poll found 56 percent of voters said AI and associated infrastructure were a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress. There is little reason to believe these concerns won’t remain on full display in the next Congress and at the state level in California, Texas, Ohio, and elsewhere.

Despite the significant Democratic gains in the election, AI skepticism transcended partisan lines, with many Republican candidates—from Michigan to Texas—advocating for slowing down the AI infrastructure buildout or increasing the regulation of the tech sector. Likewise, there are an increasing number of bipartisan policy proposals on AI safety in the current Congress—such as the FRONTIER ACT or the AI Kill Switch Act—which will likely reemerge in some form in the next Congress.

The bottom line is that, despite the increasing use and integration of AI in daily life around the country, polling as recent as last month shows that 75 percent of Americans view AI with fear or concern rather than excitement, especially when it comes to affordability, employment, education, the environment, safety and security, and many other issues. These concerns are especially prevalent among young people.

The election comes one week after one of the largest tech-driven sell-offs wiped out nearly one trillion dollars in market value due to subpar earnings reports across the AI industry. Much of that sell-off was driven by shaky confidence in whether the record borrowing and spending fueling the AI industry will translate into sustainable revenue, even as the infrastructure buildout takes time and has become a political flashpoint. Either way, the US economy is extremely dependent on whether the huge bets being placed on AI will pan out. Taken together, we’re likely in for continued market and policy adjustments related to AI.

AI is here to stay as a general-purpose technology, but it is also increasingly a determinant of geopolitical competition. As AI development outpaces institutions’ ability to manage it, we’re past due for a coherent national dialogue on AI’s impact and what US leadership in AI should look like. That debate will be on full display in the coming Congress.

US-China AI safety talks could be back on the agenda

Democratic control of Congress could strengthen political support for US-China coordination on AI safety, particularly around frontier-model risks, incident reporting, and crisis communications. The election comes at a consequential moment: During their September 2026 summit, Trump and Xi agreed to establish a bilateral AI dialogue and a communication channel for AI-related incidents, with follow-up talks scheduled for November.

Congressional Democrats have already articulated a more ambitious agenda for bilateral engagement: In September, representatives Gregory Meeks, Ami Bera, and Sara Jacobs, along with twenty-six of their colleagues, urged the administration to pursue shared AI safety standards, establish crisis communications mechanisms, address the proliferation of advanced capabilities, and facilitate exchanges between American and Chinese AI researchers. A separate initiative led by Senator Chris Van Hollen and sixteen Democratic colleagues went further, calling for a formal agreement on frontier AI testing, oversight, human control, and verification. The senators also proposed considering a mutual pause in frontier AI development, highlighting growing congressional interest in managing the risks of an accelerating technological competition.

With control of both chambers, Democrats could use committee hearings, appropriations, and legislation to press the administration to operationalize the new dialogue. Potential priorities could include defining which AI incidents trigger bilateral notifications, establishing protocols for information sharing, and supporting technical exchanges on model evaluations and catastrophic risks.

There is some bipartisan support for this approach. In September, members of the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus also called for US-China coordination on AI testing and incident reporting. Growing public backlash against current AI policy—including data center buildouts, permissive AI self-regulation, and growing concerns about the impacts of AI on employment—could also add momentum to renewed engagement on AI.

However, significant constraints remain. The executive branch controls diplomatic negotiations, while disagreements over semiconductor restrictions, technology access, and verification complicate cooperation. Democratic lawmakers also differ significantly on how far bilateral commitments should extend, with more national-security-oriented Democrats expressing greater skepticism about such a process.

The election’s most immediate effect may be to make implementation of the existing AI safety dialogue a more prominent congressional priority. Whether this develops into formal agreements will depend on the administration’s willingness to negotiate and Beijing’s readiness to accept reciprocal safeguards—a tall order, considering that Beijing has previously rejected Washington’s efforts to frame AI safety talks around US-defined priorities.

Democrats could extract some concessions on Ukraine, but don’t expect a sea-change on Europe

Europe can expect the Democrats in the next Congress to signal a more constructive US reengagement in transatlantic relations, on Ukraine, and even on trade issues. But European decisionmakers are right to have tempered expectations about how much a Democratic Congress will translate into substantial US policy changes on what matters most to the continent: support for Ukraine, US commitments to European security, and greater stability in trade and tariff policies.

Even with a strong majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats will struggle to impose meaningful limits on Trump’s conduct of foreign policy, given his constitutional powers and willingness to push the envelope. Democrats may put him and Republicans on the record with messaging bills on items such as the Russian diesel deal and waived Russia sanctions. They can put supplemental funding for Ukraine on the agenda and leverage must-pass legislation such as the NDAA to try to extract concessions on Ukraine support or US security and troop commitments in Europe related to the administration’s ongoing force posture review. The new majority will also try to claw back trade and tariff powers that Congress has ceded to the executive branch in Trump’s second term. But Trump has stated a willingness to use his veto, and hard limits on the president’s power are unlikely.

Much will also depend on where congressional Republicans go politically in response to the midterm rout. The remaining Reaganite hawks in the Senate may not continue to mute their opposition to the president’s dealings with Moscow and Beijing or his pressure on Kyiv and allied European capitals. Large Democratic majorities in both houses of Congress may make it easier to assemble the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto. Republican hawks will have more leverage to confront the White House, even if they will have to pick their battles.

Complicating matters, Europe will have to navigate two poles of power in Washington. Europe will, on the one hand, confront a Democratic Congress that wants to drive a reengagement agenda with European allies but will not be able to deliver significant policy changes on key areas of concern, at least not on its own. And on the other hand, Brussels and national capitals must be prepared to counter continued disruption from the president on trade and Ukraine, while avoiding antagonizing him with overly partisan approaches.

NATO and EU countries will continue to confront a mercurial US president who may double down on foreign policy as he is likely to come under significant pressure at home from congressional investigations, budget fights, and political gridlock under divided government. Unshackled from having to face voters at the ballot box again, Trump may shift into deal-making overdrive to cement his legacy. In doing so, he will lean into the instincts that have defined his foreign policy Weltanschauung—one of sphere-of-influence arrangements among supposedly great powers, personalized leader-to-leader dealings, and hard power realism. Trump’s deal-making mode carries both risks and opportunities for Europe and its adversaries.

Moscow and Beijing will now have to contend with a more boxed-in Trump administration. Trump’s instincts may still be to look for deals with Putin and Xi. So Europeans should assess which opportunities and deals they can shape, from Ukraine to European security and trade, even if these may turn out to be more tactical than strategic, as broader initiatives with this White House may remain elusive. But Europe simply cannot afford to fatalistically write off the next two years given the president’s powers and what is at stake for the continent in US foreign and defense policy.

Congress will double down on defense and intelligence oversight

Democratic leaders in the House and Senate will need to focus immediately on essential foreign policy issues such as Iran and Ukraine, but equally important will be the possibility of renewed oversight of core defense and intelligence issues. Expect Democrats to press on issues such as the Pentagon’s force posture plans around the globe and getting numbers on critical munitions stockpiles and associated defense production issues. Democrats are also likely to look into reports of inappropriate business practices within the department and seek out accountability on recent military actions against targets in the Caribbean and Iran. Trump’s programmatic priorities such as Golden Dome, and broader issues of personnel readiness, promotions, and recruitment, are also likely to be on the agenda.

On intelligence issues, we may see a revived bipartisan core of members who will want baseline information on how layoffs and retirements have affected US collection capacity, where AI offers expanded risks and opportunities, and how adversaries may be working together in new ways against US interests and those of the international community.

These fundamental issues won’t be easy to address. They will require urgent bipartisan attention and rapid coordination across several committees before the new Congress is even sworn in this January. Much more work lies ahead.

It’s time for bipartisan progress on immigration policy

Opinion polls have consistently made clear that the American people want an immigration system that is both just and fair, and they are prepared to vote against those who fail to deliver on that objective. Concerns about the US immigration system helped elect Trump president in 2016. Trump’s child-separation policy helped elect Joe Biden president in 2020. Chaos at the border helped elect Trump president in 2024. Cruelty in Trump’s immigration enforcement over the past two years helped create last night’s electoral triumph for Democrats.

Trump’s border adviser Tom Homan had it right two years ago: If Trump had focused on deporting only those unauthorized migrants with criminal records, he might have kept the support of the majority of Americans on this issue. Instead, Trump’s immigration policy appears to have lost the trust of the American people. As of early Wednesday morning, Democrats are expected to win in every single congressional district along the US-Mexico border, including in formerly deep-red (now looking purple) Texas.

With their new power, expect congressional Democrats to start investigations into the Trump administration’s immigration detention system.

The lesson Republicans and Democrats should learn is that only a bipartisan approach on border security and immigration will get the lasting support of the American people. The United States needs a solution along the lines of the 2023–2024 bipartisan Senate compromise or the bipartisan Dignity Act. The 120th Congress should update the 2024 compromise legislation, reallocate existing appropriations from Immigration and Customs Enforcement to other priorities, mandate a major shift in detention and asylum policy, and send it to the White House attached to whatever Trump considers must-pass legislation. Even if bipartisan immigration reform does not pass in 2027, it will help set the agenda for 2028.

Expect tougher scrutiny of Israel and Iran, and potentially more support for Ukraine

Last night’s resounding loss for the Republican Party will have some immediate impacts on foreign policy. First, the new Congress will be without a slew of experienced Republican national security voices, who either lost last night, retired, or passed away. Senators Susan Collins (ME), Thom Tillis (NC), John Cornyn (TX), Lindsey Graham (SC), and Mitch McConnell (KY), and representatives Mike Lawler (NY), Michael McCaul (TX), Ann Wagner (MO), Don Bacon (NE), and Brian Fitzpatrick (PA) have been advocates for American strength and strong alliances, including with Ukraine. That is a significant loss of expertise and experience for the Republican conferences in both chambers that will take years to rebuild.

Israel is also facing a brand-new world this morning—one with a Congress far less supportive of its causes and far more likely to cut military aid. The Israeli government and its supporters in the United States would be wise to begin immediate outreach to Democrats open to mending fences and attempt to rebuild support. Trump himself announced Tuesday that he would cut off four billion dollars in annual aid to Israel, but he will need Congress to agree, since it is actually responsible for appropriating that money. He now likely has a Congress that will.

On the war in Iran, which drove many voters to turn on Republicans, the next Congress is likely to prioritize legislation to halt, or at least significantly curtail, US military action. Still, it is unclear what that would look like beyond a resolution of disapproval, because Iran has been unwilling to have any reasonable discussions to end the conflict.

The new Congress also injects a measure of uncertainty into Ukraine policy. While Democrats have been generally solid in supporting Ukraine militarily and financially during the conflict, voters sent a resounding message in this election to focus on domestic policy and affordability. It’s unclear whether this new crop of Democrats will be interested in sending money and weapons overseas—regardless of the destination. In good news for Ukraine, the likely chairs of national security committees—particularly Representative Adam Smith (D-WA) at House Armed Services and Senator Chris Coons (D-DE) at Senate Foreign Relations—have a strong record of support. They will be powerful allies for Ukraine in the new Congress, as Kyiv fights for access to much-needed weapons.

Venezuela oil deals and military operations will come under scrutiny

Latin America policy wasn’t on the ballot yesterday, and Democrats are expected to focus on affordability and other pocketbook issues. But the Democratic-controlled House and Senate, especially with more seats flipped than expected, are likely to bring hearings, oversight, and investigations into some of Trump’s marquee policies in Latin America in at least three priority areas.

Top of that list will be Venezuela. There, investigations could stretch from looking at who benefits from oil agreements to how revenues are managed and the legal authority for those arrangements, as well as greater scrutiny of the extent to which a pathway to a democratic transition is taking shape. Senator Tim Kaine, a potential new chair of the Western Hemisphere Subcommittee in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, may push the administration on the exact timing and plan for an election.

Expect possible involvement from the House Foreign Affairs and Oversight committees, and the Senate Foreign Relations, Banking, and Finance committees. Democrats have long been asking for more information on these issues, including in a September letter from Representative Gregory Meeks and Representative Robert Garcia to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Attorney General Todd Blanche requesting more information on the management of Venezuelan oil revenue and the September oil deal announced by Trump.

But it won’t only be about Venezuela. Representative Adam Smith, in line to chair the House Armed Services Committee, has stated that, with enough backing, he would push to investigate the boat strikes and the overall military campaigns that the United States has deployed across the region since the Trump administration took office. Hearings could include the legal basis for US actions, the costs, and the casualties. Global tariffs will also be on the congressional agenda, with the implications for countries like Mexico, Washington’s largest trading partner, likely to receive greater attention.

Hearings and investigations are not the only tools available to Congress. Ahead of elections in 2028, both parties will be pressed to show concrete results through legislation—and hopefully through bipartisan alignment—on the issues that will define the continued expansion of the US presence in the hemisphere.

text:
I have always loved a simple, inexpensive, stripped-down vehicle, so I was attracted to the new Slate EV pickup truck.

The $24,950 Blank Slate EV truck starts with the essentials of a small pickup truck, comes in one color, allows you to customize it yourself and can even be converted into a five-person SUV.

Pickup trucks in the U.S. weren't always $80,000 behemoths packed with every feature possible. At the beginning of the 20th century, small-business owners began modifying passenger cars like the Ford Model T before the industry caught on to building purpose-built pickups in the 1920s. Even 60 years later, the basic idea of a small, simple truck wasn't lost on the U.S. truck industry when Ford Rangers, Chevrolet S-10s and Asian counterparts from Toyota and Nissan sold in large numbers during the '80s and '90s.

Today, there isn't a truly small pickup available to U.S. buyers. Toyota's smallest pickup today approaches the size of a full-size truck of the 1990s. The Ford Maverick, the smallest truck option available today, is about the same length as many of the company's full-size F-150s in the 1990s. The least expensive Maverick, which had a window sticker for under $20,000 for the 2022 model year, is now $28,145.

I currently own two pickups: a base-trim, slate-gray 1994 Toyota 4x4 with wind-up windows that I bought new, and a 2022 Carbonized Gray hybrid Ford Maverick. So while I definitely don't need another inexpensive gray pickup, the new small EV truck has piqued my interest.

I drove 300 miles round trip on Oct. 31 from central Pennsylvania to New Jersey for a 15-minute ride in the Slate Truck. I had previously hopped a train to New York City in August 2025 to see one in person.

I didn't actually get to drive it, but a friendly, talkative operator took me around the course, giving me a sense of how the truck handled and a few minutes to grab some video.

The test track was the oval access road of a shopping mall. The operator demonstrated the acceleration, which was brisk, as well as the one-pedal driving. It also has a mechanical brake pedal, but one-pedal driving allows the truck to slow and mostly stop through regenerative braking without using the mechanical brakes.

I was satisfied with my ride in the prototype truck. The ride is great. It isn't soft or harsh. It's just right. The truck feels solid, smooth and quiet. It's about the same length as my 1994 Toyota single-cab pickup truck, but there is way more room in the cabin.

The simplicity of this truck makes me smile. It has crank windows, and the HVAC controls are three physical buttons front and center. The truck has air conditioning, cruise control, airbags and a backup camera that's integrated into the speedometer screen. It has a key fob that opens the doors and slips into the dash to start it.

It does not have a giant touchscreen in the middle of the dashboard. Instead, you mount your phone or tablet and use your existing data plan and mobile apps. The Slate app on your mobile device will interface with the truck.

Beyond that, there is an ever-growing accessory list, from speakers to fender flares, at slate.auto. The gray plastic body panels were designed to be easily wrapped. A wrap configurator allows endless color configurations. The truck can hold five people when configured as an SUV with two different designs (think first-generation Toyota 4Runner), or it can be configured with the Open Air Kit.

Slate's concept is to roll one trim level in one color off the assembly line and then have customers add the content they want. The company will also use direct sales, meaning you purchase the truck online. According to a representative at the drive event, trucks will be delivered to regional hubs or directly to customers' homes.

Service and warranty repairs will be handled through RepairPal-affiliated service stations, while Slate University will provide online resources for owners who want to work on their own trucks. The RepairPal website currently lists six affiliated garages in the York area.

There are still many questions that will only be answered once trucks start rolling off the Warsaw, Indiana, assembly line within the next few months and land in the hands of customers. According to CarGurus, there were 180,000 reservations by mid-2026.

Would I buy one? I tend to overthink all of my large purchase decisions, so the answer is maybe. I was a reservation holder and converted my reservation to a $300 deposit, with a build date set for June 2027. I am going to wait a few months to hear about the actual ownership experience, visit some RepairPal garages in my area and see where I am by the middle of next year.

I definitely don't need another simple gray pickup truck, but I have been curious about diving into a new EV truck experience with a lower initial purchase price. You can't ignore the low cost of operating and maintaining an electric vehicle, particularly with gasoline hanging above $4 a gallon.

The real innovation of Slate is that the company dares to look back at history to see what made early pickup trucks great and has repackaged that concept for 2027 to address the soaring cost of new vehicles. Time will tell if Americans buy into the Slate philosophy.

text:
Major environmental groups submitted comments detailing the numerous legal and technical flaws in the Environmental Protection Agency’s “tectonic and unreasoned” proposal to abdicate its legal authority and responsibility to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

The proposal is “fundamentally unlawful” and should be abandoned because it contravenes Supreme Court precedent and guts important clean air protections, the groups said in comments submitted to the agency.

Clean Air Task Force, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice, Environmental Defense Fund, Environmental Law & Policy Center, NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council), Sierra Club, and Union of Concerned Scientists signed the comments.

Experts at the Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) contributed a synthesis of the latest science that shows the serious flaws in EPA’s reliance on Global Mean Surface Temperature (GMST) and Global Mean Sea Level (GMSL) as the only metrics for climate harms to people across the nation. UCS points out this is “…contrary to the scientific consensus which shows that seemingly “small” increases in GMST and GMSL translate into profound, non-linear, and compounding risks for the human health and welfare of people in the United States.” This synthesis can be found in Appendix B.

The group’s comments note that the EPA “misinterprets the Clean Air Act, ignores scientific evidence, and entirely misunderstands its own duty as the agency responsible for protecting public health and the environment,” the comments say. “The EPA must withdraw the supplemental proposal in its entirety.”

A key part of the agency’s proposal is its contention that addressing the greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S., would be “futile,” because they are responsible for only a portion of the problem of climate change.

But EPA’s futility analysis “lacks any legal foundation or rational basis and is otherwise fundamentally flawed, arbitrary and capricious, inadequately explained, and unlawful,” the groups said.

The comments include new expert modeling showing that – even assuming the EPA’s own power-plant emissions projections – uncontrolled U.S. power-plant greenhouse gases would cause massive human health and welfare harms of $20.4 trillion by 2100.

For context, the entire U.S. GDP was $29.3 trillion in 2024.

The new modeling also shows that, under EPA’s own projections, U.S. power-plant carbon pollution will cause more than 100,000 childhood asthma cases, 22,000 hospital or emergency room visits, and 1.8 million lost school days by 2100. Using other assumptions, projected damages to health and welfare are even worse.

The comments submitted to EPA late yesterday were also endorsed by Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin, and Friends of the Earth.

title: 'Seismic' blue wave triggers sinking of oil prices, energy stocks, and chances of permitting reform
description:
Anti-fossil fuel Democrats are now potentially motivated to take harder negotiating tactics.
With more clean energy-loving Democrats coming into power, renewable energy companies also were rewarded.
“We had a referendum on inflation, high oil prices, and Trump in general,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm.
Oil is down, but it’s not cratering.” Domestically, much of the focus will remain on the data center backlash and permitting reform.
That’s why a bipartisan permitting reform effort focused on expediting energy construction of all kinds was coming together.
text:
Even as Wall Street celebrated the anticipated gridlock from a splintered Congress and White House—the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 3% Wednesday—most energy companies moved in the opposite direction, especially in states such as Texas that had the most shocking Democratic wins.

The other potential loser is the bipartisan legislation to expedite the construction of energy projects—and power the AI boom—that would benefit both renewable power and oil and gas pipelines. Anti-fossil fuel Democrats are now potentially motivated to take harder negotiating tactics. TD Cowen analysts slashed their projection for passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) from 40% to 25% during the lame-duck session before the new Congress is sworn in.

Charles Hua, executive director of the PowerLines nonprofit, said the “seismic” blue wave from Congress to governors’ elections to public service commissions was a referendum on spiking utility bills, gasoline costs, and the inflationary ripple effects throughout the economy.

“You only get such seismicity in political results if something is fundamentally unsteady or unstable, and I think one of the big manifestations of that really has been energy costs,” Hua told Fortune.

In addition to voter discontent over the Iran war and fuel prices, there were more than 40 local ballot measure on restricting or regulating data centers. All but one of them—in North Dakota—passed. “That’s a staggering statistic,” Hua said.

As for Wall Street performance, there were clear winners and losers by utilities and independent power producers.

NRG Energy and Vistra, which are building out gas-fired power generation in Texas to help fuel the AI boom, saw their stock values drop precipitously by 12% and 15%, respectively. Gas turbine manufacturer GE Vernova dipped by 10%.

Analyst Julien Dumoulin-Smith of Jefferies specifically highlighted the “Texas shock,” noting that “the most impactful surprise is the magnitude by which Texas voted Democratic, imperiling the outlook for data center developments.”

Texas-based Tesla and SpaceX leader Elon Musk—after unsuccessfully spending hundreds of millions on GOP candidates—posted on X, “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

On the other hand, utilities that operate in Florida, which remained Republican, were rewarded. Florida-based NextEra Energy jumped 5% and Duke Energy rose by 3%.

With more clean energy-loving Democrats coming into power, renewable energy companies also were rewarded. First Solar rose by over 4% and solar parts manufacturer Nextpower spiked by 13%.

After President Donald Trump downplayed the potential for an escalation in Iran and Vice President JD Vance blamed his party’s election losses on the war, the global oil benchmark fell by 8% to below $100 per barrel for the first time in nearly a month. As such, oil producers and refiners suffered on Wall Street too.

ExxonMobil and Chevron dipped by 4% and 5%, respectively. Refiners Marathon Petroleum and Valero Energy, which have reported record profits of late, plunged by 9% and 7%, respectively.

“We had a referendum on inflation, high oil prices, and Trump in general,” said oil forecaster Dan Pickering, founder of the Pickering Energy Partners consulting and research firm. “It feels like Trump will have more pushback and less maneuverability around how he wants to conduct the conflict in Iran.”

What’s next?

There may be optimism for peace talks in Iran, but this war likely is far from over, Pickering warned.

There is no clear compromise yet, and Trump could easily get frustrated and opt for escalation between now and January, which is what Trump himself predicted before the election.

“I think the Iran conflict gets more complicated for the U.S. We’ve been looking for an off ramp, but we want an off ramp that doesn’t leave the Middle East in chaos,” Pickering told Fortune. “I think that issue probably transcends the election. Even with more Democrats, I don’t think they’re going to want a bad outcome for the Iran crisis. Oil is down, but it’s not cratering.”

Domestically, much of the focus will remain on the data center backlash and permitting reform. Some of the biggest states for data center growth are Texas, Georgia, and Ohio and Democratic challengers all won the governor elections in those states while pushing for data center moratoriums.

“‘Moratorium’ certainly is the buzzword,” Hua said, but it’s not clear if those efforts equate to temporary pauses or outright opposition. “How high on the priory list is electricity? I suspect that electricity vis-a-vis data centers will remain a top-of-mind issue for these new administrations.”

The AI boom has brought both parties somewhat closer together in terms of supporting all-of-the-above energy solutions. That’s why a bipartisan permitting reform effort focused on expediting energy construction of all kinds was coming together. But a Democratic wave is expected to leave more of them arguing in favor of waiting until next year to propose a version that’s less friendly to fossil fuel projects. Such an effort could be risky because it would still require Trump’s signature.

“With greater leverage heading into 2027, Democrats have less incentive to accept pipeline provisions during the lame duck, pushing the debate toward a narrower clean energy-transmission package or no deal,” Dumoulin-Smith added.

The legislation would facilitate the growth of long-distance transmission lines, which most benefit renewable energy. As such, top transmission developer Quanta Services saw its stock fall by 12% Wednesday.

The legislation’s Democratic sponsor, Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., implored his party to still support the bill on Wednesday.

“Democrats ran and won on affordability, and this bill lowers costs for families and will allow us to start delivering on our election promises,” Whitehouse told Fortune in a statement. “It’s a bird in the hand. We’d be fools not to take it.”

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

President Donald Trump’s recent executive order seeking to protect the bulk power system from foreign threats correctly identifies the risk of U.S. reliance on outside suppliers, but mitigating those risks without stalling the grid’s buildout or saddling ratepayers with even more costs will be tricky, stakeholders told Utility Dive.

Executive Order 14421, issued Aug. 26, gives Secretary of Energy Chris Wright the power to block the installation of foreign-produced equipment – “or any critical component, software, firmware, digital service, maintenance service, or remote-access capability associated with such equipment” – that poses an “undue risk” to national security, either through intentional sabotage or supply chain disruption.

It also gave the secretary the authority to order the removal and replacement of previously installed equipment.

The Department of Energy has until Dec. 24 to publish rules and regulations implementing the order. In September, DOE asked industry and other stakeholders to weigh in.

Their responses to DOE’s request show broad support for the intent of the order, but concern over how it will be implemented. A number pointed out that security standards, especially for software that would enable remote access, can be more important than country of origin since flaws in any system can be exploited by anyone, anywhere.

The vast majority of stakeholder responses that took a position on the “function over origin” question favored DOE emphasizing functional controls as opposed to a software product’s origin, according to data compiled by industry analyst Brendon Shank.

Many respondents also said they wanted DOE to take a phased approach to introducing new compliance rules and allow some vendors to “prequalify” as trustworthy. Utilities are projected to spend more than a trillion dollars on grid upgrades through 2030 and are racing to secure contracts for equipment amid rising manufacturer backlogs.

“Supply chains are already approaching a breaking point for many categories of electrical industry products,” said the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, which represents more than 300 electrical equipment manufacturers.

“[W]e strongly encourage the DOE to consider the time, money and resources it takes to evaluate, redesign, develop and produce equipment that is made for the electrical system,” it said. “At a time of high demand and longer lead times than during periods of more stable electricity growth, that is only further complicated by balancing timeliness with retooling or restructuring of production lines to meet new changes.”

Until DOE releases its determinations, the industry faces a lot of uncertainty and big questions, said Alice Wu, a manager of federal policy at the clean energy nonprofit RMI.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Utility Dive free daily newsletter

Even though the order instructs DOE to focus on transmission-related equipment and components of 69 kV or higher — not on the distribution system — it also puts distribution system components linked to the bulk system with questionably sourced software under scrutiny, she said.

“It is not feasible for generation, transmission and distribution providers to rip-and-replace every piece of equipment and for DOE to check it,” Wu told Utility Dive in an interview. “What is the secure proxy for that? … And what will the potential cost impacts to ratepayers be?”

U.S. imports billions of dollars in grid components every year

The U.S. has imported more than $22 billion in bulk-power equipment since 2025, particularly from China, which would likely be the country most impacted by the order, according to a recent Wood Mackenzie analysis.

Transformers and substations are already in an estimated market shortage of 15% and 8%, respectively, in 2026, and “restrictions on the use of Chinese built units is going to further exacerbate the supply chain challenges,” WoodMac said.

The market for 100 MVA power transformers is particularly exposed, it said, adding that the market for power transformers greater than 10 MVA has expanded nearly 300% since 2020.

A different analysis by RMI and BloombergNEF said the value of grid imports in 2025 was more than $30 billion. Together, Mexico, Southeast Asia and the European Union made up more than half of that, while China accounted for $3.5 billion and “other” countries for $7.4 billion.

Cybersecurity a key vulnerability

NEMA and other stakeholders and experts applauded the order’s emphasis on software, maintenance support and other services that introduce remote-access capabilities. They also pointed to existing security standards DOE could apply from the North American Electric Reliability Corp., the National Institute of Standards and Technology, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers and others.

Read More in Grid Security & Reliability

“Overall, this executive order focuses on the right security areas because it makes those who deploy critical infrastructure accountable for their software,” said Aaron Rose, a security architect manager with Check Point Software Technologies, which assesses security for utilities and other companies.

Check Point sees an average of about 3,000 cyberattacks per large organization per week, he said in an interview with Utility Dive.

DOE software determinations will be complicated, because “almost everything on the power system is software defined, controlled and driven,” he added.

DOE could ask for a software’s source, who maintains it, who has remote access to it, and where updates originate, Rose said. But updates for most firmware, cloud control systems, substation systems and customer-owned devices are from open-source libraries or code already written for other uses, making their countries of origin difficult to identify, and eliminating all software of uncertain origin is impractical, he said.

Power system software may also be sub-contracted to a third-party, Rose continued. Hardware manufacturers may or may not have documentation on that software’s developer or on who has remote access for updates, or be able to trace them, even with AI tools.

To avoid a complicated decompiling by a security team and still ensure critical needs are met, DOE could require future updates and remote access to be from secure sources, he added.

Rose said it is unclear whether the costs for such measures will fall on software vendors, infrastructure owners or their consumers.

An analysis of the order by the Rainey Center, a policy think tank, also questioned the logic of restrictions based on geography rather than capability and function.

Read More in Grid Security & Reliability

“The risks the order names travel through code, connections, and control, and they work the same whether a device is built abroad or at home,” it said. “A ban governs geography; a standard governs the risk, on every device.”

The report recommended DOE define risk by “a verifiable, technology-neutral standard” built on existing controls, as well as a system for vendors to prequalify through independent U.S. testing.

Protecting investments in growth

The order’s flexibilities, like phased compliance, can allow determinations that avoid negative economic impacts, said Danielle Russo, executive director of SAFE, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on U.S. national and economic security.

DOE can provide power system manufacturers and developers the clarity they need with lists of the specific supply chain equipment and components that are secure, Russo said. That will avoid slowing manufacturing investment and project development needed to meet load growth, she added.

In today’s complex investment environment, uncertainties from tariffs to changing political leadership can threaten investors with stranded assets, Russo said, adding: “It is hard to blame them for being challenged by that.”

title: Voters Send Republicans the Bill in the Energy Affordability Election - Evergreen Action
description:
Lower power bills.
Homegrown clean energy that doesn’t spike every time a war breaks out overseas.
Data centers that pay their own way, instead of passing the bill to everyone else.
Led by Trump, Republicans promised lower bills while pursuing a staggering list of policies that actually increased energy costs.
What Now: Accountability and the Groundwork for Lower Energy Bills The new majority won by offering solutions for lower bills.
text:
To: Interested Parties

From: Evergreen Action Communications Director Seth Nelson

Date: Wednesday, November 4, 2026

Re: Voters Send Republicans the Bill in the Energy Affordability Election

Democrats won the House and the Senate on Tuesday in a resounding rejection of the Republicans who spent two years driving up costs. Nobody had to tell voters what this election was about. They felt the squeeze every time they pulled up to the pump or opened a bill: more. More to fill the tank. More to keep the lights on. More for every grocery staple a diesel truck hauls. On Election Day, 87% of voters said they were concerned about the cost of gas and diesel, and 86% about the price of their utilities.

So they voted for the candidates promising relief. Lower power bills. Homegrown clean energy that doesn’t spike every time a war breaks out overseas. Data centers that pay their own way, instead of passing the bill to everyone else.

This wasn’t a fluke. Last year, Governors Mikie Sherrill and Abigail Spanberger pioneered this playbook and achieved decisive victories in races fought over the cost of living, with energy bills front and center. Now it has carried new congressional majorities. Energy affordability isn’t an issue Democrats have to play defense on. It’s an issue they win on.

The lesson of this election is simple. Voters wanted lower bills, and Democrats showed up with solutions: cheap, clean power and accountability for the data centers driving bills up. Republicans showed up with excuses. Now the work starts. For the next two years, that means making the Trump administration answer for higher bills and building support for the solutions that will bring them down.

Democrats Ran on Lower Bills, and Voters Rewarded Them

Across the map, the winners made the same argument: energy bills are too high, and here’s how to bring them down. They didn’t treat energy affordability as a side issue. They made it central to their closing argument.

Cheap, clean power was the solution, not the problem.

Led by Trump, Republicans promised lower bills while pursuing a staggering list of policies that actually increased energy costs. Democrats turned Republicans’ weakness into their strength. And they had the solutions to back it up: the fastest way to bring costs down is to build more of the cheapest power available, not prop up costly coal and gas plants. Voters responded, in no small part because so many of them had lived through Republicans’ energy agenda firsthand.

Take Michigan’s 4th District, where St. Sen. Sean McCann defeated Rep. Bill Huizenga. When the Trump administration ordered the J.H. Campbell coal plant in Huizenga’s own district to keep running past its scheduled retirement, Huizenga cheered it on. That order has already racked up at least $295 million in extra costs for ratepayers. Huizenga also falsely blamed clean energy for rising bills, insisting Michiganders “just want to keep the lights on without going broke.” They do. That’s why they elected McCann, who backs more wind and solar to lower bills and ran on “solutions that reduce costs for Michigan families—not aging coal and natural gas plants that make energy more expensive for ratepayers.”

In Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, Abdul El-Sayed pointed to price spikes as proof that the U.S. remains “uniquely susceptible” until it builds out clean energy. “We need 100% renewable energy, and we need it yesterday,” he said.

Rebecca Cooke made the same case in Wisconsin’s 3rd, tying clean energy to “good-paying local jobs” and lower costs for working families, while her opponent, Rep. Derrick Van Orden stood in the Oval Office to cheer a $700 million taxpayer bailout for coal.

Big Tech should pay its own way.

As the data center boom drove up power demand, who foots the bill became one of the defining fights of the midterms, up and down the ballot, and Democrats were clear it shouldn’t be families. Voters agreed: three-quarters opposed a new data center in their community, and they backed Democratic House candidates by 28 points, according to exit polling.

In Georgia’s U.S. Senate race, Jon Ossoff said no family “should pay a dime more” to power Big Tech’s data centers.”

In Pennsylvania’s 7th District, Bob Brooks warned against “data centers raising our energy costs while an out-of-state corporation gets rich,” while his opponent, Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, was still blaming rising electricity costs on the previous administration nearly two years into Trump’s term. Voters didn’t buy his excuses.

In the neighboring 8th District, Paige Cognetti put it bluntly: “Don’t raise our electric bills.” Her opponent, Rep. Rob Bresnahan, hailed data centers as “catalysts for economic growth” while holding up to $2 million in stock in AI and tech companies powering the boom—stock trades that Cognetti highlighted in ads and campaign messaging about profiting from data center development. New York’s 17th, Wisconsin’s 3rd, and Pennsylvania’s 8th each saw more than $1 million in ads about data centers driving up costs.

They made Republicans own their record.

The winners didn’t let their opponents hide. Janelle Stelson told voters in Pennsylvania’s 10th District that Rep. Scott Perry’s “unrelenting hostility to clean energy” could add $130 to their bills. In New York’s 17th District, Cait Conley hammered incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler for voting to slash the clean energy credits that brought billions to build new, cheap power into the state. With at least $191 million in ads about utility and energy bills on the air this cycle, most of them from Democrats, voters heard that contrast loud and clear.

The same energy affordability story played out in gubernatorial and other down ballot races across the country.

Michigan and Wisconsin voters chose governors whose plans, according to independent modeling, will put real money back into their pockets. Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson’s agenda could save Michigan households an average of $638 through 2040, while her opponent’s plan to repeal the state’s clean energy laws would have cost them $2,135. In Wisconsin, Governor-elect David Crowley’s plan to double funding for the state’s efficiency programs could save households $826, versus $3,181 in added costs under his opponent’s plan, a swing of up to $4,000 per family.

The theme ran all the way down the ballot. In Georgia, Democrats Peter Hubbard and Sheila Edwards won seats on the Public Service Commission, the body that sets the state’s power rates, by running on cheap solar, batteries, and fair rates. The victories handed Democrats majority control of the Commission for the first time in 30 years.

What Now: Accountability and the Groundwork for Lower Energy Bills

The new majority won by offering solutions for lower bills. With Trump still in the White House, its most powerful tool for the next two years is holding his administration accountable. Every energy price hike the administration has handed families, from canceled clean energy projects to costly coal plants propped up with taxpayer money, is now fair game. So are the utilities asking for rate hike after rate hike, the grid operators stalling cheap, clean power from getting online, and the tech giants whose data centers are driving up demand and costs. Voters will hear exactly who drove up their bills, all the way to 2028.

It also means putting real solutions on the floor. Democrats can pass bills to restore incentives for cheap, clean power, make data centers pay their own way, and rein in the utility profits baked into every bill. Trump is unlikely to sign them. But every vote builds the case, and the support, for the day Democrats hold both the White House and Congress again.

—

This was an energy affordability election, plain and simple. Voters were tired of paying more month after month, and they picked the candidates who offered real solutions. Cheap, clean power and making Big Tech pay its own way weren’t liabilities to manage. They were winning issues. Now the winners have to hold the people who drove up those bills accountable, and start laying the groundwork to bring them down.

text:
Following two years of anti-climate legislation from Washington, Tuesday’s blue tidal wave—giving Democrats control of both the Senate and the House—could provide an opportunity to change course.

Following his 2024 reelection, President Trump withdrew from the Paris Agreement, rolled back the landmark endangerment finding, and leased public lands for oil and gas drilling—with Democrats unable to do much about it.

The next two years likely won’t bring aggressive climate policy, nonetheless a shift is expected as a result of the midterms. “Are we going to see ambitious climate action? The answer is no,” says Ken Gillingham, professor of environmental and energy economics at the Yale School of the Environment. “We still have an executive branch with a veto power controlled by President Trump, and so anything that is done would have to make it through the veto.”

But while Democrats might be unable to reverse many of the rollbacks, the midterms now give them, “a stronger hand to play,” says Geoffrey Henderson, assistant professor of environmental policy and planning at the University of Michigan.

One priority might be to reinstate billions of dollars in climate funding that President Trump has withheld. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat who won reelection in Maine, serves on the House Appropriations Committee and has said that she plans to force the administration to spend climate money.

Democrats also have the power to focus on bulking up the permitting reform bill, which aims to overhaul the permit process to speed up energy projects. The bill appeared likely to pass even before the election, but was filled with concessions. “Prior to the election, the bill included a number of provisions to weaken core environmental laws like the National Environmental Policy Act,” says Henderson. “What Democrats can now do is basically ask for a better deal.”

Increased support for domestic battery manufacturing is also likely—which could be a key part in meeting clean energy targets. “There would be an appetite for domestic onshoring of some of the supply chain that goes into electric vehicles, and I think that this is pretty bipartisan,” says Gillingham.

Gillingham also notes that we could see Democrats pursue “all of the above” climate policies, which often include oil and gas concessions along with clean energy growth.

“There's just not going to be an appetite among a whole set of members of the Democratic Caucus for ambitious climate action, even if they may be sympathetic to climate action, they don't have the political backing to do it from where they are sitting,” he notes. “But they do have the political backing to do all of the above energy policies.”

Democrats also achieved trifectas—controlling the House, Senate, and governorship—in Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Nevada. In Pennsylvania, for example, this opens the floodgates to pass legislation to regulate data centers, allow community solar, and to require utilities to store excess electricity.

title: EPA's Second Round of Methane Rollbacks – What Oil and Gas Operators Need to Know Now
description:
Background In November 2025, EPA issued a delay rule pushing compliance deadlines for new and existing sources to January 2027.
These addressed temporary flaring of associated gas and continuous monitoring of the heating value of vent gas.
It would also offer an alternative with more targeted changes to the existing flaring limits.
