text:
On October 7, 2026, Zeldin announced the next phase of the EPA’s reconsideration of the rule.

Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin recently announced the next phase of the agency’s rollback of the Biden administration’s 2024 oil and natural gas regulations, commonly known as “OOOOb/c.” The term refers to two companion provisions of EPA’s Clean Air Act regulations: 40 C.F.R. Part 60, Subparts OOOOb and OOOOc. Together, they established methane and volatile organic compound standards for new and existing oil and gas infrastructure, including leak monitoring and retrofit requirements that reached low-producing wells, along with guidelines for states to regulate methane emissions from existing sources. It is important to note that the EPA has not yet released the proposed regulatory text or its supporting cost analysis.

Background

In November 2025, EPA issued a delay rule pushing compliance deadlines for new and existing sources to January 2027.

On April 6, 2026, EPA finalized a first round of revisions. These addressed temporary flaring of associated gas and continuous monitoring of the heating value of vent gas.

What EPA Is Proposing Now

On October 7, 2026, Zeldin announced the next phase of the EPA’s reconsideration of the rule. Based on the announcement and press reports, the key elements are:

New Well-Site Categories

EPA will put forward two options, each creating separate categories of well sites with standards tailored to each category.

No More Super Emitter Program

EPA plans to rescind the program, citing legal concerns and saying the program is not necessary to meet Clean Air Act requirements.

“Efficient” Flaring Instead of a Routine Flaring Ban

The proposal reportedly would replace the ban on routine flaring of associated gas with standards based on “efficient” flaring. It would also offer an alternative with more targeted changes to the existing flaring limits.

Significant Cost Savings

EPA estimates the changes would save the industry about $45 billion.

Litigation Risk

The rollback is moving forward while the earlier delay rule is being challenged in court. Environmental groups, including the Environmental Defense Fund, have asked the D.C. Circuit to vacate the delay rule. At oral argument on October 14, the three-judge panel was skeptical of EPA’s justifications. The judges also pressed the environmental groups to distinguish their methane lawsuit from an earlier ruling that upheld EPA’s delay of separate air toxics limits.

This matters in practice: If the court vacates the delay rule, companies could face the original compliance deadlines, possibly with little notice or transition period, creating immediate regulatory vulnerability. Moreover, once the new rollback is finalized, it is likely to draw its own legal challenges.

Key Takeaways for Operators

Keep Compliance Programs in Place

Don’t dismantle leak detection, monitoring or flaring controls until the new rules are final and the litigation is resolved.

Monitor the Comment Period

Once the proposal is published, consider commenting on the well-site categories and the flaring options, the areas most likely to affect day-to-day operations.

Check State Obligations

Federal changes do not displace state requirements. Colorado, for example, recently finalized its own methane controls for existing operations.

Review Your Contracts

Look at purchase agreements, gathering agreements and other contracts to see how they allocate the risk of regulatory change, especially if the original deadlines are reinstated.

text:
Data center approvals could remain paused in Texas until legislators pass new state laws next year if Democrat Gina Hinojosa keeps her campaign promises after winning the governor’s race in a stunning victory Tuesday.

Her statements on the campaign trail went beyond Gov. Greg Abbott’s current freeze on environmental permitting and grid connections for data centers during an audit period expected to be completed this year.

Grassroots opposition to data centers has mounted in communities across Texas, where critics across the political spectrum expressed concerns about the almost unbelievable projections for how much power the facilities could draw from the state’s grid and the unknown amount of water they would need to operate in a state with serious drought concerns.

Hinojosa attacked Abbott’s handling of the matter. She called for a data center moratorium to last until the Texas Legislature meets in January to pass “real protections so Texans can have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities.”

“When I am governor I will issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the Legislature to protect Texans,” Hinojosa said in an Oct. 22 video posted to X.

Hinojosa’s plan for data centers

The governor-elect during her campaign outlined a slate of priorities for lawmakers that included requiring data center operators to hire union workers, protecting communities’ water supplies and stopping data center companies from using nondisclosure agreements that make it harder for the public to track project developments.

Similar to Abbott, Hinojosa also said she would push to ensure Texans wouldn’t pay more for electricity because of data centers, and to stop tax subsidies that were depriving the state of billions in sales tax revenue.

“We can have economic development and we can have protections for Texans. These things are not mutually exclusive,” she said in a September interview with Politico.

Hinojosa will be working with a Democrat-dominated Texas House. She takes office Jan. 19.

Abbott slowly cracked down on the facilities, turning from a politician who in November heralded Texas as the “epicenter of AI development” to one who, starting in August, began issuing pauses on data center approvals at the state grid and then the environmental permitting agency so information about the facilities could be audited and collected.

The audit by grid regulators and operators was expected to last until December. Abbott had also demanded that officials collect information on tax incentives and water use, whether data centers were bringing their own power or water supplies and whether data centers were taking measures to reduce impacts on the neighbors for light and noise pollution.

How that information would be used remained to be seen, but Abbott had demanded data centers pay for their own electrical infrastructure — a process being worked out by state regulators — in addition to using water-efficient technology. He promised to pursue getting rid of tax breaks for data centers during the legislative session.

Data center-related donors, meanwhile, gave Abbott some $9 million since July 2025, the Texas Tribune reported. And in October, environmental and community advocates identified some environmental permits related to data centers they said had gotten approval anyway despite Abbott’s pause, forcing the permitting agency to shut down its online filing system.

Some county officials had also expressed frustration with their lack of authority under current state law to regulate data centers.

“Real anger in communities”

Data Center Watch, which researches opposition to data centers in the United States, in a Tuesday analysis said the state “offers one of the clearest examples of data center regulation becoming an election issue.” The group found that 43% of the 74 gubernatorial candidates they studied in 36 states supported a data center moratorium or ban.

“We’ve just seen real anger in communities — big, small, in solid red counties and in deep blue counties alike,” said Kathryn Guerra, the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality watchdog campaign director for Public Citizen, which identified the errant permit approvals.

“What happened yesterday just seems to have been a reflection of that anger,” she added. “We’re in a position now to listen to Texans and help advance solutions to those concerns that they have raised over the past year with the massive influx of data centers that Texas has seen.”

Jess Heck, director of government affairs in Texas for the industry association Data Center Coalition, said in a statement that data centers could continue to advance job creation and strengthen the state’s economy through investments in communities and tax revenue generation.

“The data center industry is committed to advancing America’s digital infrastructure, including here in the Lone Star State, as well as supporting energy reliability and affordability and promoting long-term, responsible economic development,” Heck said.

The coalition, Heck continued, “looks forward to working with state leadership along with local officials, stakeholders, and Texas communities to continue building trust and supporting responsible data center growth.”

text:
Americans don't want data centers in their backyards.

That's one of the clearest messages sent at the ballot box during Tuesday's midterm elections.

NBC News' exit poll found that 76% of voters would oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, and 56% said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.

As well as governors and senators who voiced opposition to data centers winning, ballots included referendums on their construction.

Goldman Sachs economists said Democratic wins at the state and local levels will likely lead to "short-term data center moratoria, potentially affecting about 45% of planned US data center capacity expansion."

More than 30 direct votes against data centers passed

Dozens of cities and small towns held referendums in which data centers were directly on the ballot.

As of 8 a.m. ET, voters had approved 33 ballot measures restricting data centers, versus one allowing them, according to an analysis by Redbud Consulting.

Most of these votes were in Ohio, home to a key data center for OpenAI's $500 billion Stargate project.

One measure stands out as being linked to a specific project. EdgeConneX wanted permits from the town of Ashville to build two data centers on a 195-acre property.

However, 82% of its 1,800 voters rejected a resolution to proceed with the development of data centers and an associated natural gas facility.

Americans look set to vote overwhelmingly against data centers in many of the referendums.

For example, in Alhambra, a city in Los Angeles County, a measure to ban data centers is also on track to be approved by 82% of voters.

A blue swing in data center hot spot Texas

Texas was one of the clearest examples of the "blue tsunami," in which Democrats exceeded expectations. It's also a major location for data centers, including Stargate's flagship site plus two others under development.

The gubernatorial race was a particular upset, where Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate, beat the incumbent Greg Abbott. She will be the state's first Democratic governor since 1995.

Her campaign included a promise to immediately pause data-center development in the state.

With 96% of the votes counted, Hinojosa had a 7-point lead, per the Associated Press — an 18-point swing from the last gubernatorial election in 2022.

James Talarico, the Democratic senator-elect, has argued that data centers are contributing to the cost of living, including by increasing utility bills. He also wants to create an "AI dividend" for people to share in AI companies' profits.

'Data Center Alley' swings further to the Democrats

Virginia has the most data centers of any state. The majority of those are concentrated in the north, giving the region the nickname "Data Center Alley."

Loudoun County has some 250 operational data centers, and over 100 more planned.

While many analysts expected the state to stay blue, Democratic Sen. Mark Warner extended his majority.

Statewide, there was a 17-point swing compared to the 2024 presidential election.

With 97% of votes counted in Loudoun County, Warner received 69% of the vote. That's a 21-point swing compared to 2024, and an 11-point swing from the state's last Senate election in 2020.

title: States Continue to Expand GHG Reporting as EPA Delays Federal Requirements Again
description:
Meanwhile, states continue to expand and revise their own GHG reporting programs, adding to the uncertainty and complexity facing companies subject to multiple reporting regimes.
State reporting requirements continue to evolve: States are revising existing GHG reporting programs and implementing new requirements, creating an increasingly fragmented reporting landscape.
Although EPA extended the 2025 reporting deadline to March 10, 2027, the deadline for reporting 2026 emissions remains March 31, 2027.
Since B&D’s July news alert, several states have taken additional steps to implement or expand reporting requirements.
Businesses operating internationally also increasingly face mandatory GHG emissions reporting requirements in other jurisdictions.
text:
Background

On October 14, 2026, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issued an interim final rule further extending the deadline to report 2025 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions under the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP) from October 30, 2026, to March 10, 2027. EPA has yet to finalize its September 2025 proposal to eliminate reporting requirements for most GHGRP source categories. The extension leaves existing federal reporting requirements in place while EPA considers its next steps. Meanwhile, states continue to expand and revise their own GHG reporting programs, adding to the uncertainty and complexity facing companies subject to multiple reporting regimes.

Key Takeaways

Status of federal reporting program in limbo: EPA extended the 2025 GHGRP deadline a second time, and EPA Administrator Zeldin indicated that the Agency is still evaluating how to proceed with its proposal to rescind most of the GHGRP.

Subsequent changes, litigation, and continued uncertainty are possible: EPA’s approach to rolling back other GHG regulations could influence its action on the proposed GHGRP rescission, and legal challenges to any repeal could further complicate the program’s future.

State reporting requirements continue to evolve: States are revising existing GHG reporting programs and implementing new requirements, creating an increasingly fragmented reporting landscape. Some of these programs are in litigation.

Implications for regulated entities: For the over 8,000 facilities subject to the GHGRP, a conservative approach in the interim is to continue collecting emissions data ahead of existing deadlines and stay informed as EPA considers options to repeal most of the GHGRP. Uncertainty as to EPA’s plans and any subsequent litigation makes it difficult to forecast reporting obligations. Businesses operating across multiple states should ensure compliance with applicable state obligations.

Continued Delays and Uncertainty for Federal GHGRP

EPA previously extended the 2025 reporting deadline from March 31 to October 30, 2026, as discussed in B&D’s July news alert. Unlike its first extension, this time EPA invoked the Administrative Procedure Act’s good cause exception to issue the extension without first providing notice and an opportunity for public comment. The Trump administration has repeatedly invoked this exception to postpone other regulatory deadlines without notice and comment while simultaneously pursuing deregulatory efforts targeting the underlying requirements. On October 22, 2026, Environmental Defense Fund and Environmental Integrity Project filed a lawsuit in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit challenging EPA’s latest extension.

Although EPA extended the 2025 reporting deadline to March 10, 2027, the deadline for reporting 2026 emissions remains March 31, 2027. If EPA issues another extension, it will likely need to extend the deadlines for both reporting years. However, the overlap between the current 2025 and 2026 reporting deadlines, combined with the recent litigation over the deadline extension, may pressure EPA to make a final decision on rescinding the GHGRP rather than keep extending the deadlines.

Current EPA Submission Deadlines

EPA cited two reasons for the latest extension: (1) additional time to consider the over 50,000 comments on the GHGRP proposed repeal, and (2) inability to prepare its electronic Greenhouse Gas Reporting Tool (e-GGRT) in time for the October 2026 deadline.

As B&D discussed in a 2025 news alert, EPA’s September 2025 proposal would eliminate reporting obligations for nearly all GHGRP source categories. As proposed, the GHGRP would continue to apply to certain petroleum and natural gas industry segments covered by Subpart W, but their reporting obligations would be suspended until 2034. Although the proposal’s comment period closed in November 2025, Administrator Zeldin reportedly indicated in October 2026 that EPA had not yet settled on the preliminary scope of a final rule, suggesting that final action may still be months away.

Other factors may also be delaying EPA’s decision. Since January 2025, EPA has gone through a major reorganization, including an overhaul of the office that administers GHGRP, and has lost nearly a quarter of its total workforce. These changes, coupled with EPA’s broader deregulatory agenda, may be affecting the Agency’s rulemaking bandwidth and, accordingly, the scope of its priorities.

EPA’s proposed GHGRP rescission has also drawn mixed reactions from industry and Congress. As discussed in B&D’s July news alert, EPA received comments from businesses requesting EPA maintain the GHGRP in whole or in part. EPA also received bipartisan congressional pushback, including from Senators Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), who urged EPA to withdraw the proposal, citing concerns about its effects on carbon capture investments and the competitiveness of U.S. energy exports. While EPA has largely moved to roll back its other GHG authorities for both mobile and stationary sources, it remains unclear how the Agency will proceed with GHGRP, particularly given that it will likely disappoint some constituents either way.

Litigation over EPA’s other GHG deregulatory efforts under the Clean Air Act (CAA) could also influence the GHGRP’s future, and vice versa. Parties are already challenging EPA’s assertion that it lacks authority to regulate GHG emissions from vehicles, with additional challenges of other proposed GHG authority rollbacks likely to come. Although those actions involve different statutory authorities, they contribute to the broader legal uncertainty surrounding EPA’s GHG regulatory authority.

Any final GHGRP rescission is likely to also face its own legal challenges, including challenges to EPA’s assertion that collecting certain GHG emissions data does not serve a statutory purpose. Depending on the rationale EPA adopts in a final rule, a future administration could also seek to restore the program, or some variation of it. Legal challenges to a GHGRP rescission would likely extend past the current administration’s tenure, creating further uncertainty for reporting entities.

The State Landscape Continues to Evolve through Rules and Litigation

States continue to revise their GHG reporting programs independently of EPA. Since B&D’s July news alert, several states have taken additional steps to implement or expand reporting requirements.

California

On August 31, 2026, the California Office of Administrative Law (OAL) approved amendments to the California Air Resources Board’s (CARB) Mandatory Reporting Regulation (MRR). The MRR Amendments became effective September 1, 2026, and support implementation of California’s Cap-and-Invest Program.

On October 12, 2026, OAL also approved CARB’s initial regulation implementing California’s corporate GHG reporting law (SB 253) and providing basic requirements for California’s corporate climate-related financial risk disclosure law (SB 261), but refrained from issuing detailed SB 261 requirements since that law remains enjoined pending appeal in Chamber of Commerce v. Sanchez, where plaintiffs are challenging the validity of both SB 253 and SB 261. Under SB 253, covered companies must submit their first Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions reports by November 10, 2026. In its new regulation and responses to stakeholder comments, CARB clarified certain statutory requirements that regulated entities should consider, such as the individualized nature of the applicability assessment. SB 253 requires publication of covered entity disclosures within ninety days of the November 10 reporting deadline. CARB’s rulemaking process for reporting under SB 253 in 2027 and beyond is ongoing.

Washington

On September 17, 2026, Washington’s Department of Ecology adopted amendments to its Reporting of Emissions of Greenhouse Gases rule (WAC 173-441)and its Climate Commitment Act Program Rule (WAC 173-446). The amendments took effect October 24, 2026. Among other changes, the amendments expanded reporting requirements for electric power entities by lowering the reporting threshold from 10,000 metric tons of CO2-equivalent emissions to anything above zero, beginning with 2027 emissions.

New York

New York’s Department of Environmental Conservation (NYSDEC) issued an enforcement discretion letter announcing that it will not enforce the June 1, 2027 deadline for reporting 2026 emissions under 6 NYCRR Part 253 until December 31, 2027. NYSDEC plans to amend Part 253 following May 2026 legislative changes to the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act. The letter delays enforcement but leaves Part 253’s substantive requirements intact.

Part 253 also faces ongoing litigation. A federal court dismissed Iowa v. James, No. 4:26-cv-00752 in August 2026 for lack of personal jurisdiction. Later that month, American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers v. James, No. 1:26-cv-07203 was filed in the Southern District of New York, similarly challenging the constitutionality of the reporting program. The case argues that the the reporting program is federally preempted by the CAA. Under an October 2026 stipulation, the parties agreed to pause litigation until April 2027. The stipulation limits certain out-of-state emissions reporting requirements and preserves the extended enforcement deadlines.

Colorado

Colorado has taken recent steps to reduce its reliance on EPA’s reporting infrastructure. Colorado has historically relied on EPA’s e-GGRT to support its state reporting program. However, as EPA acknowledged in its October 2026 interim final rule extending the federal reporting deadline, e-GGRT is not currently prepared to support 2025 emissions. Rather than push its existing October 2 reporting deadline, Colorado developed its own workbooks and reporting form for companies to use to submit data. If states continue to develop their own reporting methodologies, they are likely to diverge over time, complicating businesses’ compliance efforts.

Next Steps

Companies can submit comments on EPA’s latest GHGRP deadline extension until November 30, 2026. Regulated entities should also continue collecting emissions data for reporting years 2025 and 2026 in anticipation of the March 2027 deadlines, unless and until EPA takes further action.

Regardless of EPA’s ultimate decision on the GHGRP, companies operating across multiple states must navigate increasingly varied state reporting requirements. Businesses should assess applicable state deadlines, reporting thresholds, and calculation methodologies separately from their federal obligations. Businesses operating internationally also increasingly face mandatory GHG emissions reporting requirements in other jurisdictions.

text:
Jeenah Moon | Reuters

Stocks ripped higher on Wednesday as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections — and President Donald Trump’s acceptance of the results — removed political uncertainty risk hanging over Wall Street.

Democrats won majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate, and scored victories in key gubernatorial races like Texas. The Democrats will now be a check on the policies of Trump, who’s enacted business-friendly tax cuts, while also pursuing tariffs and a war in Iran that’s boosted inflation.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 1,570.47 points, or 3%, higher. The 30-stock index moved back above 53,000 for the first time since Sept. 8 and posted its best day since April 9, 2025, when Trump announced a pause on his so-called reciprocal tariffs. The S&P 500 gained 1.6%, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.4%.

Stocks extended their gains after U.S. crude oil fell more than 8% as Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for the election losses the Republican party suffered Tuesday. Brent futures traded more than 8% lower.

“There’s just going to be even more pressure to end the war,” said Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners. “The American people have obviously expressed their displeasure with inflation and the price of gasoline, amongst other things, and maybe this just pushes for an end to it. We’ll have to see.”

Trump told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing” to accept the results and told The Wall Street Journal that he and Republicans would work with Democrats.

The rebound “was in part due to the president’s initial tone and reaction to the results,” said Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets. “Still more uncertainty looms, but one thing is certain, there will be gridlock and historically this is good for the market.”

Shares linked to the economy that could benefit from a more stable environment led the gains. Walmart added 4%, while Bank of America rose 3% as investors looked for stocks outside of technology.

Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market, especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Investors feared a big Democratic win could mean more restrictions on data centers nationwide. The Texas governor win by Gina Hinojosa, who’s pledged an immediate moratorium in the key data center hub, added to the fears Wednesday.

Shares of CoreWeave were lower Wednesday, along with Elon Musk’s SpaceX , which is headquartered in Texas.

Another reason for the bullish sentiment Wednesday morning was that history shows the market does well under a divided government, where fewer policies and regulations are able to interfere with the business outlook.

Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the markets “like gridlock — they don’t like a party with too much power.”

Bitcoin rebound lacks new buyer support, says Bitfinex

Bitcoin has rebounded after briefly falling to the $75,000 level in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections, but the recovery has yet to attract meaningful support from new buyers, according to Bitfinex. It was last trading at about $80,000.

Analysts at the crypto exchange say gains since Oct. 30 have largely been fueled by short sellers closing their positions, while investors who recently entered the market continue to sell as prices return to their purchase levels. At the same time, outflows from bitcoin ETFs have pushed cumulative net flows for the year into slightly into negative territory, further weakening demand.

“Sustaining this bounce requires actual spot demand,” the report says. “Aggregate bitcoin futures open interest in BTC-notional terms rose to 701,548 BTC on Nov. 3, its highest since Sept. 22. Perpetual funding rates have held close to 11 percent annualized over the past two weeks despite the price correction, while spot buyers have shown little aggression. Together, these readings suggest the bid under $77,000 is primarily underpinned by perpetual futures positions, rather than spot demand.”

— Tanaya Macheel

CoreWeave credit default swaps move higher

Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can’t repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave’s CDS means investors view the debt as riskier. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 also ticked 3 basis points higher to 15.919%. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

Ballot measures on their development were also shot down in various states.

text:
This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.

The Democratic Party won a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. As of Wednesday morning, the party had secured control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. The sweep will have profound consequences for climate action in the U.S., even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing-out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Now, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could even impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats will also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump will have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down. With majorities in the Senate and the House, the party could even seek to reimpose some of the clean energy tax credits that Republicans rescinded last year.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats gained full control of the state government in Wisconsin, Arizona, and Pennsylvania, according to election analysts, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow the passage of meaningful climate policy in much of the country for the first time. In Pennsylvania, for instance, state house Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the public service commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In state races in Texas and Ohio, and in bellwether House districts like one in central Pennsylvania, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

House Democrats Could Make the Trump Administration Spend Money On the Climate

Upon taking office, the Trump administration attempted to withhold billions of dollars in climate money, much of it from the landmark Inflation Reduction Act signed into law by Joe Biden in 2022. These freezes threw a number of major climate projects into limbo — the Department of Energy halted experimental projects for hydrogen production in Pennsylvania and decarbonized cement in California, while the Environmental Protection Agency froze a $7 billion community solar program.

Those days may soon be over. Chellie Pingree, the lead Democrat who oversees funding for the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, says that she has prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin. She also intends to use the power of the purse to force the administration to spend climate money. Funding bills could include provisions that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.

“We can put a lot more teeth into the next appropriations bill,” she said. “We can say, ‘OK, fine, if you’re not going to spend the money, we have the power to withhold other funding.’”

— Jake Bittle

Texas Elects a Democratic Senator for the First Time in Nearly 40 Years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

A Wildland Firefighter Endorsed by AOC Wins a House Seat in Montana

Montana is on track to send a Democrat to the House of Representatives for the first time in over 30 years. Sam Forstag, a former wildland firefighter and union leader, claimed victory in the state’s competitive western district seat over Republican Aaron Flint, who conceded the race early Wednesday morning. The Associated Press estimates that 13 percent of ballots remain uncounted as of midday Wednesday.

Forstag ran his campaign on the affordability issues facing many Montanans and emphasized rising power bills, the need for data center regulation, and protecting public lands from attacks. The 31-year-old decided to run for office after experiencing Trump’s massive cuts to federal land management agencies, including wildland firefighting. Forstag received early endorsements from Representative Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont.

In an interview with Montana Free Press in October, Forstag said he wanted to “invest in transmission” and ensure “next-generation energy projects, wind and solar, have the actual resources that they need to get off the ground.”

— Ellis Juhlin

Two Climate Hawks Survive Republican Redistricting

Their districts were redrawn to eliminate them, but voters in Florida’s 14th and Ohio’s 9th districts respectively reelected Kathy Castor and Marcy Kaptur anyway.

Castor — referred to as a “climate hawk” by Politico — has spent much of her long career in Congress raising the alarm about climate change. Between 2019 and 2022 she chaired the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis, and has otherwise made reducing carbon pollution and preparing communities for climate impacts central to her legislative agenda. In March, she backed the Energy Bills Relief Act, which proposed restoring energy upgrade tax credits and connecting more clean energy to the grid. She has also strongly opposed data centers in the Tampa area that she serves, warning that the facilities could drive up her constituents’ utility costs while straining local water supplies.

Kaptur is the longest-serving woman in the House. She has been a leading opponent of the Department of Energy’s efforts to redirect Inflation Reduction Act money away from clean energy and toward fossil fuels. She has alleged that these redirections violate federal law, and would likely lead investigations into the Energy Department’s actions in a Democratic-controlled Congress. The Ohio state Legislature redrew her district to encompass more conservative areas along Lake Erie, but she held on to her seat comfortably.

— Jake Bittle and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A Democrat Will Become a Texas Oil and Gas Regulator

Stunning results are still coming in from the Lone Star State. For the first time in over 30 years, a Democrat has won a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, the regulatory agency that oversees the state’s oil and gas industry. Jon Rosenthal defeated Republican candidate Bo French, who made a racist social media post about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game that drew national bipartisan backlash.

“To the dude that posted the online poll last summer, asking who’s a bigger threat to America and the only two choices were Muslims and Jews — tonight this Jewish engineer sent that motherf*cker home,” said Rosenthal in his victory speech, referring to another racist post by French.

Rosenthal asserts that good jobs and clean air can — and must — coexist. He supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy and capturing natural gas. He also wants to “turbocharge” the plugging of inactive oil and gas wells, which leak methane. The Railroad Commission is currently considering rules on that, spurred by state legislation passed last year.

Rosenthal will join two Republican commissioners, meaning it’s likely he will be outvoted on many issues.

— Celeste Guajardo

Democrats Flip Control of Georgia Utility Commission for the First Time in Decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

“To the dude that posted the online poll last summer, asking who’s a bigger threat to America and the only two choices were Muslims and Jews — tonight this Jewish engineer sent that motherf*cker home,” said Rosenthal in his victory speech, referring to another racist post by French.

Rosenthal asserts that good jobs and clean air can — and must — coexist. He supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy and capturing natural gas. He also wants to “turbocharge” the plugging of inactive oil and gas wells, which leak methane. The Railroad Commission is currently considering rules on that, spurred by state legislation passed last year.

Rosenthal will join two Republican commissioners, meaning it’s likely he will be outvoted on many issues.

— Celeste Guajardo

Democrats Flip Control of Georgia Utility Commission for the First Time in Decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

text:
OTTAWA — Democrats won control of the U.S. Congress in a stunning rebuke of President Donald Trump that will create ripple effects for the Canadian economy—and restore hope for a better bilateral relationship—even if the dream of repealing tariffs remains out of reach.

Bruce Heyman, who was U.S. ambassador to Canada under Barack Obama, urged the new Congress to prioritize making things right. “Canada is our neighbour, our friend and an essential partner,” Heyman wrote Tuesday night. “The work of reconciliation should begin now.”

The president still wields a lot of power. He plans to use it. On his Truth Social platform late Tuesday night, Trump shared an image of a red, MAGA-style ball cap emblazoned with a single, all-caps word: VETO. Neither the House of Representatives nor the Senate elected enough Democrats to reach the two-thirds supermajority they would need to override such a move.

Advertisement

Tariffs on the campaign trail

The rising cost of living made the trade war a major campaign issue in several border states. In Maine, incumbent Republican Susan Collins lost her Senate seat to Democratic candidate Troy Jackson even after Trump tried to help by lifting duties on some Canadian goods.

“These elections should be a nail in the coffin for price-hiking tariffs,” Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, a coalition of some 1,200 small businesses in the U.S., said Wednesday in a statement urging Congress to deliver real cuts to duties.

If affordability remains a pressing concern, Democrats will likely step up their resistance to tariffs through symbolic legislative moves and congressional committee probes. Yet Democrats, who have historically been protectionist themselves, do not have the power to claw back the executive trade authorities that Trump used to slap tariffs on Canadian goods.

Remaining threats

Those statutes are being challenged in court, but more damaging tariffs could land well before that process plays out. In August, Trump threatened to double the Section 232 tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks to 50 per cent starting Jan. 1. He said he would extend those duties to auto parts, ending a carve-out through the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement. Last month, an executive at Honda Motor said doubling the tariffs on Canadian auto imports would be “catastrophic” for the entire auto industry and that she hoped it would not come to pass.

Trade talks

That gives Canada a reason to keep trying to secure a deal.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday that Canada and the U.S. have come closer to reaching a deal on tariffs, saying the White House has backed away from some of the “red lines” that led him to call off talks in August. “They’re asking less and they’re offering more, but we’re not quite there,” Carney said at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. Last week, however, Carney told Politico he was willing to wait for a new U.S. president if need be.

Data centres

The election results also spell trouble for Trump’s desired “era of super intelligence,” as dozens of towns and counties passed ballot initiatives restricting, or outright banning, data centre development. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made opposition to data centres a key plank in her gubernatorial campaign. She ousted Republican incumbent Greg Abbott on Tuesday night to become the first Democrat to lead the Lone Star State in decades.

Democrats are expected to push for stronger regulation of AI and more scrutiny over data centre development. Share prices for some AI firms fell on Wednesday. That could prompt hyperscalers to take a greater interest in building data centres in Canada.

Climate and energy

The Liberals under prime minister Justin Trudeau responded to the 2022 U.S. Inflation Reduction Act with billions of dollars worth of tax credits to prevent capital flight, as well as production subsidies to attract projects such as the Volkswagen-backed EV battery gigafactory in St. Thomas, Ont. Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” agenda has obliterated many assumptions and dampened demand for renewables and EVs. It also upped pressure on the Liberals to adjust climate policies to remain competitive, leading them to scrap the oil-and-gas emissions cap.

With Democrats now in control of Congress, expect stronger defence of U.S. environmental regulations and what remains of the tax incentives in the Inflation Reduction Act, including advanced manufacturing credits to lower the cost of EV production.

A key tax measure

The Qualified Small Business Stock exclusion is a U.S. tax benefit that exempts up to 100 per cent of long-term investments in high-growth domestic firms from taxes on capital gains. The Council of Canadian Innovators asked for a similar measure in the federal budget to encourage entrepreneurship and patient capital by rewarding founders and their early backers.

Imperial Irrigation District (IID) has approved nearly US$21m to refurbish one of two generators at its Pilot Knob hydropower plant near Winterhaven, California, restoring capacity that has been unavailable for three years.

The work at IID’s largest hydroelectric facility is expected to be completed in 2029. It forms part of the utility’s Powering Our Communities Together initiative, which includes plans to refurbish its 17 hydroelectric generators over the next seven years.

“Pilot Knob has been part of IID’s public power system for nearly 70 years, and this investment is about making sure it remains part of our future,” said Karin Eugenio, Chairwoman of the IID Board of Directors. “By restoring equipment that has served generations of customers, we are protecting an important public asset, strengthening the reliability of our electric system and making responsible investments that will benefit our customers for decades to come.”

Pilot Knob began operating on 31 January 1957 and will mark its 70th anniversary in 2027. It was the centrepiece of IID’s US$10m Power Development Project, approved by Imperial Valley voters in 1953 with 89% support.

The plant is located on a channel connecting the All-American Canal to the Colorado River. It generates electricity from water being delivered to Mexico under the 1944 US–Mexico Water Treaty.

After passing through the plant, the water returns to the Colorado River through the Rockwood Heading. Built in 1918, the structure originally diverted water into the Alamo Canal, which carried Colorado River water through Mexico to California’s Imperial Valley before the All-American Canal was developed.

text:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE November 4, 2026

CONTACT: EPN Press Office | epn-press@environmentalprotectionnetwork.org

EPN: Incoming Congress Must Hold EPA Leadership Accountable and Put Public Health First

Former EPA experts urge congressional oversight, restoration of scientific integrity, and withdrawal of pending pollution rollbacks that threaten families’ health and finances.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Following Tuesday’s midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, the Environmental Protection Network (EPN) calls on the incoming Congress to hold the Trump administration accountable for decisions that have weakened pollution protections and undermined the Environmental Protection Agency’s ability to protect public health.

“Voters made clear they’re deeply unhappy with the direction the Trump administration and Congress have been taking the country,” said Marc Boom, EPN’s Senior Director of Public Affairs. “At EPA, we’ve seen that play out in decisions that put the interests of polluters ahead of the health of families and communities. When EPA weakens pollution protections, the costs don’t disappear. They’re shifted onto families in the form of higher medical bills, more illness, and lives cut short.”

Over the past two years, former EPA scientists, enforcement officials, and policy experts who volunteer with EPN have documented a broad pattern of weakened safeguards against harmful pollution, exemptions for industrial facilities, the undermining of independent science and scientific expertise, the removal of critical public health information, termination and politicization of federal funding for states, Tribes and communities, and the loss of thousands of experienced EPA employees. These decisions expose people to greater risks of asthma, cancer, and other serious health problems, while leaving families and communities to bear more of the human and economic costs of pollution.

EPN calls on the incoming Congress to make public health a central focus of its oversight by:

Investigating EPA decisions that favor polluters over public health, including regulatory rollbacks, industry exemptions, weakened pollution safeguards amid the rapid expansion of AI data centers and their energy infrastructure, and the sidelining of scientific findings and career expertise.

Restoring scientific integrity and transparency, including public access to information about pollution-related cancer risks and other health threats.

Rebuilding EPA’s capacity and strengthening enforcement, ensuring the agency has the scientists, inspectors, funding, and direction needed to fulfill its legal responsibilities.

EPN also calls on EPA leadership to heed the public’s demand for stronger health protections and change course now, rather than waiting for congressional oversight. The agency should withdraw pending proposals to weaken pollution standards and abandon efforts to give polluters more leeway at the expense of public health.

“Americans understand that when corporations aren’t held accountable for their pollution, ordinary families end up paying the price,” Boom continued. “Our polling shows that 81% of registered voters surveyed believe the costs of pollution are being shifted onto families. The incoming Congress has an opportunity and a responsibility to hold EPA and the rest of the federal government accountable and make sure they’re doing their jobs to protect public health and leave families safer, not sicker.”

“Protecting families from pollution should never be a partisan issue,” Boom added. “The question for Congress is whether EPA is following the science, enforcing the law, and fulfilling its mission. That’s the standard every member of Congress should insist on, regardless of party.”

The Trump Administration Has Rolled Back Federal Support for Wind and Solar

Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has taken a series of steps to unwind federal support for wind and solar, according to a Reuters timeline. On his first day, he paused new leasing and permitting of wind projects on federal lands and waters pending a review. His administration later ordered construction to stop on Equinor’s offshore wind project off New York. In July 2025, he signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended subsidies for wind and solar projects years earlier than planned.

Under the law, projects that begin construction after July 4, 2026, must be placed in service by the end of 2027 to qualify for the tax credits. An executive order the same month directed Treasury to strictly enforce the end of the credits and Interior to eliminate preferential treatment for wind and solar. Interior added layers of review for projects on federal lands and canceled approval of the Lava Ridge wind project in Idaho, Treasury issued rules making it harder to claim the credits, Commerce opened an investigation into imported wind turbine components and the administration moved to revoke approvals for the US Wind offshore project off Maryland.

The administration has said wind and solar are unreliable, expensive and dependent on foreign-controlled supply chains, and says it favors dispatchable sources including nuclear and fossil fuels. Trump remains president and can veto legislation, so any bill to restore the credits would need his signature or a two-thirds vote in both chambers to override a veto.

text:
By Lisa Greene-Lewis for Intuit TurboTax

The passing of the One Big Beautiful Bill brought sweeping changes to the tax code and beyond. It permanently extended certain Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) provisions that were set to expire, including a higher cap on the state and local tax (SALT) deduction, and introduced changes to taxes on tips and overtime pay for certain workers. The bill also made significant changes to energy credits, Medicaid, the debt ceiling, and student loans.

As you follow the news about the One Big Beautiful Bill, you might be wondering about the key tax provisions that have passed and what provisions kick in for tax year 2026 (the taxes you file in 2027).

Intuit TurboTax shares some of the top questions we’re getting, along with the answers.

Starting July 1, 2026, federal student loan rules change too: Two new repayment plans replace the previous ones for new borrowers, and strict new limits cap borrowing.

On April 13, 2026, the IRS released final guidance on the “no tax on tips” provision of the bill. It adds the phase-out threshold for married couples, the list of qualifying occupations, and qualifying tip criteria.

Some of the new tax laws under the One Big, Beautiful Bill first kicked in for tax year 2025 (i.e., the taxes filed in 2026), and some will debut for tax year 2026. A few uncommon provisions are retroactive to tax year 2024.

What key provisions passed under the One Big Beautiful Bill?

Here are some key provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill for tax year 2026.

A new charitable contribution deduction and increased Child and Dependent Care Credit take effect in tax year 2026.

New deductions on tips and overtime apply to eligible workers.

The SALT cap increases to $40,000 for homeowners (rising to $40,400 in 2026)

Expanded family and senior benefits include a larger child tax credit and an enhanced deduction for seniors.

A permanent 20% qualified business income deduction applies to self-employed workers.

New federal student loan repayment options are available to graduates.

When do the new tax laws go into effect?

The majority of the tax provisions went into effect in tax year 2025, while some are changes for tax year 2026 (the taxes you will file in 2027). A few uncommon provisions are retroactive to tax year 2024.

What passed from the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) and what does that mean for taxes?

The One Big Beautiful Bill permanently extends certain tax provisions from the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, including:

Lower individual tax rates (10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, 37%)

The nearly doubled standard deduction

The expanded Child Tax Credit

The elimination of personal and dependent exemptions

Unreimbursed employee expense deductions (except for teachers)

If you don’t qualify for new tax benefits, your taxes will likely look similar to last year’s, but if you are eligible for any of the new tax provisions this year, you may be able to claim larger deductions and credits.

What are the new tax laws or changes that kick in for tax year 2026?

Bigger credit for child and dependent care

Starting with tax year 2026, the Child and Dependent Care Credit is getting a boost. You’ll be able to claim up to 50% of your eligible child care expenses, up from 35% before.

Here’s what that means in dollars: For one kid, the credit goes up to $1,500 (that’s 50% of $3,000), and for two or more kids it climbs to $3,000 (50% of $6,000). Previously, the max was $1,050 (35% of $3,000) for one child and $2,100 (35% of $6,000) for two or more kids.

What counts as eligible care?

Daycare, summer day camp, before- and after-school care, and even sports camps — basically, the child care that lets you work or look for work — counts. The Child and Dependent Care Credit also applies to disabled kids of any age and other disabled dependents.

Charitable giving deduction even if you don’t itemize

If you claim the standard deduction, starting in 2026, you can still deduct cash donations to charity — up to $1,000 if you’re single or $2,000 if you’re married and filing jointly.

In the past, you could only write off charitable gifts if you itemized deductions (for things like home mortgage interest). Now, if you stick with the standard deduction, your cash donations to IRS-recognized 501(c)(3) organizations can still earn you a tax break.

Higher SALT deduction cap, 2026-2029

In tax year 2025, the cap increased from $10,000 to $40,000. For tax year 2026, the cap increases to $40,400, where it will stay through 2029. The deduction begins to phase out when income is more than $500,000 ($250,000 for married couples filing separately).

This change may benefit filers in states with high state and property taxes, allowing them to deduct more of their related expenses. Some individuals who don’t own homes, but pay significant state income taxes may also see a benefit from this increased allowance.

New limits on how gambling losses offset winnings

Gambling losses that offset winnings will be limited to 90% instead of 100%. That means you’ll now owe tax on 10% of your winnings even if your losses matched or exceeded them.

Before tax year 2026, if you were able to claim itemized deductions, you could offset 100% of your gambling losses against your gains, up to the amount you won.

Education-related changes

Bigger deductions for teachers: In tax year 2026, teachers can deduct up to $350 for school supplies purchased for their classrooms under the Teachers Educator Deduction (up from $300 in tax year 2025). If you’re married to another educator, you can each claim the deduction, for a total deduction of $700.

The deduction now covers coaches and sports-related equipment. And, if you itemize, you can deduct your unreimbursed education expenses that exceed the $350 cap. Educators remain the only profession that gets this particular deduction.

Education credits: You’ll be required to have a Social Security number to claim education credits like the American Opportunity Tax Credit and the Lifetime Learning Credit.

Student loans: If a student loan is discharged (canceled or forgiven) because of death or disability, that forgiven amount won’t count as taxable income, and a valid Social Security number (SSN) is required.

Employee student loans: The law that allowed employers to help pay employee student loans was made permanent.

New kids’ savings accounts, plus a bonus for babies born 2025-2028

The One Big Beautiful Bill created a new tax-deferred savings account for kids.

Parents, guardians, and other authorized individuals can put in up to $5,000 a year for a child under 18 who has a valid SSN. And employers can chip in up to $2,500. There’s also a pilot program, which adds a one-time contribution of $1,000 for children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, who are U.S. citizens and have a valid SSN.

Bigger qualified business income deduction

The Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction lets self-employed people and small-business owners write off part of their business profit. Starting for tax year 2026, there’s a new guaranteed minimum deduction of $400 for anyone with at least $1,000 in business income.

Premium tax credit changes

Starting in 2026, there may be some situations where people will be required to pay back any excess advanced premium tax credit. Also, individuals enrolling in Marketplace insurance during a special enrollment period due to changes in household income won’t be eligible for that coverage.

What are other provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill?

Tax breaks for workers: Tips and overtime

In previous years, cash and non-cash tips were considered income subject to federal taxes, Social Security, and Medicare taxes, and were required to be reported to your employer if they exceeded $20 a month.

The new provision creates a temporary deduction to federal income tax for qualified tips up to $25,000 for tax years 2025 through 2028. This deduction is available regardless of whether you itemize your deductions.

Note that this deduction only applies to federal income tax. Tips remain subject to Social Security, Medicare, and potentially state income taxes without change. Also, if you are a worker who earns below the standard deduction ($15,750 for individual filers, $31,500 for joint filers in 2025 or $16,100 for single and $32,200 for joint filers in 2026), you may not benefit from this deduction since you probably won’t owe federal income taxes to begin with.

If you earn tips as a waitress, stylist, or in another qualifying occupation, you may be eligible to claim this deduction. For individual filers, the tax benefit begins to phase out for income above $150,000. Married couples filing jointly have a higher phase-out threshold of $300,000.

For example, if you are an individual filer and earned $5,000 in tips and are in the 12% tax bracket, your tax savings would be $600 ($5,000 x 12%).

Transportation and delivery

text:
The Democratic Party won a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections. As of Wednesday morning, the party had secured control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. The sweep will have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress will allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing-out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

Now, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could even impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats will also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump will have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down. With majorities in the Senate and the House, the party could even seek to reimpose some of the clean energy tax credits that Republicans rescinded last year.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats gained full control of the state government in Wisconsin, Arizona, and Pennsylvania, according to election analysts, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow the passage of meaningful climate policy in much of the country for the first time. In Pennsylvania, for instance, state house Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the public service commission, which regulates electric utilities.

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In state races in Texas and Ohio, and in bellwether House districts like one in central Pennsylvania, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

House Democrats could make the Trump administration spend money on the climate

Upon taking office, the Trump administration attempted to withhold billions of dollars in climate money, much of it from the landmark Inflation Reduction Act signed into law by Joe Biden in 2022. These freezes threw a number of major climate projects into limbo — the Department of Energy halted experimental projects for hydrogen production in Pennsylvania and decarbonized cement in California, while the Environmental Protection Agency froze a $7 billion community solar program.

Those days may soon be over. Chellie Pingree, the lead Democrat who oversees funding for the Environmental Protection Agency and Interior Department on the powerful House Appropriations Committee, says that she has prepared a long list of investigations and subpoenas for Trump administration officials, including EPA chief Lee Zeldin. She also intends to use the power of the purse to force the administration to spend climate money. Funding bills could include provisions that would deny agencies core operational funds or restrict travel money for leading officials unless they doled out solar and energy funding as Congress previously instructed them to.

“We can put a lot more teeth into the next appropriations bill,” she said. “We can say, ‘OK, fine, if you’re not going to spend the money, we have the power to withhold other funding.’”

— Jake Bittle

Texas elects Democratic senator for the first time in nearly 40 years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

Two climate hawks survive Republican redistricting

Kaptur is the longest-serving woman in the House. She has been a leading opponent of the Department of Energy’s efforts to redirect Inflation Reduction Act money away from clean energy and toward fossil fuels. She has alleged that these redirections violate federal law, and would likely lead investigations into the Energy Department’s actions in a Democratic-controlled Congress. The Ohio state Legislature redrew her district to encompass more conservative areas along Lake Erie, but she held on to her seat comfortably.

— Jake Bittle and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Democrats flip control of Georgia utility commission for first time in decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

A flip in an area devastated by Helene

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait — not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House District, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

— Jake Bittle

An ex-Sunrise activist wins in Michigan

William Lawrence, a co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement, appears to have prevailed in a razor’s-edge House of Representatives race in central Michigan. Lawrence, a 36-year-old progressive, ousted freshman Republican Tom Barrett in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, a bellwether area encompassing Lansing and its suburbs. He made opposition to data centers a focal point of his campaign, calling for a national moratorium on data center development. He also aligned himself with activists and residents who have opposed large-scale renewable energy projects in the Lansing area. In an interview with Grist last month, Lawrence said that many utility-scale solar projects don’t benefit the communities around them. The Associated Press has not yet called the race, but Lawrence’s campaign told Grist that Barrett has conceded.

— Jake Bittle

Democrats win after attacking Republicans on data centers

In one of the night’s biggest upsets, Texas state Representative Gina Hinojosa ousted incumbent Governor Greg Abbott after campaigning on a data center moratorium and accusing Abbott of selling out to the tech industry.

And at least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. (Bresnahan has owned stock in data center companies.) And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over incumbent Darline Graham after Andrews highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million dollars on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions, but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona, Sachi Kitajima Mulkey, and Jake Bittle

Data centers upend municipal politics

Further down the ballot, it’s hard to find a place where data centers didn’t lose. In addition to the marquee congressional and governor’s races where voter sentiment about the AI boom may have helped oust Republican incumbents, dozens of towns and cities passed pauses or bans on data center development, according to The Washington Post. In many cases, these restrictions passed by enormous margins — in Sunbury, Ohio, where Amazon proposed a $2 billion project, voters rejected the facilities by an almost 60-point margin.

The AI issue also upended local elections, and perhaps the best example is in Pine Island, Minnesota. Google has proposed building a large new data center there, one that would be powered exclusively by clean energy and would include big subsidies for electric ratepayers. But voter outrage over the project caused a previous mayor to resign and led a first-time politician to mount a campaign against the interim replacement. That challenger, Mark Lang, won with well over 60 percent of the vote.

— Jake Bittle

A FEMA defender sails to victory in Florida

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th congressional district. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries, and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, cabinet-level agency — just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance, and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Michigan gets utility money out of politics

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it will do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the 2010 Citizens United decision. And while experts are fairly confident the measure will face legal challenges and won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

— Vivian La

A governor who at least acknowledges climate change in Florida

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th Congressional District, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent Cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A MAGA loyalist who says no to drilling in Florida

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Florida Governor Ron DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
