Examine whether congressionally appropriated funds were withheld, redirected, delayed, or conditioned on objectives unrelated to public health, including commercial access, trade concessions, or critical minerals agreements. Review the administration’s handling of PEPFAR, CDC-supported global health programs, and other major health initiatives to determine whether statutory requirements and congressional intent were followed. Commission a report documenting program disruptions, funding diversions, continuity-of-care failures, and the broader diplomatic, humanitarian, and national security consequences of the administration’s actions.

Why It Matters: American global health assistance, including programs like PEPFAR, exists to prevent disease, respond to health crises, and support public health objectives that have guided U.S. policy for decades. When that assistance is restructured behind closed doors, tied to unrelated commercial and political demands, and cut without meaningful congressional or stakeholder input, the patients and health systems that depend on U.S. support are put at risk, and America’s credibility as a reliable global health partner suffers. Congress has an obligation to determine whether these taxpayer-funded programs are being administered in a manner consistent with statutory requirements and congressional intent, or repurposed to serve objectives Congress never authorized.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Foreign Affairs; Senate Foreign Relations

Section III: Democracy, Transparency, and the Rule of Law

Democracy depends on transparency, fair elections, and checks on power. Oversight is necessary when institutions are weakened, records are concealed, and lawful accountability mechanisms are ignored.

3.1 The New Jim Crow? Voting Rights After Callais

Oversight Type: Hearing

Problem: The Supreme Court’s Callais decision gutted the key remaining elements of the Voting Rights Act, effectively authorizing barely disguised racial gerrymandering, so long as it is labeled partisan. The decision led to immediate redistricting in Southern states in ways designed to strip voting power from Black voters and people of color communities.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings examining the impacts of the Supreme Court’s Callais decision and subsequent redistricting efforts that reduced the voting strength of Black voters and other communities of color. Require testimony from governors, attorneys general, state legislators, election officials, civil rights advocates, voting rights litigators, local elected officials, and affected voters from states that adopted or defended maps previously challenged as racially discriminatory. Examine both the explicit and implicit role race played in post-Callais redistricting decisions and the practical effects on representation, electoral competition, and minority political participation. Conduct legislative hearings on the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and related proposals to build a record supporting restoration of federal voting rights protections weakened by recent Supreme Court decisions.

Why It Matters: The American people would be exposed to how states used the Court’s decision to redraw districts in ways that reduced the voting power of Black voters and other communities of color, often reversing gains secured through decades of voting rights enforcement. The hearings would establish a clear record of who made these decisions, who benefited from them, and how they affected representation in communities across the country, while laying the groundwork for legislative remedies.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

3.2 Big Money, Bought Politicians, and Broken Democracy Oversight Type: Hearing

Problem: Big Money is dominating elections like never before. Outside spending overwhelms candidate spending and depends on just a handful of people—with the top 100 donors consistently responsible for 70% of Super PAC spending. Secret spending is at record levels. The world’s richest person spent hundreds of millions in the last election, a mere drop in the bucket for him. And for the first time since Citizens United was decided, corporations are opening their treasuries and spending directly in elections, a trend sure to worsen dramatically in the years to come.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold oversight hearings into the surge in Big Money spending, using case studies from the cryptocurrency, pharmaceutical, and fossil fuel industries to examine how concentrated political spending translates into favorable policy outcomes. Require testimony from Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse, Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla, Eli Lilly CEO David Ricks, ExxonMobil CEO Darren Woods, and Chevron CEO Mike Wirth regarding their political spending, lobbying activities, and policy priorities. Pair industry witnesses with campaign finance experts, former regulators, ethics officials, and advocates for election transparency. Couple the oversight hearings with legislative hearings on proposals to increase disclosure, end secret spending, support small dollar financing of elections, and overturn Citizens United and related decisions.

Why It Matters: Americans will see that many of the most significant legislative, regulatory, and enforcement outcomes of recent years have effectively been bought and paid for by powerful interests capable of spending enormous sums to influence the political process. Americans correctly perceive that Big Money is rigging elections and influencing public policy.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

3.3 Department of Injustice: Protecting Friends, Punishing Enemies Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The Trump administration has transformed the Department of Justice into a political tool. Across the department, career civil servants have been forced out precisely because of their commitment to the rule of law. The Civil Rights Division has lost upwards of three-quarters of its staff and is now working to defend white people from purported discrimination. The Department of Justice has systematically weakened its offices charged with, and its commitment to, deterring and prosecuting fraud and corporate misconduct – including by gutting the Public Integrity Section, disbanding the Consumer Protection Branch, shrinking enforcement of overseas corporate bribery, reducing oversight of corporate lawbreakers, and firing the department’s ethics adviser.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and require testimony from former DOJ attorneys, ethics officials, fraud prosecutors, Public Integrity Section personnel, Civil Rights Division attorneys, and other career officials who resigned, were reassigned, or were forced out after refusing to engage in unlawful, unethical, or politically motivated conduct. Pair those witnesses with consumers, workers, whistleblowers, civil rights complainants, and victims of corporate misconduct whose interests were harmed when the department abandoned or weakened enforcement actions. Also require testimony from individuals, organizations, and public officials who were subjected to politically motivated investigations, enforcement actions, threats, or other forms of retaliatory targeting.

Why It Matters: The American people would see how political interference within the Department of Justice allowed fraud, corruption, discrimination, and corporate misconduct to go unpunished while individuals, organizations, and public officials perceived as political opponents faced scrutiny, retaliation, or selective enforcement. The hearings would establish a clear record of who was protected, who was targeted, and the consequences of a politicized Department of Justice.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

3.4 The Revolving Door: Corporate Insiders Running Our Government Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: In the Trump administration, former energy company executives write energy policy, chemical industry lobbyists run the EPA’s chemical program, AI executives draft AI policy, and a crypto-friendly management consultant runs the SEC. This and more follows from existing ethics rules governing movement into and out of executive branch service are weak, inconsistent, and often dependent on the preferences of the sitting president through executive orders rather than permanent law. Trump declined to impose the stronger ethics pledges used by some prior administrations, contributing to recurring concerns about lobbyist influence, conflicts of interest, and officials moving between public office and private gain.

Proposed Oversight Action: Direct a congressional report and hold hearings on failures in executive branch ethics enforcement, revolving door abuses, and conflicts tied to incoming and outgoing officials. Solicit testimony from former government employees who can explain that they left because of the conflicted priorities of revolving door officials. Demand testimony from former Trump officials who have cashed in with new positions as lobbyists and consultants, to explain their ongoing lines of influence. Advance legislation codifying a minimum two-year cooling-off period after leaving government, while requiring incoming officials to recuse themselves from matters involving former employers or clients. Strengthen the Office of Government Ethics by granting enforcement authority and providing its director a fixed term removable only for cause.

Why It Matters: Public service should not be a stepping stone to private enrichment or a vehicle for corporations to place insiders inside government. When officials regulate former clients, negotiate future jobs while in office, or face weak enforcement of ethics rules, public confidence collapses, and policy can be distorted in favor of special interests.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

3.5 What Are They Hiding? FOIA Denials, Government Secrecy, and Hidden Corruption

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: Federal agencies experienced growing delays in responding to Freedom of Information Act requests during the Trump administration, resulting in rising backlogs and missed statutory deadlines. Workforce reductions have significantly impaired FOIA processing, with attorneys in multiple federal cases citing staffing cuts as a primary cause of delays. Watchdog organizations and requesters have increasingly turned to litigation to obtain records.

Proposed Oversight Action: Conduct a government-wide review and hold hearings with agency chief FOIA officers, DOJ officials, inspectors general, and transparency advocates to examine (1) FOIA processing times and backlog levels across agencies in 2025 and 2026, (2) the impact of staffing cuts on FOIA performance, (3) the increasing reliance on litigation to obtain records, and (4) whether agencies are complying with both the letter and spirit of FOIA. Request agency-level data on staffing, backlog size, response times, and use of exemptions.

Why It Matters: FOIA is one of the primary tools for uncovering corruption and holding the government accountable. When agencies delay responses, withhold records, or force requesters into court, it raises serious concerns about whether information is being concealed rather than disclosed. Congress must determine whether these delays reflect administrative failure or a broader effort to shield government activity from scrutiny.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Judiciary

3.6 Vote by Mail: Delayed Ballots, Disenfranchised Voters, and a Threat to Democracy

Oversight Type: Hearing

Problem: During the 2026 election year, the Trump administration took actions to undermine vote-by mail, including Executive Order 14399, which directed the U.S. Postal Service to limit ballot delivery to pre-approved voter lists and required states to submit eligibility data in advance of elections. Public Citizen filed a motion, based on our previous 2020 settlement, on these illegal actions. These actions, combined with prior changes to mail delivery standards, raised concerns among election officials about whether ballots would be delivered and returned in time to be counted.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold a hearing with Postal Service leadership, DHS officials, state and local election administrators, and voting rights/postal service experts to examine (1) how federal actions affected mail ballot delivery and return rates during the 2026 election, (2) whether eligible voters experienced delays or barriers that prevented their ballots from being counted, and (3) whether federal agencies interfered with state election administration. Request postal delivery data, ballot rejection data, and internal communications related to the implementation of election-related directives.

Why It Matters: Vote-by-mail is a critical access point for millions of Americans, including rural voters, people with disabilities, seniors, and military voters. If federal actions delayed or restricted ballot delivery, eligible voters may have been prevented from participating in elections. Nothing is more essential to democracy than protecting the right to vote.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

3.7 Access Denied: Restricting Public Input on Federal Regulations Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: On August 8, 2025, the General Services Administration quietly turned off the POST API on Regulations.gov, a tool that allowed advocacy groups, trade associations, and other third parties to help members of the public submit comments to federal agencies. Notice-and-comment rulemaking is one of the few formal opportunities ordinary Americans and small businesses have to shape federal regulations, yet GSA provided no public notice or explanation for removing the tool during active comment periods.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and open an investigation into the decision to remove the POST API, including whether OMB directed GSA to take the action and what justification was offered. Subpoena internal communications, policy memos, technical assessments, and correspondence between OMB, GSA, and outside stakeholders. Require agencies to explain whether comments were lost or disrupted and whether the API can be promptly restored.

Why It Matters: The POST API helped level the playing field by allowing the public to comment through simpler third-party tools. Removing it makes it harder for workers, consumers, community groups, and small businesses to participate, while benefiting well-connected corporations and lobbyists who can influence policy through private channels. When access to rulemaking is restricted, agencies lose valuable public input and democratic accountability suffers.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

3.8 401(k)s at Risk: SEC Weakens Investor Protections for Retirement Savers Oversight Type: Hearing

Problem: In November 2025, SEC Chair Paul Atkins directed staff to limit the agency’s role in reviewing shareholder proposals, allowing more than 100 public companies to exclude proposals from 2026 annual meetings. These proposals are often submitted by pension funds and institutional investors representing workers’ retirement savings, and they focus on issues such as executive pay, corporate risk, and financial accountability. Reports indicate corporate lobbyists and business groups pushed for the shift.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold a hearing with SEC leadership, investor advocates, pension fund representatives, corporate governance experts, and business and lobbying groups to examine (1) the November 2025 change to the shareholder proposal process, (2) communications between SEC officials and corporate lobbyists, (3) the number and type of proposals excluded from 2026 corporate ballots, and (4) whether the SEC is meeting its obligation to protect investors. Request communications, internal guidance, and data on excluded proposals and affected investors.

Why It Matters: Millions of Americans rely on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement security. Shareholder proposals are among the few ways investors can raise concerns and push companies to address risks to long-term value. If companies can block those proposals without meaningful oversight, it raises a basic question: are corporations accountable to their investors, or can they silence them when it is inconvenient?

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Financial Services; Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

Section IV: Big Tech, AI, and the New Corporate Threats

New technologies can deliver innovation, but without guardrails they can also magnify monopoly power, surveillance, manipulation, and public harm. Oversight must ensure emerging technologies serve people rather than exploit them.

4.1 Big Tech Writes the Rules: Conflicts of Interest in AI Policy Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: Under the influence of AI Czar David Sacks—an investor in hundreds of tech companies—the Trump administration immediately rescinded the forward-looking Biden AI Executive Order. In its place, it adopted a zero-regulation, permissive approach to AI, promoting Big Tech’s interests in energy, data centers, trade, and more. Even a very modest EO addressing national security threats was watered down under Sacks’s influence.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and conduct investigations examining the role of AI Czar David Sacks and other technology industry insiders in shaping federal AI policy. Require testimony from David Sacks regarding his financial interests, communications with administration officials, participation in policy deliberations, and role in rescinding or modifying AI-related executive actions and regulatory initiatives. Examine whether administration decisions regarding AI regulation, data centers, energy policy, trade policy, national security safeguards, and federal procurement disproportionately benefited companies in which Sacks or other administration advisers held financial interests.

Why It Matters: This hearing would expose the American people to the rampant corruption in this administration’s AI policy. Moreover, powerful new AI technologies may remake society, changing the way we work, altering culture, determining how we learn and acquire information, and more. They pose immediate and long-term threats, from political deepfakes to cybersecurity to mass unemployment. Already, they are functioning to concentrate wealth. Americans are worried about these issues and want AI policy for people, not the Big Tech oligarchy.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; House Science, Space, and Technology; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation

4.2 Preemption: Big Tech’s Escape Hatch: Stopping States from Protecting Consumers

Oversight Type: Hearing

Problem: With virtually no federal regulation of AI, Big Tech companies are working on overdrive to win federal preemption of state AI regulation. On a bipartisan basis, states are taking the lead on commonsense regulations to address political deepfakes, unauthorized intimate deepfakes, emotionally entangling chatbots, misuse of AI in health insurance decisions, frontier model risks, and more.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and require testimony from the CEOs and senior executives of major AI and technology companies, along with witnesses with bipartisan state attorneys general, state legislators, consumer protection officials, civil rights advocates, and parents whose children or families were harmed by AI-enabled fraud, deepfakes, exploitation, discrimination, or other unsafe uses of emerging technologies.

Why It Matters: These hearings would clearly identify victims harmed by Big Tech and expose this industry’s efforts to undermine consumer protection. Additionally, the Big Tech companies are racing to roll out AI technologies with very inadequate testing and safeguards, effectively conducting nonconsensual societal experiments. This is exactly what happened with social media, and it did not turn out well—and the stakes with AI are far higher. By overwhelming numbers, Americans favor strong AI regulation—something that federal preemption aims to prevent.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Energy and Commerce; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation

4.3 Procurement of Grok: Unsafe AI, Unsafe Government Oversight Type: Investigation

Problem: In 2025, the Trump administration approved the use of Grok, an AI system developed by xAI, for federal government applications including access to sensitive systems, despite documented safety risks. Reporting has highlighted that Grok and comparable AI systems have produced nonconsensual deepfake sexual images, generated harmful and misleading content, and remain vulnerable to manipulation through prompt injection and other exploits. Experts warned that Grok lacks sufficient safeguards relative to peer models, yet it was cleared for government use without transparent safety standards.

Proposed Oversight Action: Open an investigation into the procurement and approval of Grok across federal agencies, including subpoenas for internal communications, safety assessments, and risk determinations from GSA, OMB, and relevant agencies. The investigation should determine what safety criteria were applied, whether known risks were ignored or downplayed, and whether deployment complied with federal AI risk management guidance. Issue a formal report evaluating failures in the procurement process and recommending enforceable standards for high-risk AI systems.

Why It Matters: The federal government deployed an AI system with known capabilities for generating harmful content and documented security vulnerabilities, posing clear risks to national security, public safety, and government integrity. This sets a dangerous precedent that agencies can adopt powerful AI systems without meeting basic safety and security thresholds.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; House Science, Space, and Technology

4.4 Your Face, Their Database: Building America’s Surveillance State Oversight Type: Investigation

Problem: Since 2025, the Trump administration has expanded the federal government’s collection and use of biometric data, including facial recognition, fingerprints, and other identifiers, across immigration enforcement, law enforcement, and public surveillance contexts. The federal government has relied on commercially purchased data from third-party brokers to obtain sensitive personal and location information without a warrant. Documented errors in facial recognition systems have already led to wrongful identifications and arrests.

Proposed Oversight Action: Open an investigation into the scope and legal basis of biometric data collection and third-party data purchases across DHS, DOJ, FBI, and intelligence agencies, including subpoenas for contracts with data brokers, internal policies governing biometric use, and records of how such data has been deployed. Issue a report outlining the scale of biometric surveillance and recommend statutory limits on the use and acquisition of biometric and commercially available personal data.

Why It Matters: The federal government is building a de facto national biometric surveillance system without clear legal guardrails. By purchasing data from third parties and deploying flawed facial recognition tools, agencies are effectively sidestepping the Fourth Amendment and exposing Americans to wrongful identification, tracking, and targeting. Once fully built, this infrastructure will be nearly impossible to unwind.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary; House Homeland Security; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

4.5 Addictive Algorithms and Big Tech Manipulation of Children Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: Major technology companies, including Meta, have deliberately designed algorithms to maximize user engagement, even when it harms children and teens. Internal documents have shown these companies knew their platforms amplify addictive use, promote harmful content, and worsen youth mental health, yet prioritized growth and profits. In a landmark California case, a Los Angeles jury found Meta liable for harms caused by the addictive design of its platform, concluding its product was a substantial factor in causing mental health injury.

Proposed Oversight Action: Open an investigation into the design and deployment of addictive algorithms by major technology companies, including subpoenas for internal research, product design decisions, and communications demonstrating knowledge of harm. Hold high-profile hearings with executives from Meta, TikTok, and other platforms to examine how engagement algorithms are intentionally structured to drive compulsive use. Expand the investigation to AI-driven recommendation systems. Issue a report proposing enforceable product safety standards.

Why It Matters: Tech companies are actively engineering products to capture attention and drive dependency, especially among children. A California jury has already found that this design causes real world harm. Without intervention, the same addictive design principles are being embedded into AI systems, scaling manipulation and harm even further.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Energy and Commerce; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation

4.6 Robots at War: AI Targeting, Civilian Deaths, and Military Accountability

Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: In 2026, reporting raised serious questions about whether AI-assisted targeting systems were used in U.S. military strikes in Iran, including the deadly bombing of a school in Minab that killed more than 150 civilians, many of them children. Investigations indicated that the site may have been misidentified as a military target due to outdated or flawed intelligence data. The Pentagon has been increasing reliance on AI-enabled targeting tools designed to accelerate strike decisions.

Proposed Oversight Action: Open an investigation into the Department of Defense’s use of AI-assisted targeting systems in Iran and other theaters, including subpoenas for targeting protocols, human review requirements, vendor contracts, and after-action assessments related to civilian casualty incidents. Hold hearings with Pentagon officials, military commanders, and defense technology contractors to determine whether AI systems were used in the Minab strike, which safeguards failed, and whether current policy complies with the laws of armed conflict. Issue a report evaluating the risks of autonomous and semi autonomous weapons systems.

Why It Matters: The future of warfare will increasingly involve AI, but speed cannot replace judgment. If flawed data or black-box systems are allowed to drive targeting decisions, civilians will die, and the U.S. risks violating international humanitarian norms. Congress must decide now whether lethal AI tools will operate under strict human accountability or become another unchecked weapon system.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Armed Services; Senate Armed Services; House Foreign Affairs; Senate Foreign Relations

4.7 AI Search: Controlling Information, Concentrating Power Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: Major technology companies are rapidly replacing traditional search results with AI-generated summaries that answer questions directly and decide which sources users see, reducing the open-choice model that long defined the internet. Publishers and content creators fear that these systems scrape their work, summarize it without compensation, and keep users on dominant platforms, strengthening the market power of companies such as Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, and Anthropic while increasing the risk of hidden bias, factual errors, and large-scale disinformation.

Proposed Oversight Action: Open an investigation into the competitive, economic, and informational effects of AI search products, including subpoenas for internal documents on traffic impacts, source ranking decisions, training data practices, and agreements with publishers or preferred content providers. Hold hearings with major AI and search executives, independent publishers, academics, and antitrust experts. Issue a report evaluating whether existing antitrust, consumer protection, and transparency laws are sufficient for the AI search era.

Why It Matters: A small number of AI companies can determine what information people see first, what sources survive economically, and which voices disappear. If AI search tools absorb web traffic while monetizing others’ content, smaller websites, local journalism, and independent creators may become economically unsustainable. This is not only a competition issue—it is a democracy issue involving access to information, market concentration, and who controls knowledge online.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary; House Energy and Commerce; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation

4.8 Algorithmic Rulemaking: Secret Software, Hidden Decisions, No Accountability

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The Trump administration has aggressively pursued an agenda to weaken public protections through executive order, while agencies and administration-aligned entities may be using AI tools to identify regulations for rescission, draft regulatory actions, and review public comments, including reported use of DOGE’s “Sweet Rex” tool and DOT’s use of Google Gemini. There is little public transparency regarding which large language models are used, what data they rely on, whether qualified officials review their outputs, or whether any legal, privacy, or ethical guardrails apply.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings on the use of AI in the federal regulatory process, with testimony from OMB, DOJ, DOT, agency rulemaking officials, outside vendors, and administrative law experts. Subpoena contracts, internal guidance, prompts, training materials, output logs, validation studies, and communications related to DOGE’s Sweet Rex tool, Google Gemini, and comparable systems. Require a report identifying which agencies are using AI in rulemaking, for what purposes, under what safeguards, and whether such use complies with the Administrative Procedure Act.

Why It Matters: Deciding whether regulations protecting public health, worker safety, transportation safety, consumer rights, and financial stability should be repealed requires legal judgment, subject-matter expertise, and accountability that current AI systems lack. Americans deserve to know whether human experts or unaccountable software are driving decisions that affect their daily lives.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation

4.9 Data Centers, Sky-High Bills: How Big Tech’s Energy Hunger Is Draining American Families

Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: The rapid build-out of data centers is compounding increasing electricity prices and energy burden on communities across the country, with some residents seeing increases of up to 250% in their energy bills. Simultaneously, data centers are exacerbating the climate crisis by locking in more fossil fuel infrastructure, with over 50% relying on fossil fuels. Big Tech continues to expand without adequate federal oversight of community, environmental, or affordability impacts.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings, open investigations, and issue reports examining which data center operators are positioned to benefit from energy dominance programs and coal plant extensions, what the per-ratepayer cost of those extensions is in each affected state, and whether DOE conducted any cost-benefit analysis before eliminating emissions requirements from lending programs. Examine water use, light and noise pollution, and the erosion of the state and local tax base.

Why It Matters: Affordability, fossil fuel dependence, lack of transparency and community involvement, and the erosion of local tax bases are all legitimate public policy concerns. Congress should establish who is actually benefiting from current energy policy and who is paying for it.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Energy and Commerce; House Science, Space, and Technology, Subcommittee on Energy; Senate Energy and Natural Resources

Section V: Climate, Energy, and Environmental Accountability

Americans should not face higher bills, dirtier air, and greater disaster risks because of favoritism toward powerful polluters. Oversight should determine whether this administration’s public policy serves energy insiders over consumers and communities.

5.1 The Big Ugly Giveaway: Billions for Fossil Fuel Corporations, Higher Energy Costs for Everyone Else

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The OBBBA created several new tax incentives and expanded other fossil fuel giveaways, while slashing clean energy incentives that would reduce consumers’ electricity bills. Fossil fuel companies already receive an estimated $35 billion in annual federal giveaways, with over $4 billion added by Trump and Republicans in 2025—more than double the levels from 2017.

Proposed Oversight Action: The House Oversight Committee, in conjunction with House Ways and Means and other relevant committees, should collect tax data, quarterly earnings, and earnings projections to inform an investigation and subsequent hearings regarding fossil fuel industry profits from the OBBBA. The investigation should examine specific companies positioned to benefit, the total value of new incentives, and how those gains compare with any commitments to jobs or domestic investment.

Why It Matters: As more Americans foot the bill for oil shareholders and executive paychecks, Congress should conduct a thorough investigation into the profits fossil fuel companies have made since the passage of OBBBA and what they could expect to make if no changes are made. This could also be expanded to broader corporate payout from OBBBA. The committees should expose for the American people how the administration’s policies enrich fossil fuel corporations and billionaires while driving costs for households up, not down.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Ways and Means; House Energy and Commerce; House Natural Resources; Senate Energy and Natural Resources

5.2 The Grid Gamble: Fossil Fuel Bailouts for Corporations, Higher Energy Costs for Everyone Else

Oversight Type: Investigation

Problem: The OBBBA created a new “Energy Dominance Financing Program” that provides DOE loan guarantees for fossil-fuel infrastructure, replaces clean-energy grid investments with fossil-fuel-friendly alternatives, and removes emissions requirements from the Loan Programs Office. The Trump administration also issued executive orders keeping retired and retiring coal plants online, forcing ratepayers in Michigan and Pennsylvania to foot tens of millions in added electricity costs. Meanwhile, electricity demand is rising sharply due to data center growth.

Proposed Oversight Action: Investigate (1) which specific data center operators and fossil fuel companies are positioned to benefit from the Energy Dominance Financing Program and coal plant extensions; (2) what the per-ratepayer cost of those extensions is in each affected state; and (3) whether DOE conducted any cost-benefit analysis comparing fossil fuel grid investments against clean alternatives before eliminating the emissions requirement from the LPO. Request internal DOE communications and the financial terms of any loan guarantees issued under the new program.

Why It Matters: We are being told that fossil fuels are necessary for grid reliability, even as data centers—whose power needs primarily benefit large tech corporations—drive the surge in demand that justifies those investments. Congress should establish who is actually benefiting from this energy policy and who is paying for it.

Committee/Jurisdiction: Senate Environment and Public Works; House Energy and Commerce; Senate Energy and Natural Resources

5.3 Carbon Capture, Bigger Oil Profits: How the Big Ugly Law Turns Climate Policy Into Corporate Welfare

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: The OBBBA modified the 45Q carbon capture tax credit to put enhanced oil recovery— pumping captured CO2 into the ground to extract more oil—on equal financial footing with permanent geologic carbon storage. This means the federal government is subsidizing a carbon capture method whose primary output is increased fossil fuel production. The Joint Committee on Taxation estimates this provision alone could be worth $14.2 billion over ten years.

Proposed Oversight Action: Request all internal Treasury and DOE communications regarding the 45Q modification, including any industry lobbying records or communications with OBBBA drafters. Hold hearings examining (1) which specific companies are projected to claim the expanded 45Q credit for enhanced oil recovery; (2) how much additional oil production is projected to result; (3) what the net carbon accounting of the credit is when downstream combustion emissions from that additional oil are included; and (4) whether the credit as modified constitutes a net climate benefit or a net carbon increase.

Why It Matters: Congress is telling the public that carbon capture is a climate solution while simultaneously designing the federal subsidy for it to maximize oil extraction. A thorough public accounting of who benefits and what the actual emissions math looks like is essential to honest climate oversight—and to establishing the factual record for any future legislative correction.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Ways and Means; House Natural Resources; House Energy and Commerce; Senate Energy and Natural Resources

5.4 The War on Climate Science: Repealing the Endangerment Finding and Silencing EPA Experts

Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: The Trump administration pushed to repeal the endangerment finding, the foundational rule originally required by the Supreme Court and finalized under Obama that serves as the basis for U.S. climate policy. The administration repealed the rule without scientific basis, and the repeal is currently in litigation. Additionally, Congress used the Congressional Review Act to nullify California’s Clean Air waivers, raising questions about both the legality of that action and the process by which EPA and career staff were overruled.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and open an investigation into how the scientific basis (or alleged lack thereof) was determined for the endangerment finding repeal, the process by which career staff may have been overruled, and the legal consequences of the repeal and waiver revocations. Require testimony from EPA scientists, former agency officials, state regulators, and independent environmental law experts. Commission a report on the expected public health consequences of these actions.

Why It Matters: Hearings should establish a factual record on how scientific consensus was disregarded, which career officials objected and how they were treated, and what the practical legal and regulatory consequences will be for states, industries, and communities that relied on settled climate policy.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Energy and Commerce; Senate Environment and Public Works

5.5 Critical Minerals, Critical Corruption: Political Favoritism Is Driving Billions in Mining Giveaways

Oversight Type: Investigation and Report

Problem: The Trump administration has used federal mining programs and new “critical minerals” initiatives to steer lucrative deals toward politically connected companies, while weakening environmental review and public disclosure. Current congressional proposals, such as the SECURE Minerals Act and the Finding ORE Act, would codify Trump’s actions into law, and recent White House executive orders related to critical minerals and mine permitting have already directed agencies to deploy billions in taxpayer dollars for mining projects with little to no transparency or accountability. There is still no comprehensive public accounting of how much taxpayer money has been committed, who is benefiting, or how these projects are affecting communities, workers, and the environment.

Proposed Oversight Action: Congress should open a formal investigation and commission a public report to map which individuals and companies are receiving critical-minerals contracts, equity investments, and other forms of federal mining support, and under what terms. The inquiry should assess whether there are financial, political, or personal ties between recipients and administration officials, whether agencies have complied with environmental, labor, and community-impact requirements, and how proposed legislation like the SECURE Minerals Act and the Finding ORE Act would entrench or expand these preferential arrangements. The investigation should result in concrete legislative and regulatory recommendations to close loopholes, prevent self-dealing, and protect taxpayers going forward.

Why It Matters: Critical minerals are essential for the clean energy transition, advanced manufacturing, and national security, and global demand is projected to more than double by 2030. If politically connected firms and shell companies capture federal mining policy, the U.S. will become a playground for corruption and pollution, prioritizing short-term favors over long-term industrial resilience. Without robust oversight, politically favored firms can crowd out more responsible competitors, undermining market discipline and leaving taxpayers on the hook for risky or underperforming projects. Members across the political spectrum are interested in ensuring that federal mining support does not become a vehicle for self-dealing, pay-to-play schemes, or hidden liabilities that surface years after the current administration has left office.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Natural Resources; Senate Energy and Natural Resources; House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

5.6 The Climate Data Black Box: Private Risk Models, Rising Premiums, and Families Left in the Dark

Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: As climate change drives up disaster costs and insured losses, insurance companies increasingly need access to extensive federal climate data and forward-looking risk projections. As Trump cuts to climate data infrastructure, that uncertainty will drive up costs as insurers hedge by raising premiums. The lack of historical federal investment in catastrophe modeling has left insurers relying on secretive private models, leaving households and local governments in the dark.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings with climate scientists, insurance affordability experts, actuaries, and state regulators on the need for robust federal climate data infrastructure and the downstream household cost implications of data privatization. Commission a report examining the gap between federal investment in catastrophe modeling and the scale of climate-driven losses, and identifying federal steps to improve public transparency in risk modeling.

Why It Matters: The lack of historical federal investment in catastrophe modeling has left insurers relying on secretive private models. As Trump cuts funding for climate data infrastructure, that uncertainty will drive up costs as insurers hedge by raising premiums further, ultimately borne by American families.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Natural Resources; House Science, Space, and Technology; Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation

5.7 Ignoring the Climate Risk: How Deregulation Leaves Banks Vulnerable and Families on the Hook

Oversight Type: Hearing

Problem: Since the start of the Trump administration, federal financial regulators, including the SEC, FDIC, OCC, and Federal Reserve, have gutted climate-related financial regulation. These actions are unrelated to reduced climate-related financial risk, which is actually increasing as climate change goes unmitigated and physical impacts worsen. The lack of climate-related regulation exposes the financial system and the economy to increased risks and vulnerabilities.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings with federal financial regulators, independent economists, climate finance experts, and consumer advocates to examine what climate-related financial regulations have been rolled back, on what legal and analytical basis, and what the projected risk consequences are for financial institutions, households, and the broader economy. Request internal communications and analysis from the SEC, FDIC, OCC, and Federal Reserve on the basis for rollback decisions.

Why It Matters: Ignoring climate-related financial risks does not make them go away. No less than Jerome Powell, then-chair of the Federal Reserve, testified in February 2025 that, “If you fast forward 10 or 15 years, there will be regions of the country where you can’t get a mortgage, there won’t be ATMs, banks won’t have branches and things like that.” By abdicating their risk management role to do favors for the fossil fuel industry, financial regulators—who should operate independently of the executive branch—are putting the American economy at risk. It is working families that will pay the highest price if climate-driven financial risks materialize.

Committee/Jurisdiction: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; House Financial Services

5.8 The War on Wind: Fossil Fuel Buyouts, Higher Energy Costs, and Communities Left Behind

Oversight Type: Investigation

Problem: Since January 2025, the Trump administration has issued executive orders and pressured energy developers to cancel wind projects and invest in fossil fuel infrastructure instead. In 2026, Trump’s Interior Department agreed to pay several developers to abandon their offshore wind leases and redirect the money to other energy sources, such as new gas-fired power plants. Those buyouts included $1 billion for TotalEnergies, $765 million for Invenergy, and more. This aggressive anti-wind agenda blocks clean, cheap renewables that would lower Americans’ electricity bills and cut climate-warming pollution.

Proposed Oversight Action: Investigate Trump’s dirty deals with energy companies and expose how Trump’s anti-renewables agenda is hurting Americans’ pocketbooks while enriching the Trump administration and its fossil fuel billionaire cronies. Request, and subpoena if refused, the full settlement agreements, the legal memos authorizing them, and Interior and DOJ communications with the developers. Investigate who owns and profits from the pivot of renewable investments into fossil projects.

Why It Matters: The administration’s anti-renewables agenda is making life more expensive for families, putting thousands of offshore wind jobs in jeopardy, and wasting taxpayer dollars on polluting industries that are driving the climate crisis.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Ways and Means; House Energy and Commerce; House Natural Resources; Senate Energy and Natural Resources

Section VI: Corruption, Abuse of Power, and Government for Sale

Public office should serve the public, not enrich insiders or reward political allies. Oversight is needed to determine whether government power was used for private gain, donor favoritism, or corporate influence rather than the public interest. In particular, a focus on the impacts of corruption and abuse of power on the economy and on the lives of regular Americans will be well received. Hearings focused on this topic should both identify clear villains and lay the groundwork for eventual legislative reforms that grapple with oligarchy and power imbalances.

6.1 Justice for Sale: The President’s Personal Lawsuit, DOJ Resources, and the Taxpayer-Funded Slush Fund

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: President Trump filed suit against the IRS seeking damages after a contractor, Charles Littlejohn, leaked his tax returns to The New York Times. He originally sought $10 billion in damages under 26 U.S.C. § 7431, a provision that legal experts and members of Congress have noted would be unavailable to ordinary taxpayers under the same circumstances, given that Trump is pursuing the claim through the Department of Justice rather than private counsel. He chose instead to settle the matter with a $1.76 billion slush fund that could distribute taxpayer dollars to individuals alleging politically motivated targeting by the federal government.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings with Department of Justice leadership, IRS officials, Treasury Department officials, and legal experts to examine whether DOJ resources are being used to pursue a personal claim that could result in taxpayer-funded payments or special protections for a sitting president, whether similar claims or settlement arrangements would be available to ordinary taxpayers, and whether the proposed “Anti-Weaponization Fund” constituted an improper use of taxpayer resources.

Why It Matters: This lawsuit raises broader concerns about whether a sitting president can use the machinery of the federal government to pursue personal financial or legal benefit. At a time when Americans are facing real affordability challenges, Congress should examine whether public resources are being used for private financial gain or settlement structures that would not be available to ordinary citizens.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

6.2 Crypto Cash and Foreign Influence: The Risks of Government-Linked Investors in Trump-Affiliated Deals

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: President Trump and individuals affiliated with his political and business network have been linked to cryptocurrency ventures that involve investors with significant legal and regulatory exposure, including Changpeng Zhao and Justin Sun. At the same time, foreign government-linked investors have made large-scale investments in Trump-affiliated crypto ventures, including a reported $2 billion deal backed by entities tied to the United Arab Emirates and a substantial ownership stake held by a UAE royal. These investments raise concerns that foreign actors may gain financial leverage or access to U.S. policymakers through crypto markets.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings with Treasury, SEC, and DOJ officials, financial crime experts, and executives from major crypto platforms and Trump-affiliated ventures to examine (1) foreign government-linked investment in U.S. political figures’ financial ventures, (2) compliance with anti money laundering and disclosure laws, (3) the role of high-risk or sanctioned actors in these markets, and (4) whether existing safeguards are sufficient to prevent foreign influence over U.S. policymakers. Request financial records, investor disclosures, and communications between crypto firms, foreign investors, and administration officials.

Why It Matters: Foreign government-linked investment in ventures tied to a sitting president represents a potential pathway to purchase influence with the U.S. government. If foreign actors can gain financial stakes in businesses connected to political power, it creates a direct risk to national security and public trust. Congress should determine whether gaps in oversight are allowing private financial interests and foreign governments to intersect with public power in ways that undermine accountability.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; House Financial Services; Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs; House Foreign Affairs; Senate Foreign Relations

6.3 The Justice System Under Pressure: Political Prosecutions, Threats to Staff, and the Collapse of Independence

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: At the commencement of the administration, then Attorney General Pam Bondi told DOJ staff that their duty was to advocate zealously for Trump’s agenda, not the rule of law—and threatened them with discipline or firing if they failed. That zealous advocacy has included bringing bad-faith criminal charges against the president’s perceived political enemies, a preposterous prosecution against one of the nation’s leading civil rights organizations, and the issuance of various memoranda that aim to treat political adversaries as domestic terrorists.

Proposed Oversight Action: Current and former DOJ officials should be subpoenaed to testify about their decisions regarding weaponization and their coordination with the White House. At hearings, DOJ staff, including U.S. attorneys, should be asked about instructions they received to prosecute political enemies and the responses they received when they argued against such bad-faith actions.

Why It Matters: A democracy cannot function in a climate of widespread political prosecutions or the threat of such prosecutions. Weaponization of the DOJ is perhaps the pinnacle of Trump’s vindictiveness and authoritarian overreach.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

6.4 Pardons for Sale: How Trump’s Pay-to-Play System Erased Penalties and Hurt Victims

Oversight Type: Investigations and Hearings

Problem: President Trump abused the pardon power: He pardoned the January 6 insurrectionists. Outside the January 6 pardons, more than one-third of his pardons in the first year were granted to people convicted of fraud or fraud-adjacent charges. His pardons have led to the cancellation of $1.5 billion in fines and restitution, including more than $1 billion owed to victims. Pardons have been granted to those who have contributed to Trump-affiliated election committees or who have hired Trump-affiliated lobbyists. And Trump has suggested he will grant broad pardons to those serving in the current administration.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings and require testimony from recipients of controversial pardons, along with those witnesses who are fraud victims, investors, consumers, law enforcement officers, and others harmed by the underlying crimes whose restitution, accountability, or legal remedies were diminished by pardon decisions.

Why It Matters: This would be an embarrassing hearing for any member defending people who attacked the Capitol or committed fraud against consumers and investors. Moreover, Trump’s abuse of pardons drives the broad narrative about abuse of power, plus specific narratives that this administration is pro fraud and that perks are available for sale, as well as reminds the public of Trump’s embrace of the January 6 insurrection.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs; House Judiciary; Senate Judiciary

6.5 Illegal Impoundments: Depriving Communities, Trampling Separation of Powers

Oversight Type: Investigations, Hearings, and Report

Problem: Through impoundments, grant cancellations, and budgetary maneuvers, the Trump administration has refused to make hundreds of billions of dollars of Congressionally authorized and mandated investments in communities. These have hurt education, health care, VA programs, road construction, overseas humanitarian missions, and more. Many of these measures are illegal and trample on Congress’ spending power authority.

Proposed Oversight Action: Hold hearings featuring mayors, school superintendents, hospital and community health center leaders, veterans, infrastructure officials, nonprofit service providers, and other beneficiaries harmed by the withholding of congressionally appropriated funds. Pair those witnesses with former OMB officials, appropriations experts, GAO officials, and budget law scholars to examine the legality of the administration’s actions and their impact on Congress’s constitutional power of the purse. Issue a report documenting both the constitutional violations and the real-world consequences for communities denied funding that Congress had already approved.

Why It Matters: The Trump administration is thumbing its nose at Congress’s spending power, instead picking and choosing what it prefers to fund, rather than following congressional directives. It is directing federal funds on a partisan basis, attacking core safety-net programs, failing to make crucial infrastructure investments, sabotaging renewable energy programs, and undermining humanitarian programs around the world. The stakes are high for the Constitutional separation of powers and the health and well-being of communities across the country.

Committee/Jurisdiction: House Oversight and Government Reform; Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

title: STATEMENT: US Midterms Put Economic Security and Energy Affordability in the Spotlight
description:
The results will shape the political landscape for energy and climate policy at the federal, state and local levels.
Following is a statement from David Widawsky, Director of World Resources Institute United States: “The message from voters is clear: Americans want greater economic security, relief from rising costs and an energy system that works for them.
This election put a bright spotlight on how this country’s outdated energy system and dependence on fossil fuels leave families and businesses exposed to unaffordable price shocks.
From farmers in the Midwest to truckers at the pump to families struggling with household bills, Americans are feeling the strain.
“The new Congress has an opportunity to deliver on issues that cut across party lines like sky-high energy costs, data centers, promising energy technology innovations like geothermal and industrial batteries, and building a modern, resilient grid.
text:
WASHINGTON (November 4, 2026) — The United States held its midterm elections on November 3, with voters deciding control of the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate, alongside gubernatorial, state legislative and local races across the country. The results will shape the political landscape for energy and climate policy at the federal, state and local levels.

Following is a statement from David Widawsky, Director of World Resources Institute United States:

“The message from voters is clear: Americans want greater economic security, relief from rising costs and an energy system that works for them. This election put a bright spotlight on how this country’s outdated energy system and dependence on fossil fuels leave families and businesses exposed to unaffordable price shocks.

“American consumers are bearing the burden of rising electricity prices as rapid data center growth stretches the capacity of the aging US grid, while government actions have hindered the deployment of clean and affordable energy. From farmers in the Midwest to truckers at the pump to families struggling with household bills, Americans are feeling the strain.

“The new Congress has an opportunity to deliver on issues that cut across party lines like sky-high energy costs, data centers, promising energy technology innovations like geothermal and industrial batteries, and building a modern, resilient grid. These are practical solutions that can put money back in Americans’ pockets, strengthen the economy and lay the groundwork for more ambitious action.

“Some of the biggest opportunities for progress may come at the state and city level. New governors, state legislatures and mayors have the power to move quickly on solutions that address the needs of their constituents: strengthening local economies, creating jobs and lowering bills. From ensuring data centers provide real benefits to communities to expanding clean energy, modernizing the grid, enabling affordable and accessible housing, and improving public transit, state and local leaders can walk-the-talk that climate action delivers real benefits for people.”

text:
European Parliament lawmakers on Wednesday backed a relaxation of the EU's 2035 car emissions target from 100% to 87.5%, as pressure mounts on Brussels to give the struggling automotive industry more flexibility in its transition to electric vehicles.

MEPs on the Parliament's environment committee voted to ease emissions requirements for new cars and vans, allowing manufacturers more leeway to meet their climate obligations.

The move goes further than the European Commission's proposal, which would have lowered the 2035 target from a 100% reduction in emissions to a 90% cut.

Under the parliamentary compromise, manufacturers using climate-friendly steel would receive an additional 7.5% credit, while the target for vans would fall from 90% to 80%.

The vote marks a significant shift in EU climate policy and the balance of power in Parliament, where a broad political consensus once supported progressively tighter CO2 emissions standards.

With soaring energy costs threatening Europe's industrial competitiveness, lawmakers are increasingly focused on protecting the automotive industry. EU car production remains roughly 19% to 20% below pre-pandemic levels in 2019, according to the think tank Bruegel.

Related

Seven EU countries pressure European Commission to rethink 2035 diesel and petrol car ban

EU carmakers to comply with 90% emissions reduction by 2035 as full combustion engine ban scrapped

The compromise was negotiated by the centre-right European People's Party (EPP), the centre-left Socialists and Democrats (S&D) and the centrist Renew Europe group, reflecting the EPP's longstanding demands for greater flexibility for carmakers facing fierce competition from China, sluggish electric vehicle sales and rising production costs.

The three groups had already reached a compromise, with a similar version approved by Parliament's transport and industry committees on October 22.

Italian MEP Massimiliano Salini, the EPP's lead negotiator on the legislation, hailed the vote as a victory for his group's campaign to relax the restrictions on combustion engines.

"The EPP Group managed to bring Europe's political centre together behind a clear objective: backing our car industry, protecting European jobs and giving manufacturers the freedom to develop the best technologies," Salini said.

The EPP, which previously helped sustain EU climate legislation alongside the Socialists, Liberals and Greens, has increasingly challenged the pace and design of the green transition, at times joining forces with the far right.

The Greens have warned that the move threatens the cross-party consensus that underpinned Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's Green Deal.

Breaking with the past

The vote marks a shift away from the EU's original plan to effectively end sales of new combustion engine cars from 2035, despite backing from several EU countries and electric lobby groups.

The Green Deal was a flagship achievement of the 2019–2024 European Parliament, when the Greens held 18 more seats than they do today.

The original 2035 zero-emission target for new cars and vans was ultimately adopted in 2023, despite resistance from parts of the centre-right. The Greens were among its strongest defenders, seeing it as essential to give manufacturers a clear investment signal and accelerate the shift to electric vehicles.

Related

What went wrong for the EU election-losing Greens and Liberals?

However, the current reversal is also a reflection of the political pressure that has built up since then, with several critics arguing the EU lacks adequate charging infrastructure for the uptake of EVs.

Faced with mounting demands from carmakers and national governments, particularly Germany and Italy, the Commission rolled back its original proposal in December 2025, proposing instead to weaken the 2035 target from a 100% to a 90% reduction in tailpipe emissions.

The remaining 10% could be compensated through credits linked to EU-made low-carbon steel and sustainable fuels. This would allow plug-in hybrids and even diesel- and petrol-powered vehicles to remain on the market beyond 2035 — a significant concession to the argument that the green transition must not come at the expense of industrial competitiveness.

EPP push tech flexibility

The EPP argues that carmakers need more technological leeway to remain competitive and protect jobs. The compromise with the S&D and Renew suggests that concerns about industrial competitiveness are increasingly cutting across traditional political divisions in the Parliament.

Overall, the political agreement forged on Wednesday reflects growing unease among EU governments and lawmakers about the speed and cost of the automotive transition.

Germany and France, home to two of Europe's largest automotive industries, have been among those calling for greater flexibility, carving out their own Franco-German car deal, in which climate-friendly steel plays a much smaller role.

Veteran German MEP Peter Liese, the EPP's climate policy spokesperson, hailed the political will from the different groups.

"We want climate neutrality, but with the rules we have now agreed on, we are also ensuring technology neutrality. I am personally convinced that the future belongs to electric cars. But electric vehicles with range extenders and plug-in hybrids with a long electric range will also have a role to play in 2035 and beyond," Liese said.

Related

Exclusive: EU Commissioner Hoekstra defends scrapping 2035 ban on combustion engines

France and Spain back 2035 diesel and petrol car ban, letter reveals

Green lawmakers have criticised the proposed changes, warning that weakening the 2035 requirements could slow the transition to electric mobility and undermine investment certainty for manufacturers that have already committed to electrification.

German Green MEP Michael Bloss described the vote as a "bad deal" for the European car industry, saying the political back-and-forth is more harmful than the high production costs in Europe.

"While sales of electric cars are skyrocketing, the majority of the European Parliament is sending a signal of uncertainty. The fact that Social Democrats and Conservatives are helping to jeopardise investment security and industrial jobs is a contradiction that could hardly be more glaring," Bloss told Euronews.

"Europe has the factories and skilled workers to build top-of-the-line cars for the electric age, but it needs clear political support for this direction."

The deal must still secure the backing of Parliament's full plenary and survive negotiations with EU member states before becoming law.

text:
India has set ambitious clean energy and climate targets, including achieving 500 GW of non-fossil fuel-based electricity capacity by 2030 and attaining net-zero emissions by 2070. Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) serves as one of the key policy instruments to accelerate renewable energy adoption by mandating obligated entities to procure a specified percentage of their electricity from renewable energy sources.

With the evolving regulatory landscape—including the introduction of Renewable Consumption Obligation (RCO), Energy Storage Obligation (ESO), the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), and increasing emphasis on distributed renewable energy- obligated entities are required to remain updated on changing compliance requirements, reporting mechanisms and upcoming technologies. Strengthening institutional understanding of these developments is essential to ensure effective implementation, regulatory compliance, and achievement of Uttar Pradesh’s renewable energy goals.

To support this objective, Uttar Pradesh New and Renewable Energy Development Agency (UPNEDA), in collaboration with the Centre for Science and Environment (CSE), is organizing another one day capacity building workshop in Ghaziabad, covering stakeholders in Western Uttar Pradesh. The workshop will provide participants from the region with an overview of the evolving renewable energy policy landscape, demonstrate the Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) Portal, and explain compliance procedures. It will also showcase successful renewable energy interventions from obligated entities, facilitate peer learning from other states RPO compliance experiences, and create a platform for panel discussions among regulators, brokers, vendors, technical experts, and obligated entities to address implementation challenges and explore emerging opportunities in renewable energy procurement, storage, and carbon markets.

Join our free webinar The Post-Election Playbook: Opportunities to Advance Clean Economy Policy on Thursday, November 12 at 4PM ET. Ceres experts will deep dive into the election results and what they mean for the private sector. This webinar is free and open to the press. Register here.

BOSTON — The U.S. election results show decisive support for clean, affordable energy, as voters elected leaders nationwide committed to lowering energy costs and meeting rising demand with clean solutions.

Ceres urges the incoming Congress to refocus federal policy on reducing costs for businesses and consumers by modernizing the power grid, doubling down on clean manufacturing, and deploying affordable, homegrown wind, solar, batteries, and efficiency solutions. New state policymakers also have opportunities to strengthen successful clean energy policies to build modern, more affordable, and more reliable energy systems.

“Energy was a top issue this election season, and voters delivered a clear mandate for Congress to bring electricity prices down by deploying clean, affordable power.” said Ceres CEO and President Mindy Lubber. “They can begin this year by passing the Senate’s bipartisan permitting deal, which includes strong provisions to ease transmission development and ensure permit certainty for urgently needed clean energy projects. But lawmakers must also work together to develop the next generation of clean energy and pollution reduction policies, which will insulate American businesses and consumers from volatile prices and geopolitical conflict. The future of the American economy depends on it.”

Ceres and its Policy Network, along with other corporate and investor leaders from across the economy, will engage leaders on Capitol Hill to fine tune the next round of clean energy and grid modernization policies to bring down energy prices and to ensure they are enacted at the next available opportunity. Our federal priorities for the end of 2026 and the new Congress starting next year include:

Passing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act before the end of 2026. Enacting this strong bipartisan deal this year would allow lawmakers to use 2027 and 2028 to ensure robust implementation and work on the next round of policies to bring down prices by deploying affordable, homegrown clean energy. Ceres and our Policy Network will continue to support this effort and advocate on Capitol Hill through the end of the year, and we will work with policymakers to address some of the concerns raised across the environmental community.

Restoring targeted clean energy incentives to address high prices and rising electricity demand from data centers. The new majority in Congress has an opportunity to take lessons from the past few years to shape new, long-term solutions that ensure America has durable clean energy and climate policy that reduces costs for years to come.

Expanding home efficiency programs and distributed energy resources. Lawmakers should look to data centers to pay for home energy upgrades for consumers and programs to modernize the grid and deploy smart appliances and rooftop solar.

Addressing the growing bipartisan call to protect the freedom to invest. Lawmakers should bring legislation to the floor of both chambers addressing both state laws that limit investor voices and the SEC’s continued rollback of shareholder rights. Ceres and our Freedom to Invest initiative will continue to educate state and federal lawmakers on the importance of both issues.

Building a more resilient economy. Lawmakers must use this opportunity to reduce climate pollution and secure supply chains for the future by accelerating both manufacturing and deployment of cost-saving clean solutions.

Ceres and major businesses will also encourage new governors and state legislators to continue strong efforts around the country to deploy clean energy and address rising prices.

“In the states, the work to tackle energy affordability has already begun. Now, it’s time to double down,” said Lubber. “States like Virginia, Illinois, Arizona, and California have strong proposals on the table to tackle energy affordability right now, and Ceres will be working across the country to educate a new slate of governors and state legislators on why these policies matter and how they should be implemented. The business perspective is uniquely valuable in the states at this decisive moment. This election is an opportunity to work together to build a cleaner, more resilient economy.”

In 2026, more than two dozen major companies working with Ceres called on state policymakers around the country to tackle rising energy prices by optimizing the power grid, accelerating clean power deployment, and expanding energy efficiency programs. Ceres led business advocacy efforts to educate governors and state legislators on many of these priorities. They are laid out in more detail in Powering Affordability: A Business-Backed Playbook for a Modern Clean Energy System.

Working together with businesses and investors, the election results present an opportunity to educate a new slate of state policymakers on these priorities — and on the benefits of strong state clean energy policies already in place.
