name: Texas and Evs
title: The UAW needs a strategy for the future of manufacturing - MR Online
authors: Editor, Andy Merrifield, Michael D. Yates
description:
But the union-management collaboration that grew during this period of class struggle now has a stranglehold over the UAW.
In this period of limited class struggle, what does it mean for workers to organize themselves with a goal of developing class struggle?
SEEDS OF CLASS STRUGGLE STRATEGY Workers looking to go on offense for the long haul ought to revive the class struggle unionism of the further past.
One of its core efforts is their rank-and-file project, helping militants secure jobs in strategic workplaces—like EV plants—to build power.
Finally, it is crucial to see the strategy of class struggle unionism and the vision of collectively controlled manufacturing as parts of the same whole.
text:
The UAW has a problem: The future of the auto industry.

The crisis facing autoworkers is unfolding on many fronts. Beyond the chaotic corporate-led electric vehicle (EV) transition, there is also the ongoing restructuring toward nonunion manufacturing in the South, continued labor-replacing reorganization, and growing international competition. Workers bear the brunt on every front, most recently weathering plant closures, mass layoffs, and cross-border supply chain shocks.

UAW President Shawn Fain—whose entire slate swept the recent election for top office—has rhetorically distanced himself from UAW’s legacy of concessions: “Keep in mind how far we’ve come in the last four years,” Fain said at the June UAW Constitutional Convention. “We’ve gone from defense to offense.”

In reality, after decades of managed decline, the UAW has only just started to play defense. Fain’s administration, which came to power in 2023 through the organizing of Unite All Workers for Democracy (UAWD), has revived splashy, agitational contract campaigns. Yet the long-standing culture of union-management collaboration has left the UAW unable to resist the harm from the EV rollbacks and the corporations are restructuring the industry faster than the union can build power.

Nonunion production is nearing two-thirds of the market share as UAW’s renewed push to organize the South faces setbacks, including its loss at Mercedes and its withdrawal from some campaigns. There is still no plan for the heavily nonunion parts sector. If a 2028 strike against the Big Three wins back the retirement benefits Fain campaigned on, it would essentially bring unionized assembly work to pre-2008 standards. But it would cover fewer workers and inflation-adjusted wages would likely still be lower (Figure 1).

The situation is grim. Even with its renewed dynamism, the UAW’s current trajectory is a continued loss of leverage on an industry-wide scale. If the next administration tries to accelerate EV development again, corporations will cite the Trump-era rollback as a reason to demand more federal guarantees at labor’s expense. If protectionist policies prevail, a zero-sum market dynamic will force competition over jobs and devastate solidarity among North American workers, trapping the union into tailing corporations as they jolt back toward fossil fuels. The United States will continue to produce overpriced trucks to sell at home while Chinese companies sell better and cheaper EVs around the world. The result will be a weakening union presiding over a slow decline.

But there is an opening for workers: the recent pivot away from EVs reveals the corporate-led transition’s fundamental inability to deliver clean and safe transportation for the working class. This impasse is an opportunity to introduce political solutions that long seemed out of reach. If workers are serious about going on offense, they must look to UAW’s roots: a strategy of class struggle unionism that breaks with union-management collaboration, invests in militant shopfloor leaders, and fights for worker control alongside bread-and-butter demands.

Shopfloor militancy is necessary, but not enough on its own. The deeper problem is capitalist competition and workers face too many threats at once to beat them with one-off bargaining pushes. The way out is to chart a path toward collectively controlled manufacturing that serves the working class. This could look like building affordable EVs and public transit needed to improve working people’s lives and address the climate crisis, with public procurement enabling planning for decades to come. Such an approach would both break the zero-sum market trap and enable the rebuilding of worker-led solidarity at home and abroad.

HOW WORKERS EXPERIENCE THE CORPORATE-LED EV TRANSITION

Between the EV restructuring and uncertainty from the trade war, plant shutdowns, mass layoffs, and production pivots have roiled the industry over the last three years. Employment in the entire US auto sector decreased by over sixty-five thousand jobs, though the decline has recently plateaued and is slowly recovering. This number represents an expansive picture of the sector that includes parts and assembly subsectors, union and nonunion jobs, and production workers and supervisors.

In the Midwest, thousands of workers face temporary or indefinite layoffs as EV production at several factories is spooling down and multiple plants are being re-retooled from EV assembly back to combustion engine vehicles. GM laid off over one thousand workers at one Ultium Cells battery facility, closed another to retool for energy storage, and sold off a third. Reneging on its 2023 agreement with the UAW, Stellantis canceled plans for their EV assembly lines and battery plant in Belvidere, IL, eventually leading to the UAW’s “Keep the Promise” campaign.

Perhaps most illustrative of the current moment is the recent closure of the Kentucky BlueOval electric vehicle battery facility co-owned by Ford and a South Korean company. The 1,600 workers who were fired had previously voted to unionize with the UAW in the face of rabid antiunion corporate tactics. But now, Ford is using the closure as an opportunity to bust the union, claiming to reopen the facility in 2027 for battery storage manufacturing, in part supplying data center construction driven by AI speculation. Workers from the plant held a rally with the help of the UAW, but other Ford Locals have not mobilized in solidarity, leaving the fired workers with little leverage.

When I worked at General Motors Factory Zero, which produces gigantic luxury EVs like the $100,000 Electric Hummer, I experienced the plant shifting from mandatory overtime in 2024 to mass layoffs in 2025. The company used a loophole in the contract, which allows for waiving overtime restrictions when launching new vehicles—forcing workers to work six days a week for 12.5 hour shifts (including a half hour of unpaid lunch) for almost a year. GM also relied on the inability of over a thousand new hires to get relief through the federally protected Family Medical Leave Act (FMLA), which only kicks in a year into employment.

Local 22 union officials were uninterested in organizing against the brutal mandatory overtime, even when the death of one of our union siblings while driving home after a long shift galvanized anger on the shopfloor. The rank-and-file formation I was a part of, anchored by UAWD members, put out a petition demanding easing of the mandatory overtime schedule and raising striking as a threat. Local officials quashed the organizing despite more than seven hundred workers signing the petition. Officials pushed through a vote to adjourn during one membership meeting to avoid discussing the matter. In the monthly newsletter, the Local president claimed that signing the petition may result in workers getting fired. Regional leadership was made aware of these actions and the conditions the workers faced, but did not support the campaign either.

After Trump’s EV policy reversals came into effect, management at the plant started to ramp up layoffs in 2025, ultimately impacting over a thousand workers. In union newsletters and from the front of the room during membership meetings, Local union officials blamed the downsizing on so-called “absenteeism” rather than fighting to keep workers in the plant. Many workers were finally able to take time off with FMLA after a brutal year of mandatory overtime. This boom and bust dynamic over the span of just two years revealed deep cultural challenges at the Local level: instead of the corporations’ decision to make luxury EVs with limited market appeal or the Trump administration’s anti-EV policies, workers were being blamed for their own layoffs, weakening solidarity and pitting the union against itself.

A union that put the blame where it belonged and oriented around expanding worker control would have fought for strong work sharing provisions to spread the downturn’s burden across the workforce, and over the longer term, for a say in the product decisions that caused the bust in the first place.

At the Local level, organizers face the profound challenge of breaking with business unionism—the ideology that seeks labor peace with the boss and narrowly confines the union to bargaining better deals for its own members. Some of our strongest opposition came from proud union members who have been in the Local for decades and many come from UAW families. Their positions on the Local Executive Board or as union stewards kept them from grueling work on the shop floor, which in turn made them worried about losing their union role. This reinforced the conservative belief that fighting management is more destabilizing than smoothing over conflict.

Such was the reality on the ground, despite UAW’s claim that a “just transition” was won. The 2023 national agreements gave the UAW little contractual standing to resist the EV-related mass layoffs and plant closures, as the companies used “market condition” exception clauses to explain their restructuring. UAW’s current focus on contracts ultimately obscures that management’s control over workers is a question of power, not legalism.

The biggest experiment in resistance was UAW’s aforementioned Stellantis Keep the Promise campaign. After the Stand Up strike, Stellantis began a wave of layoffs, reversed its decision to reopen the Belvidere Assembly Plant, and dropped other product commitments. Fain tried to unite Local presidents around escalating strike threats in solidarity and the UAW reported that 28 Locals passed resolutions that put them on track to strike over violations of the contract’s product commitment provisions. Two Locals of parts-distribution workers cleared the strike authorization threshold, but assembly-plant workers were more conflicted.

As a co-chair of UAWD’s Organizing Committee at the time, I worked with others to support rank-and-file workers in launching a small bottom-up campaign across assembly plants to build support for Fain’s strategy—convening meetings, handing out flyers, and intervening at membership meetings. While some in the rank and file grasped the importance of cross-Local solidarity, many were resistant and skeptical, especially as officials fear-mongered about further layoffs. Decades of business unionism atrophied the muscles for bottom-up deliberation. Without a meaningful democratic process, the campaign felt like an imposition and the chance for political education and buy-in was lost. UAW’s top leadership cut it short after Stellantis agreed to some demands, while cancelling plans for a battery plant and parts megahub in Belvidere.

The inability to resist the corporate-led EV restructuring while the Big Three continue to profit reveals the overall weakness of the UAW, especially between contract negotiations. The ideology internalized across UAW workers, staff, and union officialdom is that management has a right to do what it wants and workers can only ride the boom and bust cycle of the industry and hope they make it out on the other side.

ORGANIZING SETBACKS AND THE WAY FORWARD?

UAW’s organizing drive in the South is one of the most ambitious and important endeavors in the labor movement today. Coming out of the recent Constitutional Convention, in June 2026, where delegates approved an increase in the organizing budget from $60 to $100 million over four years, UAW’s current organizing approach should be critically evaluated.

In 2024, UAW homed in on new organizing, claiming to focus on more than a dozen nonunion assembly and battery plants, mostly in the South. As multiple analyses have revealed, this increased funding also came with a pivot in strategy emphasizing worker-led organizing, leadership identification, workplace mapping, public pressure campaigns, and the use of experienced staff (primarily coming from the higher education sector).

The big breakthrough has been the Volkswagen plant in Chattanooga, Tennessee, where workers recently settled a contract after nearly two years of bargaining with the company. A parts plant down the road from the Volkswagen facility also unionized with the UAW, showing the possible ripple effect of southern organizing wins. Workers at Daimler Truck plants in North Carolina and elsewhere in the South ran an animated contract campaign that secured significant wins. The unionization victory at BlueOval, mentioned above, eked out with an 11-vote margin, and would have continued the pattern if the company did not deliberately shut down the factory for retooling.

Yet, in the face of unrelenting union busting, the UAW appears to have reassessed its strategy and pulled resources from certain organizing drives. A UAWD member leading an organizing drive at an Alabama plant recently told Daily Struggle, “I feel there was a ton of enthusiasm from International at the start, but when things got hard, like they inevitably do in new campaigns, they kind of folded to the adversity. We don’t dislike our staff, they’ve just been hard to reach for months, they’re managing multiple campaigns across the South and they’re not down here that much. They sometimes have advice for us when we get them on the phone, but, beyond that, there aren’t organizing resources flowing to us as workers.”

A similar pattern is playing out at a Rivian electric vehicle plant in Normal, IL. The UAW has pulled back support for the organizing drive, after establishing a neutrality agreement that will only kick in once the company reaches a threshold of profitability. Certain Rivian workers publicly disagreed with this strategy, telling WGLT: “Money’s not in the Top 5. I want a say in what goes on in my work life and my home life. Right now, I don’t have any of that. They can change your schedule. They can do whatever they want because I don’t have a seat at the table.”

The Mercedes unionization drive in 2024, which failed by a margin of about six hundred votes out of five thousand voters, is an important recent case study. There have been many insightful analyses by workers and labor researchers assessing the loss. As the campaign is regrouping for another push, the organizing demands are worth analyzing more deeply.

Mercedes organizers picked eliminating the wage and healthcare tier that was instituted in 2020—or what they dubbed the “Alabama discount”—as a key target of their campaign. Under pressure from the organizing drive, the company eliminated the tiers and went on a charm offensive after replacing their CEO. According to organizers, who were able to secure a large majority of “yes” commitments, the company’s pivot swung many voters to “no” in the weeks leading up to the election. Then, months after the election, the company reasserted its control by, for example, forcing excessive Saturday work and dragging its feet on addressing shopfloor issues. The defeat at Mercedes closed the chapter on what organizing leaders in the Fain administration had previously called a “movement moment,” raising questions about the way forward.

One aspect of the way forward would include parts plants. Briefly, the 2008 crash and subsequent restructuring drove a wave of closures and mergers, leaving a more centralized parts sector with fewer, but larger, facilities across the Midwest and South. Yet, despite the organizing advantage of a more concentrated supply chain and recent signals of rank-and-file militancy, the UAW has not pursued a sectoral effort to organize parts plants.

While not mutually exclusive, these setbacks and missed opportunities point to an underlying weakness of more narrowly targeting “bread-and-butter” demands (like wages and benefits), rather than issues of workplace conditions and control (like maintaining production standards, protections from new technology and outsourcing, union control over training, immigrant protections, product decisions and commitment, and so on). It is a lot easier for the company to shift its finances to take the wind out of the sails of an organizing drive than to fundamentally relinquish control over its operation. Campaigns like these take longer because they depend on developing ideological worker-leaders, but that work is essential to waging class struggle on a larger scale.

THE ZERO-SUM TRAP

Given the challenges posed to organizing and by the EV transition, the UAW has turned to supporting protectionist trade policies in hopes of tipping the balance in its favor. But in doing so it has accepted a false premise: that North American autoworkers are locked in a zero-sum competition for jobs.

In a comprehensive policy paper, the UAW argues that, “If the production-to-sales ratio in the United States were 1-to-1, we would manufacture nearly 6 million more cars per year. ” But because most of the current imbalance comes from a highly integrated supply chain across North America, they are essentially saying that Mexican and Canadian workers should give up their jobs to American workers.

Shawn Fain’s administration, aligning with past UAW presidents Bob King and Ron Gettlefinger, is right to blame NAFTA and other pro-business trade policies for undermining labor’s strength. But it is actually UAW’s lack of international solidarity and inability to avoid harms to workers from technological advancement and industry restructuring that led Fain to cheer on Trump’s tariffs.

Even if we accept the UAW’s reshoring premise, corporations would need billions of dollars of investment to ramp up domestic production (as was the case when investment flowed for Mexican auto industry expansion). But the automakers have already been burned by whiplash from Biden to Trump. The rollback of the Inflation Reduction Act and tariffs have cost them billions in their scramble to restructure under Trump’s new policies. If the state makes an onshoring push or attempts to accelerate EVs again, corporations will extract concessions from the federal government and demand strong assurances before moving forward. Such state-capital alignment premised on appeasing corporations would surely further undermine labor.

The scant evidence of reshoring under the current 25 percent tariffs on Mexican and Canadian vehicles and Trump’s inability to push his nationalist agenda further are signs of capitalism’s strength and inertia. The conditions that limit a Mexican autoworker’s daily pay to what a Michigan autoworker makes in an hour cannot be undone without class struggle. And, in any case, to bankroll such a massive pivot in a short period would require either increasing vehicle prices or massive amounts of federal subsidies and loans, or both.

Why accept this zero-sum framing? And if the federal government is going to cough up billions, why let them give it to corporations again and not workers?

BEYOND PROTECTIONISM AND COMPETITION

The recent uptick in protectionist policies is already eroding the possibility of cross-border solidarity, perpetuating the downward spiral of union power. The impact on the United States’s “most loyal ally” has led former research director of the Canadian Auto Workers, Sam Gindin, to conclude that, “Canadian auto isn’t in ‘crisis’, it’s in danger of extinction.” With pressure from Trump’s tariffs, GM’s CAMI and Stellantis Brampton plants each recently shuttered. The same month as Canadian workers rallied against these shutdowns, UAW cheered the move of these jobs from Canada to the United States, enabling cross-border whipsawing. At the same time, US trade policy has already led many Mexican parts plants at the border to close, impacting tens of thousands of workers. Lear Corporation is relocating a Juarez plant to find cheaper labor in Honduras, threatening the possibility of bigger capital flight.

If a substantial increase in domestic production does occur, it will likely happen at nonunion plants in the South, like Toyota’s recent expansion in Texas or Hyundai’s in Georgia. This will continue to erode unionized market share if organizing drives do not pick up, and corporations will continue to use every restructuring period to advance their technological frontier, which arcs towards requiring fewer work-hours to produce a single vehicle.

What’s more, a protectionist orientation subordinates the union to state interests. At a Rutgers University bargaining training in November 2025, Chris Brooks (Fain’s former Chief of Staff) revealed that the Trump trade officials the UAW was negotiating with would stop responding whenever Fain said something that the Trump administration did not approve of. This kind of engagement belies the misguided view that the ‘antiworker’ Trump administration will be swayed through lobbying and that the union’s strength can grow through alignment with whichever party is in power.

But the backdrop to Trump’s and UAW’s turn to protectionism are the deeper forces of capitalist competition that continue to shift control away from workers toward management. As Kim Moody convincingly argues in On New Terrain, the lion’s share of the decrease in the manufacturing workforce over the last few decades is due to increasing work intensification, new management tools to control workers, and the continued rise in “productivity,” rather than offshoring or increased imports. Even through waves of offshoring, the US light-vehicle annual production rate trends modestly upward (if you smooth out the ups and downs of the market).

Today, the evolving technological frontier entails a combination of cobots (collaborative robots), humanoid robots, AI-modified manufacturing processes, and new assembly platforms like the one Ford is launching, all of which are already displacing or on track to displace future work. I witnessed the leading edge of automation when I worked in the “Body” department at Factory Zero. My work involved aligning and staging stamped sheets of metal for robots to pick up and weld. In so-called “dark factories” in China, this part of the process has been essentially fully automated, meaning workers are not needed and the lights can be turned off.

Neither US automakers nor the UAW has an answer to increasing competition from Chinese corporations, which now build three out of every four EVs produced globally. Without a secure plan for workers, if the United States were to suddenly drop its auto tariffs against Chinese vehicles, or let Chinese companies enter the United States (as Trump recently toyed with), conditions for US workers would enter a tailspin. For the labor movement, solidarity with Chinese autoworkers is a true puzzle, but a necessary one to solve.

To make headway on these questions, workers must realize their power actually lies in class independence and solidarity with their working class allies internationally. So far, however, the UAW has sided with short-term gains over long-term power building. The UAW must rethink its zero-sum assumptions and understand that the way to break the false choice between protectionism and international competition is through a commitment to fighting over workplace and industry control with a path toward collectively controlled manufacturing that meets working-class needs.

Of course, these ideas are not new: Through the late 1940s, workers set their own pace on machines, which allowed them to establish simple forms of workers’ control over the speed of work. In the 1960s, the UAW helped organize World Auto Councils to unite workers across countries in shared fights against multinational corporations. French and German autoworkers have made progress on reducing their workweek. And workers around the world, like in the UK, Canada, Italy, Argentina, and elsewhere have long fought for collectively controlled manufacturing.

Some starting points for such a program within the UAW could include political education campaigns, preparing stewards and rank-and-file members to take over plants threatened with closure, or pressure against the next administration to launch manufacturing facilities controlled by UAW workers. While the specific implementation lies beyond the scope of this analysis, such an effort must expand capacity for worker self-organization rather than simply replace a capitalist boss with a state technocrat. Even one success would be significant, as it would demonstrate how public funding enables planning of socially useful manufacturing, while shifting the paradigm away from both business unionism and protectionist cooperation. Paired with winning policies like a shorter workweek, this path would build working-class power and could secure millions of jobs for decades to come.

LIVE TO FIGHT ANOTHER DAY?

“We did what we had to do to get to tomorrow,” said Ron Gettlefinger, UAW president who oversaw the negotiations of the concessionary contracts following the 2008 crash. Tomorrow has now arrived, and the depth of the well-documented UAW decline should be an alarming call to action. The union had 1.5 million active members primarily in the auto industry in 1979, but today has roughly 400,000, with only about 150,000 in the Big Three.

Over the last twenty years, unionized US plants have dropped dramatically from around forty-five down to below twenty-five, with nonunion plants in Mexico and the US South increasing to fill the gap (Figure 2).

This restructuring is easily seen by comparing auto employment in a few major states in the Midwest and the South (Figure 1, bottom-left panel). The Midwest workforce dramatically decreased leading up to and during the 2008 crash. Southern states, like Alabama, Kentucky, and Texas, now surpass Ohio and Missouri in assembly worker counts.

With the exception of the recent expansion into the Volkswagen plant, the union foothold has been set by the number of Big Three assembly workers, as well as some parts plants. In 1990, over half a million workers across the entire sector were unionized, including assembly and parts plants. Today, that number is below two hundred thousand.

Average real wages across the entire assembly subsector, accounting for inflation, were relatively flat around $25 per hour from 1990 until the 2008 crash; after the collapse, wages dipped below $20 per hour (in 2000 dollars; Figure 1, upper-right panel). They have still not recovered, and even the top rate from the UAW-GM contract in 2028 will be below the precrash inflation-adjusted average.

Meanwhile, although more challenging to interpret due to periodic economic fluctuations, the productivity rate increase (or the decrease in the number of work-hours required to produce a vehicle) since 1990 outpaces sales growth roughly by a factor of three—1.7 percent to 0.6 percent per year (Figure 1, bottom-right panel). The decrease in productivity over the last decade—likely due to the launch of new EV manufacturing—is becoming less of a factor, especially with the recent EV reversals. This is further evidence that with each restructuring, corporations continue to need fewer workers.

LABOR PEACE AND THE SEEDS IT BURIED

To best respond to the shifting terrain, the UAW would do well to tend to seeds planted about a century ago.

The GM sit-down strike of 1936 took place during a time when industry-wide wins were born from class struggle waged by ideologically-minded militant workers willing to take collective risks and execute aggressive tactics during upsurges. This layer of worker-leaders was made up of organized socialists and other militant trade unionists ready to build fighting strategies. Studying history shows that such working class breakthroughs did not rely solely on spontaneity, but required years of organization building, political education, and deep connections to the surrounding community.

But the union-management collaboration that grew during this period of class struggle now has a stranglehold over the UAW. This tendency finally won out when UAW President Walter Reuther signed the Treaty of Detroit in 1950 codifying a regime of labor peace in exchange for a bigger cut of capital’s growth. The UAW agreed to longer contract durations, “no strike” clauses during the life of the contract, stronger management rights provisions, and an increasingly bureaucratic grievance procedure. Decades later, this ideology of labor peace was eventually institutionalized through joint programs, the system of cogovernance between the UAW and management that became the vehicle for union corruption and led to further cooptation of the union bureaucracy.

At my UAW-GM orientation, the joint programs official said nothing about the grievance procedure or shopfloor fights, but repeated the following phrase for what felt like a hundred times: “don’t be late, be on time, do your job.” The lesson he imparted to hundreds of new UAW members, many of whom were young Detroiters who had never been in a union before, was simple: management is in charge.

Even as individual workers stayed relatively well-off, labor’s aggregate share of capital’s gains plummeted along with UAW membership count after its 1970s peak. Worse, over the last two decades, the average share per worker has declined (Figure 1; top-right panel). Yet, throughout this decline, the union’s culture of collaboration and business unionism has prevailed. This perspective has resulted in the UAW focusing narrowly on wage and benefit fights, rather than control over jobs or production decisions.

Under the current UAW administration, the lack of a plan for the future of auto manufacturing is concomitant with Fain’s political approach: a form of progressive bureaucratic unionism that, despite its militant rhetoric, has ultimately been captured by the top-down bureaucracy he previously ran against. This limitation stems largely from Fain’s orientation toward internal union maneuvering rather than the rank and file—an approach that quickly ran into political headwinds. The fact that only about 7 percent of the UAW membership voted for him in the recent election with 90 percent not voting at all, shows the deep disconnection between the membership and his slate’s program. More importantly, Fain’s perspective—as well as recent proposed strategies from UAW organizers—does not grapple with labor’s key barrier: the continued avoidance to fight for worker control over capital’s decision-making power.

In this period of limited class struggle, what does it mean for workers to organize themselves with a goal of developing class struggle?

SEEDS OF CLASS STRUGGLE STRATEGY

Workers looking to go on offense for the long haul ought to revive the class struggle unionism of the further past. Key to this work is continuously identifying where workers have been organizing themselves to fight collectively over their material conditions. Even in a time when the organized left is weak, workers in nonunion Toyota plants in the South have been staging walkouts against mandatory overtime, GM workers fought job mergers through work-to-rule campaigns, and parts workers voted down three contracts, to name a few instances.

In the absence of either a working class party or a socialist party with a broad working-class character, building independent left organization within industrial workplaces is a way to develop worker-leaders who see both the possibilities and limitations of shop floor struggles. Shop floor militancy can improve conditions and win reforms, but will not challenge capital’s exploitation at scale on its own. Coming up against those limits advances the conclusion that the fight is not against a single boss but the system that every boss answers to, and that winning it requires a revolutionary rupture with capitalism.

Independent self-organized working-class formations anchored by socialists and radicals take years to build and are important both to resist the coercive forces of the union bureaucracy and the ruling class parties and to introduce bold class struggle strategies to fight for the working class’s future.

Worker-led formations like Unite All Workers for Democracy and the Southern Workers Assembly (SWA) are putting such class struggle strategies to the test. At their core, these strategies begin by recognizing that the working class and capitalist class are fundamentally at odds and focusing on bottom-up militant approaches to expand worker control. Vying for control starts small—for example, resisting unilateral management decisions on the shop floor or winning job security during downturns—but it must expand to decisions over production, the industry, and ultimately over society as a whole. This control concerns political questions about the movement of people and wars abroad as much as economic organization.

UAWD is committed to a “vision of class struggle unionism and fighting to build a militant, democratic UAW.” Rather than focusing on reforming the UAW, it has prioritized developing worker-leaders who can draw their coworkers into shop-floor struggles over working conditions and workplace control. That means running work-to-rule campaigns, resisting mandatory overtime, fighting layoffs, and preparing members to strike over economic and political issues like ICE escalations. It also laid out a long-sighted vision for a worker-led transition to EVs and public transit. UAWD pursues this program in three ways: it supports worker-leaders in building chapters in UAW Locals that are rooted in shop-floor action; it runs trainings on class struggle unionism; and it carries out a political education program by producing and distributing its publication, Daily Struggle, online and to more than one hundred UAW workplaces.

There is a fundamental difference between class struggle unionism and reform-based strategies —like that of a group of leaders who split from UAWD in April 2025 to form UAW Member Action, a Labor Notes-backed project. Reform strategies focus on installing better leaders, improving grievance handling, or making the union more democratic: on their own these strategies cannot challenge the paradigm of labor peace or address the crisis facing working people. Class struggle strategies seek to transform relations between capital and labor in the workplace and beyond.

SWA’s scope is broader than the UAW, but some of its main organizing targets are nonunion auto plants in the South, emphasizing that fights must be anchored in communities and expand beyond the contours of existing labor law if workers are to win. One of its core efforts is their rank-and-file project, helping militants secure jobs in strategic workplaces—like EV plants—to build power.

Finally, it is crucial to see the strategy of class struggle unionism and the vision of collectively controlled manufacturing as parts of the same whole. Without an internationalist worker-led program, a zero-sum trade logic will short circuit the possibility of expanding solidarity and will trap workers into competing against each other as new technology and industry restructuring continues to erode jobs. On the other hand, these goals cannot be achieved by simply asking nicely. They can only be won through militancy, self-organized working-class formations, and a cohesive vision for the future of manufacturing shared by rank-and-file workers. Ultimately, these efforts build toward a socialist horizon: transforming the entire industry to be run for social benefit rather than private profit.

For the UAW and the entire working class, it will be impossible to reverse the decline of the labor movement, let alone go on offense, through piecemeal reforms or tinkering with organizing tactics. As we approach the 2030s, a new layer of committed worker-leaders with a political vision is direly needed to lead their coworkers in the fight for control over the future of manufacturing.

text:
The Federation Says Intensifying Competition Could Erase 2.2 Trillion Won In South Korean EV Exports by 2030, Calling for Tax Credits And Other Support To Strengthen Domestic Production Base

An analysis has shown that if the trend of expanding exports of Chinese electric vehicles continues, about 2.2 trillion won (aboiut $1.64 billion) of South Korea’s electric vehicle exports in 2030 could be eroded due to intensifying competition. The Federation of Korean Industries suggested that tax support and other measures should be considered to strengthen the domestic electric vehicle production base.

The Federation of Korean Industries stated this on Nov. 4 through its analysis titled ‘Current Status and Implications of South Korean Electric Vehicle Exports and Competitiveness.’ The target of the export analysis is electric vehicles, which combine battery electric vehicles (BEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), while the domestic market share was based on battery electric vehicles.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the proportion of electric vehicles in global new car sales expanded about tenfold from 2.6% in 2019 to 25.0% last year. It is projected to increase to 29% this year.

In contrast, the domestic and international market share of South Korean electric vehicles has declined. In the domestic battery electric vehicle market, the proportion of domestic cars decreased by 16.7%p from 73.7% in 2019 to 57.0% last year. During the same period, South Korea’s share of the global electric vehicle export market also fell by 4.3%p from 8.9% to 4.6%. In particular, the export share has dropped for two consecutive years after recording 8.1% in 2023.

The gap with China has also narrowed in export comparative advantage indicators. The Revealed Comparative Advantage (RCA) index of South Korean electric vehicles, calculated by the Federation of Korean Industries using UN Comtrade data, dropped by nearly half from 2.92 in 2023 to 1.48 last year.

The RCA is an indicator that compares the proportion a specific item takes up in a country’s total exports with the proportion that the item takes up in global exports. If it is greater than 1, it is interpreted that there is a comparative advantage in the export of the relevant item.

The RCA of Chinese electric vehicles rose from 0.19 in 2019 to 1.49 last year, reaching a level similar to that of South Korea. This contrasts with South Korea’s non-electric vehicle RCA, which increased from 1.76 to 2.54 during the same period.

Differences also appeared in the Trade Specialization Index (TSI), which shows the export and import structure. The TSI is the value obtained by dividing net exports by total exports and imports, and the closer it is to 1, the higher the level of export specialization.

The TSI of South Korean electric vehicles fell from 0.70 in 2023 to 0.50 last year. On the other hand, China rose from -0.79 in 2017 to 0.97 last year. The analysis indicates that while China transitioned from being import-centric to export-centric in electric vehicles, South Korea’s level of export specialization weakened.

The Federation of Korean Industries estimated South Korea’s exposure to competition risk by assuming a scenario where the upward trend in China’s global electric vehicle export share from 2023 to 2025 continues until 2030. As a result, it found that about $1.61 billion, or about 2.2 trillion won, could be exposed to competition risk. This is equivalent to 14.7% of South Korea’s electric vehicle export value last year.

This estimate is the result of a scenario analysis applying China’s additional market share increase based on last year’s export value. The Federation of Korean Industries explained that this analysis focused on examining the relative export specialization of domestic production and did not evaluate the global competitiveness, technology, or productivity of companies themselves, including overseas production and sales.

Lee Sang-ho, head of the Economic Affairs Division at the Federation of Korean Industries, emphasized, “The Chinese electric vehicle industry is rapidly pre-empting the future automotive market thanks to strong support from its government,” and added, “It is necessary to consider policy support measures such as domestic production tax credits to expand the domestic electric vehicle production base.”

text:
The UK Battery Industrialisation Centre (UKBIC) will hold an online seminar examining the trends expected to shape the battery industry over the next 12–24 months.

The webinar will take place from 11–11.45am GMT on 24 November 2026. UKBIC chief technology officer Richard LeCain will present the market outlook, with external affairs director Jonathan Smith also taking part.

Topics will include the slowdown in the automotive market and the increasing convergence of electric vehicle and battery energy storage system technologies. LeCain will also consider China’s position in the global battery sector and the emergence of battery innovation driven by defence requirements.

Other subjects on the agenda include the commercial prospects for sodium-ion cells, electrification in aviation and advanced air mobility, and the effect of Foreign Entity of Concern regulations on the development of sovereign battery supply chains.

The presentation follows a battery market outlook delivered by LeCain in 2025. UKBIC said the forthcoming session would offer an updated perspective on the challenges and opportunities facing the industry through 2027 and beyond.

Based in Coventry, UKBIC is an open-access facility intended to bridge the gap between battery research and high-volume manufacturing. It forms part of the UK government’s Battery Innovation Programme, funded by the Department for Business and Trade and delivered by Innovate UK.

text:
In 2021, across much of the country, Winter Storm Uri caused utilities to scramble for power as the use of electricity and natural gas increased. In addition to facing transmission constraints, utilities couldn’t generate enough power due to issues with fuel supply and equipment malfunctions. In Nebraska, in an effort to preserve the grid and prevent a system-wide failure, the Omaha Public Power District, or OPPD, conducted rolling blackouts. Afterward, the Southwest Power Pool, which manages the region’s grid reliability, required its members to keep more power capacity in reserve in case of future emergency situations.

In the following years, the data center boom, electrification, and growth from other industries have brought utilities around the country the promise of new customers and the challenge of a huge spike in demand. As a result, OPPD, which serves about 419,000 customers across eastern Nebraska, is running low on the amount of energy capacity it can promise to new and expanding economic development projects. The shortage is threatening the region’s ability to develop economically, attract companies, add jobs, and grow.

What’s more, OPPD is facing the same challenges that are plaguing utilities and electric grids across the country: Power plants and other electric grid infrastructure are aging. Demand for energy is still growing. Climate change is straining the grid in real time. All the while, communities in Nebraska oppose the renewable energy developments that could solve some of these issues.

OPPD currently projects it has less than 100 megawatts of available power capacity for new or expanding large customers for the next few years. (For reference, a large data center could require as much as 1,000 megawatts of capacity, and manufacturing facilities can range from a few megawatts to over 100 megawatts.) That figure could vary depending on customer commitments and new energy generation coming online, and OPPD asserted that the utility has enough power capacity to support typical residential and commercial growth. But essentially, OPPD president and CEO Javier Fernandez said, any new or expanding development requiring 2 megawatts or more might have to wait to receive service. Fernandez will be leaving the utility at the end of the year, according to a recent internal announcement.

Economic development leaders are concerned that if power capacity in Nebraska’s largest metropolitan area remains limited, the Omaha area and the state as a whole will be put at a competitive disadvantage for growth opportunities like new businesses, jobs, and increased tax revenue. This comes as the state is projected to face a $208 million deficit next year. Compared to 2022, state income tax revenues this past year were $703 million lower.

“We are bending over backwards. We’re trying to figure out creative solutions,” Fernandez told Grist. “How do we bridge this? Can we buy capacity from other utilities? Literally, no one has excess capacity. Everyone is in the same boat as we are, so now the pinch, so to speak, it’s, well, growth has to slow down, maybe?”

At the same time, OPPD is doing long-term planning to determine what its energy and system needs will be over the next 10 years. To meet the demand, the utility and its board face a decision about how much to expand OPPD’s energy portfolio. On the low end, the utility could add about 1,000 megawatts, but, according to OPPD’s initial planning results, the utility might more than double its portfolio. For context, OPPD’s portfolio currently contains 4,583 megawatts of energy capacity

And while more generation capacity is coming online over the next few years, the projections for energy demand remain high. Companies with nearly 2,000 megawatts of economic development projects are planning to come to the area and are actively in OPPD’s queue through 2031, according to a September presentation. There are about 5,000 megawatts worth of other potential projects on the radar that are considering the area.

Fernandez said the utility knows that not all of the projects will actually come to fruition. Nevertheless, if the utility builds too small, the Omaha metro could end up back in the same shortage for economic development. If the utility builds too big and the usage from big customers doesn’t materialize, OPPD’s ratepayers will likely have to eat the costs.

Nailing the projections and actually building new generation — such as renewable energy and natural gas sources — will be a big challenge. Two OPPD board members said it would be helpful if state and local leaders were on the same page with clear economic development plans to guide priorities for how much energy the region will need.

OPPD declined to comment on what portion of its queue is made up of data centers, manufacturers, or other types of customers. According to a presentation in March, a chart of the utility’s current peak demand shows industrial customers represent 32 percent, residential customers make up 41 percent, and commercial customers are 27 percent. By 2035, industrial customers are expected to make up 52 percent.

“Clearly, data centers have been a very, very big force on that increase,” Fernandez said.

“The biggest question my board is likely going to have to answer is going to be how big of a plan we approve,” Fernandez said. “And that is going to be informed by… state, counties, cities, chambers: How much do you want us to grow?”

In September, Heath Mello, the Greater Omaha Chamber’s president and CEO, sent a letter to OPPD’s board calling for the utility to plan farther out than 2036 and strongly consider building for more growth. Paul West, chair of the chamber’s board, said that the chamber hopes to recruit and expand industries like manufacturing.

Economic development could help solve big problems – the state’s budget shortfall, high property taxes, and brain drain. But energy is one of the top two reasons that the chamber loses deals to other locations. And any new manufacturing will have to compete for power with potential data center customers considering the region. This matches a trend being seen across the U.S., said Larry Gigerich, chair of the Site Selectors Guild.

Utilities like OPPD have an obligation to serve all customers, but state and local governments can incentivize and disincentivize for the kind of growth they want to see, Fernandez said. The competition for electricity with data centers is “causing manufacturing companies now to be more proactive and to use their voice more directly with utilities versus the way they have done it for decades,” Gigerich said. “Now it’s a true competition, and we can’t generate enough new power fast enough to meet everybody’s needs.”

Projecting demand is one thing. Getting electricity-generating projects built is quite another. To meet the growing demand and to keep costs low, OPPD is looking at building more natural gas and renewables. Both of these options come with their own challenges.

The current popularity of natural gas has constrained the equipment supply chain, which means it could take the utility much longer to build. And while renewables face some up-front cost increases, they remain the lowest cost energy source to operate. However, OPPD has struggled to bring these projects online, because some communities in the state have turned them away. The tension has been building for years as misinformation has spread and projects were kept secret by developers. Residents across the state have rejected clean-energy proposals over concerns about fire risks and potential damages to prime agricultural land and local infrastructure.

Fernandez said that some community leaders have rejected renewable generation only to ask for more power capacity to attract new economic development. “Everyone is saying no, and then we end up in a really bad place,” he said.

With the demand for power growing, something has to give, otherwise OPPD might not be able to generate the power it needs to help Nebraska grow.

“If Omaha doesn’t grow, if Omaha doesn’t prosper, the rest of the state very likely won’t,” Fernandez said. “What the state wants versus what the city wants versus what the chambers want — well, they all want different things. But the one common denominator that I keep hearing is jobs and income.”

title: HizonSun Expands OEM and ODM EV Charger Manufacturing for Global Brands - Detroit Free Press
description:
Growing Demand for Customized EV Charging Equipment The expansion of electric mobility has created different charging requirements across international markets.
These varying requirements have increased the importance of OEM and ODM manufacturing in the EV charging industry.
A Diverse Portfolio of AC and DC EV Chargers Product diversity is another important consideration for global brands selecting an EV charger manufacturing partner.
Compared with conventional AC charging, DC charging systems are designed to deliver higher power levels for applications that require shorter charging periods.
HizonSun brings together AC and DC charging equipment, integrated manufacturing processes, proprietary technical resources, and OEM and ODM customization services.
text:
KUNSHAN, JIANGSU, CHINA, November 4, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ — As electric vehicle adoption continues to reshape the global automotive industry, demand for reliable and customizable charging infrastructure is increasing across residential, commercial, and public applications. For automotive brands, charging network operators, and equipment distributors, finding a manufacturing partner capable of delivering flexible product configurations and consistent production quality has become an important part of market development. HizonSun, officially known as Suzhou HizonSun Tech Co., Ltd., provides OEM and ODM EV charger manufacturing services supported by in-house research and development, integrated production capabilities, and a diverse portfolio of AC and DC charging equipment.

Growing Demand for Customized EV Charging Equipment

The expansion of electric mobility has created different charging requirements across international markets. Residential users generally prioritize convenient installation, compatibility, and ease of operation, while commercial operators focus on charging efficiency, equipment capacity, operational management, and long-term reliability. Public charging networks also require solutions that can accommodate different vehicle standards, site conditions, and traffic volumes.

These varying requirements have increased the importance of OEM and ODM manufacturing in the EV charging industry. OEM services allow brands to develop products under their own identities while utilizing an established manufacturer’s production capabilities. ODM services provide additional flexibility through product design, engineering development, and customized configurations.

HizonSun addresses these requirements by offering customized manufacturing services for automakers, charging brands, operators, real estate developers, and other customers. Its product development and manufacturing capabilities support different charging scenarios, allowing customers to evaluate suitable equipment configurations according to their target markets and project requirements.

Integrated Manufacturing and Research Capabilities

Founded in 2018, Suzhou HizonSun Tech Co., Ltd. is a high-tech enterprise integrating research and development, production, and sales of new energy vehicle charging equipment. The company has established branches in Jiangsu, Shenzhen, Wuhan, and Gansu, building an operational foundation for its charging equipment business.

An important part of its manufacturing development was the launch of a new 10,000-square-meter factory in 2021. The production base in Kunshan, Jiangsu, incorporates manufacturing facilities covering multiple stages of the production process. Rather than relying entirely on external suppliers, HizonSun operates an integrated industrial chain that includes research and development, mold design, injection molding, surface-mount technology (SMT), sheet metal processing, cable assembly, and final product assembly.

This integrated structure supports coordination between product engineering and manufacturing. It also provides a foundation for managing customized specifications, component integration, and production consistency. According to the company’s published information, its annual manufacturing capacity exceeds 500,000 units, providing production support for different customer requirements and market segments.

HizonSun also reports having more than 50 intellectual property rights, including invention patents, design patents, utility model patents, and software copyrights related to AC/DC charging systems and cloud service platforms. These technical resources contribute to its ability to develop charging equipment and supporting software solutions.

A Diverse Portfolio of AC and DC EV Chargers

Product diversity is another important consideration for global brands selecting an EV charger manufacturing partner. HizonSun’s product portfolio covers AC EV chargers and DC charging piles, with configurations designed for residential, commercial, and public charging applications.

AC EV Chargers for Residential and Commercial Applications

AC EV chargers are widely used in homes, workplaces, parking facilities, and other locations where vehicles can remain connected for extended periods. HizonSun offers AC charging equipment with power options ranging from 3.5 kW to 44 kW across its listed product categories and configurations.

Its product range includes wall-mounted and floor-standing models, as well as different connector and charging configurations. The company also lists customizable 22–44 kW AC charging stations designed for European, American, and Chinese market standards, including IEC/Type 2, SAE/Type 1, and Chinese-standard options.

For OEM and ODM customers, these product variations provide a basis for developing charging equipment that reflects regional requirements, installation environments, and brand positioning.

DC Fast Chargers for Public and Commercial Networks

DC fast charging equipment plays an important role in public charging stations, highway service areas, commercial parking facilities, and fleet charging operations. Compared with conventional AC charging, DC charging systems are designed to deliver higher power levels for applications that require shorter charging periods.

HizonSun’s product range includes integrated DC charging stations from 20 kW to 240 kW and other configurations reaching 360 kW. The company also lists split-type DC charging systems with power configurations ranging from 360 kW to 720 kW.

These products offer different approaches to equipment installation and power distribution. Integrated systems combine major charging components within a single unit, while split-type configurations separate the power cabinet from charging terminals. This provides project developers with different options depending on available space, charging demand, and site layout.

Additional product configurations include dual-gun charging stations, advertising-screen-equipped DC chargers, and models supporting different charging standards, such as GB/T, CCS1, CCS2, and IEC-related configurations, depending on the specific product.

Energy Storage Integrated Charging Solutions

Energy storage is becoming increasingly relevant to charging infrastructure planning, particularly where grid capacity, electricity demand management, and renewable energy integration are important considerations.

HizonSun’s portfolio also includes energy storage integrated charging equipment, with listed configurations of 100 kWh and 200 kWh. These systems combine energy storage and EV charging functions within an integrated solution concept.

For commercial projects, this type of equipment can provide additional flexibility in energy management and charging infrastructure planning. Its suitability depends on local electricity conditions, system configuration, and project-specific requirements.

OEM and ODM Services for International Brands

Beyond its standard product range, HizonSun provides customized manufacturing services intended to support different business models in the EV charging market. For international brands, OEM manufacturing can help establish a product line without requiring the buyer to independently develop every production process and manufacturing facility.

ODM cooperation offers another approach for customers seeking more extensive product customization. Depending on the project, relevant considerations may include charging power, equipment structure, enclosure design, connector standards, installation methods, and software-related functions.

HizonSun also reports having an independently developed DC control system and an intelligent control platform. Its software capabilities support remote upgrades, remote control, automatic settlement, and customized development. The company has additionally developed an EV Charging Network cloud management and operation supervision platform, connecting charging equipment with digital management functions.

These capabilities are relevant to operators and brands that need to consider not only the physical charger but also equipment monitoring and operational management. However, the specific functions and integration requirements should be evaluated according to each customer’s project specifications.

Quality Certifications and Global Market Development

Product compliance is a significant consideration for EV charger suppliers serving multiple international markets. Different regions may apply different electrical safety requirements, charging standards, and certification procedures.

HizonSun states that it holds ISO 9001, CQC, CE, CB, and UL certifications. Its product portfolio also includes models designed for different regional charging standards. For international buyers, confirming the certification scope and applicable product model before procurement remains essential.

The company reports that its products are exported to more than 40 countries and regions, including markets in the United States, Europe, and Southeast Asia. It also operates 36 global sales and service centers, supporting its international business development and customer service activities.

With its combination of manufacturing infrastructure, technical development, product diversity, and customized production services, HizonSun continues to position itself as an EV charging equipment manufacturing partner for global brands and project developers.

Supporting the Next Stage of EV Charging Infrastructure

As electric vehicle markets develop, the requirements for charging equipment manufacturers are becoming more diverse. Buyers increasingly need manufacturing partners that can coordinate product engineering, regional specifications, production management, and intelligent charging functions within a connected supply chain.

HizonSun brings together AC and DC charging equipment, integrated manufacturing processes, proprietary technical resources, and OEM and ODM customization services. Its product portfolio serves multiple charging scenarios, from residential wallbox installations to high-power public charging stations and energy storage integrated systems.

For international distributors, automotive brands, charging operators, and project developers evaluating manufacturing cooperation, these capabilities provide a foundation for exploring customized EV charging solutions aligned with different market requirements.

title: Democrats sweep US midterms, lift Korea batteries while tariffs stay firm - CHOSUNBIZ
description: Democratic sweep seen boosting Korea’s green energy suppliers while presidential control keeps tariffs and autos steady In the U.S.
text:
In the U.S. midterm elections held on the 3rd local time, a landslide victory by the opposition Democratic Party appears all but certain. As the Democratic Party, which advocates pro-environment energy policies, is projected to sweep both the House and Senate, many expect Korea's battery makers and companies related to renewable energy such as solar and wind to benefit. The impact on industries such as autos, steel and shipbuilding is expected to be limited.
On the 4th, a screen at the Woori Bank dealing room in Jung-gu, Seoul displays a video related to the U.S. midterm elections along with the KOSPI and other indexes. /Courtesy of Yonhap News
Major U.S. outlets including CNN and NBC reported after 10 p.m. on the 3rd local time that the Democratic Party is projected to take control of not only the House but also the Senate. The "blue tsunami," a blowout victory surpassing a narrow "blue wave," has materialized. It is the first time in 20 years since 2006 that the opposition has recaptured both the House and Senate in a midterm election.
President Donald Trump effectively conceded defeat in an interview with the New York Times (NYT) that day, saying, "I fully accept the results. We will work with the Democratic Party."
◇ Pro-environment policies expand again… battery and solar stocks surge
Samsung Securities said in a report released last month, "If the Democratic Party wins the midterms, policies such as the Republican-led reduction of subsidies for renewable energy and the end of the investment tax credit (ITC) could be revised," adding, "This would act positively for Korean companies in related sectors."
The ITC, which applies to renewable energy such as solar power generation, is a program under the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) that deducts up to 30% of initial facility investment expense from taxes. The ITC had been set to remain in place through 2032, but last June, under Republican leadership, the scheduled end date was moved up by four years to 2028. With the Democratic Party now controlling both chambers, there is a possibility that the end date will be extended again or support will be strengthened.
A view of the Qcells factory in Cartersville, United States /Courtesy of Hanwha Solutions
The production tax credit (PTC) that supports onshore wind power generation has also grown more likely to be extended due to the Democratic victory. The PTC likewise faced early termination under the "One Big, Beautiful Bill (OBBBA)," pushed through last July by the Trump administration and Republicans. OBBBA is a bill that significantly revises or moves up the expiration of renewable energy tax credit programs contained in the existing IRA.
Samsung Securities analyzed, "If the Democratic victory changes the makeup of Congress, we can look forward to easing the schedule for ending subsidies or readjusting support measures for renewable energy," adding, "If expectations for policy changes grow, new project development will also resume."
Many also expect the battery industry to benefit. The Democratic Party, through an energy agenda released in May, outlined plans to expand investment in the national power grid and energy storage systems (ESS). In addition, the Trump administration and Republicans will likely find it harder to push additional legislation that suppresses demand for electric vehicles, which appears helpful for the battery industry.
Hyundai Motor Securities projected, "If the Democratic Party takes control of both chambers, it is expected to pursue the restoration of renewable energy tax credits and an expansion of ESS investment," adding, "Both Democrats and Republicans have previously toughened tariff policies on Chinese batteries, so the direction of blocking China's supply chain will remain after the election."
Shares of renewable energy and battery manufacturers rose in Korea's stock market that day. Hanwha Solutions jumped 22.7% from the previous day, and HD Hyundai Energy Solutions climbed 16.3%. LG Energy Solution rose 4.3% and Samsung SDI gained 9.3%, ending regular-session trading higher.
◇ Tariffs are an executive-branch power… autos and steel unlikely to see major changes
Industries such as autos and steel, which were hit hard by high tariffs after the Trump administration took office, are not expected to see major changes. That is because changes to energy-related programs fall under Congress, but tariffs and trade policy are the sole authority of the president and the executive branch.
Authorities over tariffs and trade policy, such as Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act, are unlikely to undergo a major shift even if the Democratic Party sweeps both chambers. Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (MUFG) also said in a report released that day, "Tariffs and trade policy are areas under presidential control," adding, "In any case, the impact from the election will be limited."
Chung Eui-sun, chairman of Hyundai Motor Group, attends the completion ceremony for Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America (HMGMA) in Ellabell, Georgia, United States, on Mar. 26, 2025 (local time), and signs a commemorative autograph on a produced IONIQ 5. /Courtesy of Hyundai Motor
There are also projections that the electric vehicle market is unlikely to rebound. The Trump administration ended the tax credit of up to $7,500 for new EV buyers at the end of September last year.
As a result, with U.S. sales of electric vehicles— a downstream industry— plunging, Korean battery makers were also hit hard. Emissions and fuel economy regulations were eased, further reducing demand in the EV market.
Hana Securities said, "Even if the Democratic Party wins the midterms, it will be difficult to expect a recovery in the EV market," adding, "Fuel economy regulations are a matter of executive orders and are unrelated to a change in congressional power."
The shipbuilding sector is also expected to see little change. As the Trump administration reached out to bolster the competitiveness of U.S. shipbuilding, Korean shipbuilders had grown more hopeful about rising demand.
If Republicans had won the midterms, the Korea-U.S. shipbuilding cooperation project "MASGA" might have gained speed, but with the Democratic Party's landslide, significant changes are unlikely for the time being.
◇ AI data centers could contract… cautious views say "Democrats have limited interest in green policies"
There are concerns that investment in AI-related infrastructure such as data centers will face setbacks. The Democratic Party has shown moves to toughen regulations on AI.
According to a poll by Reuters last month, about 80% of Democratic supporters favored stronger AI regulation. Resistance has grown over higher electricity bills and environmental damage stemming from building AI data centers.
KB Securities also projected in a report last month that "if the Democratic Party takes both chambers in the midterms, regulations on data center construction will be strengthened and AI infrastructure investment could contract."
Some also say that even with a Democratic landslide, expectations for benefits to green energy-related sectors should not be excessive. Another limitation is that President Trump could veto congressional demands.
Hana Securities said, "Although the Democratic Party has traditionally advocated pro-environment policies, in this election they were not treated as key agenda items compared with inflation and immigration," adding, "The chances of immediate, major changes are small."

title: Potable Water and Refrigeration To be Added to Gentilly “Microgrid Beehive,” Deployed in ...
description:
A microgrid beehive, trademarked by Footprint Project, is made up of stationary microgrids that serve as the hive.
Beehive Deployed in Gentilly Neighborhood of New Orleans In 2023, the organizations installed one of the first microgrid beehives at the NET Charter High School in the Gentilly neighborhood of New Orleans, where Reynolds had previously served as principal.
Beehive deployed as alternative to roof-mounted solar panels The project has yielded many benefits, including helping train young people in solar.
In 2022, a tornado hit New Orleans, knocking out power, and Groundwork New Orleans and Footprint Project deployed the microgrid and mobile units for charging and backup power.
The microgrid project also received funding from multiple organizations, and Schneider Electric donated materials and design assistance.
text:
After Hurricane Ida hit New Orleans in 2021, the city lost 19 community members to heat exposure while the power was out, and Groundwork New Orleans, partnering with Footprint Project, started investigating ways to provide microgrid resilience.

At the time, the nonprofit Footprint Project–which equips areas hit by disasters with clean energy–was developing the microgrid beehive idea, said Todd Reynolds, executive director at Groundwork New Orleans, which focuses on creating green and resilient neighborhoods, along with developing an environmental youth workforce.

A microgrid beehive, trademarked by Footprint Project, is made up of stationary microgrids that serve as the hive. A group of portable microgrids—known as the “bees”--can charge or discharge energy at the beehive and then travel where they’re needed. The stationary microgrids have a permanent location, and the “bees” can be stationed at the beehive until they’re needed in the surrounding community.

As part of the microgrid beehives, the organizations often loan out “pollinators,” which are solar batteries in a metal cabinet that also includes inverters and a charge controller, Reynolds said.

Beehive Deployed in Gentilly Neighborhood of New Orleans

In 2023, the organizations installed one of the first microgrid beehives at the NET Charter High School in the Gentilly neighborhood of New Orleans, where Reynolds had previously served as principal. The Gentilly neighborhood is a large, historically residential and disadvantaged neighborhood located in central New Orleans, where mobile “bee” trailers could easily be dispatched to neighborhoods that needed resilience during power outages, he said.

The school project included a semi-permanent “Queen Bee” unit, a 30-foot-long off-grid trailer that will remain at the school. It has 15 kW of solar and 55.5 kWh of storage. A bee trailer was also deployed.

The Queen Bee microgrid powers the school’s outdoor classrooms and Groundwork New Orleans’ office on the school grounds. The mobile unit has also powered community events.

Two new trailers are expected to be added to the project. One trailer will be a solar-powered refrigeration freezer trailer that will allow people to store their medicine and food, Reynolds said.

The other unit will include atmospheric water generation technology, allowing the organization to produce potable water during outages when water pumps go down or when water infrastructure isn’t available. It will produce about 200 gallons of water a day. Plans also call for Groundwork New Orleans to add a larger unit to the school site that can produce 600 gallons a day, he said.

Beehive deployed as alternative to roof-mounted solar panels

The project has yielded many benefits, including helping train young people in solar.

“Under my workforce development program, we worked with Footprint Project and my young folks actually built a solar bee while learning solar, learning the concepts, learning construction,” Reynolds said.

The microgrid hive and bees have had one opportunity to help out during an emergency. In 2022, a tornado hit New Orleans, knocking out power, and Groundwork New Orleans and Footprint Project deployed the microgrid and mobile units for charging and backup power.

While power was out, Groundwork New Orleans loaned out the “pollinators” — or battery kits — to people who could use them to charge phones and other items, Reynolds said.

Funding sources include the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency

A $500,000 grant from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Justice Collaborative Problem Solving Cooperative helped pay for the project, which initially called for six bees, Reynolds said. In February 2025, the Trump administration issued a termination notice and the project team scaled back the design to two bees.

In 2022, the project received $7,500 through Clean Energy Group’s Technical Assistance Fund for a feasibility assessment.

The microgrid project also received funding from multiple organizations, and Schneider Electric donated materials and design assistance.

“It was a great combination of groups coming together to get this grid operational,” Reynolds said.

Microgrid beehives deployed to disaster areas

In addition to completing the Gentilly beehive in 2023, Footprint Project has deployed numerous microgrid beehives to disaster areas, including for desperate Texans during the state’s February 2021 deep freeze and other crises. It also came to the rescue in Ukraine when the war with Russia broke out in February 2022.

Plans now call for connecting the Gentilly microgrid to the grid.

“The goal is now to create a bypass to tap into the school system so that when the power goes out, we can just switch it and it'll power their essential services,” Reynolds explained.

Reynolds hopes that the new projects will be funded by grants, and is taking an unconventional approach to funding.

“I don't wait till we get 100% of the funding. I receive X amount to do X amount of a phase,” Reynolds said. “What happens in that scenario is as you start building and as you start doing, you're able to attract more interest in your project instead of this conceptual thing that you're asking people to support.”
