title: Carney Wants Ten New Nuclear Reactors. Who Will Build Them? - The Walrus
description:
A month earlier, the Darlington New Nuclear project had been among the first added to the federal government’s list of major projects.
“Clean technology is the future.” The vision extends well beyond Darlington; across the country, nuclear power is having a moment.
Saskatchewan is advancing plans for small and large nuclear reactors, while, in New Brunswick—home to the only operating nuclear plant outside of Ontario—the province is investigating ways to expand nuclear as it phases out coal.
Keefer says he’s pleased to see the federal interest in new nuclear reactors, especially to maintain emissions-free energy over the coming decades.
After the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, nuclear energy proponents proclaimed the dawn of a nuclear renaissance.
text:
Last fall, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ontario premier Doug Ford gathered in a cavernous space in Bowmanville, Ontario, a line of hard-hatted workers assembled behind them. Though the scene had many of the familiar set pieces of political theatre, the announcement concerned something novel: a new nuclear project, in a country that hadn’t seen one in over thirty years.

Standing at the dais, Carney pitched the project—a four-reactor nuclear plant in Darlington, Ontario, funded by a $3 billion federal and provincial investment—as part of Canada becoming master of its own destiny in a dangerous and unpredictable world. A month earlier, the Darlington New Nuclear project had been among the first added to the federal government’s list of major projects. At the announcement, it seemed a new chapter in Canada’s nuclear history was being written. “We are an energy superpower, and we are only getting stronger,” Carney proclaimed. “Clean technology is the future.”

The vision extends well beyond Darlington; across the country, nuclear power is having a moment. In Port Hope, Ontario, the provincial utility has proposed a new 10,000-megawatt nuclear station, while on the shores of Lake Huron, one of the world’s largest nuclear plants—the Bruce Power nuclear power plant—is advancing a plan to double the plant’s output to 4,800 megawatts. In Alberta, a proposal to generate a similar amount of power via four large-scale reactors near the town of Peace River has begun the impact assessment process. Saskatchewan is advancing plans for small and large nuclear reactors, while, in New Brunswick—home to the only operating nuclear plant outside of Ontario—the province is investigating ways to expand nuclear as it phases out coal.

Federally, that’s echoed by a rhetorical embrace of nuclear. In June, the federal government released a (unfunded) strategy for Canada to capitalize on the “global nuclear renaissance,” including ten large-scale reactors, with construction starting by 2035.

Worldwide, governments are looking to nuclear to support increased electrification and decarbonization, as part of a wider move away from fossil fuels. Increasingly, nuclear is also being pitched as a solution to the voracious energy appetite of artificial intelligence, an application that has helped unleash billions in private investment. But in Canada, the appeal of nuclear has an especially outward-facing tone; proponents suggest Canada, as a one-time leader in nuclear energy, can use the industry as a low-carbon path to not just energy sovereignty but global energy dominance.

Still, this vision for the future faces challenges, not least of which is the history of the industry itself, replete with bloated budgets and unfulfilled promises. On top of that, Canada hasn’t had experience with building a new reactor in decades. “There are a lot of opportunities to learn from the failures of the past, but ultimately it will come down to execution,” says Brendan Frank, vice president, policy at the think tank Clean Prosperity. “We need the workforce, the skilled trades, the project management expertise, the public financial support. A lot of things have to come together for this to go as intended.”

Canada’s role in developing nuclear energy dates to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when physicists at McGill University made pioneering discoveries about the nature of radioactivity. Then, in 1942, a nuclear laboratory was moved from the United Kingdom, where war was encroaching, to Montreal, where a team of scientists worked on a reactor that could produce material used in atomic bombs.

That reactor—the first operational reactor outside the United States—wasn’t up and running until after the war ended, when focus shifted to electricity production. Two decades later, Canada became one of a handful of countries to develop its own commercial reactor. The CANDU reactor was designed to make use of the country’s abundant reserves of natural uranium and to avoid dependence on foreign suppliers for the element’s enriched counterpart.

A station using a prototype of the reactor began feeding power to the grid in 1967; five years later, CANDU reactors at the country’s first major commercial generating plant spun into operation in Pickering, Ontario. The industry then expanded at, by nuclear’s standards, a breakneck pace, with twenty-three nuclear plants commissioned in twenty-two years in Ontario, Quebec, and New Brunswick, partially as a response to the 1973 oil crisis. “[It was] just extraordinary the pace at which we built this out,” says Chris Keefer, an Ontario emergency room physician and president of the advocacy group Canadians for Nuclear Energy. “It was one of the fastest decarbonizations, in terms of adding low carbon electricity, per capita, that the world’s ever seen.”

As a result, nuclear now produces about 13 percent of the country’s power—and close to 50 percent of Ontario’s, a proportion only exceeded in France and Slovakia (in New Brunswick, the only other province currently generating power from nuclear, the share is about 15 percent). A dozen CANDU reactors have also been exported to countries like China, South Korea, and Romania.

Still, until Carney’s major projects push, it seemed the energy around nuclear had fizzled; no new nuclear plants have been constructed in Canada since the 1990s, while several have been taken offline (the number of operating nuclear stations in the country is down to seventeen). Canada’s nuclear industry has focused instead on refurbishing existing installations, and, at times, even that has seemed tenuous. The Pickering plant, for instance, was meant to shut down in 2025, but, inspired by the birth of his son and fuelled by the climate crisis, Keefer and the nonprofit he started with “a peppy group of a few people on Twitter” led a multi-year advocacy campaign to do a “nuclear power plant refurbishment” instead. In November, the Ontario government approved near $27 billion to refurbish four of the plant’s reactors, work on which is supposed to start in 2027, to keep the plant in operation.

Keefer says he’s pleased to see the federal interest in new nuclear reactors, especially to maintain emissions-free energy over the coming decades. “Nuclear, in certain jurisdictions and Ontario, is really a no brainer,” he says.

For now though, new large-scale reactors are a hypothetical. The only project under construction is at Darlington, where work has started to prepare the site for a novel approach to nuclear energy: four small modular reactors (SMRs), each generating about the third of a large reactor’s power, with an expected cost of $20.9 billion, including $7.7 billion for the first reactor.

On paper, SMRs address some of nuclear’s most intractable challenges: they’re meant to be constructed wholly or partially in factories, reducing complexity and shortening the decades-long process to build a large-scale plant. They require less land than a large nuclear facility and can be deployed incrementally to meet energy demand as it increases. For small grids that cannot easily accommodate the amount of power that would come for a single large reactor—like Saskatchewan and New Brunswick—SMRs also offer flexibility.

But the technology has risks, says Mark Winfield, professor in the faculty of environmental and urban change at York University. For one thing, “there’s this small existential problem of non-existence.” Because no SMRs are yet operational anywhere in the G7, they carry an unanswered series of questions around how much they will cost, how long they’ll take to build, and whether they’ll work. The technology requires enriched uranium, which Canada doesn’t produce and would have to import; meanwhile, the reactors themselves are not Canadian but are a Japanese-American design.

“I think it’s reckless,” says Winfield, pointing to the high costs of power from SMRs, which, in some estimates, would be higher than renewables, gas, or large-scale nuclear. “This cascade of geopolitical, technological, economic risks which are being introduced by going down this pathway . . . it just makes no sense.”

The World’s Largest Nuclear Plant Comes to Small-Town Ontario

The Truth Behind UFO Sightings over Canada’s Nuclear Facilities

Avi Lewis Wants to Save the Planet. It’s Tearing His Party Apart

Past instances where promising nuclear technologies were commercial failures offer a clue to the obstacles ahead, says Mahdi Khelfaoui, professor at the Université du Québec à Trois-Rivières and nuclear historian. In the 1960s, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited (AECL), a Crown corporation, developed a small reactor intended to have a similar output to today’s SMRs. It was considered one of the most elegant designs at the time, says Khelfaoui, but was abandoned because AECL decided it lacked an international market.

In the latter half of the twentieth century, another obstacle emerged, when public sentiment turned on nuclear after accidents at Three Mile Island and Chernobyl in 1979 and 1986. At that time, the AECL was developing a small reactor for district heating—an experiment that also foundered, both due to cost and because of a lack of social acceptance in the countries Canada wanted to export it to. That suggests we should be careful with technological promises, says Khelfaoui. “Technical feasibility is not the same thing as commercial viability.”

Allison Macfarlane, former chair of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission and current director of the school of public policy and global affairs at UBC, was also dismissive about the viability of SMRs. “There’s a reason that we only have large reactors around the world, and that reason is economies of scale. It is simply much cheaper to build one large reactor pressure vessel than it is to build six small ones for the same amount of electricity generated.”

Despite the rosy projections from what Macfarlane calls the “nuke bros” (the numerous SMR startups that have emerged in the past decade), it’s just not straightforward to build a nuclear reactor in a factory, she says, noting that in her tenure as chair, she watched the American company Westinghouse go bankrupt over its attempt to build a reactor in a factory in the state of Georgia.

While GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, the company behind the Darlington project, is an established player in the nuclear industry, she’s still skeptical whether the project can deliver on its promises. “We really don’t know how much [SMRs] will cost. What will be the safety issues associated with them? How much waste will they produce? All of these things are still big question marks because nobody’s ever built one.”

In a statement, Natural Resources Canada said by making Canada the first G7 country with an SMR, the Darlington New Nuclear Project will create “significant advantage for Canada’s economy, security, and clean power generation goals,” strengthening Canadian supply chains and building expertise that will be in high international demand as nuclear power generation increases.”

Still, Macfarlane says she’s heartened by the federal government’s interest in large scale reactors, though she’s unsure what the long-term role is for nuclear, given advances in wind, solar, and battery storage—all of which are cheaper than nuclear energy. “Frankly, I’m really perplexed why the government of Canada is not investing more heavily in renewables,” she says.

In a statement, Natural Resources Canada pointed to programs such as a $4.5 billion program to support deployment of energy storage and renewable energy technologies (federal investment in the Darlington New Nuclear Project alone, by contrast, is nearly half that). The department also highlighted the Clean Electricity Investment Tax Credit, meant to spur investment in renewables—though this can also be applied to nuclear projects.

But renewables don’t offer the same advantage to the Canadian economy, says Keefer; imported turbines, solar panels, and batteries don’t prop up domestic supply chains, and jobs in wind and solar are often itinerant and temporary. Work in nuclear energy, particularly on large scale CANDU reactors, would create a domestic supply chain with large numbers of long-term, unionized jobs, as well as the potential to export uranium and reactor design abroad.

For that reason, Keefer says he’s most hopeful about the federal government’s strategy to build ten new large-scale reactors and increase uranium export, which the government has said will be accompanied by a draft federal financing policy for new projects by 2027.

Yet with large reactors, Canada faces much the same issue. Though the country once turned out CANDU reactors at a rapid clip, it hasn’t produced a new reactor in decades, and the new generation of Canada’s technology—the CANDU MONARK—has never been built. Complex technological projects are risky, says Khelfaoui. In his research on Canada’s last attempt at a reactor build—the failed MAPLE reactor, which was abandoned in 2008—he found that, in going from design to construction, commissioning, and testing, engineers encountered problems that could not have been anticipated, driving up costs and lengthening timelines. “Between what is on paper and what will be built,” he says, “actually, there is a whole world of uncertainty.” For an investment in the tens of billions, the risk may just be too great.

History is instructive in showing what can happen to the enthusiasm around nuclear. After the 1997 Kyoto Protocol, nuclear energy proponents proclaimed the dawn of a nuclear renaissance. But projects encountered delays and spiralling costs, and the 2011 Fukushima disaster—in which a powerful earthquake and tsunami damaged Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi nuclear reactor, causing widespread contamination—turned public opinion. By 2013, analysts concluded that the nuclear renaissance had been a fantasy.

Given the skyrocketing demand for electricity, Frank says there’s reason to think this time might be different. In the short term, as investors balance risk against the growing appetite for energy, Darlington will be important in demonstrating whether the new generation of nuclear can bear fruit, he says. “The sector needs to prove that it can actually build things on time and on budget for scale to be possible in the long run.”

In that long run, though, he suspects most of the new nuclear energy in Canada will come from large reactors, not SMRs. That means it could be decades before those projects begin sending power to the grid, at a time when wind and solar are being deployed at comparatively breakneck pace (with electricity from wind and solar reaching record highs in 2025) and the 2050 deadline to decarbonize is fast approaching. Nonetheless, Frank says nuclear is a long-term play: a hedge against renewables getting us all the way there.

In a way, nuclear has always been a bet: on technology, on policy, on the future that will exist after the long years between construction starting and the reactor starting up. Betting on anything in the future feels risky right now. But with pressure mounting from all sides, Canada appears ready to take those odds.

text:
In 2022, Ron Lamberty, then chief marketing officer for the American Coalition for Ethanol, led a project that included traveling over 40,000 miles in a hybrid electric flex-fuel vehicle affectionately named HEFF. Lamberty says the goal was to find out how low the real-world, on-road emissions could be for a hybrid electric vehicle when that hybrid’s internal combustion engine—and the source of its battery charge—was powered by high ethanol blends, namely E85.

HEFF (a used 2019 Ford Fusion with an after-market eflexfuel.com E85 converter) consumed about 1,518 gallons of fuel averaging 71.4% ethanol over 40,007 miles, resulting in tailpipe CO2 emissions of about 200 grams per mile. If HEFF had been able to use E85 consistently on its journey, tailpipe CO2 would have dropped to 176 grams per mile. The figures were comparable to results of a similar test done by Car and Driver on a 2019 Tesla Model 3 LR electric vehicle, and even beat the Tesla’s long-range results in higher-CI electricity markets like Wisconsin and Missouri, which allow up to 260 grams per mile.

“HEFF shows that anyone truly interested in reducing carbon pollution should be interested in flex-fuel hybrids,” Lamberty wrote in a column about the project for Ethanol Producer Magazine in late 2024.

Then, the allure of flex-fuel hybrids was mostly about climate—reducing tailpipe CO2 emissions. Two years later, with ethanol hovering around $1.50 per gallon less than gasoline at the rack, and E85 regularly selling for a dollar cheaper than regular (E10)—why are flex-fuel hybrids still not offered in the U.S.?

Auto industry analysts say consumers are, in fact, very interested in hybrids, but the flex-fuel component is missing from the U.S. market. Reuters reported in mid-September that hybrids are “on a tear,” making up 19% of August 2026 vehicle sales, up from 16% before the Iran conflict began in February. Automakers are capitalizing on this trend, Reuters reported, specifically Toyota, Hyundai/Kia, Ford and Honda.

Kelley Blue Book reports that in the first half of 2026, 22% of potential buyers said they would consider a hybrid vehicle, up from 20% in 2025.

Hyundai, Ford and Stellantis (owner of several auto brands including Jeep, Dodge and Ram) announced earlier this year that they will introduce larger EVs with gas generators, known as extended-range EVs. These new vehicles would presumably be suitable for E15 but not E85.

Finally, Chevrolet announced the launch of what it calls mild hybrid models that can run on up to E100. Stellantis is also launching a Fiat hybrid FFV it calls a “bio-hybrid.” Both vehicles, however, will only be available in South American markets, specifically Brazil, where hybrid FFVs have a growing presence.

“It’s been very frustrating to see the lack of leadership and lack of vision from both the automotive sector here in the U.S. and our policymakers on these topics,” says Geoff Cooper, CEO of the Renewable Fuels Association. “We look at this trend and just scratch our head and wonder why in the world are the automakers not building flex-fuel capability into these hybrid vehicles.”

The Case for Hybrid FFVs

Similar to ACE’s HEFF project, the RFA released a study in 2024 that illustrated the advantages of a plug-in hybrid flex-fuel vehicle over fully electric vehicles. RFA converted a 2022 Ford Escape plug-in hybrid to flex-fuel and ran a 15-month study.

The results showed GHG emissions that rival or outperform that of EVs; lower cost of ownership than that of EVs; and no meaningful loss of fuel economy.

Fast forward to today, with gas prices well over $6 in California while E85 hovers around $2.50 to $3. For a standard 21-gallon tank, that amounts to a savings of up to $74 to fill up.

“You’re paying half the price for E85,” Cooper says. “If you put that in a hybrid FFV that has a high-compression ratio engine and some turbocharging, which most of them do, you are not going to see the kind of fuel economy loss that gave E85 a bad name back in the old days.”

Cooper adds that a hybrid FFV combines the best of both technologies—electrification and a low-carbon liquid fuel—and marries them together in one vehicle.

Soaring gas prices are already incentivizing traditional hybrids, says Lamberty, now ACE's chief strategy officer. “Now, you make those economics even better by making them a flex-fuel hybrid, and they would probably sell.”

But automakers in the U.S. are not incentivized to make hybrid FFVs in the current policy framework, Cooper and Lamberty emphasize.

“It comes down to some bad policy decisions made years ago at the federal level,” Cooper says, adding that hybrid FFV production does come with a modest added cost. “The automaker has no incentive under the current policy framework, to make even that modest investment to add flex-fuel capability to their vehicles.”

The FFV boom in the early 2000s was prompted by compliance credits for tailpipe standards, Cooper says. In 2014, one out of every six vehicles sold in the U.S. was an FFV, with nine major automakers producing more than 2.8 million FFVs, Cooper cites in a 2023 Ethanol Producer Magazine column. Between 2010 and 2014, automakers received substantial credits based on E85 displacing petroleum.

The Obama administration initiated a phase-out of those credits over a decade ago, and the number of FFVs produced has since dwindled precipitously.

“Today, there is no regulatory benefit for an automaker to build FFVs,” Cooper adds. “Policymakers decided 10 years ago that they wanted to shift all incentives to fully electric and remove any incentive for any liquid fuel vehicles.”

Dave VanderGriend, founder and chairman of ICM, which works extensively in the Brazilian market, says numerous factors, chief among them the lack of an FFV production incentive, have stifled hybrid FFV adoption in the U.S.

But intense consumer demand for more affordable fuel options should be incentive enough for an FFV reboot, Cooper and Lamberty agree.

“Currently, hybrids are not being widely promoted by auto manufacturers here in the U.S., but it is coming,” VanderGriend says. “The economics for hybrids are here today.”

“We do think, if over time, automakers see there is consumer demand for hybrid FFVs, they’ll build them,” Cooper says.

For consumers, hybrids are selling now without incentives. “The incentive is the economics of having a hybrid,” Lamberty says.

In fact, Cooper says the top E85 conversion kit makers in the U.S. have hit record sales as consumers realize the savings potential in a $6-per-gallon gasoline market.

Doug Durante, longtime executive director of the Clean Fuels Development Coalition, argues that hybrid FFVs are not the solution to high gas prices. He instead encourages a national high-octane fuel standard that pairs E30 with hybrid vehicles. The idea being that E30 would be compatible with typical, non-FFV engines.

The Hybrid FFV Boom In Brazil

The hybrid FFV environment in Brazil is much different.

Stellantis’ bio-hybrid launch in South America is part of a record €5.6 billion ($6.3 billion) investment that supports more than 40 new products.

The bio-hybrid will not be available in the U.S., where Stellantis will instead focus on traditional hybrids, battery EVs and extended-range hybrids, the company announced in 2026.

Chevrolet’s Brazilian hybrid FFV launch will include Tracker and Montana models, expected to be available soon.

Brazil is the target market for these new hybrid FFVs, Lamberty says, as the country blends at 32%. “Brazil has two types of fuel: Fuel that has a lot of ethanol and fuel that’s just ethanol.”

About 85% of vehicles on the road in Brazil are already FFVs, he adds.

VanderGriend echoes that conclusion: “The hybrid FFV was introduced originally in Brazil as an efficiency upgrade, so it had a headstart.”

The Market Move

While U.S. automakers could offer hybrid FFVs in response to rising consumer interest, policies to incentivize both production and purchases might also be necessary. “We should be seeing if there’s a way that the federal government can incentivize hybrid and flex-fuel vehicles as much as they’ve incentivized electric vehicles,” Lamberty says.

It should be of interest to an administration of either party, Cooper says, regardless of priorities. “Improving fuel efficiency, reducing GHGs, reducing costs, domestic energy and fuel supplies—E85, flex fuels check all of those boxes.”

President Trump rolled back the Biden-era fuel economy and tailpipe emissions standards and is likely to put new ones in place, Cooper says. “When a new set of regulations are put together, we do think there’s an opportunity to get our story out there. Restoring some incentive for flex-fuel capability, be it in hybrid vehicles or be it in conventional internal combustion engine vehicles, should be a high priority.”

Lamberty says the ethanol lobby tends to be necessarily myopic in focus and is currently concentrated on getting year-round national E15 legislation approved.

But both Cooper and Lamberty agree the timing is excellent for a hybrid FFV effort.

“The blending economics are more attractive than they’ve ever been,” Cooper says.

And Lamberty adds, “If you’ve got a flex-fuel vehicle, you can always buy the cheapest fuel. That’s the beauty of it.”

title: Groups Cancel $1-Billion Gas-Fired Power Plant Project in Wisconsin
description:
Two groups behind construction of a proposed $1-billion natural gas-fired power plant in northern Wisconsin told state officials they are pulling the plug on the project.
The power plant was sited in Superior, in Douglas County, near Lake Superior, and also near Duluth, Minnesota.
The commission had granted certificates of public convenience and necessity for construction of a natural gas-fired power plant with generation capacity of between 550 and 625 MW.
Several Gas-Fired Power Stations Move Forward Other gas-fired power plant projects are moving forward in Wisconsin.
The Red Oak Ridge Energy Center project would be a nearly 1.2-GW facility; the Foundry Ridge Energy Center would have 324 MW of generation capacity.
text:
Two groups behind construction of a proposed $1-billion natural gas-fired power plant in northern Wisconsin told state officials they are pulling the plug on the project. Dairyland Power Cooperative, headquartered in La Crosse, Wisconsin, and South Shore Energy—a subsidiary of Allete—the parent of Minnesota Power—in a letter to Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission told commissioners the groups would not move forward with the Nemadji Trail Energy Center (NTEC).

The power plant was sited in Superior, in Douglas County, near Lake Superior, and also near Duluth, Minnesota. The letter to the PSC was filed Oct. 28 by Daniel McCourtney, manager of strategic environmental initiatives at Allete, which had distanced itself from the project late last year.

“No construction has occurred on NTEC or the [generation tie line],” McCourtney wrote in the letter to the PSC. “Accordingly, the owners respectfully request that the commission acknowledge their relinquishment of all rights associated with the [plant approvals].”

The PSC had approved the project in 2020. The commission had granted certificates of public convenience and necessity for construction of a natural gas-fired power plant with generation capacity of between 550 and 625 MW. The utilities had proposed the NTEC as a way to provide baseload electricity to replace retiring coal-fired generation, and support power reliability as they made more investments in renewable energy.

Several Gas-Fired Power Stations Move Forward

Other gas-fired power plant projects are moving forward in Wisconsin. Regulators recently approved Invenergy’s request to build two new gas-fired stations in the southern part of the state, and We Energies—the state’s largest electric utility—has said it would buy the plants. The Red Oak Ridge Energy Center project would be a nearly 1.2-GW facility; the Foundry Ridge Energy Center would have 324 MW of generation capacity.

We Energies also received approval in 2025 for two new gas-fired facilities, in Oak Creek (1,100 MW) and Paris (128 MW). POWER previously reported on the utility’s plan to build a gas-fired plant in Outagamie County; the Fox North Energy Center would have 750 MW of generation capacity.

Invenergy in August filed an engineering plan with the PSC for two gas-fired stations in Calumet County in northeast Wisconsin that would have a combined generation capacity of nearly 2 GW. We Energies has included the power plants in its regulatory filings, and has said the 1,200-MW Forest Junction Energy Center and the 750-MW Union Depot Energy Center could be online by December 2031.

Legal Challenges

Indigenous and environmental groups, including Clean Wisconsin and the Sierra Club, had filed legal challenges against the NTEC facility. The groups also had asked the state’s Supreme Court to hear a lawsuit that challenged the PSC’s approval of the plant, though the court declined to take the case. There also was local opposition, and the NTEC also had permitting delays.

Jennifer Cady, vice president of public policy for Minnesota Power, in a December filing to the PSC said that air, wetland, and construction permits for the project had expired due to delays. Minnesota Power also nixed an agreement with its subsidiary South Shore Energy to buy power from the plant.

City officials in Superior also had denied approval for the plant, amid concerns from local residents about noise and pollution, and the impact on surrounding wetlands. Regional tribes and environmental groups also raised those concerns. The plant’s location would have been near a cemetery in Superior in which some 200 ancestors of the Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa are buried.

Project supporters had said the facility would have benefited the area with about 350 jobs during construction, and another two dozen full-time jobs once in operation. Officials who supported the plant said it would have generated about $1 million in annual tax revenue.

name: Clean Energy
title: An Electric Ride to the Polls: First Votes, First EV Rides at VotaFest
description:
In Lilburn, Georgia, Poder Latinx celebrated Vote Early Day with VotaFest, a community celebration bringing together music, art, culture, community resources, and early voting support.
An Electric Ride to the Polls Poder Latinx’s broader Vote Early Day efforts included free EV rides to early voting locations in participating communities, including Georgia, as a way to help address transportation barriers while introducing voters to clean transportation.
The IONIQ 5 itself also offered a connection to Georgia’s growing clean transportation economy.
Clean energy, transportation, household energy costs, infrastructure, and other issues that affect communities are shaped in part by decisions made by elected officials and public agencies.
VotaFest demonstrated how clean transportation, culture, community, and civic engagement can come together in one space.
text:
This year, the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy (SACE) joined Poder Latinx to celebrate a lot of firsts for some members of Lilburn, Georgia’s Latin American community — taking their first ride in an electric vehicle, casting their first vote in a midterm election, and even voting in their first U.S. election.

On Saturday, October 24, 2026, communities across the country celebrated Vote Early Day, a nonpartisan civic holiday dedicated to helping eligible voters understand their early voting options and make a plan to cast their ballots before Election Day.

In Lilburn, Georgia, Poder Latinx celebrated Vote Early Day with VotaFest, a community celebration bringing together music, art, culture, community resources, and early voting support.

VotaFest created a welcoming space for community members to celebrate their culture while learning more about civic participation and the upcoming election. Participants celebrated with music and traditional Latino folkloric dancing, food and crafts from local Latino vendors, and even a mechanical bull — but there was another kind of ride available that day.

An Electric Ride to the Polls

Poder Latinx’s broader Vote Early Day efforts included free EV rides to early voting locations in participating communities, including Georgia, as a way to help address transportation barriers while introducing voters to clean transportation.

SACE supported transportation for the event by providing free rides to an early voting location in a Hyundai IONIQ 5, giving voters the opportunity to cast their ballots while also experiencing an electric vehicle firsthand.

The rides to the polls served multiple purposes: In addition to practical, free transport to voting locations, the rides also gave participants opportunities to experience the comfort, quiet ride, and technology of an EV, while talking with experts about electric transportation and clean energy in Georgia. The IONIQ 5 itself also offered a connection to Georgia’s growing clean transportation economy.

New Experiences, One Ride at a Time

Each ride and each rider carried their own story. Riders brought different life experiences but shared excitement about participating in the voting process and riding in an EV for the first time.

Bernardino, who moved to the United States 30 years ago, was surprised to learn that the vehicle we were riding in was 100% electric. He was also unaware of previous federal incentives that helped make EVs more affordable. The ride sparked a broader conversation about how decisions made by elected officials can influence clean energy and transportation policies, incentives, and investments. For Bernardino, it was another reminder of why he felt participating in this election was too important to miss.

We also gave a ride to an older couple who were excited to vote together. It was the husband’s first time voting, while his wife had cast her first ballot during the 2024 presidential election. They were thrilled to participate in their first midterm election and were already enthusiastically talking about future elections, including the 2028 presidential race. They were just as excited about their first EV experience and surprised to learn that there are increasingly affordable new and used EV options available. After only about five minutes in the IONIQ 5, the husband excitedly exclaimed, “We need one of these!”

Julian, a young local mechanic originally from Oaxaca, Mexico, took advantage of the EV ride to vote, sharing that without the ride, he might have gotten busy and missed the opportunity. He also expressed interest in becoming an electrician, which sparked a conversation about career opportunities in EV manufacturing, battery production, charging infrastructure, and other clean energy industries that have expanded in recent years, in part due to federal investments in clean energy and domestic manufacturing.

Each rider brought a different background and lived experience, but everyone experienced something new while taking part in the civic process and thinking about the future of their communities.

Clean energy, transportation, household energy costs, infrastructure, and other issues that affect communities are shaped in part by decisions made by elected officials and public agencies. Poder Latinx’s 2026 voter education work similarly connected energy and environmental issues with opportunities for civic participation.

VotaFest demonstrated how clean transportation, culture, community, and civic engagement can come together in one space. By meeting people where they were and offering a hands-on EV experience alongside transportation to the polls, the event created an opportunity for community members to experience electric mobility while exercising their right to vote.

Sometimes a ride can do more than get someone from one place to another. It can introduce a new technology, start a conversation, remove a transportation barrier, and increase participation in shaping a community’s future.

description:
Millions of dollars of settlement money from the largest known methane leak in the United States are now available to affected residents to replace gas-powered appliances with electric ones.
In total, the program will make $40 million available to help people install heat pumps that cool and heat homes, electric stoves, water heaters and other appliances.
Evan Kamei is the director of TECH Clean California, a state program helping distribute the settlement money.
He said the incentives "will help create healthier homes, lower energy costs, deliver cooling, and create local jobs by replacing aging gas appliances with efficient electric appliances."

text:
Millions of dollars of settlement money from the largest known methane leak in the United States are now available to affected residents to replace gas-powered appliances with electric ones. Organizations involved in distributing the money say it will help create safer and cleaner homes.

The announcement makes available the first $20 million in incentive funding from the Aliso Canyon settlement to help home and building owners impacted by the 2015 Los Angeles-area blowout. In total, the program will make $40 million available to help people install heat pumps that cool and heat homes, electric stoves, water heaters and other appliances.

Evan Kamei is the director of TECH Clean California, a state program helping distribute the settlement money. He said the incentives "will help create healthier homes, lower energy costs, deliver cooling, and create local jobs by replacing aging gas appliances with efficient electric appliances."

Anyone in the affected area with a single-family home will be eligible for the incentives, and certain income-qualifying residents will be eligible for extra funding. Access for multi-property owners will come later.

The Aliso Canyon gas leak took nearly four months to control, sickened thousands of families and forced them from their homes near the San Fernando Valley to escape a sulfurous stench and maladies including headaches, nausea and nose bleeds.

The natural gas storage well failed and uncontrollably released nearly 100,000 tons of methane and other substances into the atmosphere for more than 100 days. Methane is a potent, heat-trapping gas that contributes to extreme weather events worldwide through climate change. The natural gas facility involved in the blowout temporarily closed and later reopened at reduced capacity after being deemed safe to operate.

In 2021, thousands of families reached a settlement of up to $1.8 billion with the Southern California Gas Co. and its parent company, Sempra Energy. Some 35,000 plaintiffs were compensated after complaining of personal injury and property damage to their homes. SoCalGas spent more than $1 billion on the blowout, with most of the money going to temporarily relocate 8,000 families.

Weldon Kennedy is the co-founder and chief marketing officer of Copper, a California startup that sells electric induction stoves and ovens. He said his company got involved with the program to distribute settlement money after the group Energy Solutions highlighted how hard it would be to get people to switch their cooking appliances from gas to electric.

"People have a cultural attachment to gas when it comes to cooking," Kennedy said. The kind of appliances Copper sells may help mitigate that attachment because they can be plugged into a regular outlet without the expense of rewiring that is usually associated with switching from gas-powered appliances to electric ones.

Cooking with electricity comes with health benefits. Gas stoves, which 47 million Americans use, release pollutants like nitrogen dioxide that's been linked to asthma and cancer-causing benzene.

Products like electric appliances are one way to address the significant amount of pollution driving climate change that comes from cooking, heating and cooling living spaces and providing hot water in buildings.

Income-qualified residents affected by the Aliso leak are eligible for up to $31,800 worth of incentives to cover the cost of electric installations in their homes.

Switching from gas to electricity can save energy and lower bills.

Carol Kamei, Evan Kamei's 72-year-old mother, has lived for 46 years near the Aliso Canyon Natural Gas Facility and was one of the plaintiffs in the case against SoCal Gas. She remembers smelling gas and getting nose bleeds. When she read in the news that the leak was also spewing cancer-causing benzene, she knew it was time to go.

Carol Kamei said her nose bleeds went away after moving in with her sister in Hollywood for three months. She recently participated in a health study by the University of California, Los Angeles and found out she has diminished lung capacity, one of the health impacts researchers look for, she said.

"I do know some people that have died from blood-borne illnesses, cancer since then," Carol Kamei said.

Kamei hopes to use the incentive funding to replace her oven with an electric one. "I'd rather not use gas," she said.

title: New ANSI Report Charts Progress on Standards for Electric Vehicles at Scale - Supply Chain Digest
description: As electric vehicles become more integrated into the nation's ... Although Texas has three schools with undergraduate programs in the top ...
text:
The report, issued by the ANSI Electric Vehicles Standards Panel (EVSP), providupdates on standards, research, and conformity assessment activities against 30 previously identified gaps.

For each of the 30 current gaps tracked, you get something like this:

Gap V3: Safe Storage of Lithium-ion Batteries

No standards or guides have been identified that address the safe storage of damaged (i.e., unknown condition) lithium-ion batteries, whether at warehouses, repair garages, recovered vehicle storage lots, or auto salvage yards.

R&D Needed: Yes. Assess various known failure modes and appropriate battery storage procedures. modes. Resulting consequences from failures should be determined and associated mitigating measures such as explosion control should be explored. Research should consider gas and fire detection and suppression technologies / systems.

Recommendation: A standard or guide for the safe storage practices for EV batteries must be developed, addressing damaged batteries and the wide range of storage situations that may exist, including when the batteries have been separated from their host vehicle.

It's good stuff.

This report also proposes three new gaps for consideration:

·Damaged EV Battery Triage, Monitoring, Storage, and Transfer, addressed in the report’s Vehicle Systems chapter

Accessible and Inclusive EV Charging Equipment and Interfaces, addressed in the report’s Charging Infrastructure chapter

Public Unattended Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) User Experience, Operations, and Serviceability, addressed in the report’s general section

“As EV adoption grows, the standards questions are shifting from whether the technology works to how it performs in the real world, for every driver and at every charger,” said Christine Bernat, ANSI director of standards facilitation. “Damaged batteries, accessibility, and charger reliability are the kinds of issues that are easier to solve together and early, and we encourage more stakeholders to join ANSI in this work.”

(See More Below)

CATEGORY SPONSOR: SOFTEON

Tracking progress as EV adoption scales

The report builds on the EVSP’s 2023 Roadmap of Standards and Codes for Electric Vehicles at Scale, developed with input from more than 130 organizations across federal agencies, national laboratories, standards developers, industry, and academia. The roadmap identified 37 standardization gaps across vehicle systems, charging infrastructure, grid integration, and cybersecurity.

It is intended as a living document, updated as standards work advances, until the EVSP undertakes its next full roadmap.

The next gaps progress report is expected to be issued May 2027. For more information, visit www.ansi.org/e

title: Company withdraws application to build battery storage project in Madison County
description:
A company that proposed two battery energy storage facilities in Madison County has withdrawn its application.
Audio Player Jupiter Power wanted to build two separate facilities that hold surplus energy from a local power grid.
Before voting unanimously for an unfavorable recommendation, the Madison County Planning Commission raised questions about the safety of the project and any future land sales.
Officials from Jupiter Power have not given an exact reason for the withdrawal.
At past meetings, Madison County officials, and community members spoke at length about long-term risks of these facilities, including lithium fires that burn hotter and longer than wood fires.
text:
A company that proposed two battery energy storage facilities in Madison County has withdrawn its application. As IPR’s Thomas Ouellette reports, that’s after it received an unfavorable vote from local officials.

Audio Player

Jupiter Power wanted to build two separate facilities that hold surplus energy from a local power grid. The energy is stored in large lithium batteries until it’s needed in times of peak power use.

Before voting unanimously for an unfavorable recommendation, the Madison County Planning Commission raised questions about the safety of the project and any future land sales. The majority of public comment was also firmly against the proposal.

Officials from Jupiter Power have not given an exact reason for the withdrawal. In a statement, the company says “Indiana’s need for more power has not changed, and we will continue to evaluate how best to help meet this challenge and support everyone who depends on a reliable grid for their families and businesses.”

Jupiter officials had said the completed project would have resulted in a $500 million investment in the county, with no tax abatements requested.

The rezoning was proposed in September, but Jupiter Power developers at that meeting requested a continuance to better respond to concerns and questions.

At past meetings, Madison County officials, and community members spoke at length about long-term risks of these facilities, including lithium fires that burn hotter and longer than wood fires.

Indiana Michigan Power had signed an agreement to purchase one of the finished facilities.

title: EPA worked with White House on Clean Air Act exemptions, group says - C&EN
authors: Alex Music, special to C&EN, Alex Music, special to C&EN
description:

The EDF maintains that the exemptions made under the Trump administration are illegal, despite the presidential exemption provision.
She maintains that the exemptions are “harmful and unlawful" in their implementation.
“We can advance American manufacturing and protect people’s health at the same time with commonsense limits on pollution,” Murphy says.
“The health and well-being of the people who live near these facilities shouldn’t be the cost of doing business.”
text:
President Donald J. Trump has used the presidential exemption provision to temporarily excuse over 200 facilities—including petroleum refineries, medical sterilization plants, and coal-fired power plants—from pollution standards since March 2025, when the EPA opened a portal for facilities to request exemptions.

When asked about the EDF report and the EPA’s role in the exemptions, an agency spokesperson said in a written statement that it “played no role in the determinations set out in the statute and specifically vested in the President.” But the spokesperson did not deny EPA officials’ collaboration with the White House as shown in the records published by the EDF. The White House did not respond to a request for comment to confirm the EPA’s role.

The EDF maintains that the exemptions made under the Trump administration are illegal, despite the presidential exemption provision. “The sweeping proclamations issued by President Trump do not include any specific analysis or explanation showing that the exempted facilities meet” the standard under section 112 of the CAA, says Erin Murphy, lead counsel and clean air and energy markets director with the EDF. She says that many of the standards exempted by the Trump administration "simply require companies to implement commonsense work practices” and are not dependent on technological advances.

The American Chemistry Council (ACC) provided a written statement to C&EN in support of the administration’s use of the Clean Air Act’s presidential exemption provision around the 2024 Hazardous Organic National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (HON) rule, which adds air pollution regulations for chemical manufacturing plants and certain other facilities.

“The two-year exemptions that have been granted provide an achievable compliance pathway for certain sources to design, permit, procure, install and implement the controls and operational changes required by the rule where those actions cannot feasibly be completed within the rule’s original timelines, consistent with Congressionally enacted provisions of the Clean Air Act,” the ACC says in its statement. “Regulations that lack a proper foundation in sound science or advance unrealistic requirements on infeasible timelines can jeopardize important economic production and impose significant unnecessary costs throughout supply chains, ultimately affecting the availability and affordability of products that Americans rely on every day.”

Murphy says that the EDF is currently challenging the exemptions in court. She maintains that the exemptions are “harmful and unlawful" in their implementation.

“We can advance American manufacturing and protect people’s health at the same time with commonsense limits on pollution,” Murphy says. “The health and well-being of the people who live near these facilities shouldn’t be the cost of doing business.”

title: The Value of Electric Power Transmission in a New Energy Context - Rhodium Group
description:
Because the regionality and scale of transmission benefits differ depending on energy market conditions, we evaluated the value of transmission expansion across a range of potential energy system futures.
Together, these scenarios represent a range of possible energy system outcomes given current energy market trends.
The expanded transmission environment allows us to evaluate how the US energy system would evolve with fewer barriers to transmission development.
We quantified the value of transmission expansion by comparing capacity additions, electricity prices, reliability costs, and transmission deployment in the expanded transmission and BAU environments for each scenario.
Our expanded transmission scenarios envision a world in which it’s easier and cheaper to build out transmission infrastructure, but this world is far from guaranteed.
text:
Surging electricity demand and constraints on generator supply are increasingly challenging access to affordable, reliable electricity in the US. Evolving natural gas dynamics at home and abroad also have implications for the power sector. Though considerable work has been appropriately focused on expanding new generation on the grid in response, a more robust transmission system also plays a critical role in meeting demand and reducing costs. We find that expanding transmission capacity has the potential to help mitigate rising electricity prices while supporting electricity reliability, especially under conditions that add extra strain on the grid. Easing transmission barriers reduces total US power system costs by $82-130 billion from 2026 to 2040, resulting in 2-3% lower electricity prices nationally in 2040, with greater price impacts in some regions. Expanded transmission drives these lower costs by enabling 9-43% more capacity deployment on the grid through 2040. More extensive interregional transmission networks also allow regions to meet reliability requirements at up to 12% lower costs, since they facilitate the sharing of capacity resources between regions. At the same time, expanded interregional transmission enables access to lower-cost sources of electricity in neighboring regions, driving different decisions on where generators are built and how they are operated.

Transmission value in a dynamic energy environment

After a couple of decades of effectively flat electricity demand growth, surging US electricity demand, largely driven by current and anticipated growth in large AI data centers, has increasingly dominated energy conversations and begun to reshape the US power sector. But electricity demand growth isn’t the only factor driving rapid change in the energy sector. Elsewhere on the grid, supply chain challenges, interconnection queue delays, and inflation are driving up the costs to bring new generating capacity onto the grid—at a time when the country needs all the electrons that it can get. Taken together, these dual challenges are intensifying the focus on rising electricity bills and what can be done about them. At the same time, demand for US liquefied natural gas (LNG) and the corresponding build-out of new LNG export terminals are reshaping domestic natural gas production trends and stand to put upward pressure on domestic gas prices. All of this is playing out against a backdrop of a dynamic energy policy environment, with legislative and executive decisions that are poised to shape how the US meets this increasing demand.

There has been considerable attention on how the US can expand electricity generating capacity in response to these trends—building more gas turbines, batteries, solar farms, and the like—but that only tells part of the story. These electrons need to move from generators to end users efficiently and in real time—underlining the critical importance of a robust transmission system for delivering affordable, reliable electricity. The recently released Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) includes meaningful improvements to federal policy to help bolster the transmission system, underscoring how important a strong grid is for meeting future energy needs. In this note, we briefly describe the new energy context the US is facing and then unpack modeling results that demonstrate how increasing transmission capacity on the grid can help bring more power to the grid, reduce costs, and contribute to reliability.

AI data centers are driving increasing electricity demand but are not the only source

The evolution of US electricity generation since 1960 can be divided into three distinct phases. From 1960 to 2005, electricity generation grew steadily, averaging just over 70 TWh per year, driven by economic and population growth, widespread adoption of electric appliances, and increasing commercial building floorspace (Figure 1). From 2005 through 2019, load growth was flat, averaging just 11 TWh (or about 0.1%) more demand per year due to increasing efficiency of appliances and lighting, a continued shift away from electricity-intensive manufacturing, and the Great Recession. The country is now on the precipice of increasing load growth that could dwarf the previous era of sustained growth, and has already seen a rebound to 50 TWh (2.1%) of year-on-year growth this decade.

AI data centers drive the bulk of future load growth, and assumptions around just how quickly that demand will materialize have an outsized impact on aggregate power demand. That said, the reshoring of electricity-intensive manufacturing (like chipmaking and battery manufacturing) and ongoing electrification of oil and gas operations in the Permian Basin also contribute step changes in demand growth. Increasing demand from large loads is superimposed on broader trends toward electrification via technologies like electric vehicles and heat pumps. All these factors contribute to higher electricity consumption, tighter reliability conditions, and greater pressure on electricity prices in many regions than the US has experienced over the past few decades.

This electricity demand growth varies meaningfully by region, largely driven by expectations around where data center development will take place and at what scale. Under our baseline data center assumptions, which represent a reasonably conservative pace of expansion compared to other recent data center demand projections, Virginia accounts for 23% of data center demand growth through 2040, doubling already high electricity growth rates in the South Atlantic. Data center expansion in Texas (15% of the total) helps maintain high levels of demand growth in West South Central, while expansion in Ohio and Indiana (11% of the total) more than doubles demand growth in East North Central.

Data center demand expectations are highly uncertain and vary widely. Under high data center demand assumptions aligned with the upper range of recent projections, the pace of national electricity demand growth could increase by 80% compared to baseline rates, widening regional differences. This new era of data center-driven demand growth raises the stakes for building cost-effective and rapid grid infrastructure to ensure delivery of reliable, affordable energy.

Abundant, low-cost US natural gas plays an increasingly prominent role in the global energy system

Alongside the need for more electrons, demand is also expanding for US natural gas abroad, and investments to increase export capacity that have been underway for years are well-timed to meet that increased demand. US LNG export volumes have surged in recent years, growing from effectively zero in 2015 to more than 5.5 trillion cubic feet—14% of domestic natural gas production­­—­in 2025. The war in Iran and ensuing closures and limitations on the Strait of Hormuz have amplified demand for US gas. From January through June 2026, LNG exports were up 23% compared to the same period in 2025, driven by increasing demand from Asian markets that were previously largely served by Qatari LNG. This trend looks poised to continue, enabled by currently under-construction projects coming online over the next few years. As discussed further below, we consider two LNG export capacity pathways and find volumes could more than double by 2040, increasing by 121-145% over 2025 levels (Figure 3).

This increasing demand for US LNG does not reduce the amount of natural gas available for use in the power sector. We model increasing demand for LNG along with demand from other sectors and estimate domestic production of gas will increase by 7-8 trillion cubic feet in 2040 (18-20%) in response, building on a period of immense growth in gas production over the last decade. Rather, this global demand drives producers to drill higher-cost wells and increases competition with domestic consumers. As a result, Henry Hub spot prices increase by 10% ($0.50) on average from 2030 to 2040 in the high LNG case compared to the baseline LNG case. In turn, the power sector makes somewhat different investment and operational choices, with power generation from natural gas decreasing by 7% in the high LNG case in 2040. As we unpack below, more available transmission has a different impact on this less gas-heavy grid.

The US needs a grid that provides affordable, reliable electricity

The grid is made up of three interconnected systems: generating assets that convert natural resources into electricity; the transmission system, which connects these generating assets to concentrations of electricity demand; and the distribution system, which moves electrons from the transmission system to end users. While adequate supply of generating capacity is necessary to provide affordable and reliable energy, the transmission system plays a crucial role in connecting supply and demand. It ensures that generation can meet load reliably, at the right time and place, and at the least cost. Our focus in this analysis is on the importance of transmission to the grid.

The transmission system can be further subdivided into three major categories of assets: lower-voltage lines that connect individual generators to the bulk power system (spur lines), medium-voltage lines that make up the bulk of the transmission system moving electricity around within an individual grid region (regional lines), and higher-voltage lines that connect larger grid regions together (interregional lines; in our case 25 individual electricity regions).

Taken together, these components add value to the grid in several important ways. First, the transmission system supports the reliability of the entire power system by enabling power to flow from places where it is abundant and cheap to places where it is needed—both of which might change depending on the time of day or time of year. By sharing resources across regions, the grid as a whole can meet its reliability standards at a lower overall cost.

Second, transmission can expand access to geographically diverse supplies. Some types of generators, especially renewables like solar, wind, geothermal, and hydroelectric power, have resource endowments that are not located proximate to population centers and other sources of load. Adding transmission can enable new and existing resources to meet increasing demand. Finally, transmission can help reduce costs by reducing congestion at key chokepoints on the grid, allowing lower-cost generation to places that would otherwise be reliant on more expensive generation, helping to improve grid asset utilization.

Despite the value that transmission brings to the power system, the US has been building less transmission in recent years (Figure 4). Part of this is because transmission expansion has been less critical in a period of low load growth. Beyond that, federal, state, and local siting and permitting challenges have also slowed the pace of deployment and now represent a major bottleneck in this new era of surging demand.

Despite these challenges, some meaningful transmission investments are moving forward. ERCOT, the grid operator in Texas, has plans to build a 765-kV transmission backbone across the state, largely to help serve increasing load associated with oil and gas production in the Permian Basin. The Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) approved nearly $22 billion in transmission investments aimed at improving reliability, interconnection, and market efficiency. And construction is underway on the TransWest Express transmission project to connect grid regions in the West.

Building new transmission lines represents one of a number of solutions that can improve the performance of the grid by increasing access to generation, relieving congestion, and enabling interregional sharing of resources. Deploying grid-enhancing technologies (like dynamic line rating and advanced power flow controls) and reconductoring existing transmission lines can all improve the efficiency of the existing grid. The use of high ampacity conductors in transmission expansion can maximize the impact of these investments. Increasing the installation of energy storage of a range of durations and scaling up grid flexibility efforts can help strategically shape the demand that the grid needs to serve. Though the focus of this report is specifically on transmission build-out, an all-of-the-above approach leveraging each of these solutions can help respond to emerging urgent energy system needs.

Scenarios to assess transmission value

There is a considerable body of work that discusses the importance of transmission to an efficient, reliable, low-cost power sector. We aim to add to that work by examining the importance of transmission specifically in the new energy context that we’ve described above, representing both the current federal and state policy environment and macro drivers of energy system change.

Because the regionality and scale of transmission benefits differ depending on energy market conditions, we evaluated the value of transmission expansion across a range of potential energy system futures. We developed a set of scenarios that capture uncertainty in key dimensions of the US energy system. The central scenario largely mirrors our mid emissions scenario from Taking Stock 2026 and assumes moderate oil and gas price projections, moderate clean technology costs, baseline data center demand growth, and planned LNG export capacity that includes all under-construction facilities. We also incorporated additional electricity demand in the Permian Basin from the ongoing electrification of oil and gas operations.

All other scenarios start from the central scenario assumptions and explore a more extreme outcome for one component of the energy system (Table 1). The high data center scenario assumes data center demand grows at a faster pace, with total data center demand rising 133% above the central scenario by 2035. The high LNG scenario assumes planned LNG export capacity that includes both under-construction and permitted facilities, increasing planned export capacity by 43% and increasing Henry Hub spot prices by 10% ($0.50) on average from 2030 to 2040 relative to central assumptions. The constrained supply scenario represents an environment where adding new generating capacity to the grid is more expensive by imposing a cost premium on all new additions when installations exceed thresholds derived from historical annual deployment levels. Together, these scenarios represent a range of possible energy system outcomes given current energy market trends.

To assess the value of transmission expansion, we used RHG-NEMS, Rhodium Group’s US energy system model, to model this set of scenarios under two transmission environments:

Business-as-usual (BAU): Transmission expansion continues at a similar pace to historical levels.

Expanded (Exp.): Interregional and intraregional transmission infrastructure, including spur lines, can be developed faster and at lower cost than today.

The expanded transmission environment allows us to evaluate how the US energy system would evolve with fewer barriers to transmission development. We quantified the value of transmission expansion by comparing capacity additions, electricity prices, reliability costs, and transmission deployment in the expanded transmission and BAU environments for each scenario.

BAAJA, the current bipartisan federal permitting reform bill, includes changes to transmission planning requirements, cost allocation approaches, and the federal government’s role in permitting interstate transmission lines. We modeled those transmission reforms as part of a broader set of policy changes and recently released a note discussing our findings. We do not model explicitly BAAJA provisions in this analysis and instead take a policy-neutral approach to representing the potential to increase transmission, but our findings here are generally consistent with our BAAJA modeling.

RHG-NEMS captures many benefits of transmission, and it has the advantage of reflecting dynamic natural gas prices to the grid—a key driver of power sector decision-making. However, its representation of transmission is limited relative to more specialized production cost models and, naturally, the actual electricity grid and its operations. RHG-NEMS does not capture benefits that play out on highly granular scales, either in terms of time or geography. RHG-NEMS does not capture within-region congestion, one well–documented source of costs that better transmission access can help improve. Similarly, recent work from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory has shown that around 40-60% of the benefits of expanded transmission accrue in just 5% of hours in a year (in their retrospective modeling approach)—and 20-30% accrue in just the top 1% of hours. RHG-NEMS takes a reduced-form approach to modeling hourly dispatch that doesn’t fully capture the benefits that occur in these narrow time slices. Similarly, RHG-NEMS does not anticipate unexpected weather events, which can strain the resilience of the grid and which can be at least partly mitigated by transmission investments. As a result of these limitations, this analysis provides a conservative estimate of the value of transmission.

Expanded transmission reduces prices and enables more capacity on the grid

We find that making transmission easier and cheaper to build reduces electricity prices by transforming the US electric grid. Capacity additions increase as it becomes easier to connect power plants to demand centers. The transmission network grows, strengthening existing connections and expanding to connect new regions. Increasing trade between regions impacts the capacity and generation mix while reducing reliability costs.

Lower electricity prices

Making transmission easier and cheaper to deploy reduces costs across the electricity system. We unpack changes to the grid in the sections that follow, but in general, increased solar and natural gas-fired capacity displaces generation from older, inefficient, more expensive fossil plants, reducing fuel costs. Increasing connections between regions allows regions to share resources for reserve margins. Trade between regions also impacts capacity deployment and operating decisions in ways that favor cheaper resources. Taken together, these dynamics combine to lower total system costs in the expanded transmission scenarios relative to BAU by $82-130 billion from 2026 to 2040, a 2-3% reduction.

This reduction in total system costs flows through to electricity prices. Electricity price represents the average amount customers ultimately pay per kilowatt-hour after accounting for the various components of their electricity rates, including fixed and volumetric charges. Between 2027 and 2040, expanded transmission decreases economy-wide national electricity prices modestly across all sectors, with average economy-wide prices falling by 1.6-3.4% (0.2-0.5 cents) in 2040 (Figure 5). Put another way, the average residential customer saves up to $40 on their electricity bill in 2040 with expanded transmission. These price gaps widen over time as cheaper transmission allows more renewable capacity and more efficient natural gas plants to come online, compounding the benefits of transmission investment. From 2035 to 2040, lower electricity prices save residential and commercial customers $4-5 billion and $5-9 billion per year on average, respectively. Like the dynamics in the previous section, transmission expansion reduces electricity prices most in scenarios where the electricity system is most strained: the constrained supply scenario sees the largest price impact, while the central scenario sees the smallest price impacts. Put another way, the affordability implications of expanded transmission are amplified if data center demand or LNG exports grow at a faster pace.

Unplanned solar additions increase by 20-24% (59-75 GW) in the central, high data center, and high LNG expanded transmission cases compared to BAU in 2040. In the constrained supply scenario, solar capacity doubles (170 GW) over the same period with expanded transmission, owing to lower transmission barriers and reduced spur line costs decreasing overall project costs, balancing this scenario’s higher supply-related costs and allowing solar capacity to deploy more readily.

Natural gas plants also benefit from a more connected grid. Unplanned natural gas-fired additions increase by 10-19 GW (7-21%) with expanded transmission relative to BAU. Combined cycle plants comprise most of these additions, but peaker plants deploy as well to balance the additional solar capacity and maintain grid reliability. Natural gas additions increase the most with expanded transmission in the high LNG scenario. In this scenario, higher LNG exports drive the average Henry Hub spot price up by 50 cents (10%) compared to prices in the central scenario from 2030 to 2040. As a result of higher natural gas prices, the high LNG scenario under BAU sees the lowest gas-fired capacity of all scenarios. Coming from this lower baseline, expanded transmission has a differential impact on natural gas additions in the high LNG scenario, but total natural gas capacity remains the lowest of all scenarios.

In our modeling, emerging clean technologies like nuclear technologies and enhanced geothermal systems remain too expensive to compete with more conventional resources: nuclear capacity doesn’t expand beyond planned uprates and restarts, and geothermal capacity grows meaningfully from today but still represents only a small share of the market by 2040. However, these technologies also benefit from expanded transmission, which can reduce the time and costs associated with grid connection. The economic viability of geothermal projects in particular, which are often located in rural areas, partially depends on the build-out of transmission infrastructure required to connect these resources to demand centers.

These capacity changes impact the generation mix in each scenario. Solar generation shares increase by 2-7% in 2040 relative to BAU, largely displacing gas generation shares despite the increase in gas capacity. Across scenarios, transmission expansion allows older, more inefficient gas-fired generators to run less frequently while increasing generation from new gas plants and solar capacity. Instead of retiring, these older gas plants stay online to provide reliability for growing shares of renewable energy and amid increasing demand. Coal generation also falls slightly as coal retirements increase modestly, and surviving plants operate at lower capacity factors. This shift towards zero-marginal cost resources and more efficient gas power plants reduces generation costs, which helps drive down electricity prices.

Meeting reliability targets at lower cost

Beyond reshaping the generation mix, making transmission cheaper and easier to deploy also lowers the cost of maintaining grid reliability. Across all scenarios, our model optimizes to meet the same targets for resource adequacy and spinning reserves. Expanded transmission reduces the costs of achieving these by up to 12.2% (Figure 8). Enhancing connections between regions allows regions to rely on some capacity in neighboring regions to meet reliability requirements, driving down costs associated with building out extra in-region peaking generation or long-term planning of generation to meet growing load. Regional grid operators currently utilize this strategy to cut costs. For instance, the Southwest Power Pool saved $8.5 billion in additional generation capacity investment in 2025 by sharing resources across its footprint. Expanded transmission allows for greater resource sharing and increased cost savings. In our modeling, the high LNG and constrained supply scenarios see the biggest reductions in reliability costs with expanded transmission, because transmission mitigates some of the high generation costs associated with high gas prices or a generation-limited power sector.

By 2035, regional transmission and spur lines together expand by 2.9-6.7 TW-mi (22-35%) relative to BAU scenarios. Like the interregional transmission results, the high data center scenario sees the greatest regional transmission and spur line impacts in 2035, as easier access to transmission allows grid capacity to expand and meet high electricity demand at lower cost. However, transmission impacts in this scenario fall after 2035 as the expanded grid becomes increasingly sufficient to accommodate load growth. By 2040, the constrained supply scenario experiences the greatest impacts to regional transmission and spur line build-out, with lower voltage transmission expanding by 53% compared to BAU. In this scenario, impacts accumulate over time as capacity additions continue to diverge from the supply-limited BAU.

Conclusions

In this era of surging US electricity demand—coupled with increasing pressure on natural gas prices from expanding LNG exports, elevated costs from supply chain inflation, and non-cost barriers like lengthy interconnection queues—energy reliability and affordability have become critical concerns across the country. A robust transmission network is an essential tool for alleviating some of these cost and supply pressures, as well as accommodating rapid electricity demand growth.

Expanded transmission lowers electricity prices by 2-3% in 2040 compared to BAU, though some regions see larger price impacts. While our modeling doesn’t capture local congestion, transmission expansion can also reduce price impacts from congestion, further reducing electricity prices beyond what we’ve modeled here. These price impacts result from changes in the grid mix and grid operations enabled by expanded transmission.

Strengthening and expanding transmission systems enables more capacity to connect to the grid—mostly solar and natural gas in our modeling. Enhancing interregional connections allows regions to share their generation more readily, improving the relative economics of certain types of power in areas with better-quality, cheaper resources than their neighbors.

The grid capacity build-out and changing electricity trade dynamics, driven by expanded transmission, improve electricity affordability. Expanded transmission enables more efficient natural gas plants and renewables to connect to the grid faster, allowing less-efficient, higher-cost resources to retire and reducing the total system costs required to meet growing demand. At the same time, greater trade between regions allows cheaper energy to be delivered to demand centers. Expanded interregional transmission also allows regions to share resources for reserve margins, reducing the costs required to meet reliability standards.

We find that transmission expansion offers the greatest benefits when the US energy system is stressed (e.g., by skyrocketing data center demand or constraints on supply of new capacity). As demand growth continues to accelerate, driven by AI proliferation, domestic manufacturing, and electrification, and global conflicts continue to strain supply chains, the risk of longer-term systemic stressors increases. Our expanded transmission scenarios envision a world in which it’s easier and cheaper to build out transmission infrastructure, but this world is far from guaranteed. The path from our current environment to this imagined world requires focused resources and policy development at the federal, state, and local levels.
