The outcome of Tuesday's midterm elections could have serious implications for utilities, as candidates in both parties seek to capitalize on widespread concerns about energy affordability.

Policy areas that could see the biggest impact include data centers, energy tax credits and permitting reform, experts told Utility Dive.

Hasan Nazar, head of policy at Crux, a finance technology company that connects tax credit buyers and sellers, said he believes energy affordability will be "determinative" in this election.

Polls have given Democrats a strong chance of taking control of the House and possibly also flipping the Senate, but even if they do, Nazar noted that there would still be a split government with a Republican administration in place. He hopes broad support for reform will lead to bipartisan cooperation on energy policy.

"History shows us that energy crises create policy openings, and we think the conditions are probably in place for a window of policymaking," Nazar said.

What candidates are telling voters

All U.S. House seats are up for grabs, along with one-third of the Senate and 36 gubernatorial seats.

An Oct. 8 poll from Pew Research Center found that 74% of U.S. adults surveyed were concerned about the price of gasoline and energy, the largest share of concern among all surveyed issues.

As candidates campaigned this year, energy issues were central in many races.

During an Oct. 8 debate, Georgia Senate candidates Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., sought to tie each other to controversial data center projects, according to Atlanta News First. Collins said Ossoff had a "data center billionaire" donor and promised to protect Georgians from having their electricity infrastructure "destroyed" by the projects. Ossoff noted Collins had voted in favor of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and said the legislation contained a "data center tax scam."

In Wisconsin's gubernatorial race, David Crowley, D, has proposed requiring data centers to be powered with renewable energy, and a 2050 net zero goal for the state. His opponent Tom Tiffany, R, has strongly opposed data center development, saying "data centers, solar and wind farms should not be built on Wisconsin's farmland," the Wisconsin Examiner reported.

Ohio gubernatorial candidates Vivek Ramaswamy, R, and Amy Acton, D, have both campaigned on data center and energy issues — the next governor will appoint a full slate of commissioners to the Ohio Public Utilities Commission. Ramaswamy has promised free electricity to those who live near a data center, while Acton proposed a conditional moratorium on data centers if certain requirements aren't met, reported the Ohio Capital Journal.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, D, has applied pressure to utilities requesting rate hikes, while his opponent, state treasurer Stacy Garrity, R, proposed lowering rates by eliminating the state tax on electricity, and said she would intervene in a utility's rate case if she disagreed with a hike, according to reporting from Spotlight PA. An ad from Garrity's campaign said Shapiro "sold us out" to data center interests, while an ad from Shapiro's campaign called Garrity "Pennsylvania's No. 1 fan of data centers," The Hill reported.

Dylan Reed, Advanced Energy United's managing director overseeing federal and political affairs, said Pennsylvania's race is also significant given the role that Gov. Shapiro has played in the ongoing debate over the PJM Interconnection's surging prices.

In 2025, Shapiro was one of the PJM state governors who threatened to pull out of the grid operator's markets.

"Affordability is the message that we see out here very clearly," Reed said. "I think when you are looking at high prices when it comes to your utility bill, the number one office that can impact that right now is the governor."

How elections could shape federal policy

Nazar said he thinks that following the election, in Congress "there's probably going to be at least a discussion about new kinds of tax credit incentives that could be deployed."

In 2022, then-Vice President Kamala Harris cast the tie-breaking vote in the Senate to pass the Inflation Reduction Act, which received no Republican votes and established long-horizon tax credits for clean energy along with new tax credit mechanisms like transferability.

In 2025, a Republican-controlled Congress passed the OBBBA, which shortened the horizon for some of the IRA's clean energy benefits. Now, if Democrats take back control, they could seek to revise the OBBBA's impacts, observers say.

"A flipped Congress where both houses are with the Democrats could have a dramatic turn on the energy policy landscape, and particularly with federal energy tax credits," said Heather Cooper, a partner at the law firm McDermott Will & Schulte. "We have seen pretty dramatic flip-flopping in the last five years as Congress has gone back and forth."

However, Cooper — who advises clients on federal income tax issues related to the energy transition — said she thinks the clean energy industry is prepared for the possibility of future flip-flopping.

"Most of the players who are in this market … The reality is all of their business models are kind of used to a world where these tax credits have 1, 2, 3, 4-year horizons," she said.

The IRA, which created a longer runway for the first time, resulted in a "phenomenal amount of money poured into this industry," she added.

Carl Fleming, global co-head of McDermott Will & Schulte's energy and project finance group, said, "A number of folks have already worked out scenarios where some of these projects pencil out regardless of tax credits."

"I do think you'll probably see an extension of the solar credit," he said. "Solar took a good hit under OB3, but with rising energy costs, I think all that stuff's on the table because if I'm running for office or trying to get back into office, and I can find a technology that can help bring those energy costs down … whatever it takes to kind of get these energy costs down, that's going to be on the table."

Election rhetoric or something lasting?

Some utility executives have suggested that the furor over data centers and affordability could die down after the elections.

Fleming said he thinks there may be a more fundamental shift happening. He pointed to Texas' pause on data center grid interconnections, aimed at weeding out speculative requests, as a potential policy model.

"You could question whether [the pause was] driven by the midterms or just normal processes, but I think that's going to be the way folks will look at this at the state level going forward — taking a kind of investment-type approach to these projects," he said.

"It's no longer a race to power; it's a race to bankable power," he continued. "Data centers are coming along so fast, much faster than people had anticipated. It's tough for legislation to keep up with."

Reed said that the question of how to achieve speed to power, while preserving grid reliability and affordability, is what "every policymaker should be asking."

Nazar said that post-election, he sees the chance for "durable" bipartisan legislation.

"I think it is actually quite an interesting opportunity next year to have a necessarily bipartisan approach to these policies, where energy is top of mind for voters," he said. "I think the [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act] is a good signal of potentially a return to cross-party substantive, serious and impactful energy policymaking that I could foresee carrying into next year."

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act aims to speed federal permitting for energy and infrastructure projects, protect permits for approved projects and expand the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's power to eliminate obstacles to new transmission. It was announced in September, the result of careful negotiation between Republicans and Democrats.

But bill co-sponsor Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., warned in October that the deal could be "[blown] up" by the Trump administration's moves to revoke federal permits for offshore wind farms.

The bill has also been criticized by some consumer and clean energy advocates who say it would favor oil and gas projects, weaken environmental laws, undermine state and Tribal authority and limit the judiciary's ability to intervene to prevent harm.

Nazar said he thinks the potential for BAAJA to be amended "seems like that's an ongoing conversation that appears to be in play."

"That said, I think we will see how the dynamics shift after tomorrow, if they shift at all," he added.

According to Crux's conversations with developers, Nazar said, "Predictability is the most important thing they could ask for from the federal government."

text:
The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) has introduced a $237 million funding opportunity designed to increase manufacturing and strengthen supply chains for critical electric grid components.

The Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance (Grid SCALED) funding opportunity will incentivize the refurbishment and reuse of critical equipment and encourage the adoption of alternative materials and sub components that are sourced and made in America. These efforts will lower costs, strengthen grid reliability, and meet growing electricity demand.

“The Energy Department is investing in American-made technologies and modernizing our grid to reduce reliance on foreign suppliers and deliver affordable, reliable, electricity,” U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said.

The funding opportunity will support projects in two key areas:

Up to $50 million will be provided to projects that promote greater refurbishment and reuse of existing grid equipment and materials;

Up to $187 million will be provided to projects that will increase the use of alternative materials and subcomponents sourced and made in the U.S, reducing dependence on imports.

“America should never have to rely on foreign suppliers to keep the lights on,” Office of Electricity Assistant Secretary Katie Jereza said. “We’re putting American ingenuity to work, developing next-generation grid technologies that strengthen our domestic supply chain, help lower costs, and make our grid more reliable. The power to secure our energy future should be in our own hands.”

This is the first funding opportunity in the DOE’s Grid Supply Chain Program, which is authorized to provide up to $375 million to strengthen domestic supply chains for the manufacturing of distribution and power transformers, grid components, and materials.

In 2027, additional funding announcements are anticipated for next-generation technologies, including solid-state transformers, and promote common configurations to streamline manufacturing.

The investment is expected to deliver an estimated $125 million in annual utility savings. Further, it would keep about $50 million per year in the U.S. economy that would otherwise go to foreign suppliers.

Applicants must submit a concept paper by Nov. 20 to qualify to submit a full application. Full applications are due by Feb. 8, 2027.

text:
The election will also be a test of how voters respond to Democratic candidates tying the biggest issue of the election — affordability — to the climate crisis.

Here are five things to know about the climate crisis and the midterms:

1. If Democrats do well, they could gain leverage to oppose Trump’s anti-climate agenda

If Democrats take control of the House or Senate, they won’t be able to overturn previous Republican actions like gutting the Inflation Reduction Act, and they can’t pass new legislation that Trump would veto, but they will have more cards to play to oppose Trump’s pro-fossil fuel agenda going forward.

If Democrats take back the House, it will mean the White House has to compromise with Democrats in order to pass budgets. This would give Democrats the power to add climate provisions into appropriations legislation, said Michael Gerrard, founder and director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “Many appropriations begin in the House, and these are huge bills that have to pass, so it’s possible that some pro-climate provisions could be put in some of the appropriations legislation,” he said. “Often presidents sign appropriation bills that have provisions they don’t like because they need to get the budget passed.”

Democrats could also use their power in the House to launch investigations and subpoena witnesses and documents. Dan Farber, a law professor at the University of California, Berkeley, suggested they could investigate possible conflicts of interest or corruption, like the Trump administration intervening in a federal lawsuit to allow Elon Musk to continue using portable gas generators in his Mississippi data center, which the suit alleges is a violation of the Clean Air Act.

If Democrats win the Senate, they could oppose further confirmations of federal judges, cabinet officers, and sub-cabinet positions. “That gives [Democratic] senators some leverage to stop appointments they don’t want,” Farber said. “But you can also hold appointments hostage in return for other things.”

Preventing appointments of anti-climate judges would leave more vacancies for the next president to fill, he added. “That can have a big long-term effect on the environment.”

Gerrard said a power shift in the House and Senate could change negotiations around the permitting reform bill, which could clear hurdles for both clean energy and fossil fuels projects. The bill would significantly weaken the National Environmental Policy Act, making it impossible for a court to halt a project due to a Nepa violation, he said. “But if the Democrats are in charge of both the House and the Senate, that bill might look different.”

Farber and Gerrard said state climate policy was also hanging in the balance this November. The Cook Political Report found that Democrats could gain two-to-four governor’s seats this cycle. “If some of the governor’s offices flip from Republican to Democrat, that could yield a profound change in state climate policy,” Gerrard said.

2. If Republicans do well, expect more environmental rollbacks

If the Republicans buck polling predictions and manage to keep control of the House and Senate, it would embolden Trump to continue his anti-climate agenda.

Trump could continue his favoritism toward polluting companies, because Democrats would lack the investigative and subpoena powers to hold him accountable.

And he could continue appointing conservative justices: “Trump has been packing the lower courts with anti-regulatory, super conservative judges,” Farber said.

Under this administration, Republican lawmakers have backed Trump on policies that were unfavorable to their constituents — such as voting to repeal clean energy tax credits that created jobs in their districts. If Republicans win in the midterms, Republicans would continue to vote in support of Trump. “Maybe even more so, because I think this would be seen as a big win for him personally,” Farber said.

“They have not just been sitting on the sidelines ‚ they have helped Trump, in terms of repealing the Inflation Reduction Act from Biden, and overturning some specific regulations by Congress. We could see more of that kind of thing coming from them. So it would be another big step backwards,” Farber said.

“I keep thinking, how much worse could they do? But they always find something,” he added.

3. As affordability remains a key issue, voters feel the pinch of Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration’s constraints on renewables are forcing consumers to spend more on energy. A study by Nera predicted that between 2027 and 2033, economy-wide household energy costs would increase on average by $11.6 billion annually from constraining the deployment of solar and wind. The region hardest hit by these constraints is Texas, where rates are forecast to rise as much as 22 percent, the study found.

Trump’s attacks on clean energy have also led to mass job losses, including many in battleground states. The US clean energy workforce lost nearly 37,000 jobs last year — the first annual job loss in America’s clean energy economy since the pandemic, according to a September report from E2, a business advocacy group for the clean economy that analyzed Department of Energy data.

A report from Climate Power puts that number even higher, with 173,000 clean energy jobs either cut or delayed since Trump took office. The report found that Texas saw the most jobs lost from Trump’s war on clean energy.

The Nera report found that increased reliance on natural gas capacity and generation raises reliability risks and increases exposure to price volatility. According to Climate Power, since Trump took office, gas and electric utilities have raised or sought to increase bills by more than $92 billion, affecting more than 100 million customers across the country.

4. Voters in battleground states want to hear more from candidates about the climate crisis

Polling shows that Democrats and Republicans in battleground states want candidates to talk more about the climate crisis. And even though one in three US adults have been directly affected by extreme weather, midterm candidates are avoiding talking directly about climate change in what’s known as “climate hushing.”

But researchers from the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability have found that there are three groups of Democratic candidates and officeholders who are talking about the climate crisis in subtle instead of direct ways: energy populists like Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio are using data centers and utility bills to connect the issues of climate and affordability, climate champions like Arizona Democratic candidate JoAnna Mendoza are promising bold action like investing in clean energy, and candidates who are advocating for an “all-of-the-above” approach to energy, like Amy Acton in the Ohio governor’s race.

“The one thing that they all have in common is a focus on affordability … and talking about energy issues in the context of affordability,” said Geoffrey Henderson, an assistant environmental policy and planning professor at the University of Michigan.

He noted that a few candidates, like Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa, were emphasizing how extreme weather events worsened by the climate crisis are driving up the cost of insurance.

With various quiet climate messages being tested in battleground states, this election could be a test of how voters respond to these messages. Henderson expects political analysts will study the data after the election to draw lessons from it. “The climate message has in a number of ways been brought into alignment with the affordability question, and so I think this is a test of whether that combination resonates,” he said.

The issue of climate hushing has come up election after election, but Henderson believes it’s a positive thing that candidates are still finding ways to talk about climate, even indirectly. “It’s better that candidates are tying climate to affordability than not mentioning it at all, and I do see how different parts of the country lend themselves to different strategies.”

5. Whatever happens at the polls, some of the big US climate fights ahead will be in the courts

Environmental laws are being tested in US courts like never before. “We’re now at a stage where every significant environmental regulation is challenged in court by one side or the other,” Gerrard said.

The Trump administration has set out to weaken and revoke environmental regulations, triggering a wave of litigation attempting to undo those actions. If a future Democratic president tries to restore those regulations or issue new ones, they would also be challenged in court, Gerrard said.

Gerrard is closely watching the fight over Trump’s repeal of the endangerment finding, which stated that the buildup of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere endangers public health, allowing the Environmental Protection Agency to limit greenhouse gas pollution from various sources. “There’s a case before the DC circuit on Trump’s revocation of the endangerment finding — that’s a very big case,” he noted.

Samsung SDI has started mass production of LFP batteries at its $6.3 billion StarPlus Energy plant in Kokomo, Indiana. The company started prismatic LFP cell output in October. The step is part of a two-track approach for both LFP and NCA chemistries. The Indiana location is now Samsung SDI’s “ESS battery production hub.

The transfer is a solid quarter closer. In the third quarter of 2026, Samsung SDI reported its best operating profit for the quarter in three years. Revenue increased 52.6 percent from the previous year. After posting an operating loss last year, operating profit stood at KRW 407.8 billion, or $304 million. The battery division alone accounted for KRW 4.41 trillion in revenue, which rose by 55.3 percent, and an operating profit of KRW 361.9 billion.

Other Projects.

Another major energy project is taking place in Texas. Waaree Solar Americas has started commercial production on two new 800 MW solar module manufacturing lines at its Brookshire facility in Texas, USA. The expansion doubles the plant’s annual manufacturing capacity to 3.2 GW. Production on the new lines began on October 29, 2026. The development strengthens Waaree’s domestic manufacturing footprint as the company targets growing demand from US solar developers, utilities and engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors.

Scope of implementation on the Samsung SDI StarPlus Energy Plant

The Kokomo complex houses two StarPlus Energy gigafactories, built with Stellantis under their battery joint venture. They have a combined investment of more than $6.3 billion and a combined capacity of 67 gigawatt hours. The first plant, which has a capacity of 33 GWh, was opened in early 2025. Stellantis schedules the second, at 34 GWh, to start production in early 2027. It will employ 1,400 more workers.

The pivot was driven by demand. The factories that produce mobility cells are no longer profitable in the United States, where EV sales have been sluggish. Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solutions have thus moved their lines towards LFP for stationary storage. LG made a similar move at its joint venture with Stellantis in Canada. Samsung will speed up the conversion of EVs to LFP in the fourth quarter.

The company has also ensured its supply chain. Next, supply chains. To avoid Chinese import tariffs and meet Foreign Entity of Concern rules, Samsung SDI said it has “signed long-term supply agreements for LFP cathode materials with major Korean materials companies.” The objective is to meet U.S. demand “independent of China.

Orders back the strategy. Samsung SDI has received over 60 GWh of orders for energy storage in the United States in 2026. The tally includes a 1 GWh agreement with Alpha Omega Power for its NCA-based Samsung Battery Box 1.7. It also includes a US cell supply deal with inverter manufacturer Sungrow.

Outlook for the Samsung SDI business

Today, data centers are driving the growth narrative. The turnaround was driven by orders for utility-scale ESS and battery backup units for AI facilities. Samsung SDI has also launched cylindrical LFP cells for data center BBUs.

Furthermore, the company is pursuing additional deals. It is looking to finalize more long-term ESS and UPS deals before the end of the year. It is also bidding in South Korea’s third government-led ESS procurement round.

The pieces therefore fit together. The cells come from Kokomo, the cathode chain is provided by Korean suppliers, and the output is taken by grid plus data center customers. Now Samsung SDI has to prove that the hub can operate at scale with the continued softness of EV demand. Despite this, it has a head start with the order book and the profit swing.

text:
Q&A with Adam Webb, Head of Battery Raw Materials, Benchmark Mineral Intelligence

Battery raw materials expert Adam Webb of Benchmark Mineral Intelligence says the long-term outlook for lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and phosphate remains strong despite a slowdown in electric vehicle (EV) growth. Webb argues that battery energy storage systems (BESS) have become a major demand driver, pushing lithium into deficit and helping lift prices as global battery deployment accelerates.

This interview explores how export restrictions are reshaping cobalt and nickel markets, where future supply is likely to emerge, and the key risks facing the sector. Webb identifies lithium as the standout battery metal, forecasting demand growth from around 2 million tonnes (Mt) today to 5Mt by 2040, requiring significant new mine supply globally.

To listen to the interview, click here:

Give us a quick introduction to yourself and your work in this space.

For those unfamiliar with Benchmark Mineral Intelligence, we cover critical minerals and are particularly focused on battery supply chains, as well as materials outside and adjacent to them, including copper and rare earths.

My role within the company is to look after our fundamental research into those raw materials, specifically looking at supply, demand, market balance forecasts, price forecasts, and cost analysis. This also covers a broad spectrum of critical minerals, including lithium, nickel, cobalt, and graphite.

There’s been a lot of talk about the EV revolution, which has gained pace in many ways, but also faltered in others. What are some of the broader trends you’re seeing today?

On the EV side, you’re right. The market has grown massively over recent years. We’ve seen a huge uptick in EV sales globally, but there has been somewhat of a slowdown in that growth this year.

But if you look at this on a regional basis, China, which is by far the biggest EV market, has seen growth almost flatline this year. That’s because certain subsidies were removed towards the end of last year.

In North America, we have a similar picture. The Trump administration removed some tax credits for EVs. So, we saw a big uptick in sales just before the tax credit was removed and then subsequently a downturn.

But if you look at Europe, EV sales have risen significantly this year. That’s because of high fuel prices driven by the war in Iran, subsidies in various European Union (EU) countries, and imports of Chinese EVs.

That picture is reflected in the rest of the world as well. For example, in Australia, New Zealand, and South America, sales are strong. This is again due to a combination of relatively competitively priced Chinese imports and high fuel prices.

So it’s a really mixed picture.

Overall, we’re expecting 7% growth in global EV sales this year. While there is a slowdown, there are different regional dynamics, and the market is still growing pretty strongly.

Let’s look at some of the supply and demand dynamics for some of the key metals that are needed like lithium, graphite, cobalt, etc. Where are the biggest supply gaps?

We look at the raw materials needed for batteries used in EVs, but also in BESS, which is another massively growing segment driving demand.

When we’re talking about raw materials, number one is lithium. It’s used in all lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries, regardless of the battery type.

That’s probably the commodity most tied to this sector, with about 90% of lithium demand coming from batteries.

What we’re seeing for lithium is that the market has been in deficit this year, meaning demand has exceeded supply. That has been driven not by the EV sector, but by BESS. We’ve seen new BESS deployments increase by around 40% year-on-year. We’re expecting that this year, the supply of those batteries will increase at an even greater rate.

There’s been a big ramp-up of production, particularly of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries in China. That’s pushed up lithium demand significantly this year. We’re talking around 30% growth in terms of demand.

On the supply side, we’ve also seen growth as projects come online. Some projects that previously closed due to low lithium prices have also returned, particularly in Australia. This has pushed supply up by around 20%, but not at the same rate as demand.

The lithium market is in deficit and that’s caused prices to increase. We’ve seen prices more than double, rising from around US$10,000 ($14,170) per tonne of lithium carbonate in mid-2025 to above US$20,000 by mid-2026.

There’s been a recent pullback in prices, but we see that as more sentiment-driven. The fundamentals are still showing that the lithium market is in deficit.

The dynamic differs for other commodities. Nickel and cobalt, for example, are used in battery cathodes, but not in LFP batteries. Instead, they’re used in nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries, which are used in EVs rather than the energy storage sector.

The dynamic that we’ve seen is the increase in the use of LFP batteries in EVs in China, particularly in the more economic models, and that means that the share of NCM batteries has fallen.

Even so, battery types that contain nickel and cobalt are still growing. For example, I think cobalt-containing batteries are expected to grow 10% this year, which feeds through to rising demand for nickel and cobalt.

There are a few dynamics that are quite interesting on the supply side.

About 75% of cobalt comes from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which imposed an export ban early last year before introducing a quota system that has reduced how much cobalt can reach the market.

These measures have switched the market into a deficit, leading to a strong rally in cobalt prices. A couple of years ago, cobalt hydroxide was as low as US$14,000 per tonne, but this year, it’s reached as high as US$60,000.

It’s a similar picture for nickel, but for different reasons. That market is dominated by Indonesia, which has really ramped up its refining capacity in nickel and now accounts for around 60% of global supply.

Indonesia has introduced a quota system called the Rencana Kerja dan Anggaran Biaya (RKAB), which dictates how much ore can be mined to supply its smelters. The quota was significantly lower this year than the previous year and fell short of the smelters’ requirements.

So, we’ve seen some operations having to curtail production, with a resulting drop in Indonesian output.

In addition, the Fort Saskatchewan refinery in Canada has closed because the US imposed sanctions on Cuban oil imports. The refinery relied on a mine in Cuba and it basically ran out of fuel and couldn’t produce any ore.

So, for those two reasons, we’ve had a small drop in nickel output this year, around 1%. At the same time, demand has risen, driven by batteries and stainless steel, which remains the biggest demand sector for nickel. This has essentially balanced the market.

By our estimates, the market is in a very narrow deficit but to all intents and purposes remains balanced.

Again, that’s supported prices, which we’ve seen rise by about 15% from the 2025 average to the 2026 average.

Graphite is another interesting and often overlooked material. While the other materials that I’ve mentioned go into the cathode side of the battery, graphite goes into the anode.

There are two types of graphite: natural and synthetic. Synthetic graphite is produced from coke, so from the hydrocarbon industry, while natural graphite is mined as flake graphite.

We’ve seen rising demand from batteries, which account for about 40% of global graphite demand. There is also significant industrial demand for flake graphite, so demand is rising. However, 70% of supply comes from China. We’ve also seen a big ramp-up in production in East Africa, leaving the market in a bit of a surplus and weighing on prices.

Prices have been very stable. I would say that flake graphite prices for the -100 mesh, which goes into the battery supply chain, have remained at about US$400 per tonne, reflecting the industry’s price floor.

The last one to mention is purified phosphoric acid, which is important to LFP cells and is becoming more significant as LFP use rises. That market is essentially in deficit. It’s important to know that with purified phosphoric acid, there are a lot of other uses as well, including fertilisers. The battery use of phosphate rock is relatively small, but it’s an important raw material to consider, particularly with that rise in LFP.

You spoke about export bans and quotas in the DRC and Indonesia specifically. What’s the overall impact of these policies on the industry overall? Is substitution an option?

With cobalt, on the substitution side, the industry has been looking at that for a long time because cobalt is quite a volatile commodity. The market is small, with a total demand of about 300,000 tonnes. Compare that with lithium, which is at 2Mt, and nickel, at close to 4Mt. So, cobalt is a really small market.

What comes with that is price volatility. A small change in supply or demand can move prices significantly. For that reason, and because supply is concentrated in the DRC and linked to artisanal mining, original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) have been looking to move away from cobalt for quite some time. That’s one of the reasons why we’ve seen a shift from NCM chemistries containing more cobalt to those containing less.

In terms of the broader impact, I think nickel and cobalt are similar when it comes to pricing. If you have that much control of supply and can control how much reaches the market, you can influence supply and demand dynamics and, therefore, prices.

Cobalt hydroxide prices were as low as US$14,000 per tonne due to a massive glut of supply from primary copper mines in the DRC, which produce cobalt as a byproduct. The DRC Government wanted to generate more revenue from its cobalt resources, so it introduced export bans and quotas, which have led to prices rallying.

That was always the plan. The risk, though, is that pushing prices up increases the incentive to substitute cobalt with other materials.

I think there’s a balancing act on the nickel side of things. Indonesia’s RKAB quota system is another way to support the price. What we saw last year is nickel prices dropping to a point where a lot of the Indonesian nickel industry was not making any money or was operating at a loss.

The Indonesian Government can use the RKAB quota system to better manage its natural resources and prevent them from being overexploited. It can also control supply to support prices and keep the Indonesian nickel industry profitable.

But there is always the risk that if you pull that lever too much, it pushes the prices too high and then you destroy demand for the very thing you’re trying to monetise.

So, with these export controls and regulations in producing regions, where do you see emerging opportunities or projects?

While demand in the lithium market is currently around 2Mt, it’s expected to reach 5Mt by 2040. That means we’ll need to more than double supply to meet demand.

The scale of growth is similar for other commodities, although a little lower for nickel and cobalt. Natural graphite and purified phosphoric acid are also expected to see significant growth.

We’re going to need more supply to come online to meet that demand, which will naturally create opportunities for project developers across the world.

Where that supply comes from is based on geology and where the deposits are located.

For lithium, it’s quite a diverse supply landscape. The bottleneck is refining, particularly in China. In terms of mining, Australia is currently the biggest producer, with China the second- or third-largest. Then you’ve got Chile, Argentina, and Zimbabwe, so lithium is quite diverse in terms of where the mineral resources are located, with opportunities around the world.

At the moment, the biggest growth we’re seeing is in Argentina, where the country is becoming quite supportive of the industry, as well as in the US, particularly around the Smackover Formation in Arkansas, and in parts of Africa. We’re expecting AVZ Minerals’ (HM:3A2) Manono Lithium Project to come online in the DRC, along with several more projects in West Africa.

On the nickel front, this has become a clearly Indonesian-focused story. However, there are several projects in Canada, for example, that differ from those in Indonesia. They’re exploiting sulphide resources, whereas nickel resources in Indonesia are laterite.

Western governments have been looking to diversify away from Chinese supply, particularly. Within Indonesia, there’s also quite a heavy influence of Chinese companies through joint ventures. So there’s that strategic aspect as well.

We’re expecting growth in Indonesia to continue, particularly from high-pressure acid leach operations, which are feeding the battery supply chain. So, that’s where we’re seeing the biggest growth in terms of nickel.

For graphite, we’ve seen huge growth in East Africa, including Mozambique, Tanzania, and Madagascar, and we expect that to continue. In North America, Nouveau Monde Graphite (NYSE:NMG) has secured funding for its project, which is tied to this move away from Chinese control, particularly in graphite.

If you look at the natural graphite side, around 70% of mine supply is coming from China, with refined supply bringing that up to 90%. So, that’s part of a strategic move as well.

Finally, in the purified phosphoric acid industry, China accounts for around 40% of supply. Morocco is the second biggest producer, but if you look at the global reserve base, Morocco has about 70% of reserves. So, there’s a real opportunity there for Morocco to become a source for Western markets.

But, in terms of growth at the moment, China is still going to be the dominant player in that space.

What are some of the biggest risks for the future growth of the industry?

The opportunities for growth that I’ve outlined represent our base case — especially where we’re talking about a doubling of demand by 2040.

On the risk side of things, the number one risk is EV adoption and BESS rollouts. One risk that I’ve been talking about a lot this week is basically the oversupply of batteries, particularly within China, and this is largely on the BESS side.

This year, we’re expecting battery production to reach around 3 terawatt hours (TWh), but demand for those batteries is much lower, around 2.3TWh. So, we’re getting this oversupply.

Obviously, the production of the batteries is what dictates the demand for the raw materials. The risk is that if battery production is curtailed to bring it closer to demand, we may not see a decline in demand, but rather a slower rate of growth. This is because continuing to produce well above demand is not sustainable in the long term. However, this could be a gradual trend rather than a dramatic shift, and China has a history of overproducing in various sectors.

The other risk is technological. When we look at different battery types, there’s a lot of talk about sodium-ion batteries instead of Li-ion batteries. These are unlikely to be as relevant for EVs, although there may be some adoption. That’s because they tend to have lower energy density, meaning a car would have less range with the same size battery. However, they could have applications in BESS.

We’re seeing growth in the sodium-ion battery, but we’re not seeing it replacing LFP or Li-ion in the BESS space. There is a risk that if sodium-ion suddenly takes off, becomes commercialised, and costs less than LFP, it could displace some demand for Li-ion batteries, shifting requirements for raw materials.

To wrap it up, can you pick a favourite metal? What do you find most exciting?

I like looking at them all! They all have different dynamics when it comes to the energy transition and the EV and BESS market. Intrinsically, the one that is fundamental to all of this is lithium. As I said at the start, lithium is used in every single one of those Li-ion batteries and that’s a market that has grown massively.

By the time we get to 2040, that market is going to be 5Mt, which is more than the current nickel market, an established commodity.

We’ve seen the market grow from a very niche sector to the size of an established commodity. Along the way, we’ve seen projects emerge in various countries, different technologies being used, and even financial instruments, hedging, and futures contracts around lithium.

So, this rapid development of a niche or speciality commodity is quite exciting to be involved in.

Write to Amy Rotman at Mining.com.au

text:
Ford is installing a completely new production system at its at its Louisville Assembly Plant, which will make the Ford Fathom midsize electric truck in 2027. As part of a $2 billion overhaul of the plant, which began in late 2025, the carmaker says the Universal EV Production System radically simplifies the assembly process. Prototype production will begin in the first quarter of 2026, with customer models following by mid-year.

Fix first, predict later: Five predictive maintenance lessons from AMNA 2026

Lucid, Tenneco, Gestamp, Autoliv and Ford discussed where predictive maintenance pays back and where it stalls. The consensus was that prediction is the last step in a plant's digital journey, not the first.

The UEV Production System transforms the traditional assembly line into an ‘assembly tree’. Instead of one long conveyor, teams simultaneously build three subassembly vehicle sections in parallel before bringing them together – the front and rear sections, and the third containing the structural battery, seats, consoles and carpeting.

The sections arrive in front of the operator as a kit, with parts in the right orientation, and fasteners, scanners and power tools included.

Advertisement

Ergonomic benefits

Building the three sections separately in parallel also facilitates access to the overall surface area to be worked on, enabling more operators to work at the same time, which speeds up the process. Ford says the UEV Production System removes the cumbersome restraints of working inside a frame, as seen in the example of installing a seat, where operators typically have to squeeze through the doorway and work around the structure of the vehicle with tools in hand to secure it. In the UEV Production System, the seat goes on the rear clip and gets secured in place without the vehicle structure in the way. Likewise, to install components on the dashboard, which has the most parts per section of the vehicle, operators can stand facing the front clip with a direct line-of-sight, optimising installation.

The three main sections of the body marry together only when the bulk of components are already installed. This is possible, in part, thanks to the use of large unicastings where a single large aluminium casting replaces what was once dozens of individually stamped and welded pieces to help form two of the main sections of the vehicle.

Assembly operatives have been trained at the New Model Product Development Center (NMPDC) on the new assembly method.

Faster Fathom output

Ford has redesigned specific parts of the vehicle as part of its assembly streamlining, a move that has also reduced production costs. Each unicasting is structurally whole on its own and does not to be welded into a complete body shell before work can begin inside. On the third line, interior components are installed on top of the battery, which serves as the vehicle’s floor. The battery itself is then installed into the vehicle from the bottom.

The UEV Production System and its assembly tree will allow Ford to assemble the Fathom 40% faster than LAP’s current products, and the company has reinvested some of that time into insourcing and automation to improve quality and cost. Ford says that gives LAP the highest level of automation in final assembly across all Ford plants globally. Ultimately, it means the Fathom’s assembly will net out at 15% faster than previous production times at the Louisville plant.

The UEV Production System features more than 5,000 metres (17,000 feet) of conveyor in final assembly and Ford has built around 21,500 sq. m (230,000 sq. ft) of concrete floor on which to stand the assembly equipment.

Advertisement

Module flash station

For the first time, a software module flash station will ensure vehicles have the latest software prior to module installation. Previously, this software flash happened after the vehicle was built, and if issues were detected, updates took 10 minutes per vehicle. With private 5G in the plant, operators can perform quality tests like these as a vehicle rolls down the three branches of the assembly tree.

To support this, Ford has tripled WiFi coverage at LAP from 385 to 1,080 access points to provide constant, high-bandwidth, low-latency connectivity. Network capability will be the latest-generation WiFi-7, which is more resilient and three times faster than previous generations. LAP has more access points than any other Ford plant globally. It means Ford can make more on-the-spot quality checks along the assembly tree to make the build of each vehicle more efficient.

Battery pack rethink

Ford has also been working on how to get more miles out of a smaller battery to simultaneously address the range anxiety of customers who are weighing up the pros and cons of buying an EV, while at the same time addressing the weight and cost issues of the battery itself. The average lithium battery accounts for somewhere around 40% of an EV’s total cost and upwards of 25% of its weight, according to Ford.

AMNA ’26: Building resilience through speed, flexibility and disciplined digitalisation

Day 1 of Automotive Manufacturing North America’26 brought together a clear message for North American automotive manufacturing: the industry must adapt faster, but it cannot afford to confuse activity with progress

Alan Clarke, vice-president of Advanced Development Projects at Ford and designer of the UEV Production System, says his team approached the design engineering and manufacturing of the vehicle together from a completely new perspective. That includes equipping every engineer working on the project with what are called Bounties – numerical metrics assigned to key factors, such as vehicle mass and aerodynamic drag, that directly translate to efficiency and the range and the cost of the battery. Clarke says the aim is to reduce overall energy consumption of the vehicle as a system, not simply the optimisation of a single part.

Ford is making the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for the Fathom at BlueOval Battery Park in Michigan with technology licensed from battery supplier CATL. LFP batteries are built on a lower cost chemistry, having no nickel or cobalt content. The prismatic battery pack designed by Ford also has a very efficient cell-to-structure architecture, which turns the battery into an integral part of the truck skeleton.

The battery pack uses a multi-layer, single piece, flexible circuit board, which integrates low and high voltage, as well as thermal sensing connections, reducing hundreds of bus bars and wires into a single part. According to Clarke, the architecture reduces non-cell cost and has a very compact, power electronics unit inside the battery pack, which eliminates extra connectors, enclosures, mass and overall volume.

Advertisement

Module focus

Reduced manufacturing complexity is also helping to drive up quality. The Fathom architecture has 50% fewer connections and 20% fewer parts than a typical vehicle programme. Combined with the replacement of pre-opened pre-positioned (POPP) clamps with quick connects, there is a lower risk of faulty connections.

This has helped reduce the wiring harness by more than 1,200 metres (4,000 ft) and made it almost 10kg lighter than in the first-generation electric SUV.

Ford says that the time saved using the new UEV Production System is being reinvested into insourcing and automation to improve quality and cost. The architecture of the system incorporates a five-fold increase in Ford’s own module design, providing five times more control over critical semiconductors.

Ford’s electronics team has produced 35 million Ford modules. That includes a High-Performance Compute Center unifying infotainment (IVI), the advanced driver assistance system (ADAS), audio and networking into a single, compact powerhouse.

At the same time, the team has decreased the total number of physical modules in the vehicle. This approach delivers significant cost savings of 10-15% per module.

By combining parallel assembly, a new production line architecture and a new battery pack design, Ford aims to produce the Fathom faster, at lower cost and with higher quality. Once full production is up and running in the middle of next year and plant performance is analysed, Ford will be looking at the lessons learned and what it can apply at other plants in North American and further afield.

description:
WASHINGTON (Nov. 3, 2026) – Major environmental groups submitted comments detailing the numerous legal and technical flaws in the Environmental Protection Agency’s “tectonic and unreasoned” proposal to abdicate its legal responsibility to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.
The proposal is “fundamentally unlawful” and should be abandoned because it contravenes Supreme Court precedent and guts important clean air protections, the groups said in comments submitted to the agency late yesterday.
The EPA “misinterprets the Clean Air Act, ignores scientific evidence, and entirely misunderstands its own duty as the agency responsible for protecting public health and the environment,” the comments say.
But EPA’s futility analysis “lacks any legal foundation or rational basis and is otherwise fundamentally flawed, arbitrary and capricious, inadequately explained, and unlawful,” the groups said.
The comments submitted to EPA late yesterday were also endorsed by Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin, and Friends of the Earth.
text:
WASHINGTON (Nov. 3, 2026) – Major environmental groups submitted comments detailing the numerous legal and technical flaws in the Environmental Protection Agency’s “tectonic and unreasoned” proposal to abdicate its legal responsibility to regulate greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

The proposal is “fundamentally unlawful” and should be abandoned because it contravenes Supreme Court precedent and guts important clean air protections, the groups said in comments submitted to the agency late yesterday.

Clean Air Task Force, Center for Biological Diversity, Earthjustice, Environmental Defense Fund, Environmental Law & Policy Center, NRDC (Natural Resources Defense Council), Sierra Club, and Union of Concerned Scientists signed the comments.

The EPA “misinterprets the Clean Air Act, ignores scientific evidence, and entirely misunderstands its own duty as the agency responsible for protecting public health and the environment,” the comments say. “The EPA must withdraw the supplemental proposal in its entirety.”

A key part of the agency’s proposal is its contention that addressing the greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, the second largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in the U.S., would be “futile,” because they are responsible for only a portion of the problem of climate change.

But EPA’s futility analysis “lacks any legal foundation or rational basis and is otherwise fundamentally flawed, arbitrary and capricious, inadequately explained, and unlawful,” the groups said.

The comments include new expert modeling showing that – even assuming the EPA’s own power-plant emissions projections – uncontrolled U.S. power-plant greenhouse gases would cause massive human health and welfare harms of $20.4 trillion by 2100.

For context, the entire U.S. GDP was $29.3 trillion in 2024.

The new modeling also shows that, under EPA’s own projections, U.S. power-plant carbon pollution will cause more than 100,000 childhood asthma cases, 22,000 hospital or emergency room visits, and 1.8 million lost school days by 2100. Using other assumptions, projected harms to health and welfare are even worse.

The comments submitted to EPA late yesterday were also endorsed by Clean Air Council, Clean Wisconsin, and Friends of the Earth.

text:
U.S.-based solar technology and manufacturing company Inox Solar Americas LLC is progressing with the construction of its 3 GW annual-capacity solar cell manufacturing facility in North Carolina.

According to a press release, the company has advanced the project to the equipment installation phase and reaffirmed that the facility remains on schedule to begin production in the second quarter of 2027. As part of its efforts to establish a more vertically integrated U.S. solar manufacturing platform, Inox Solar Americas is developing the 515,460-square-foot facility.

Once operational, the facility's domestic advanced solar cell production will complement the company's existing U.S. solar module manufacturing capabilities. The investment aims to provide customers with greater access to U.S.-manufactured solar technology while supporting a more transparent, resilient and reliable domestic supply chain.

Inox Solar Americas Builds On Boviet Solar's U.S. Manufacturing Assets in North Carolina

Founded in 2026 in the United States, Inox Solar Americas specialises in advanced monocrystalline photovoltaic (PV) cells and high-performance Gamma Series™ monofacial and Vega Series™ bifacial PV modules.

Its photovoltaic solutions are designed for residential, commercial, industrial, community solar and utility-scale applications, with a focus on efficiency, reliability and long-term value.

Inox Solar Americas acquired Boviet Solar's U.S. PV manufacturing assets in Greenville, North Carolina. These include 3 GW of annual PV module manufacturing capacity and a planned 3 GW of annual PV cell manufacturing capacity, which is expected to become operational in 2027.

Through localised manufacturing, resilient supply chains, operational excellence and efficient logistics, the company aims to strengthen the U.S. solar supply chain and address growing domestic demand.

Inox Solar Americas is part of the broader renewable energy platform of Inox Clean Energy and the India-headquartered INOXGFL Group. Backed by the group's financial strength, business stability, manufacturing capabilities, technological innovation and industry expertise, the company aims to deliver high-quality, reliable and sustainable solar solutions across the U.S. solar energy market.

Navigating FEOC Regulatory Compliance

The addition of domestic PV cell manufacturing capabilities is expected to further support customers in addressing evolving U.S. domestic-content requirements, Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) and Prohibited Foreign Entity (PFE) considerations, applicable trade requirements and federal energy-policy provisions.

The company's approach emphasises qualified sourcing, documented manufacturing processes and compliance readiness to help customers navigate increasingly complex procurement and project requirements.

The Greenville manufacturing platform will integrate advanced Galaxion™ monocrystalline PV cell technologies with Inox Solar Americas' U.S.-manufactured Gamma Series™ monofacial and Vega Series™ bifacial PV modules.

Advanced automation, precision cell processing, integrated inspection and testing, process controls, documented quality procedures and production traceability are intended to provide greater manufacturing control, from PV cell production through finished-module assembly.

This integrated approach is designed to support consistent product quality, high efficiency and energy yield, durability, and dependable performance across demanding U.S. solar applications.

Supply Chain Security, Transparency and Traceability

Integrating U.S. PV cell and module manufacturing will provide greater visibility and control across critical stages of the solar supply chain. Inox Solar Americas is strengthening supplier qualification, component-origin documentation, material traceability, production records and supply-chain due diligence.

Through these efforts, the company aims to support customers seeking greater transparency into where and how their products are manufactured.

It also intends to increase domestic production to reduce dependence on imported solar cells, mitigate exposure to global supply disruptions and trade-related risks, and ensure more reliable product availability for U.S. project pipelines.

Bankability, Supply Reliability and Customer Confidence

Inox Solar Americas is building its manufacturing capabilities to support large-scale, multiyear customer requirements. Its strategy focuses on expanding manufacturing scale, ensuring supply continuity, strengthening domestic-content capabilities, improving traceability and compliance readiness, and providing product support.

Together with product performance, quality systems, warranty support and its commitment to the U.S. market, these capabilities are intended to strengthen the confidence of customers, developers, investors and lenders in Inox Solar Americas and the projects supported by its products.

"Our continued progress on U.S. PV cell manufacturing represents an important step in building a more integrated and resilient domestic solar supply chain," said Ashok Nair, President & CEO of Inox Solar Americas.

"By bringing advanced cell technology, high-performance module manufacturing, and rigorous quality control together within our U.S. manufacturing platform, we are strengthening our ability to support customers with reliable supply and the bankability required for their project pipelines."

Dive Brief:

The U.S. Department of Energy is launching a new initiative to speed development and deployment of advanced battery technologies, DOE Assistant Secretary Audrey Robertson told Utility Dive.

The Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan, aims to strengthen domestic supply chains for battery materials and components, reduce manufacturing costs and shorten commercialization timelines, the department said on Wednesday.

U.S. demand for batteries across transportation and grid management applications is expected to increase from 179 GWh in 2025 to 707 GWh in 2035, according to a June analysis from Bloomberg NEF that DOE cited in a white paper published last month.

Dive Insight:

A secure, scaled-up domestic battery supply chain is critical for U.S. economic growth and security in the years ahead, DOE said in the white paper, “A National Strategy for American Leadership in Batteries.”

For utilities, batteries are increasingly indispensable for improving grid reliability and shifting load, particularly in regions where data center loads threaten to disrupt power flows, DOE said in the paper. Data centers themselves could account for one-quarter of total U.S. battery demand by 2030, according to a Benchmark Mineral Intelligence forecast cited in the paper.

The U.S. today is heavily dependent on external trade partners — particularly China — for battery materials and components, which “poses substantial supply chain risks,” DOE said in the paper.

Recent investments in U.S. battery cell and pack manufacturing have not been matched by investments in U.S. production of precursor components, creating gaps in the supply chain, DOE said.

“We have substantial work to do to secure the materials and manufacturing capabilities [lithium-ion batteries] require,” Robertson said in an email. “China currently controls between 60% and 100% of global production capacity across several critical stages of battery materials and component manufacturing … [which] represents a serious vulnerability for American industry and national security.”

China and other Asian countries host nearly all global lithium-ion battery cathode, anode and separator manufacturing and nearly 93% of electrolyte manufacturing, DOE said in 2024.

Robertson said the BattMan consortium, which has support from DOE’s Office of Critical Minerals and Energy Innovation, would expand the Trump administration’s efforts to boost domestic sources of battery materials and components.

The Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads the consortium, with participation from Argonne National Laboratory, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies, formerly known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. BattMan’s research university partners include the University of Alabama, Arizona State University, Binghamton University, the University of Michigan–Dearborn and the University of Washington.

DOE says the consortium will advance three strategic objectives: establish a “mine-to-market” domestic supply chain by 2030; develop new battery technologies that are “more affordable, longer lasting, higher performing, and less reliant on critical minerals;” and scale deployment of advanced battery technologies in sectors critical to national security.

“We’re excited about technologies that use more abundant domestic materials, reduce dependence on foreign supply chains, and can be manufactured competitively here in the United States,” Robertson said in an email.

In August, DOE announced $500 million in funding for seven projects to expand U.S. critical minerals and materials processing, battery manufacturing and recycling projects. Award recipients include a California-based company expanding lithium-ion battery anode manufacturing with U.S.-sourced materials and another firm piloting battery production using ultra‑thin lithium‑metal films and “prelithiated” material.

The latter “could enable higher-energy, faster-charging batteries,” Robertson said.

According to PNNL, BattMan will work to overcome barriers that have kept promising, U.S.-developed energy storage technologies like these from reaching commercial scale.

This is the latest installment in Waste Dive’s Biogas Monthly series.

Seven members of Congress recently joined together to urge the U.S. EPA to allow more maritime fuel uses to qualify for credits under the federal Renewable Fuel Standard, the latest push to open up a new market for biogas uses.

The letter, dated Oct. 15, comes as the industry continues to push for wider adoption of biofuels in the maritime sector, as the market for alternative fuels in the on-road transportation sector nears saturation.

Marine engines are divide into three categories for emissions regulations, with Category 3 considered the largest. The letter notes that the RFS already includes certain marine fuels as eligible under the RFS, but said there is insufficient regulatory clarity for fuel used in Category 3 engines, which power container ships, cruise ships and other large ships.

The representatives said their intent was to affirm the use of biofuels primarily on inland waterways or along U.S. coasts as eligible for credits under the RFS. They also said EPA should narrow the definition of ocean-going vessel to ensure that fuel “used predominantly in domestic commerce (including operations between U.S. ports or within U.S. coastal and inland waters) may qualify under the RFS regardless of whether a vessel uses a Category 3 engine.”

Doing so would further boost the domestic market for renewable natural gas, renewable diesel, ethanol, and other advanced biofuels, according to the letter.

The American Biogas Council praised the letter in a statement on Oct. 19, saying the proposed changes would open up a new market for liquefied natural gas produced from biogas and other renewable fuels.

“This helps put millions of tons of waste to beneficial use,” Patrick Serfass, ABC’s executive director, said in a statement.

The company is in the final stages of permitting its Sunnyside, Washington, RNG plant. Documents released by the host city indicate it would generate between 800,000 and 950,000 mmBtus of RNG annually, and would accept dairy manure from up to 25 local dairies as well as cellulosic feedstocks.

The project, which could become the nation’s largest, has received pushback from some local residents. It’s also not far from Divert’s Longview, Washington, anaerobic digestion plant. Divert is a portfolio company of Ara Partners, a separate strategy overseen by the same firm.

Purpose Energy partners with Danone for digester

Purpose Energy announced plans to build a $40 million digester to process wastewater and organic food waste residuals piped directly from a Danone facility in Minster, Ohio. The facility, which represents the first collaboration between the two companies, would receive material piped directly from Danone’s largest U.S. yogurt manufacturing facility.

Once online, the project is designed to process up to 250,000 gallons per day and produce about 50,000 mmBtus of RNG annually. The gas will be used in a boiler on site and displace fossil-based natural gas.

“This project is an excellent example of PurposeEnergy’s role in creating circularity benefits for food and beverage manufacturing,” Eric Fitch, founder and CEO of Purpose Energy, said in a statement.

Purpose Energy is backed by infrastructure investor Quinbrook. Purpose has built several digesters in the Northeast, including a plant that offtakes residuals directly from ice cream manufacturer Ben & Jerry’s plant in St. Albans, Vermont.

Publicly traded Aemetis announced it began operations of two new dairy digesters in California. The sites are expected to feed into its central biogas processing facility in Keyes, California.

The company has built out a network of 14 digesters through its hub-and-spoke biogas strategy. The system takes advantage of state and federal incentive programs, including the California Low Carbon Fuel Standard and federal Renewable Fuel Standard.

The newest digesters also used equipment purchased from from NPL Construction, a subsidiary of infrastructure services company Centuri Holdings. Aemetis expects to use a dozen more cleanup and compression systems from that transaction to speed up development of additional digester installations.

The company is also planning to bring its first RNG fueling station online at Keyes in the coming weeks.

Executives from Waga Energy and other project partners gathered to celebrate the ribbon cutting for a landfill-gas-to-energy plant at the Decatur Hills Landfill in Greensburg, Indiana. The landfill is owned by Best Way Disposal, a waste company based in Kalamazoo, Michigan.

The plant replaces a flare system for the landfill’s gas. Waga’s system can process up to 1,000 standard cubic feet per minute of gas and is expected to produce up to 203,000 mmBtus of RNG annually. Waga will own and operate the plant through a 20-year agreement.

CHARLOTTESVILLE, Va. (CBS19 NEWS) — Charlottesville is looking to expand its electric vehicle fleet over the next several years while addressing reliability concerns with some of its older public transit buses.

During a Charlottesville City Council work session on Monday, officials discussed an updated fleet and equipment replacement plan that projects the purchase of 24 additional electric vehicles between 2028 and 2030.

The city currently has 14 electric vehicles in its fleet, including vehicles used by several departments and electric buses operated by Charlottesville Area Transit.

Public Works Director Steven Hicks said the city is taking a phased approach to replacing vehicles based on their condition, reliability, safety and operational needs.

That includes addressing problems with older transit buses, which can leave riders waiting when vehicles break down. Garland Williams, director of transit, says that happens every day.

The city is also weighing the costs of transitioning to electric vehicles.

A city fleet electrification study estimates an electric passenger car could cost about $1,500 more than a comparable gas-powered vehicle. A larger electric SUV could cost about $18,000 more.

However, the study estimates replacing vehicles with electric models could save an average of $2,800 per vehicle over 10 years through lower fuel and maintenance costs.

"Just a year ago we were able to buy in bulk, diesel, for about $2.35. We're buying diesel now about $5.50 in bulk. That's unsustainable for us," said Williams.

Expanding the electric fleet also means investing in the infrastructure needed to keep those vehicles charged.

The city is requesting approximately $390,000 through its Capital Improvement Program for additional charging infrastructure. That includes about $225,000 for 17 Level 2 charging stations and $165,000 for one fast charger.

The proposed electric vehicle purchases and charging infrastructure would be considered through the city’s annual budget process. Officials say the timing of replacements will depend on vehicle conditions, department needs, available funding and whether electric options are needed.

On October 15, 2026, Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER), the Environmental Data & Governance Initiative (EDGI), and ToxicDocs.org launched Eyes on Environmental Enforcement, “a new online search portal that gives the public direct access to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) enforcement records that have been historically difficult to obtain and were not previously available in a searchable, centralized format.” According to PEER’s October 15, 2026, press release, the portal includes inspection reports, notices of violation, and related documents obtained by PEER from EPA through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). The press release states that the website:

Makes enforcement records about inspections and violations searchable in one place;

Helps communities near polluting facilities understand a facility’s enforcement history; and

Supports journalists and researchers investigating oversight and enforcement trends.

Records under the Clean Air Act (CAA), the Clean Water Act (CWA), and the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) from 2021 through 2025 are available, with some records from 2026. Additional records will be added as PEER obtains them.

The press release notes that an analysis “of just one small part of those holdings, EPA’s landfill inspections, has already turned up striking findings.” Although large landfills must control methane levels exceeding 500 parts per million (ppm), according to PEER, EPA inspectors measured methane above that limit at 677 locations at just 12 landfills, and at 200 locations within the 12 landfills, levels ran from 5,000 to over 200,000 ppm. At eight of the 12 landfills, “the largest leaks exceeded 50,000 ppm, methane’s lower explosive limit.”

text:
BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models.

Electrek’s Take

While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.

China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.

With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.

text:
Texas voters will make a historic choice in Tuesday’s gubernatorial election: Give Republican incumbent Greg Abbott a fourth term or elect Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who would become the state’s first Latina governor and the first Democrat to hold the office in more than three decades.

If Abbott wins and completes another four-year term, the Republican would become the longest-serving governor in Texas history. But beyond the historical milestones, the outcome could shape the future of public education property taxes and household costs for everyday Texans — issues at the heart of the candidates’ competing pitches to voters.

"I think the central question is about affordability and which candidate is going to be able to bring down the cost of living," said Austin Bussing, an assistant professor of political science at Trinity University.

Both candidates spent the final days of the campaign bringing that message to rallies across Texas, while encouraging supporters to head to the polls.

Hinojosa campaigned alongside Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico in Houston on Saturday and inSan Antonio on Sunday. Meanwhile, Abbott campaigned in Midland on Sunday, with stops in Texarkana, Houston andSan Antonio.

As governor of Texas, the winner will have the power to sign or veto legislation, recommend a state budget and make appointments across state government, including the education commissioner.

But the winner’s ability to carry out their agenda will depend on the Texas Legislature, which will likely remain under Republican control. Gov. Abbott has spent nearly 12 years working with Republican majorities. A Hinojosa victory, however, could leave the Democrat facing Republican lawmakers who oppose many of her priorities, making her legislative priorities difficult to fulfill.

Different visions for Texas public schools

On education, the candidates offer sharply different approaches. Abbott champions the school voucher program created in 2025, which allows families to use public money for private education expenses. He argues that the program gives parents more options.

Abbott also signed an$8.5 billion public-school funding package in 2025 that includes teacher pay raises, special education and school safety money.

Hinojosa opposes vouchers and state takeovers of local school districts, in which Texas education officials can replace locally elected school boards with appointed managers. She pledges to replace Education Commissioner Mike Morath with an educator and put more resources into the state’s public schools.

Abbott, Hinojosa on making Texas more affordable

Both candidates promise to make life more affordable, but their proposals take different paths.

Abbott wants voters to decide whether toeliminate school district property taxes for homeowners through a constitutional amendment. His plan also calls for tighter limits on appraisal increases. But eliminating those taxes would leave the state responsible for filling billions of dollars in lost property tax revenue that currently helps fund Texas public schools.

Hinojosa has also said she wants to reduce or even eliminate homeowners’ residential property taxes, although she has acknowledged that eliminating them entirely may not be achievable. She proposes reducing corporate subsidies to help pay for property tax cuts. She also wants one-time$1,500 payments to Texas households from the state's Rainy Day Fund — a proposal her campaign estimates would cost around $17 billion and need legislative approval.

But neither Abbott nor Hinojosa would have complete control over the cost of living in Texas, which is also shaped by national economic conditions.

"I don't know that I would blame or credit Abbott for the economy because that's a national thing," said David Crockett, a political science professor at Trinity University.

Texans who haven’t already cast their ballots can do so on Tuesday, Nov. 3.

Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time. Anyone in line when polls close can still vote.

Election results will begin rolling in after the polls close on Tuesday evening. The winner could be clear on Tuesday night, but a close contest between Abbott and Hinojosa could take longer to call.
