text:
On November 2, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance and Economy Lee Hyoung Il visited the Hyundai Motor and Kia R&D Center in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, and held a meeting with industry representatives to discuss ways to strengthen the competitiveness of the electric vehicle (EV) industry.

The visit and meeting were organized to review the current state of the EV industry and autonomous driving technology development, as well as to gather industry feedback on challenges facing businesses and areas where government support is needed.

During the visit, Deputy Prime Minister Lee inspected autonomous driving test vehicles* scheduled to be deployed in Gwangju Autonomous Driving Demonstration City starting in November 2026 and reviewed progress in vehicle production and technology development. He also received briefings on plans by Hyundai Motor and other Korean companies to develop next-generation EVs and autonomous vehicles.

* EV-based test vehicles designed to validate autonomous driving technologies, with 200 vehicles scheduled for deployment by the end of 2026 and a cumulative total of 3,000 by 2027.

At the subsequent meeting, Deputy Prime Minister Lee stated, “EVs represent the next key battleground for boosting Korea’s potential growth rate.” He noted that Korean companies must achieve technological capabilities on par with those of global leaders within the next two to three years to remain competitive, making rapid adaptation and technological innovation more critical than ever.

Representatives from the EV, autonomous vehicle, and automotive parts industries emphasized the need for swift government support to help Korean companies survive intensifying global competition and requested the introduction of production tax credits for EVs. They also called for expanded support to help automotive parts suppliers transition to future mobility technologies, the establishment of a legal framework for introducing a battery leasing system, and an increase in specialized personnel at the agency responsible for autonomous vehicles.

In response, Deputy Prime Minister Lee reaffirmed the government’s commitment to making every effort alongside businesses. He stated that the government would carefully review the industry’s proposals in consultation with relevant ministries and take prompt steps to address them. Regarding production tax credits for EVs, the government would actively participate in discussions at the National Assembly and engage in substantive deliberations. In addition, the government would formulate and announce measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the EV industry in November, reflecting industry feedback raised at the meeting. These measures would include initiatives to enhance autonomous driving technologies and expand R&D in core components and technologies.

text:
Good morning! It's Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

In this morning's edition, car companies are all in favor of the Trump administration's rollback of fuel economy rules while they simultaneously urge Congress to pass the permanent ban on Chinese vehicle imports they've been whining about. Also, Europe has all but forgiven Tesla CEO Elon Musk and a chip shortage at Stellantis could hamper Fiat output in Italy.

If you'd like a recap of the latest auto news sent to your inbox each weekday, you can sign up for Jalopnik's free Morning Shift newsletter here.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a group representing some of the biggest automakers in the world, including General Motors, Toyota, Hyundai, Ford, Stellantis and Volkswagen, said it was backing the Trump administration in a legal challenge to its sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards that had been filed by California, New York and two dozen other states, cities and counties around the country. I'll tell ya what, I'm not surprised, but I'm sure those automakers will be once those fuel economy rollbacks are changed in the next administration (whenever that comes).

Last month, the U.S. Department of Transportation said it was finalizing a fleet-wide fuel economy average of 34.9 mpg by 2031. That's down from the 50.4 mpg mark that was set by the Biden administration in 2024. The group argued that automakers require "certainty and stability" in standards. From Reuters:

It added that if the standards were set aside, it "would affect automakers' ​business, endangering the capital investment planning, product development, and performance validation for hundreds of ​new vehicle models intended for the US market."

The states said the Trump administration was ignoring the presence ‌of millions ⁠of electric vehicles, "leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the 'maximum feasible' fuel economy level." The automaker group said the court should reject those arguments.

The revised Trump administration standards seek to reverse Biden's push toward greater fuel efficiency and electric vehicles. A coalition of environmental ​and consumer groups ​also filed a separate ⁠lawsuit challenging the new rules.

The Transportation Department said the regulation reduces manufacturers' average cost per vehicle to comply by $1,289 but increases fuel ​costs by more than $1,600 over the life of the vehicles.

The department ​said the ⁠rule would increase US gasoline consumption through 2050 by 4.6%, or about 121 billion gallons, compared with the Biden rules but also boost new car sales.

The American Petroleum Institute, an oil ⁠and natural ​gas industry trade group, also filed in support of ​the Trump administration's rules, saying they ensure the government sets standards that "do not force consumers to purchase vehicles that ​consume less fuel than they would otherwise choose."

Automakers can talk all they want about being environmentally sustainable and eco-friendly, but at the end of the day, it's very clear that what it all comes down to is the bottom line. It'll certainly be interesting to see what the fallout will be once a new, more eco-conscious administration enters the White House in a few years' time.

That same group, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, is currently on a heater. Not only are they going after fuel economy standards. They're also continuing their push to get Congress to ban the import of Chinese EVs to the U.S. Automakers have been whining about this for years at this point, and now they'd like the bill to pass when lawmakers return next week for a quick session following today's midterm elections.

Back in September, the Senate sponsors of a bipartisan bill to effectively ban Chinese-made vehicles from entering the U.S. agreed to delay the effort to fast-track the bill until November, despite the fact it had overwhelming support from other congresspeople who apparently aren't a fan of a free market or freedom of choice for the consumer. There are some officials who believe that if Dems win control of Congress, there may not be enough time to approve the ban before the session ends in December. Whatever will these OEMs do??? From Reuters:

"We need to ​protect the US market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry ​surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in ⁠American communities," said John Bozzella, who heads the Alliance for Automotive Innovation.

[...]

"Given the ​obvious national security risk and China's pattern of unfair behavior, Congress should protect ​our defense and advanced manufacturing base and stop Chinese automakers from doing here what they've gotten away ‌with ⁠in Europe," Bozzella said.

Bozzella said in the first eight months of 2026, the EU imported more than 1.1 million vehicles from China — more than all of 2025.

A Senate committee passed the bill, which has significant momentum, in July and a House version now tops 100 co-sponsors. ​Automakers and legislative aides ​hope to win full ⁠passage this year.

[...]

A regulation imposed by the former ​Biden administration ⁠in early 2025 effectively banned Chinese automakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the US because they could send sensitive driver data to China. Washington also maintains more ⁠than 100% ​tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.

The Chinese foreign ministry ​has previously urged the United States "to respect the laws of the market economy and principles of fair competition," ​criticizing previous proposals against Chinese companies as "unreasonable suppression."

President Trump, wildcard that he is, sparked a hell of a lot of worry among key stakeholders when he said he would accept Chinese automakers building cars in the U.S., but so far no one has taken him up on the offer.

Of course, the whole "national security angle of this story is just steeped in irony. After all, I'm writing this article on my Chinese-made laptop, and you're reading it on your Chinese-made phone.

It would seem that Europe has all but forgiven Tesla CEO Elon Musk for all of the nasty crap he's pulled over the past few years, as registrations for his vehicles rose sharply across several European countries in October. It's an extension of the Austin, Texas-based automaker's recovery in the region, but the gains were admittedly a bit uneven as Chinese rivals continued to expand their market share. From Reuters:

Tesla registrations soared 248% in Sweden, 131% ​in Norway and 34% in Denmark, data from Mobility Sweden, Norway's OFV and Denmark's bilstatistik.dk showed.

The ⁠automaker also recorded strong growth elsewhere in Europe, with registrations rising 271% in Spain, 186% in Portugal and 94% in Italy, according to data from ANFAC, ​ACAP and Italy's Transport Ministry.

The rebound has been aided by easier year-ago comparisons, higher fuel prices, government incentives ​and continued growth in EV demand. But the pace of recovery varied significantly between markets, underlining the increasingly fragmented nature of Europe's EV sector as Chinese brands broaden their presence.

Tesla remains one of Europe's strongest EV brands, though its reliance on the ​Model 3 and Model Y has left it facing growing competition from rivals with broader lineups.

The automaker ​said in October it had ended the third quarter with its largest passenger vehicle order backlog in four years.

Norway remained a bright ‌spot ⁠for Tesla. The carmaker recorded its best October on record and was the country's top-selling car brand with a 9.8% market share, according to OFV. Chinese brands continued to expand their footprint, accounting for 22.5% of new passenger car registrations, their highest monthly share on record.

[...]

"Northern Europe is quite open to the new players as long as they ⁠are efficient ​EVs. That's what allowed Tesla to get to a leading position ​and it's what is allowing the Chinese to gain ground fast," industry analyst Felipe Munoz, who runs the Car Industry Analysis platform, ​told Reuters.

I guess time really does heal all wounds. Well, that, and staying out of the spotlight as best as Elon really can.

Stellantis is partying like it's 2021 again, because it's going through its own chip shortage in Italy. It says a shortfall for an electronic component used in an engine control unit is causing "significant" disruption to production of some Fiat models in Italy, and the issue could persist through the end of the year.

The shortage from a supplier has already weighed on October sales, especially for the Italy-made Fiat Pandina, one of the brand's best-selling models. There's a possibility that the shortage could lead to further issues, including production halts in the coming months at its plants in Pomigliano and Mirafiori — where it builds the Fiat 500. From Reuters:

"Stellantis and Fiat ​are working with the highest priority to identify alternative solutions and gradually restore normal operations," the group ​said.

[...]

The disruption could also impact Stellantis plants in Italy making ​engine components, including ​Termoli, ⁠where the N3 GSE engine used in both the Pandina and ​the 500 is assembled.

Mirafiori is currently ​undergoing ⁠a three-week production halt that started in mid-October due to a separate component shortage, with unions ⁠pointing ​at weak demand for the ​Fiat 500 as one of the factors behind the ​stoppage.

Mama mia! That's a spicy production nightmare — one an ailing company like Stellantis can hardly afford right now.

Gas prices are continuing their slow retreat back to relative normalcy, but certainly not at the pace the Trump administration would have hoped. Perhaps that's something to keep in mind while you're voting today. Usually the President has very little to do with fuel costs, but in this case, he's directly involved with the fact that WTI Crude Oil futures and Brent Crude prices remain elevated, sitting at $96 and $103, respectively, at the time of publication. You can thank his war with Iran for that.

Anyway, here's where national average prices stand right now, according to AAA:

AAA

This all shakes out to the average price of a gallon of gas dropping another 2 cents overnight to $4.15, according to AAA. Diesel, on the other hand, saw prices remain virtually the same at $6.29. Trump has said for a while now that prices will come down post-election, so I suppose we'll see what that's all about in the coming weeks and months. I wouldn't hold my breath, though.

text:
Siemens announced that JSW Greentech Limited has selected Siemens Xcelerator software to establish an integrated digital foundation for the development of commercial electric vehicles. The initiative will support JSW Greentech as it builds capabilities for electric buses, trucks and other sustainable mobility solutions under the brand AMPSTAR through its R&D center in Pune and its state of the art greenfield manufacturing facility in Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, India.

JSW Greentech is undertaking a digital transformation program designed to connect engineering, product development and manufacturing processes through a unified product lifecycle management (PLM) strategy. The company aims to improve collaboration across teams, enhance engineering quality, reduce development cycle times and accelerate the delivery of new electric vehicles to the Indian market.

"The future of commercial electric mobility will be shaped by how effectively we integrate technology across the value chain. By building a digitally connected enterprise from the outset, JSW Greentech is creating a foundation for smarter, more efficient and scalable electric vehicle manufacturing under the brand AMPSTAR. Our collaboration for Product Lifestyle Management (PLM) with Siemens will enhance operational efficiency and accelerate the development of next-generation electric commercial vehicles, reinforcing our commitment to a future-ready mobility ecosystem in India.” said Sumit Mittal - CEO, JSW Greentech Limited.

JSW Greentech’s implementation includes Teamcenter® software for product lifecycle management and Mendix™ software to support supplier and business process collaboration. Together, these technologies will help create a connected digital thread across product development while supporting greater visibility and traceability throughout the organization and the supply chain.

Siemens’ Teamcenter will provide the digital thread backbone, connecting sources of product and engineering information, supporting bill of materials (BOMs) and product structures, and delivering capabilities for requirements management, program planning, change management and collaboration across mechanical and electrical engineering disciplines. Another key element of the initiative is integration between Teamcenter and the company's ERP system, helping synchronize engineering and business data across the organization while improving the flow of information between engineering and business functions. Teamcenter also supports supplier collaboration through a Mendix-based portal, extending digital processes beyond internal teams and across the broader product development and supplier ecosystem.

"Commercial EV manufacturers have a unique opportunity to establish digital transformation as a core business capability from the outset," said Mathew Thomas, vice president and managing director for India, Siemens Digital Industries Software. "By connecting engineering, product lifecycle management and collaboration across the enterprise, JSW Greentech is creating a scalable digital foundation that can help accelerate innovation and support the efficient development of next-generation commercial electric vehicles."

text:
In September 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) took two actions to repeal greenhouse gas emission standards for power plants. The first action finalized the repeal of key greenhouse gas standards for power plants because EPA changed its position regarding the standards’ technical feasibility and cost reasonableness.

In the second action, EPA proposed to repeal all remaining greenhouse gas emission standards for fossil-fuel-fired power plants. EPA argues that Section 111 of the Clean Air Act does not authorize EPA to prescribe emission standards to address global climate change. EPA attempts to support this position by asserting that Section 111 must be interpreted to address only local or regional air pollution, that regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants implicates the major questions doctrine, and that regulating these emissions is futile because global climate change is such a large problem.

In our comments on EPA’s proposal, we offered the following insights:

EPA’s proposal relies on a novel and incorrect interpretation of the Clean Air Act. Statutory text, legislative context, and regulatory history all affirm EPA’s authority to use Section 111 to address global climate change and other air pollution problems that endanger public health or welfare through means other than local or regional exposure. Existing statutory constraints allow the agency to avoid regulating de minimis emissions without adopting EPA’s new interpretation—as evidenced by the agency’s longstanding practice.

Contrary to EPA’s assertions, the major questions doctrine does not preclude EPA from regulating greenhouse gas emissions under Section 111. The Supreme Court has effectively held that the major questions doctrine does not prohibit such regulation. And because such regulation was neither unprecedented nor transformed EPA’s regulatory authority, it did not trigger the major questions doctrine when EPA began to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under Section 111.

EPA’s finding that it is futile to regulate power plants’ greenhouse gas emissions is arbitrary and erroneous. EPA departs without adequate justification from its long-standing use of social cost of greenhouse gases, a peer-reviewed, state-of-the-art tool to measure climate change damages. EPA proposes to measure welfare effects, but discusses only the physical effects of sea level rise and global temperature that would inform actual welfare effects. EPA also ignores other climate change impacts and relies on fundamentally flawed underestimates of sea level rise and temperature change effects from power sector emissions. EPA inappropriately trivializes the climate benefits of Section 111 regulations by comparing them to global baselines, but its own approach to assessing the 2026 Proposal’s cost savings demonstrates the fallacy of that approach.

Power plant greenhouse gas emissions clearly contribute significantly to air pollution that endangers public health or welfare. Using EPA’s own models for estimating climate change damages and projections of power sector emissions, greenhouse gas emissions from the power sector will cause over $20 trillion in damages. The U.S. power sector’s unregulated emissions could also cause over 100,000 additional U.S. mortalities by 2200. And even these substantial figures are likely underestimates because these models do not comprehensively capture all important effects of climate change. For over five decades, EPA has recognized much smaller shares of large pollution problems to merit regulation under Section 111.

EPA fails to consider important effects of its proposal. EPA should analyze the effects of its proposed action under possible future scenarios, including the addition of new coal generation and the vacatur of EPA’s partial repeal of the Carbon Pollution Standards. When doing so, EPA should quantify and monetize all significant impacts, including the climate costs and the costs of increased co-pollutant emissions that result.

text:
The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) has announced a US$37 million investment to build 515 more public EV charging points across five Pennsylvania counties.

The investment is part of the Community Charging portion of the federal National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (NEVI) programme. To date, 54 stations in Pennsylvania have built using NEVI funds, with 34 currently in planning or construction phases. Pennsylvania’s first NEVI-funded station opened in December 2023.

The latest investment was announced by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation secretary Mike Carroll, and joins over US$100 million in federal funding for the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania's build-out of public EV charging. To date, US$58 million for EV charging initiatives has come in the form of federal investment under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) allocation of funds designed to encourage moves towards alternative transport technologies.

The BIL includes a provision of US$2.5 billion, spread over five years, destined for distribution under the FHWA's (Federal Highway Administration) Charging and Fueling Infrastructure (CFI) grant programme. The CFI, in turn, is split evenly between the Community Program, of which the latest tranche of EV public charging is part, and the Alternative Fuel Corridor (AFC) programme.

The AFC provides funds to promote the deployment of alternative fuel infrastructure including EV charging, hydrogen, natural gas and propane, along designated transport 'corridors'.

In Pennsylvania, some of the largest funding awards among the most recent funding announcement include US$1 million for eight fast charging ports in Bensalem, Bucks County, US$7.2 million to build 54 fast charging ports at various sites in Philadelphia County, US$1.8 million for eight fast charging points in Drexel Hill, Delaware County, and US$1.6 million for Thorndale, Chester County.

"These awards expand opportunity for southeastern PA visitors and residents alike by reducing range anxiety for current EV owners and making EV ownership possible for others," said Ariella Maron, executive director of the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission (DVRPC). "DVRPC applauds [the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation]'s leadership in expanding transportation options across Pennsylvania and serving as a national leader in NEVI implementation."

Secretary Mike Carroll said: "The Shapiro administration hit the ground running with EV funding and the results speak for themselves."

Federal Community Charging funding, which has been running since 2021, is allocated by region, with the specific areas designated funding determined by local transport planning agencies.

description:

Fuuse’s onboarding team will assess each customer’s charging infrastructure requirements, confirm service arrangements and guide customers through the migration process.
Through its partnership with Drax, Fuuse will provide customers with access to service and maintenance support.
This includes continued support for existing hardware warranties and maintenance of previously installed charging infrastructure.
“With nationwide field service capabilities and continued hardware warranty support, we can help keep charging infrastructure maintained, supported and operational.”
text:
Was BP ever serious about its “beyond petroleum” marketing slogan? It’s too early to say, but in July 2025, the oil giant decided to get out of the fleet EV charging market, leaving former customers unplugged, so to speak. Fortunately, other companies stepped in to help former bp pulse corporate customers migrate to new platforms.

Fuuse and Drax Electric Vehicles, part of energy provider Drax Group, have announced a partnership to support the transition of nearly 1,000 former bp pulse fleet depot-charging customers, which collectively operate more than 14,000 charging sockets.

Fuuse will lead the migration of the charging infrastructure to its platform, allowing fleets to retain and manage their existing charging equipment.

The partnership follows more than a year of hardware testing and platform development between bp’s EV charging business and Fuuse to prepare customers for the transition. Fuuse’s onboarding team will assess each customer’s charging infrastructure requirements, confirm service arrangements and guide customers through the migration process.

Through its partnership with Drax, Fuuse will provide customers with access to service and maintenance support. This includes continued support for existing hardware warranties and maintenance of previously installed charging infrastructure.

“Being selected as the migration partner reflects the work of our team and the capabilities of our platform,” said James Chapman, Strategic Sales Director at Fuuse. “Through our existing partnership with Drax, we can also provide hardware maintenance support while honoring existing warranties. This is about more than software. It’s about protecting customer investments, maintaining operational continuity and making the transition straightforward.”

“Ensuring former bp pulse fleet depot-charging customers can move forward with confidence is our priority,” said Adam Hall, Energy Services Director at Drax Electric Vehicles. “With nationwide field service capabilities and continued hardware warranty support, we can help keep charging infrastructure maintained, supported and operational.”

title: Plant-inspired natural coatings can beat forever chemicals - The Source - WashU
description:
Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are known as “forever chemicals” because of the impact they make on the environment and human bodies.
“It’s not going to stay in the environment forever and it can be degraded,” Yuan added.
To make SLIP, Yuan and his team, including first authors Puneet Dhatt and Weiwei Li, took inspiration from plant vascular tissue called xylem.

text:
Polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are known as “forever chemicals” because of the impact they make on the environment and human bodies. Much of modern manufacturing relies on these substances for safe packaging, fire protection and waterproof coatings.

Despite the billions of dollars in economic burden PFAS place on human health and the environment, the PFAS materials themselves are relatively affordable and abundant. So when WashU chemical engineers wanted to come up with an alternative that meets manufacturing needs, they turned to a different material that is also affordable and abundant: lignin, or plant waste material. In new research published in Matter, researchers from Washington University in St. Louis outline the chemical processes used to turn lignin and fatty acids into a viable PFAS replacement called SLIP, or superhydrophobic lignin-integrated particles.

“We actually use this waste material to turn it into a valuable product,” said Joshua Yuan, the Lucy & Stanley Lopata Professor and chair of energy, environmental and chemical engineering at WashU McKelvey Engineering. Yuan, who serves as director of the NSF Carbon Utilization Redesign for Biomanufacturing (CURB) Energy Research Center at WashU, has long taken inspiration from the natural world to find solutions to replace petrochemical-based materials.

In SLIP, the researchers found a viable waterproof coating to replace PFAS and lose the toxic side effects. “It’s not going to stay in the environment forever and it can be degraded,” Yuan added.

To make SLIP, Yuan and his team, including first authors Puneet Dhatt and Weiwei Li, took inspiration from plant vascular tissue called xylem. Within xylem is a waterproof molecule called suberin, which transports water throughout the plant. The team incorporated suberin’s structure into lignin particles by linking lignin to fatty acids and further added a polylactic acid (PLA) binder. The resulting material demonstrated a highly superhydrophobic performance and included features of mechanical robustness and ultraviolet stability.

That’s not everything PFAS does, but it’s a substantial start, the researchers said, especially considering the sheer number of waterproof coatings used in modern manufacturing.

Tests show water literally bouncing off the new SLIP material. “The water will just run off,” Dhatt said, adding that the material was tested with wood-degrading fungus that showed the coating can break down into harmless organic matter within the expected time period.

Lignin and fatty acid “evolved to degrade in the environment for a long time,” Dhatt noted, saying that the replacement material could help avoid the societal cost of forever chemicals.

The WashU team collaborated with researchers at Texas A&M University to estimate the cost savings of replacing PFAS. Looking at the global impacts to human health and the environment from forever chemicals, the Texas researchers estimated that total societal damage avoided by replacing forever chemicals with SLIP in waterproofing could reach $1.1 billion annually.

For now, the scientists will continue to add attributes to this new coating. SLIP could be used in packaging and for construction material coatings, but the next step will be to make it oil- and fireproof to vastly expand its applications. The team also is working to scale up the process and integrate it with biorefinery and paper and pulping industries.

“This study represents the perfect example, where we learn from nature and design a sustainable material critical to our society, with a life cycle similar to nature polymers, where everything can degrade without causing harms,” Yuan said.

Dhatt PS, Li W, Chen Y, Meng X, Liu M, Fei C, Ragauskas A, Dai SY, Yuan JS. Bioinspired and biodegradable fluorine-free superhydrophobic coatings. Matter, 2026, 103068. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matt.2026.103068

Several congressional Republican senators support maintaining a stable and predictable tax framework to help promote domestic energy development.

“While we support fiscal responsibility and prudent efforts to streamline the tax code, we caution against the full-scale repeal of current credits, which could lead to significant disruptions for the American people and weaken our position as a global energy leader,” wrote U.S. Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), John Curtis (R-UT), Thom Tillis (R-FL), and Jerry Moran (R-KS) in an April 9 letter sent to U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD).

A wholesale repeal, or the termination of certain individual credits, would create uncertainty, jeopardizing capital allocation, long-term project planning, and job creation in the energy sector and across the nation’s broader economy, they wrote, noting that many American companies have made substantial investments in domestic energy production and infrastructure based on the current energy tax framework.

“Our country is blessed with abundant natural resources and an entrepreneurial spirit that uniquely positions us to power both our economy and the world — enabling U.S. leadership in innovation, energy production, and manufacturing alike,” wrote the senators. “Many of the investments that make this possible are enabled by current tax provisions, including some from the Inflation Reduction Act.”

The Republicans also pointed out that for energy credits that provide a direct passthrough benefit to ratepayers, repeals would translate into immediate utility bill increases, placing additional strain on hard-working Americans.

As discussions on budget reconciliation continue, they urged Thune to consider each existing tax credit for its ability to: spur new domestic manufacturing and investment; reduce utility bills for consumers, especially in rural remote communities; and ensure certainty for businesses that have already made meaningful U.S. investments based on the current credit structure.

“We believe the final reconciliation bill can support smart policies that enable private sector investment in domestic energy to help meet future U.S. energy needs and strengthen the global competitiveness of American companies,” they wrote.

text:
Lightstar Renewables, a community solar solar developer specializing in agrivoltaics and battery energy storage, and the Paxton City Council are collaborating on a 4.95-MWAC community solar project on approximately 35 acres of privately owned land in Paxton, Illinois. The Baltimore Drive Solar Project will co-locate hay growing and a community solar project on the same site.

The previously unincorporated site is being annexed as city property, so Paxton will receive tax revenue from the site. The project will occupy 30 of the 35 acres of land, avoiding a wetland on the property. Hay will be grown between solar module rows, which are planned to use single-axis solar trackers. Residents will be able to subscribe to the solar project with promised savings on their electricity costs.

“Paxton showed what a strong partnership looks like,” said Kyle McAdam, senior development manager. “This agreement keeps tax revenue in the city, delivers real savings to local subscribers, and puts the project on a site that works for the community. That is the kind of project we want to build across Illinois.”

text:
NORMAN, OKLA. – U.S. Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright visited the University of Oklahoma on Friday, Oct. 30, to meet with OU researchers and students involved in the DOE Genesis Mission, a national initiative to accelerate scientific discovery through artificial intelligence, supercomputing and quantum technologies. The roundtable, which also included Rep. Tom Cole, R-Oklahoma, and OU President Joseph Harroz Jr., showcased how OU research is helping advance American energy and scientific discovery.

“Energy has always been central to Oklahoma’s story, and the University of Oklahoma has been part of that story for more than a century,” said Harroz. “Our selection for the Genesis Mission reflects the extraordinary talent and research expertise we have at OU, as well as our commitment to advancing discoveries that will strengthen our state and nation. We are honored to welcome Secretary Wright and Congressman Cole to campus as we work together to write the next chapter of Oklahoma’s energy story.”

“The University of Oklahoma has a proud history of energy innovation, and its role in the Genesis Mission will help drive the breakthroughs needed to strengthen American Energy Dominance and secure our nation’s energy future,” said U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright.

“Since shortly after statehood, energy has been a driving force in Oklahoma’s economy. Furthermore, the University of Oklahoma has helped build on that legacy through its investments, groundbreaking research, and longstanding commitment to the energy sector. There is no university more deserving of selection for the Genesis Mission than OU,” said Congressman Cole. “I’d like to thank DOE Secretary Wright for joining us in Oklahoma today for this roundtable discussion and I look forward to seeing OU continue to lead the way in advancing our nation’s energy future.”

The visit highlights OU’s long-standing leadership in energy and its growing investment in research. The university’s Mewbourne College of Earth and Energy is home to nationally ranked petroleum engineering programs, and enrollment in the college has grown 84% over the past four years. Earlier this year, OU launched Project 200, the largest investment in research talent in the university’s history. Over the next five years, the initiative will bring about 200 leading researchers to OU in four areas of strategic importance: health, weather, national security and defense, and energy.

The roundtable followed the August announcement that OU was among 168 universities selected for Genesis Mission funding. Two OU-led research teams received nearly $1.4 million in Phase I funding. Ahmad Ghassemi, McCasland Chair Professor of petroleum engineering in the Mewbourne College of Earth and Energy, is leading a project using machine learning and physics-based modeling to improve enhanced geothermal systems. Grant Biedermann, Homer L. Dodge Endowed Chair and associate professor of physics in the Dodge Family College of Arts and Sciences, is leading a project using AI to control arrays of trapped atoms for quantum computing. Xuguang Wang, Robert Lowery Chair Professor and Presidential Research Professor in the School of Meteorology, is a research partner on a project led by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory using AI to model turbulence and clouds for Earth-system prediction.

title: Midterms unlikely to undo OBBB business breaks, expert says - Thomson Reuters
authors: Tim Shaw, Checkpoint News, Tim Shaw, Checkpoint News
description:
Energy credit limits could draw pressure Making green energy credits transferable under the Inflation Reduction Act, P.L.
Many expected the OBBB to end transferability, but it survived, he said, though the law bars transferring them to specified foreign entities.
Boccaccio said if he were a congressional Democrat next year, he would push to repeal the foreign entity rules.

He also advised buying 2026 credits now to avoid making the December 15 estimated payment.
text:
Whatever the outcome of Tuesday’s midterm elections, permanent business deductions in the One Big Beautiful Bill (OBBB) are likely safe, while foreign entity limits that have slowed green energy credit trades could come under pressure, a corporate tax adviser told Checkpoint.

Ian Boccaccio, principal and practice leader of income tax at Ryan LLC, said he expects slimmer majorities in Congress, with the House likely going to Democrats. “I think the general feeling is we’re moving toward gridlock,” he said, which has “one benefit in that you have consistency for the next couple of years.”

Permanent deductions seen as secure

Lawmakers made 100% bonus depreciation under IRC § 168(k) permanent in the OBBB for property acquired after January 19, 2025. A new IRC § 174A also lets businesses immediately deduct domestic research and experimental expenditures, which they had been required to capitalize starting in 2022.

“Bonus depreciation at 100% was fantastic for U.S. taxpayers,” Boccaccio said, adding that “being able to deduct R&D in the U.S. has been a huge benefit to U.S. companies.”

Neither provision is likely to change, he said, because historically “it’s very hard for a divided Congress or one with slim majority to make big changes to permanent things in the code.”

Republicans also have little interest in reopening the law, according to Boccaccio. “I think that’s their landmark legislation of this session. It’s done. They don’t want to open it back up.” Technical corrections remain possible, however, including a wagering-loss fix approved by the House Ways and Means Committee.

Energy credit limits could draw pressure

Making green energy credits transferable under the Inflation Reduction Act, P.L. 117-169, in 2022 was “one of the biggest changes to the corporate tax planning process in a long time,” Boccaccio said. Developers that can’t use the credits sell them at a discount to companies that owe tax.

Many expected the OBBB to end transferability, but it survived, he said, though the law bars transferring them to specified foreign entities. Boccaccio said the law’s new restrictions and shorter credit lives are “the areas that I would expect after the midterms we could see pressure on.”

Wind and solar facilities that begin construction after July 4, 2026, can’t claim the clean electricity credits under IRC § 45Y and IRC § 48E if placed in service after 2027. Democrats would like to extend that window, Boccaccio said, and some Republicans could support it because most green energy development is in Republican districts, “creating jobs, creating tax base.”

Foreign entity rules and credit transfers

The OBBB also denies those credits for facilities beginning construction after December 31, 2025, if the construction includes material assistance from a prohibited foreign entity. Older credits not subject to the rules are “trading fast,” Boccaccio said, while newer credits facing the test are “almost untradeable.”

Buyers won’t pay for credits that could be disallowed once regulations are issued, he said. The IRS issued interim safe harbors in Notice 2026-15 and plans proposed regulations. Credits still trade if an investment-grade seller “puts up a no-fault indemnity and wears the risk,” but few developers have that rating, Boccaccio said.

By statute, the IRS must issue safe harbor tables by December 31, 2026. Boccaccio said members of his Washington team expect guidance between mid-fourth quarter and the first quarter of 2027, before extended 2026 returns are due in October 2027. “If this didn’t get solved by next summer, it would be a real, real problem,” he said.

Boccaccio said if he were a congressional Democrat next year, he would push to repeal the foreign entity rules. “It’s not like we’re creating a new credit. It’s not like we’re extending the life of the credit. We’re just reducing one complexity that would make the market much more liquid,” he said.

Year-end planning under current law

Expecting “no material changes” for 2026, Boccaccio said taxpayers should “use what you know is law … and optimize it to the absolute hilt,” including taking all R&D deductions and bonus depreciation. Electing out of bonus depreciation under § 168(k)(7) can preserve taxable income to use credits before they expire, he said.

He also advised buying 2026 credits now to avoid making the December 15 estimated payment. “Now is the time to contract for 2027 tax credits,” he said, because buyers who contract now and pay later still get the discount rate and can cut estimated payments in 2027, “effectively getting a float.”

For more information on business tax credit transfers and eligibility, see Checkpoint’s Federal Tax Coordinator 2d ¶ L-17991.

title: Volkswagen's Is Giving Retired Cars a Second Life as Parts Donors | GreenCars
description:
Workers methodically disassemble vehicles across eight stations so parts can be refurbished and resold as service parts.
Instead of brand-new parts, used parts may be available at a much lower cost.
Cheaper Repairs, Better Recycling VW wants to use these vehicles to supply verified used parts to the repair market.
Dismantling also helps separate materials such as aluminum, steel, and plastics, so unusable parts can be recycled more effectively.
VW plans to invest 90 million euros in dismantling at Zwickau, and the Free State of Saxony is adding another 10.7 million euros.
text:
Fast Facts | Volkswagen's Zwickau Dismantling Line

Location: Zwickau, Germany, where VW builds six EV models for VW, Audi, and Cupra

The Line: Eight stations that take vehicles apart so parts can be refurbished and resold

Volume: About 4,100 vehicles in 2027, growing to about 15,000 by 2030

Recycling: Cleaner separation of aluminum, steel, and plastics

Investment: 90 million euros from VW, plus 10.7 million euros from the Free State of Saxony

What If Retired Cars Became Parts Warehouses?

Those of us who love cars and doing things ourselves know scrapyards and pick-and-pull lots well. They're where vehicles often end up when they've reached the end of their useful lives. But until the last of a car's carcass gets crushed, melted down, and made into something new, it can still be an organ donor that keeps other vehicles alive. Now, Volkswagen is bringing that idea to the factory by turning its plant in Zwickau, Germany, into a vehicle organ-donation facility.

EV Pioneer to Circular Economy

The Zwickau assembly plant in eastern Germany was one of the first in the company to convert to electric vehicle production, starting ID.3 production in 2019. Today, it builds six models for the VW, Audi, and Cupra brands, all based on the company’s MEB electric vehicle architecture.

Earlier this year, VW announced plans to make the plant its center of excellence for the circular economy. The concept is that materials never get completely disposed of. Instead, they keep getting reused, recycled, and repurposed.

Vehicle reuse is only one part of the circular economy, and EV batteries have their own second-life and recycling paths, so see what happens to an EV battery after its automotive life ends ➜

An Assembly Line in Reverse

Zwickau's first circular economy effort is a new line that does the opposite of its assembly lines: It takes cars apart. Workers methodically disassemble vehicles across eight stations so parts can be refurbished and resold as service parts. The dismantling line is starting with preproduction vehicles.

As it ramps up to volume production, a manufacturer builds anywhere from dozens to hundreds of preproduction vehicles. Employees typically use them for several months before the manufacturer gets approval to begin customer deliveries.

This phase helps find last-minute issues, solve production problems, and validate the quality of both supplier parts and the finished product. These vehicles represent what customers will get, but they haven’t been fully certified for sale.

After that, they may work as transport and utility vehicles at factories or other company facilities. When they reach the end of their useful life, they get crushed. But they often have a lot of valuable parts that could fix customers' vehicles.

For example, a crash damages a customer's vehicle, and it needs a new door or other bodywork. Instead of brand-new parts, used parts may be available at a much lower cost. That’s where scrapyards are often useful.

Cheaper Repairs, Better Recycling

VW wants to use these vehicles to supply verified used parts to the repair market. It's starting small, with plans to dismantle about 4,100 vehicles in 2027 and grow to about 15,000 by 2030. As volumes ramp up, VW will add end-of-life vehicles from other use cases.

Parts from those vehicles could help keep tens to hundreds of thousands of other vehicles useful for many years to come, and at a much lower cost. Dismantling also helps separate materials such as aluminum, steel, and plastics, so unusable parts can be recycled more effectively. VW plans to invest 90 million euros in dismantling at Zwickau, and the Free State of Saxony is adding another 10.7 million euros.

text:
The West of England is expected to need more than 45,000 to 50,000 additional green jobs to meet its Net Zero ambitions. Clean energy is one of the region’s five priority growth sectors, supported by around 400 clean energy businesses.

The West of England Careers Hub is playing a fundamental role in translating the region’s clean energy and Net Zero ambitions into practical, high-quality careers education for young people.

Through the Green Futures programme, the Hub acted as a strategic connector across education, employers and regional partners, creating a coordinated programme that raised awareness of clean energy careers, strengthened employer engagement and helped build the future talent pipeline needed by a rapidly growing sector.

At its core, the programme demonstrates the value of the Careers Hub as a regional system leader: convening schools, colleges, employers, teachers, parents and careers professionals around a shared workforce challenge. By aligning careers education with labour market priorities, the Hub enables young people to understand the breadth of opportunities within clean energy and the wider green economy, from engineering and construction to digital, project management, communications, policy and sustainability roles.

Early evaluation shows strong impact against a clear baseline need. Before the programme, only 27% of students felt able to explain what a green job was and just 8% believed they had the information needed to pursue a green career. Following participation, 85% of young people reported they could explain what a green job is, 74% could give examples of green jobs, 64% understood pathways into green careers, 69% understood the skills green employers are seeking and 64% felt they had the information needed to pursue a green career pathway.

The programme also strengthened career readiness: 78% of participants reported understanding workplace expectations, 63% believed they had the skills required to pursue a green job in the future and 64% felt confident discussing their skills and qualities with future employers. Employer engagement was also sustained, with 91% of employers indicating they were more likely to continue providing workplace experiences and employer encounters in future.

Employers valued the Careers Hub’s ability to broker meaningful connections with schools and young people, helping them communicate the breadth of clean energy roles, address misconceptions about green careers and contribute directly to the development of future local talent. Feedback also indicates that employers gained greater confidence in engaging with education providers, with 91% saying they were more likely to continue offering workplace experiences and employer encounters because of the programme.

Green Futures provides a scalable model for how Careers Hubs can respond to emerging economic priorities: turning strategic intent into accessible careers learning, improving social mobility by reaching young people who face additional barriers, and helping employers develop a more diverse and locally rooted talent pipeline. In doing so, the Careers Hub has positioned itself as a critical delivery partner in supporting clean energy growth, inclusive opportunity and the transition to a cleaner, more sustainable regional economy.

description:

text:
Houston-returned entrepreneur sees opportunities as Nigerian banks, telecom operators and major businesses reassess long-term energy costs.

HOUSTON, TX, UNITED STATES, November 3, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- Nigeria’s longstanding electricity challenges may be creating one of the country’s most significant emerging private-sector investment opportunities as businesses increasingly evaluate solar generation, battery storage and independent power systems against the rising cost of conventional energy.

That is the outlook of Hakim Ali, an American-born Nigerian entrepreneur who relocated from Houston, Texas, to pursue opportunities in Nigeria’s renewable-energy and electric mobility industries.

Ali, a Director of Abuja-based Sora Green Energy Projects Limited, believes the next major shift in Nigeria’s renewable-energy market may come not only from households adopting solar power, but from banks, telecommunications operators, hospitals, hotels and other institutions reconsidering how they finance and manage electricity over the long term.

From Houston to Nigeria’s Energy Opportunity

Ali’s decision to relocate from the United States reflected his belief that Nigeria’s large population, expanding commercial requirements and persistent electricity challenges created opportunities for businesses capable of providing practical energy solutions.

However, entering the market required patience.

Customers unfamiliar with newer technologies often needed education about equipment reliability, battery performance, maintenance requirements and the economics of replacing conventional energy systems.

Ali believes this initial hesitation is gradually giving way to a more financially focused discussion.

For many Nigerian businesses, electricity is not simply a utility expense. It is an operating requirement that can involve generators, fuel purchases, equipment maintenance and the financial consequences of service interruptions.

He believes these recurring costs are encouraging more organizations to examine whether alternative energy systems can offer greater predictability over time.

Why Institutional Buyers Could Transform Solar Adoption

Ali sees particularly significant opportunities among institutions with substantial and recurring electricity requirements.

Banks operating multiple branches, telecommunications companies maintaining mobile network infrastructure, hospitals requiring dependable electricity and hotels serving customers around the clock all face different versions of the same challenge: maintaining reliable power while controlling operating expenses.

For these organizations, Ali believes the financial case for solar energy should be evaluated over five- to ten-year periods rather than solely through initial installation costs.

Such assessments can include electricity consumption, generator fuel expenditure, maintenance, financing, battery replacement, equipment lifespan and the cost of power interruptions.

Properly designed solar and battery-storage systems may offer financial advantages where the total cost of ownership compares favorably with existing arrangements.

The economics are not identical for every institution, and system design, financing terms and operating requirements remain important considerations.

Nevertheless, Ali believes institutional demand could become a significant driver of Nigeria’s renewable-energy market as more businesses incorporate long-term electricity costs into capital investment decisions.

Solar Energy and Electric Mobility Are Becoming Connected Markets

Sora Green’s operations illustrate another development Ali considers important: the growing relationship between renewable-energy infrastructure and electric transportation.

Solar energy remains the company’s original and principal business, providing residential and commercial electricity-generation and storage solutions.

The company has expanded into electric vehicle distribution, charging infrastructure and related automotive services.

According to management, Sora Green has delivered more than 300 electric vehicles since late 2024, including models from Hongqi, Xiaomi and Avatr, alongside its relationship with Chinese automotive manufacturer FAW.

Ali believes this combination of energy and transportation services reflects the practical requirements of Nigeria’s emerging electric mobility market.

Electric vehicles require dependable charging, while solar generation and battery storage can provide alternative electricity sources where grid supply is inconsistent.

Rather than treating the two industries as separate opportunities, Sora Green is developing services intended to address them together.

Off-Grid Charging Infrastructure in Abuja

The company’s planned electric vehicle charging facility in Maitama, Abuja, provides a practical example of this integrated approach.

Designed to operate independently of Nigeria’s national electricity grid, the facility is expected to combine more than one megawatt of solar generation capacity with over 1.3 megawatt-hours of battery storage.

Initial plans include four 120-kilowatt DC fast chargers, with the company also considering a future increase in charging capacity.

The project is intended to serve the wider electric vehicle market, including motorists who purchased vehicles from other distributors.

The facility is not yet operational, with an opening targeted for early 2027.

For Ali, the development illustrates how private investment in renewable-energy infrastructure may help address limitations that would otherwise slow electric vehicle adoption.

Financing and Commercial Partnerships

Ali believes access to financing will be important to the wider adoption of electric mobility and renewable-energy technology.

Sora Green reports an existing agreement with Jaiz Bank that provides financing facilities for eligible customers purchasing vehicles through the company.

According to management, Jaiz Bank has also purchased vehicles from Sora Green.

The company has additionally supplied vehicles to Nigeria’s Rural Electrification Agency.

These activities reflect the development of commercial relationships alongside the company’s energy and mobility operations.

Ali believes similar attention to financing and long-term operating economics will be important as institutional customers consider larger renewable-energy investments.

A Long-Term Opportunity Beyond Equipment Sales

Ali’s outlook extends beyond the immediate sale of solar panels, batteries or electric vehicles.

He believes Nigeria’s energy market may increasingly reward companies capable of delivering integrated solutions that combine equipment, technical support, maintenance, financing access and dependable long-term performance.

The transition is unlikely to happen immediately.

High initial costs, financing constraints, technical requirements and customer uncertainty remain important barriers.

Nevertheless, Ali believes the country’s energy challenges are creating incentives for businesses to reconsider conventional approaches to electricity supply.

For institutions facing substantial recurring energy expenditure, the decision to invest in alternative power infrastructure may increasingly become a question of financial planning rather than environmental preference alone.

Ali sees this as a potentially important shift in Nigeria’s energy economy: from treating electricity shortages primarily as an operating problem to evaluating dependable energy infrastructure as a long-term commercial investment.

About Sora Green Energy Projects Limited

Sora Green Energy Projects Limited is an Abuja-based renewable-energy and electric mobility company providing residential and commercial solar-energy solutions, electric vehicle distribution, charging infrastructure and automotive support services.

text:
Flojaune "Flo" Cofer and Sacramento City Councilmember Eric Guerra are facing off Tuesday for Sacramento County's District 1 supervisor seat.

The winner will replace Phil Serna, who is leaving the Board of Supervisors after 16 years and did not seek a fifth term. The district covers much of the city of Sacramento.

Cofer, an epidemiologist, was the runner-up in Sacramento's 2024 mayoral election against Kevin McCarty. Her campaign has emphasized keeping people housed, protecting access to healthcare and creating clean-energy jobs.

Guerra was first elected to the Sacramento City Council in 2015. His campaign emphasizes affordable housing and addressing homelessness by converting encampment sites into housing and expanding shelter capacity. He has also highlighted his work on public safety, including efforts to crack down on human trafficking.

The five-member board oversees county services, including public health and social services.

title: Pulling together: A European partnership model for decarbonisation
