text:
Research effort will explore recycling materials from spent nuclear fuel into fuel for future molten salt reactors.

ABILENE, Texas, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Natura Resources today announced its participation in a Texas A&M Engineering Experiment Station (TEES)-led research effort, Turning Nuclear Waste into Fuel with a Thorium Molten Salt Reactor, selected to receive $5.4 million in funding from the U.S. Department of Energy's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E). The funding, provided through ARPA-E's High-performance Optimized Recycled Nuclear Isotopes for Gen IV reactors (HORNIG) program, is part of an up to $50 million investment across eight selected projects to advance next-generation nuclear fuels.

The effort will develop a fuel form compatible with Natura's technology that could help reduce America's spent nuclear fuel stockpile while minimizing the creation of new long-lived radionuclides. The work supports HORNIG's goal of accelerating the commercial deployment of advanced reactors and strengthening America's domestic nuclear fuel supply chain.

"Texas A&M has played an important role in Natura's journey from our company's founding," said Jordan Robison, CEO of Natura Resources. "Our work together through the Natura Resources Research Alliance has established a strong foundation for collaboration, and with the Department of Energy's investment, this gives us another opportunity to turn advanced research into action. With Texas A&M also being identified as one of the proposed sites for our MSR-100, we see this as part of a much larger partnership focused on bringing advanced molten salt technology to market."

"Texas A&M University and Natura Resources have established a strong and successful partnership, and this new project builds upon that foundation. Natura Resources will serve as our technology commercialization partner, contributing not only to research and development but also to data collection, validation, and documentation in accordance with industry standards. This seamless integration of academic research, industry standards, and technology commercialization is a distinctive feature of our project and one of the key strengths of our team," said Lin Shao, Regents Professor of nuclear engineering and associate dean for research in the Texas A&M University College of Engineering.

"America's energy future depends on bold innovation and strong partnerships between the federal government, national laboratories, universities and industry," said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Energy James P. Danly in announcing the award. "This project demonstrates how we can address long-term nuclear waste challenges while advancing technologies that strengthen our nation's energy security. The Department of Energy is proud to support research that has the potential to unlock new value from existing nuclear materials and accelerate the deployment of advanced reactor systems."

"The Energy Department is delivering on President Trump's vision to unleash an American nuclear renaissance by investing in next-generation nuclear technologies that strengthen our energy independence and bolster our national and economic security," said ARPA-E Director Conner Prochaska. "These projects will help bring tomorrow's reactors online faster and power American prosperity for decades to come."

Over 36 months, researchers and engineers from TEES, Savannah River National Laboratory and Natura Resources will explore how materials found in spent nuclear fuel could be recycled and used as fuel in advanced molten salt reactors. Natura's portion of the work is valued at $1 million. The research could help address one of the nuclear industry's longstanding challenges while creating new opportunities to make better use of existing nuclear material.

Unlike conventional approaches that treat these materials primarily as a disposal challenge, the research will study how long-lived transuranic materials found in spent nuclear fuel could be incorporated into a thorium-based molten salt fuel and consumed in an advanced reactor. The work will help build the scientific and engineering foundation needed to qualify this type of liquid fuel for future reactor use, including understanding its chemistry, performance and compatibility with reactor materials.

The research will begin at Texas A&M using cerium as a non-radioactive surrogate for plutonium to develop and validate methods for understanding the fuel's chemistry, performance and compatibility with reactor materials. The work is then expected to move to Savannah River National Laboratory, where those methods will be validated using plutonium-bearing fuel salts.

Natura will serve as the effort's industrial partner and prospective commercial end user, helping bridge laboratory research and commercial reactor deployment. Natura will help integrate the research findings into reactor design and lead the techno-economic and commercialization work, including evaluating licensing, manufacturing, supply chain and deployment considerations.

About Natura Resources

Natura Resources LLC is a leading advanced small modular reactor developer committed to answering increasing domestic and global demands for reliable energy, medical isotopes, and clean water. Natura's reactors are liquid-fueled and molten salt-cooled, which enhances safety and reduces waste. With the first construction permit for a liquid-fueled reactor from the NRC, Natura has established itself as a leading force in the advanced nuclear industry, fueled by a commitment to support America's energy future. The company is privately owned and has secured more than $120 million in private funding and a commitment of $120 million from the State of Texas. For more information, www.naturaresources.com.

text:
Federal EV tax credits are gone for most buyers, but state EV rebates are still paying out. The New Clean Vehicle Credit, the Previously-Owned Clean Vehicle Credit and the Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit are generally unavailable for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025. Reporting from BlackPressUSA and TechRadar this week steers shoppers toward state programs in California, Illinois, Oregon and Colorado that still knock money off the sticker price.

Timing matters more than usual today, November 3, 2026. Oregon’s Clean Vehicle Rebate Program window closes tomorrow, November 4. Illinois runs through December 31. California’s MyFirstEV discount has been live since August 7. Buyers who were waiting for the market to settle now face a patchwork of deadlines, price caps and income tests. That caution looks reasonable given an SBD survey we covered, where only 11% of gas-car owners named an EV as their next purchase.

This analysis walks through what each program pays, who qualifies, where the gaps sit and what the patchwork means for EV demand. It also flags what we could not confirm, including New York and utility rebates. Every figure below comes from the verified program details for each state, and anything outside those details stays general on purpose.

Federal EV Credits Ended: What Actually Changed

Three federal credits covered the EV market before the cutoff. The New Clean Vehicle Credit applied to new cars. The Previously-Owned Clean Vehicle Credit covered used ones. The Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit served fleets and businesses. All three are generally unavailable for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, according to the federal program notices summarized in the research behind this story.

The wording “generally unavailable” carries weight. It does not mean every edge case disappeared overnight, and a buyer with a binding contract or an unusual lease structure should ask a tax professional. For the typical shopper walking into a dealership in November 2026, though, the federal discount is off the table. That shifts the whole conversation to the state level.

The gap is now roughly 13 months old. In that time, automakers, dealers and state agencies have had to rebuild the incentive picture from scratch. Some states already had programs in place. Others, like California with MyFirstEV, built new point-of-sale discounts and recruited manufacturers to run them. The result is a market where the best deal depends heavily on the buyer’s zip code.

State EV Rebates at a Glance: Four Programs, Four Designs

The four programs confirmed for this report look different from each other. California hands the discount to buyers at the point of sale through automakers. Illinois runs a rebate cycle with a fixed calendar and a price cap. Oregon uses a short open window. Colorado, according to Edward Piersa, who oversees the state’s vehicle exchange program, delivers its incentive at the point of sale as well.

Read the table as a map of structure, not a ranking. The headline savings claim, that state rebates still save you money, holds up across the listed programs. The exact savings depend on the state, the vehicle, the buyer’s income, the purchase or lease date and whether program funding lasts. That caveat applies to every row.

California MyFirstEV: $3,500 Off a New Zero-Emission Vehicle

California’s MyFirstEV program offers $3,500 off a new zero-emission vehicle with an MSRP up to $50,000. For a used zero-emission vehicle sold for up to $25,000 through a manufacturer’s pre-owned program, the discount is $1,750. The state announced the program as available on August 7, 2026. Run the math and both tiers work out to 7% of the maximum qualifying price, which suggests a deliberate design rather than two unrelated numbers.

The key word in the name is “first.” The rebate is for a Californian buying their first zero-emission vehicle. A household that already owns an EV or another zero-emission model should not count on it. The discount is applied at the point of sale through participating automakers, so buyers do not file a separate claim months later.

Which Automakers Participate in MyFirstEV

Twelve brands are listed as participating: Ford, General Motors, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Lexus, Toyota, Lucid, Nissan, Rivian, Subaru and Volvo. Note who is missing from that list. Tesla does not appear among the participating automakers in the verified details, so a buyer eyeing a Tesla should not assume the discount applies. We did not confirm any reason for the omission, and we are not guessing at one.

Why the Used-Car Tier Matters

The $1,750 used-vehicle rebate runs through manufacturers’ pre-owned programs, not through private sales. That routes buyers toward certified inventory, where warranties and inspections come standard. For a first-time EV shopper, that is arguably the lower-risk way into the market. A price ceiling of $25,000 also keeps the tier aimed at ordinary budgets rather than late-model luxury trade-ins.

Illinois EV Rebate: $2,000 Standard, $4,000 for Low-Income Buyers

Illinois runs the most clearly scheduled program of the four. The Electric Vehicle Rebate Program’s current cycle covers August 1, 2026 through December 31, 2026. That leaves about 59 days from today. An eligible new or used all-electric vehicle earns a $2,000 rebate. An eligible low-income applicant buying an all-electric vehicle that is not an electric motorcycle gets $4,000 total. An eligible electric motorcycle earns $1,500.

Two rules trip up applicants. First, the vehicle’s base purchase or selling price must not exceed $80,000. Second, the purchase must come from an Illinois licensed dealer. A private-party sale or an out-of-state purchase breaks the second rule, no matter how attractive the price. The low-income tier doubles the standard rebate, which makes it the clearest fixed-amount deal for budget-constrained buyers among the four programs. Colorado’s “up to” ceiling is higher, but it is not a guaranteed figure.

Note the phrase “$4,000 total.” The wording indicates the low-income figure is the full rebate, not an add-on stacked on the $2,000. Buyers should confirm that reading with the Illinois program office before they count on $6,000.

Oregon’s November 4 Deadline: The Window Is Almost Shut

Oregon is the urgent one. The 2026 open period for the Clean Vehicle Rebate Program runs from August 25 through November 4, 2026. Vehicles purchased or leased outside that period are not eligible for that rebate cycle. Counting both ends, the window spans 72 days, and as of today only two remain, today and tomorrow.

The verified details do not establish a dollar amount for Oregon, so we are not printing one. What they do establish is the rule that matters most right now. A buyer who signs after November 4 falls outside this cycle. Anyone who has a purchase or lease deal pending in Oregon should check the paperwork date today, not next week.

The short window also tells you something about program design. Oregon is betting on a concentrated burst of demand rather than a year-round discount. That approach gives the state tighter control over spending but punishes anyone who shops on a slower timeline.

Colorado’s Point-of-Sale Rebate: Up to $9,000 New, $6,000 Used

Colorado posts the biggest headline numbers. Edward Piersa, who oversees Colorado’s vehicle exchange program, said the point-of-sale rebate is “up to $9,000 for a new EV or up to $6,000 for a used EV.” The words “up to” do the heavy lifting there. The verified details do not spell out which buyers land at the top of that range or what vehicle price limits apply, so readers should treat $9,000 as a ceiling and not an expectation.

Even so, the gap with the other states is plain. Colorado’s used-EV ceiling of $6,000 is more than three times California’s $1,750 used tier and three times Illinois’ $2,000 standard rebate. A buyer in Colorado with the right profile may be looking at the best state incentive in this group. A buyer without it may see a far smaller number. The only responsible advice is to get a written figure at the dealership before signing.

Point-of-sale delivery also changes the economics for buyers. A rebate that reduces the amount financed lowers the loan principal immediately. A rebate mailed weeks later does not. Piersa’s description of the program as point of sale is therefore more than a procedural detail.

What We Could Not Confirm: New York and Utility Rebates

A fair analysis marks its blind spots. No specific rebate amount, eligibility rule or current availability was established for New York. The same goes for utility rebates, which many power companies run separately from state programs. Those incentives may exist and may be worth chasing. We simply have no verified details, so we are not putting numbers on them.

Readers in New York should check the state’s current program pages directly and treat anything they read second-hand, including this article, as a prompt to verify. The same applies to Oregon’s dollar amount. Missing data is a reason to ask questions, not a reason to assume the answer is zero.

Market Impact: What Patchwork Incentives Do to EV Demand

Replacing one national credit with a collection of state programs changes how EV demand spreads across the country. Buyers in states with rich, easy-to-use rebates get a real price advantage. Buyers elsewhere do not. Automakers respond by concentrating marketing, inventory and lease offers where incentives exist. California’s list of twelve participating brands shows how quickly manufacturers will line up when a state builds a point-of-sale channel.

The effect is already visible abroad, where incentive design drives sales mix. Coverage on our site of Tesla’s 248% registration jump in Sweden as Chinese rivals gained ground shows how fast a market can swing when pricing and policy shift. The US picture is not identical, but the lesson carries over. Price signals move buyers, and a single price signal removed from the market tends to leave a visible dent.

For hardware watchers, the interesting angle is what happens to the price tiers. California’s $50,000 MSRP cap and $25,000 used cap steer demand toward mainstream models. Illinois’ $80,000 ceiling is looser and reaches into premium territory. Colorado’s larger amounts, if buyers can actually reach them, could pull volume toward whichever vehicles fit the program’s price rules. Automakers watch those thresholds closely when they set trim levels and pricing.

Competitive Comparison: Which State Program Fits Which Buyer

No single program wins for everyone. The right pick depends on income, the car’s price and how soon the buyer plans to sign. The table below sorts the four programs by buyer profile, using only the confirmed details.

On raw ceilings, Colorado leads, Illinois follows for low-income buyers and California offers the most predictable flat amount. Oregon’s value cannot be ranked without a confirmed dollar figure. Illinois and California both state their caps clearly, which makes them easier to plan around than programs that say “up to.”

Historical Context: From One Federal Credit to Many State Programs

For years the US relied on a nationwide federal credit as the backbone of EV purchase support, with states layering extras on top. September 30, 2025 ended that arrangement for most new purchases. States that had already built programs kept them. States that had not scrambled to fill the gap, and several of the programs in this story, such as California’s MyFirstEV announced August 7, 2026, are recent builds.

Other big EV markets are also shaped by policy and not by price alone. Our coverage of China’s EV share heading to 75% to 80% by 2030 shows how much weight forecasters place on that backdrop. The US now leans on a layered model of its own, with far more variation from state to state.

Readers who follow vehicle technology and pricing can find related analysis in our hardware coverage, which tracks the components and price pressures that sit behind these incentives.

How to Claim a State EV Rebate: A Buyer’s Checklist

The programs differ, but a short routine reduces the risk of losing money to a technicality. Work through these steps before signing anything.

Check the purchase or lease date against the program window. Oregon’s cutoff is November 4, 2026, and Illinois’ cycle ends December 31, 2026.

Confirm the vehicle price against the cap. California requires a new-car MSRP up to $50,000 or a used price up to $25,000, and Illinois caps the base price at $80,000.

Verify the seller. Illinois requires an Illinois licensed dealer, and California’s discount runs through participating automakers.

Ask whether you qualify as a first-time zero-emission buyer in California or as a low-income applicant in Illinois.

Get the rebate amount in writing before you sign, especially in Colorado, where the figure is “up to” a ceiling.

Ask whether the incentive reduces the price at the point of sale or arrives later as a payment.

Used buyers have an extra step, which is to check the vehicle’s condition and battery health. That is one reason certified channels look attractive. We covered how Hyundai’s certified used cars now add 90-day driver scores and EV battery data, the kind of disclosure that helps a first-time buyer judge a pre-owned EV before a rebate is applied.

Finally, run the long-term math instead of focusing only on the discount. A study we reported on found that an old gas car versus a new EV reaches break-even at 18,000 miles on emissions. Cost break-even is a separate calculation, but the point stands that the sticker price is only one part of ownership.

Risks and Caveats Buyers Should Weigh

State rebates carry risks that the federal credit did not. Funding can run out. Windows can close, as Oregon’s does tomorrow. Eligibility rules can change between announcement and checkout. The verified details support the view that savings are real, and they equally support the view that savings are conditional.

Another risk is stacking confusion. Buyers in some states may be eligible for more than one incentive, such as a state rebate plus a utility offer. The verified details do not confirm how these combine in any of the four states, so nobody should budget for stacked savings until a dealer or program office confirms the arithmetic in writing. Counting on a discount that later disappears at signing is the costliest mistake a buyer can make.

Finally, remember that a rebate is not a reason to buy a car you cannot afford. A $3,500 or $2,000 discount helps with the sticker price, but insurance, charging access and financing terms still decide whether the purchase works month after month.

Predictions: Where State EV Rebates Go Next

These are our own forecasts, not reported facts, and they rest on the structure of the programs described above.

More states will copy California’s point-of-sale model. A discount applied at checkout through automakers removes paperwork for buyers, and twelve participating brands show manufacturers will cooperate.

Short windows will become more common. Oregon’s 72-day window gives agencies tight budget control. Expect more programs to run in bursts rather than year-round.

Income tiers will spread. Illinois’ $4,000 low-income rebate, double its standard tier, points to a policy direction that targets money at buyers who need it most.

Used-EV incentives will grow in importance. With caps like California’s $25,000 used ceiling, states are courting buyers who would never consider a new EV, and that pushes demand into the certified pre-owned channel.

Battery cost trends will shape how big rebates need to be. As suppliers such as CATL, which holds 39.1% of the EV battery market in our January to September tracker, push pack costs around, states can adjust rebate sizes up or down.

The takeaway: state EV rebates will keep carrying the load that the federal credits dropped, but unevenly. Shoppers who match the right program to their income, location and calendar can still capture real savings. Shoppers who ignore the fine print will not.

FAQ: State EV Rebates After the Federal Credit Ended

Are federal EV tax credits still available?

Generally no. The New Clean Vehicle Credit, the Previously-Owned Clean Vehicle Credit and the Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit are generally unavailable for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025. Buyers with unusual circumstances should confirm with a tax professional.

How much is California’s MyFirstEV rebate?

The program offers $3,500 off a new zero-emission vehicle with an MSRP up to $50,000, and $1,750 off a used zero-emission vehicle sold for up to $25,000 through a manufacturer’s pre-owned program. It is for Californians buying their first zero-emission vehicle.

What does Illinois pay for an electric vehicle?

An eligible new or used all-electric vehicle earns $2,000. An eligible low-income applicant gets $4,000 total on an all-electric vehicle that is not a motorcycle. An eligible electric motorcycle earns $1,500. The base price cannot exceed $80,000 and the seller must be an Illinois licensed dealer.

When does Oregon’s EV rebate window close?

The 2026 open period for the Clean Vehicle Rebate Program runs August 25 through November 4, 2026. Vehicles purchased or leased outside that period are not eligible for that cycle, so the deadline is tomorrow.

How big is Colorado’s EV rebate?

Edward Piersa, who oversees Colorado’s vehicle exchange program, described the point-of-sale rebate as “up to $9,000 for a new EV or up to $6,000 for a used EV.” The actual amount depends on the buyer and vehicle, so get the figure in writing.

Do New York or utility rebates still exist?

We could not establish a rebate amount, eligibility rule or current availability for New York or for utility rebates. Check the official program pages or your utility directly before counting on either.

Can I stack more than one EV incentive?

The verified details do not confirm stacking rules for any of the four states. Ask the dealer or program office to confirm in writing which incentives combine and how the final price is calculated.

Eugene voters will decide tomorrow whether to create a clean energy fund by charging certain large businesses a 2% fee, a proposal supporters say would help pay for climate and energy projects but opponents warn could raise costs for customers.

Measure 20-388 would create a clean energy fund to support climate and energy projects in Eugene. The money would come from a new fee on certain large businesses, though voters will decide on the measure before knowing exactly which businesses the fee would apply to.

Under the measure, the fee would apply to businesses with more than $1 billion in national gross profits and more than $500,000 in Eugene gross profits. The measure exempts most groceries, medicines, health care, and residential garbage and recycling services.

“The Eugene clean energy fund allows Eugene to do their part, make these investments, invest in their community directly and also reduce climate emissions, which will improve our health and our environment and create good-paying jobs along the way,” said Britney Vancitters, a steering committee member for the Eugene Clean Energy Fund.

If approved, the fund would allocate 60% to renewable energy and energy-efficiency programs, 25% to clean-energy job training and contractor support, 10% to green infrastructure and 5% to future innovation.

Stop the Hidden Tax, the opposition campaign, says it supports clean energy but argues the measure could hurt Eugene’s economy. “The tax is on gross profit which is calculated before rent wages or utilities,” opposition spokesperson Laura Sedwick said. “Small businesses buy their insurance supplies and equipment from these same companies a cost like that doesn't disappear. It shows up in prices that we all pay.”

Supporters dispute that the fee would lead to local price increases. “These big corporations are setting their prices at a regional or national level, and we have Portland to look at. Portland has not seen these types of price increases,” Vancitters said.

Portland’s clean energy fund was enacted in 2019 and is funded by a 1% surcharge on large retailers’ Portland sales.

In Eugene, the city would decide which businesses meet the measure’s definition of a “large retailer,” a process that could take up to six months. Potential businesses could include Walmart, Target and some banks.

The Oregon Bankers Association says the measure would put banks at a disadvantage to credit unions. In a statement, the association, which contributed $15,000 to the opposition, said: “We are concerned that the measure would impose a new tax on qualifying banks serving Eugene while specifically exempting competing credit unions – this would make the unfair tax gap separating banks and credit unions even larger.”

If the measure passes, a nine-member appointed committee would review funding proposals and recommend to the mayor and City Council how the money is spent. The measure could generate between $15 million and $40 million a year for the clean energy fund. If approved, the fee will take effect Jan. 1, 2029.

By David Shepardson

WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) – A group representing General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major automakers on Monday backed the Trump administration in a legal challenge to its sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards filed by California and other states.

Last month, the US Transportation Department said it was finalizing a fleet-wide fuel economy average of 34.9 miles per ⁠gallon (14.7 km per liter) by 2031, down from 50.4 miles per gallon (21.4 km per liter) that had been approved under then-President Joe Biden in 2024.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents GM, Toyota, Volkswagen, Hyundai, Ford, Stellantis and other major automakers, backed the effort by President Donald Trump’s administration after California, New York and two dozen other states, cities and counties sued last month.

“Automakers require certainty and stability in the standards,” the group said in the filing with the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals.

It added that if the standards were set aside, it “would affect automakers’ business, endangering the capital investment planning, product development, and performance validation for hundreds of new vehicle models intended for the US market.”

The states said the Trump administration was ignoring the presence of millions of electric vehicles, “leading to a ‌flawed, dramatically ⁠distorted analysis of the ‘maximum feasible’ fuel economy level.” The automaker group said the court should reject those arguments.

The revised Trump administration standards seek to reverse Biden’s push toward greater fuel efficiency and electric vehicles. A coalition of environmental ​and consumer groups also filed a separate lawsuit challenging the new rules.

The Transportation Department said the regulation reduces manufacturers’ average cost per ​vehicle to comply by $1,289 but increases fuel costs by more than $1,600 over the life ​of the vehicles. ⁠

The department said the rule would increase US gasoline consumption through 2050 by 4.6%, or about 121 billion gallons, compared with the Biden rules but also boost new car sales.

The American Petroleum Institute, an oil and natural gas industry trade group, also filed in support of the Trump administration’s rules, saying they ensure the government sets standards that “do not force consumers to purchase vehicles that consume less fuel than they would otherwise choose.”

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by Jamie Freed)

text:
Trump is making pollution great again (and again, and again…)

OAKLAND — California Attorney General Rob Bonta today joined a coalition of 27 states, counties, and cities in opposing the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) supplemental proposal to rescind its 2015 finding that greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from fossil fuel power plants drive climate change and endanger public health and welfare, which would eliminate and prevent regulation of these emissions. The 2015 finding, known as the Endangerment Finding for power plants, acknowledged that fossil fuel power plant GHG emissions significantly contribute to the pollution that is changing the climate and triggered EPA’s duty to set limits on those emissions. EPA proposed rescinding the finding on different grounds last year, at the same time it proposed repealing the Biden Administration’s GHG emissions standards for certain fossil fuel-fired power plants. Although EPA finalized the repeal of the Biden-era emissions standards, it did not finalize its proposed recission of the Endangerment Finding, instead choosing to supplement its proposal with arguments borrowed from EPA’s rescission of the Endangerment Finding for motor vehicles that it finalized in February 2026. If EPA finalizes the supplemental proposal, it will effectively abandon Section 111 of the Clean Air Act — the statutory tool that speaks directly to those emissions, as affirmed by the U.S. Supreme Court in Massachusetts v. EPA — and preclude future federal regulation of fossil fuel power plant GHG emissions. Attorney General Bonta and the coalition urge EPA to withdraw the proposed rule and preserve its ability to use the Clean Air Act to limit power plant greenhouse gas emissions.

“The President can’t keep burying his head in the sand and ignoring the truth. Climate change is real, it’s caused by greenhouse gas emissions, and decades of settled science warned us this was coming. This proposal is a dangerous retreat from science, the law, and common sense,” said Attorney General Bonta. “EPA’s plan to rescind the Endangerment Finding for power plants puts Trump’s Big Oil friends before the American people, who are already dealing with the impacts of destructive wildfires, scorching heat, and severe floods. That’s why we’re opposing this proposed rule and urging EPA to withdraw it.”

Fossil fuel-fired power plants in the United States are one of the largest contributors to climate pollution in the world — if these power plants were a country, they would be the sixth-highest emitter on the planet. The power sector is the largest stationary source and second-largest overall source of GHG emissions in the United States, accounting for a quarter of all domestic emissions. Failing to control the sector’s GHG emissions will exacerbate significant threats facing California, including intensifying and increasing heat waves, wildfires, severe storms, flooding, disease, air pollution, and harm to regional ecosystems. Last year, two of the most destructive fires in state history — the Palisades Fire and the Eaton Fire, both in Los Angeles County — killed at least 30 people, destroyed over 16,000 homes and other structures, and damaged over 37,000 acres. Just recently, record-breaking tides — amplified by sea level rise and ocean warming — have inundated streets and flooded homes along Southern California’s coastline.

Meanwhile, President Trump and EPA have taken many actions that accelerate climate change and further endanger hundreds of millions of Americans — particularly communities that are disproportionately burdened by environmental harms. These actions include the illegal repeals of the Endangerment Finding for motor vehicles and of the 2024 GHG emission standards for fossil fuel-power plants, and now this attempt at withdrawing the Endangerment Finding for power plants.

In today’s comment letter, Attorney General Bonta and the coalition assert that:

The Clean Air Act directs EPA to regulate GHG emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants under Section 111, and the U.S. Supreme Court and D.C. Circuit have interpreted Section 111 to effectuate this plain meaning. EPA cannot rewrite the Clean Air Act or overrule the U.S. Supreme Court, and EPA’s arguments for doing so — including its invocation of the major questions doctrine — all fail.

Futility is an impermissible reason not to regulate GHG emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants, particularly given that the U.S. power sector’s GHG emissions are the sixth largest source of GHG emissions in the world.

EPA’s supplemental proposal is arbitrary and capricious because EPA failed to adequately explain its change in position or to consider serious reliance interests, failed to quantify or monetize GHG, ozone, and particulate matter impacts, and failed to consider impacts of the proposal on grid reliability or electricity affordability.

In submitting the comment letter, Attorney General Bonta joins the attorneys general of New York, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawaiʻi, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and the District of Columbia, along with the Chief Legal Officers of the City of Chicago, the City and County of Denver, the City of New York, and the Bay Area Air Quality Management District.

"Automakers require certainty and stability in the standards," the group said in the filing with the 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals.

It added that if the standards were set aside, it "would affect automakers’ business, endangering the capital investment planning, product development, and performance validation for hundreds of new vehicle models intended for the US market."

text:
With Chinese-made electric vehicles led by Tesla eroding domestic market share below the majority threshold, lawmakers from both the ruling and opposition parties called in unison at this year's national audit for EVs to be included in the domestic production tax credit. Amid growing alarm that the foundation of Korea's auto manufacturing base could be shaken, the National Assembly's tax subcommittee is expected to take up the question of whether to add EVs when it reviews tax code amendments this month.

The domestic production tax credit is a key campaign pledge of President Lee Jae Myung and has been dubbed Korea's version of the Inflation Reduction Act. It grants tax credit benefits to companies that produce and sell strategic goods domestically, scaled to their production output. The government's 2026 tax reform plan, announced last August, however, covered only six sectors: solar power generation, wind power generation, secondary batteries, semiconductors, core materials and AI robot components.

People Power Party lawmaker Ahn Sang-hun said at the Finance and Economy Planning Committee's comprehensive audit of the Ministry of Economy and Finance on Oct. 22 that major advanced economies were deploying tariffs, tax deductions and subsidies to protect their domestic EV industries. "There is in effect no country that has defended its market without an active response," Ahn said.

Bae Jun-young, who leads the People Power Party's side on the Finance and Economy Planning Committee, said the government had once primed the pump for the semiconductor industry when it was struggling. "I believe support should be provided where an EV tax credit or similar measure is needed to help compete against other countries or where the government needs to play a priming role," Bae said.

The same call came from the Democratic Party of Korea. Moon Jin-seog said the current government plan appeared to be pushing domestic finished-vehicle makers — who must compete against Chinese automakers with strong price competitiveness — off a cliff. "To genuinely strengthen competitiveness, EVs should be eligible for the domestic production tax credit regardless of whether capital investment in facilities has been made," Moon said.

According to the National Assembly's bill information system, 24 amendments to the Restriction of Special Taxation Act that would add EVs and other next-generation vehicles to the domestic production tax credit have been filed across both parties since the 22nd Assembly convened. Even after the government's tax reform plan — which excluded EVs — was made public, seven lawmakers from both parties led by Ahn Do-geol filed a string of related bills.

Eight of the 24 bills were introduced by lawmakers who sit on the tax subcommittee, which directly reviews tax legislation. The amendments are expected to clear the tax subcommittee, then pass through the full Finance and Economy Planning Committee and the Legislation and Judiciary Committee before a final floor vote in December.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il visited Hyundai Motor and Kia's Namyang R&D Center in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, on Monday to meet with Hyundai Motor Group Chairman Euisun Chung and hold a roundtable with the EV industry. At the Oct. 22 comprehensive audit, Lee had said he was considering visiting the scene to hear firsthand about actual conditions and was reviewing how to reach a conclusion after confirming that the EV sector faced serious difficulties over the next two to three years.

Industry executives from the EV, self-driving car and parts sectors who attended the roundtable requested support through the EV production tax credit. They also called for expanded support for the parts industry's transition to next-generation vehicles, a legal framework for introducing battery leasing, and an increase in specialist personnel at agencies dedicated to self-driving cars.

Lee said the government would actively participate in and engage in in-depth discussions during the National Assembly's deliberations on EV production tax credit support. The government plans to announce a package of measures to strengthen the competitiveness of the EV industry this month, reflecting opinions raised at the roundtable.

The rapid pace at which Chinese-made EVs are capturing the domestic market is cited as the backdrop to the industry's push for tax support. According to the Korea Automobile Manufacturers Association and the Korea Automobile Importers & Distributors Association (KAIDA), Chinese-made passenger EVs newly registered in Korea from January through September this year totaled 112,417 units — 2.2 times the 51,535 units recorded in the same period last year. Their market share rose 8.4 percentage points to 43.5 percent. Domestic passenger EV market share, meanwhile, fell 6.2 percentage points to 48.7 percent, dropping below the majority mark.

Tesla is driving the surge. According to KAIDA, 89,148 Tesla vehicles were newly registered in Korea from January through September this year, up 104.4 percent from the same period last year — already 1.5 times the full-year 2025 registration figure of 59,916 units. The Tesla Model Y and Model 3 sold in Korea are produced at the company's Shanghai factory. While Kia's Sorento has held on to the top-selling position in the domestic market, the gap with the Tesla Model Y has narrowed to just 1,810 units, fueling concern that a Chinese-made EV could dislodge a domestic model from the annual top spot.

The industry has long urged the government to introduce a production tax credit of around 4 million won ($2,990) per vehicle — on par with Japan's level. In the National Assembly, Democratic Party of Korea lawmaker Lee Eon-ju introduced a bill in September setting the base credit at 4 million won per EV.

Japan serves as the industry's benchmark. In 2024, Japan introduced its "Strategic Sector Domestic Production Promotion Tax Regime," which provides a corporate tax deduction of 400,000 yen ($2,540) per vehicle for EVs and hydrogen-powered cars produced and sold domestically, and 200,000 yen per vehicle for compact EVs and plug-in hybrid vehicles, for a period of 10 years. The deduction is capped at 40 percent of corporate tax liability.

An industry official said Korea, with its export-oriented industrial structure unlike the United States or Europe, finds it difficult to adopt the same trade measures as major economies, making it a concentrated target for Chinese EV makers. "If policy support across the entire auto industry — including the domestic production tax credit — is not provided in a timely manner, the domestic automotive ecosystem will wither away," the official said.

text:
Wind, solar and a small battery could meet 70-90% of a typical electricity demand profile for an average delivered cost of $56/MWh, offering an affordable way for Kazakhstan to meet rising demand and reduce reliance on its ageing coal fleet.

Astana, 3 November 2026: Kazakhstan could meet much of its growing electricity demand with wind power supported by solar and battery, at a lower cost than building new coal power, according to new analysis by global energy think tank Ember. The modelling finds that wind hybrid plants could meet 70-90% of typical electricity demand hour by hour at an average delivered cost of $56/MWh, with projects built close to demand centres and existing power lines, rather than in the windiest locations, to limit the need for major new transmission infrastructure.

Kazakhstan has some of the world’s strongest wind resources, but wind generated just 4.4% of its electricity in 2025, compared with a global average of 8.6%. “Kazakhstan has a vast untapped high-quality wind resource that with some solar and a small battery can reach similar reliability to what solar and more batteries can do in sunny places at an affordable cost. Wind resources are great across most of its territory, so hybrid projects can be built close to demand, minimising major additional transmission lines”, report author Kostantsa Rangelova said.

Wind resources are rich enough to bring power closer to demand

Around 66% of Kazakhstan’s territory has average wind speeds above 7 metres per second at 100 metres above ground, excellent for commercial wind projects. In comparison, less than a third of Germany has wind speeds above this level.

Ember tested the local weather data of 15 sites across Kazakhstan near demand centres and existing power lines, simulating the hourly output of 125 hybrid power plant configurations that combine different wind, solar, and battery capacity to evaluate their ability to meet a typical demand profile. The results from the simulations, matching supply and demand hour by hour across a 30-year project lifetime, show that the country’s strong wind resources could provide an affordable source of electricity near demand. This could reduce the need for major new transmission lines to connect remote power plants to consumers.

By combining wind with solar and a small battery, these hybrid plants can provide electricity more consistently than wind alone. The modelling finds that hybrid plants can meet 70-90% of demand, depending on the site, at an average delivered cost of around $56/MWh – under $60/MWh at every site, lower than the cost of new coal power, estimated at $70-170/MWh.

Smartly operated hybrid plants can be a source of system flexibility

The simulations showed that the best-performing hybrid plants deliberately build more wind and solar capacity than can be absorbed by the demand profile every hour. Their generation cost averages $45/MWh, in line with Kazakhstan’s recent wind auctions. Delivering a reliable supply adds about $11/MWh, taking the average delivered cost to $56/MWh. That extra cost is the price of the surplus capacity that is curtailed in windy or sunny hours: it is a design choice made by the plant, and fundamentally different from grid-ordered curtailment without compensation.

At system level, a single project does not need to meet all demand with 100% reliability on its own. 70-90% is the most a single project can meet for under $60/MWh.The remaining 10-30% can be provided more efficiently by a more flexible, interconnected power system, which Kazakhstan has yet to build.

Wind hybrid plants offer a unique opportunity for Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan’s electricity demand increased by 16% between 2020 and 2025, from 107.3 TWh to 124.6 TWh. The country has been a net electricity importer since 2022 and aims to achieve electricity self-sufficiency by 2027 and potentially become a net exporter by 2029. Coal accounted for 62% of electricity generation in 2025, and the country’s coal fleet is more than 50 years old on average. Wind hybrid plants offer a unique opportunity to meet these challenges and by providing a way to build an affordable and reliable source of home-grown electricity quickly and at scale near to where demand is.

Kazakhstan has a target for renewables to supply 15% of electricity generation by 2030, but has no dedicated target for wind and solar beyond that date. The report recommends a clear target for wind and solar beyond 2030 that would give investors greater certainty and help Kazakhstan make better use of its wind resources. Market rules that reward flexibility would also help integrate more renewable electricity and make it a source of flexibility.

text:
Eloy, AZ - Congressman Juan Ciscomani recently toured the Kitt Solar project currently under construction in Eloy, underscoring his commitment to advancing Arizona’s energy future. The Congressman highlighted the project as a model for supporting American energy production and driving economic growth in local communities across Southern Arizona, including Eloy. Once complete, Kitt Solar will deliver up to 100 megawatts of clean electricity paired with advanced battery storage, enough to power approximately 32,000 Arizona homes. The project supported nearly 500 well-paying jobs at peak construction earlier this year, while boosting business for local restaurants, markets, and small businesses throughout Eloy.

"Arizona’s energy needs are growing rapidly, and projects like Kitt Solar are essential to meeting that demand while creating good-paying jobs and attracting investment to our communities," said Congressman Juan Ciscomani. "It was inspiring to witness the progress underway in Eloy and to learn about the opportunities this project brings to local families. In Congress, I have worked to protect the incentives that make initiatives like Kitt Solar possible. We need an all-of-the-above approach that keeps energy affordable, reliable, and made in America."

Ciscomani has been a vocal advocate for protecting domestic energy production of all kinds and ensuring American businesses have the certainty to invest and expand. During the debate on the Working Families Tax Cuts Act, he signed multiple letters to Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith and House leadership, urging them to safeguard clean energy tax incentives and prevent abrupt disruptions that could hinder growth.

In Congress, Ciscomani also spearheaded efforts to support American energy production and strengthen domestic manufacturing, particularly for battery storage components. His advocacy helped preserve critical incentives that benefit projects like Kitt Solar, which utilizes federal tax credits for its battery systems and the overall project. Earlier this year, the Congressman was awarded the American Energy Champion Award by the American Energy Alliance for his all-of-the-above energy approach.

"We are proud to bring the Kitt Solar project to Eloy and invest in the community and Arizona’s energy future," said Antonia Castro-Graham, Senior Vice President of Policy & Regulatory Affairs at Avantus. "We were glad to welcome Congressman Ciscomani to see firsthand the impact this project is having, from nearly 500 construction jobs to decades of local tax revenue. Kitt Solar exemplifies how clean energy investment delivers lasting benefits to local communities and helps meet the rising demand for reliable electricity."

Arizona’s continued growth relies on robust energy infrastructure to support new homes, businesses, and industries. Investments in energy generation and storage are vital to meeting these needs. Projects like Kitt Solar are expanding the resources necessary for Southern Arizona’s future and bringing new economic opportunities to communities like Eloy.

authors: John Lushetsky, R. Neal Martin, John McEachern, Adrianna Swartz

text:
October brought significant developments across federal permitting, critical materials, and federal energy financing. Stakeholders began weighing in on the Senate’s Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, while the Trump administration’s continued actions on offshore wind projects tested the bipartisan permitting proposal. The US Department of Energy (DOE) designated helium as a critical material amid supply disruptions, and the Export-Import Bank of the United States (EXIM) spotlighted Mesabi Metallics’ new iron ore operations. DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing announced more than $14 billion in new loan commitments and closings for nuclear projects, and DOE launched a $237 million funding opportunity to strengthen US supply chains for critical grid components. Finally, House Energy and Commerce Democrats escalated their investigation into DOE’s October 2025 grant terminations, potentially setting the stage for oversight hearings after the November elections.

Stakeholders Mobilize on Permitting Reform

The debate over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA), which would make major reforms to the federal energy permitting landscape, kicked into gear in October in preparation for Congress’s return after the midterm elections.

Despite the intense buildup to its bipartisan release in the Senate at the end of September, the Trump administration has given only tacit support for the deal as written, while House Republicans have largely refrained from commenting on the legislation. Rather than endorsing the legislation directly, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) highlighted the committee’s own permitting agenda; by contrast, House Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.) described the bill as “encouraging.”

The bill has received broad backing from labor and industry groups. Business organizations such as the US Chamber of Commerce, the National Mining Association, and the Steel Manufacturers Association have endorsed the legislation. The American Clean Power Association and the American Petroleum Institute have also voiced support, a rare alliance in the energy sector. Lastly, labor unions, including the Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA) and the United Association, have expressed support.

Opposition has come primarily from environmental organizations, Tribal groups, and state officials. The Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC) lauded the bill’s transmission provisions but criticized provisions that would change existing environmental laws, reduce Tribal authority, and support fossil fuels. Similar concerns have been raised by the Native American Rights Fund and the National Congress of American Indians. At the state level, the Environmental Council of the States submitted a letter to congressional leaders objecting to several provisions, particularly those affecting the Clean Water Act. Democratic attorneys general from nine states issued a similar letter.

BAAJA has a credible path forward through the Senate, given its bipartisan sponsorship. A procedural vote is scheduled for November 9 which is expected to kick off debate and amendments in the Senate. On the House side, Natural Resources Committee ranking member Jared Huffman (D-CA) has signaled that Democrats will not support the bill as written, highlighting the expected change in the House majority from the upcoming midterms. All sides, however, have a strong motivation to reach consensus during the lame-duck session to avoid the outcome from the previous Congress, which failed to reach agreement on the Barrasso–Machin permitting reform bill.

Trump Moves on Solar and Wind Projects

A key point of contention in the permitting reform bill negotiations has been the Trump administration’s targeting of wind and solar projects. Approximately 300 wind and solar projects have been awaiting Department of Defense review, according to reports surrounding the negotiations. Although the White House has pledged to advance those projects, Pentagon officials reportedly advanced only two on October 22 — one in Maine and one in South Dakota. The projects were not publicly identified, and the reported action did not establish that either had received final clearance or that the remaining projects had advanced.

Separately, the Interior Department has sought court action to reconsider or withdraw federal approvals for four offshore wind developments: Revolution Wind, Atlantic Shores, the proposed 2.2-gigawatt Maryland Offshore Wind project, and New England Wind. These requests place existing approvals under further review but do not, by themselves, constitute completed project cancellations.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and a participant in the permitting negotiations, has warned that the administration’s actions threaten a bipartisan agreement. He described the Pentagon’s advancement of the two projects as “a start” while calling for additional action on the backlog.

DOE Designates Helium as a “Critical Material”

On October 23, 2026, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright designated helium as a critical material under authority from the Energy Act of 2020. While no specific funding assistance was announced, the announcement unlocks eligibility for federal financing, supply chain monitoring, and grant opportunities for US producers.

Helium’s notable applications include semiconductor chip manufacturing, cooling spaceflight and defense machinery, leak testing in natural gas infrastructure, and medical imaging. The designation comes as supply disruptions continue due to the Iran war. Spot prices for helium have nearly tripled since March 2026, though the full effects of the shortage remain to be seen.

Helium is primarily produced as a byproduct of natural gas processing. The United States is the largest helium producer globally, producing 81 million cubic meters, or around 43.8% of global production, in 2025. Qatar’s supply, the second largest at around 34.6% of global production, has come under threat. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, along with Iranian strikes on Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas facility, has rattled supply chains. The Qatari government said it would take at least three years to get the facility back in operation.

EXIM Chair Touts Mesabi Metallics’ Projects

As part of the Trump administration’s effort to expand US industrial capacity, on September 17, EXIM Chair John Jovanovic toured Mesabi Metallics’ iron ore mine and pellet plant in Nashwauk, Minnesota, as the facility began operations. The project is notable as the first new iron ore mine and pellet plant to commence production in the United States in approximately 50 years and is expected to produce up to 7 million tons of iron ore pellets annually for use in modern steelmaking.

On September 28, Jovanovic also joined President Trump in the Oval Office to announce Mesabi Metallics’ planned $15 billion steel plant in Iowa, which will be supplied by the Minnesota mine. The announcement followed EXIM’s approval of a $770 million direct loan supporting development of the Minnesota operation.

Energy Dominance Financing Announcements

DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) on October 5 announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $4.2 billion to finance nuclear uprates and modernization across Vistra’s fleet at Beaver Valley in Pennsylvania and Davis-Besse and Perry in Ohio. DOE said the projects will preserve nearly 4 gigawatts (GW) of baseload power and add 433 megawatts (MW) of new capacity in the PJM region, with an option to finance future uprates at Vistra’s Comanche Peak plant in Texas.

On October 27, EDF followed with a conditional commitment of up to $5 billion to Constellation Energy to finance uprates across eight nuclear plants in Illinois, Maryland, and Pennsylvania, adding nearly 1.1 GW of capacity across the PJM and MISO regions. Like the Vistra commitment, it includes an option to finance additional facilities, and Constellation must satisfy technical, legal, environmental, and financial conditions before definitive financing documents are executed and funds are disbursed.

The next day, EDF announced the financial close of a $5.1 billion loan package to Alliant Energy’s Iowa and Wisconsin utility subsidiaries to support new natural gas-fired power plants, energy storage systems, and upgrades to existing generation. DOE projects the investments will add more than 2.6 GW of new or upgraded capacity and deliver over $1 billion in electricity cost savings. The package, which exceeds the $3 billion conditional commitment offered under the Biden administration in January 2025, marks the administration’s 10th financial close. These announcements build on the September 8 close of a loan of up to $1.9 billion to NextEra Energy to restart Iowa’s Duane Arnold nuclear plant, and they signal that EDF will remain a significant source of capital for nuclear and firm-power projects, including for utilities managing rising load growth

DOE Launches Grid Supply Chain Funding Opportunity

On October 30, DOE announced a $237 million funding opportunity to boost US manufacturing and strengthen supply chains for critical electric grid components. The Grid Supply Chain Alternatives to Lead Energy Dominance (Grid SCALED) funding opportunity will provide up to $50 million for projects that promote refurbishment and reuse of existing grid equipment and materials, and up to $187 million for projects that increase the use of alternative materials and subcomponents sourced and made in the United States. DOE estimates the investment will deliver $125 million in annual utility savings and keep $50 million per year in the US economy that would otherwise go to international suppliers.

Grid SCALED is the first funding opportunity under DOE’s Grid Supply Chain Program, which is authorized to provide up to $375 million for domestic manufacturing of distribution and power transformers, grid components, and materials. DOE anticipates additional announcements in 2027 targeting next-generation technologies, including solid-state transformers. Concept papers are due November 20, 2026, and full applications are due February 8, 2027.

Grant Cancellations

On October 26, House Energy and Commerce ranking members Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.), Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), and Yvette D. Clarke (D-N.Y.) sent a second letter to Energy Secretary Chris Wright. They wrote after DOE missed the October 6 response deadline set in their September 22 letter.

The members accuse DOE officials of misleading Congress by denying that politics drove the October 2025 grant terminations. They cite filings in Thakur v. Trump (N.D. Cal.) in which DOE admitted the decisions were "based solely" on partisan considerations and argued they were permissible "as leverage to end a government shutdown." The members point to the court’s October 27 briefing deadline on DOE’s statutory authority. title: Republicans' Anti-Clean Energy Policies Hurt their Own Constituents the Most
description:
Javier Orozco, Research Analyst Republicans’ assault on clean energy through policies like the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA) has adversely impacted thousands of clean energy manufacturing and power projects and sites across the country.
However, the cost of Republicans’ anti-clean energy policies like OBBBA is falling mostly on their own districts and constituents.
The stakes for working people extend from the factory floor to the energy bill, with OBBBA putting a significant amount of planned utility-scale clean energy capacity additions at risk.
Utility-scale clean energy is associated with lower retail rates thanks to lower transmission, distribution, and maintenance costs relative to other sources.
Republicans’ attacks on clean energy are putting manufacturing jobs and planned power projects at risk, with the greatest impacts falling on the constituents of Republicans who voted for OBBBA.
text:
Javier Orozco, Research Analyst

Republicans’ assault on clean energy through policies like the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” (OBBBA) has adversely impacted thousands of clean energy manufacturing and power projects and sites across the country. We track and map these impacts in our recent database release, Fallout: Where Attacks on the Clean Economy Hit Home.1 Now, an analysis of our database has found that most of the impact has fallen on states and districts represented by Republicans who voted to pass OBBBA. Republicans are attacking these important projects and sites at a time when working people, including their own constituents, are already hurting—and facing fewer manufacturing job opportunities and higher electricity rates across the country.

The Trump administration and Republicans have taken unprecedented action to punish political opponents through funding cuts and freezes aimed at Democrat-led states. For example, more than $7 billion in clean energy grant cancellations were found by a federal court to be illegally targeted at states where a majority of the electorate voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.

However, the cost of Republicans’ anti-clean energy policies like OBBBA is falling mostly on their own districts and constituents.

An analysis of our database shows that whether you look at project count, private investment, federal award funding, or jobs, most of the impact falls on projects and sites located in the districts of OBBBA-supporting Republicans. Notably, more than 80% of impacted private investment and jobs are in districts of GOP members.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA) claims that, thanks to GOP policies, “American manufacturing is BOOMING.” 2 Yet, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data shows that as of September 2026 U.S. manufacturing employment was down about 21,000 jobs compared to the start of Trump’s second term, with motor vehicles and parts manufacturing alone seeing a decline of 13,000 jobs. Investment in new manufacturing is also on the retreat, with the annualized rate of manufacturing construction spending as of August 2026 down more than 28% since the start of Trump’s second term. 3

Our data shows that projects and sites impacted by OBBBA supported thousands of clean energy technology manufacturing jobs, especially in the vehicles industry. Jobs like these offer an important wage advantage, with one report finding that “clean energy factory workers earn 35% more than the average American worker.” An analysis of our database found that 29,269 permanent clean technology manufacturing and industrial jobs could be lost to project cancellations and stalls in states and districts represented by OBBBA-supporting Republicans. Additionally, 5,478 jobs may be vulnerable due to an at-risk or cancelled federal grants or loan awards, and another 122,819 jobs may be vulnerable due to curtailed federal tax support. Vehicles and closely related industries, including batteries and critical minerals, account for 73% of jobs associated with impacted projects and sites.

The stakes for working people extend from the factory floor to the energy bill, with OBBBA putting a significant amount of planned utility-scale clean energy capacity additions at risk. An analysis of our database found that in states and districts represented by OBBBA-supporting Republicans, 206,964 MW of planned capacity face curtailed federal tax support, and 19,651 MW of planned capacity have already been cancelled. Utility-scale clean energy is associated with lower retail rates thanks to lower transmission, distribution, and maintenance costs relative to other sources. Households face rising energy bills, paying about $110 more in 2025 than in 2024 with further increases expected this year. In August 2026, all but four states recorded higher retail rates compared to last August, 5.1% higher on a national basis.

Republicans’ attacks on clean energy are putting manufacturing jobs and planned power projects at risk, with the greatest impacts falling on the constituents of Republicans who voted for OBBBA. At a time when working people are in critical need of good paying jobs and affordable electricity, these policies undermine both in the very communities OBBBA-supporting Republicans represent.

text:
Australian Class 8 truck conversion company Janus selects Mississauga-based battery manufacturer for its move into Canada and the U.S.

Electrovaya Inc. will supply lithium-ion battery systems for heavy-duty electric trucks under a new strategic agreement with Australia’s Janus Electric, opening a new market for the Mississauga-based battery manufacturer.

The agreement, announced last week, comes with about US$26 million in initial purchase orders to meet demand for Janus products in the U.S. and Canada.

Janus converts diesel Class 8 trucks to battery-electric and powers them with swappable battery packs so fleets can exchange batteries in minutes rather than wait hours to recharge. Each conversion will use around 600 kilowatt-hours of Electrovaya batteries, split between two packs.

Electrovaya has also agreed to invest about US$1.4 million in Janus for up to 4.2 million shares, plus up to 6.3 million warrants.

A different solution

Janus has orders and commitments for 118 truck conversions in the U.S. and Canada.

“It’s a new vertical for the company,” Electrovaya CEO Dr. Raj Das Gupta said in an interview with Electric Autonomy. “Class 8 trucks are huge consumers of diesel, big emitters and have been a challenge to electrify.”

The big hurdles for electric trucks are range and charging time: batteries big enough to haul heavy loads take a long time to charge and fast charging them would require multi-megawatt chargers that just aren’t available.

Janus’s swap system sidesteps the problem.

The first shipments are going to California for drayage operations, where trucks haul containers on short, repeat routes between ports and nearby warehouses. That kind of predictable work is “the low-hanging fruit,” Das Gupta said, noting a single container ship can generate at least 2,000 truck trips.

The advantages of Infinity Battery Technology

Electrovaya uses something it calls, Infinity Battery Technology, which, the company claims, has three core advantages over other batteries, according to Das Gupta. The first is safety: conventional lithium-ion batteries use plastic separators between the positive and negative electrodes that can shrink when overheated, resulting in short circuits and fires. Electrovaya’s separators are more than 90 per cent ceramic by weight.

“That makes the material much more resilient for thermal exposure,” Das Gupta said.

The second is cycle life. Electrovaya’s batteries can do about 15,000 charge cycles before their capacities drop; a typical phone battery can do 1,000 cycles. That high number of cycles matters in a swapping model, where packs may be exchanged several times a day.

“That longevity really does play a role in a lower lifecycle cost,” he said.

The third is power density, which lets the batteries charge faster.

A ‘strategic’ investment

While the Electrovaya investment in Janus is relatively small, Das Gupta calls it “strategic.” Heavy-truck battery swapping has taken off in China, led by CATL, and Electrovaya wants to lead it in North America.

“If you look at their product and the cost structure, the batteries are the vast majority of the cost structure,” he said. “So already we’re somewhat intertwined at that level.”

U.S. production plans

The first Janus systems will be built at Electrovaya’s factory in Mississauga. Longer term, some will come from Electrovaya’s upcoming plant in Jamestown, N.Y., which will make cells, modules and packs and is expected to come online next year. Most of its output is expected to go to energy storage.

Das Gupta said Canada-U.S. political tensions have not affected the project. “We have both flags in front of the buildings” he said, adding that Electrovaya’s real competition is in Asia, especially China.

U.S. tax credits also make scaling production there attractive. “We’ve had a lot more support from the U.S. government than we’ve had from the Canadian side,” he added.

In 2027, Electrovaya expects to deliver batteries for more than 100 Janus vehicles, likely early in the year, with more demand to follow.

“I think it’s just the start,” Das Gupta said. “Trucking has been a difficult piece to electrify, and I think Electrovaya is the right company.”
