text:
This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletters.

By Vivien Ayers, Inside Climate News.

TAYLOR, Texas—A red thresher cuts across the countryside off County Road 401 in Taylor, leaving behind tufts of discarded stalks as farmers prepare to plant seeds for the next year’s harvest.

Less than five miles away, mom-and-pop antique shops open their doors on North Main Street, welcoming residents and tourists alike to glance into the city’s historic past as a 19th-century railroad town known for its cotton fields.

The day has begun in what seems to be, at first blush, an iconic rural town of roughly 17,000.

It was that idyllic picture that drew many of the city’s newer homeowners post-pandemic to the area about 35 miles northeast of Austin, the booming Texas capitol, including Sarah Medina and her family.

“We wanted some land, and so we had looked in different pockets outside of Austin,” said Medina, 38, a creative director for an Austin-based hospitality group who bought land in south Taylor with her husband five-and-a-half years ago. “It just seemed like it was potentially up-and-coming and cool, and had some kind of artsy fun stuff happening. We found some affordable land, so that was really what did it.”

Medina and her husband, Tate Green, a career and technical teacher at the junior high and high school in Coupland about 10 miles south of Taylor, nurtured a garden on about an acre of land, raising pigs, chickens, guinea hens, goats and geese. They built their homestead intending for it to be theirs for the rest of their lives—a place to raise their two kids, continue their careers and eventually retire.

But that vision has been slowly fracturing over the past few years as they’ve faced the impacts of Samsung breaking ground in 2022 on a semiconductor facility, a $17 billion project on a sprawling 1,200-acre campus, around a mile from their house.

“We moved for a small-town feel, for a tighter-knit community, for the ability to afford some land and do some agricultural stuff, and to have space for our kids to run around,” Medina said. “We did not move here to be closer to any kind of tech. It’s not part of the appeal.”

Now, that same county road surrounded by farmers working their land is clogged by delivery trucks, concrete mixers and flatbeds hauling building materials to the Samsung facility site. The beeping of construction equipment echoes across the flatland, with construction visible and audible from Taylor High School and the newly built houses surrounding it less than two miles away.

But Samsung’s arrival was only the beginning of Taylor’s transformation from small town to big tech. Since then, the city has approved the development of three data centers south of the railroad tracks cutting through the city, raising resident concerns about what the constructions mean for the community. Together, the three projects by some estimates would consume 1.42 gigawatts of electricity, enough to power 950,000 Texas homes a year, or about the annual electricity footprint of Austin.

Texas has seen an influx of data center construction over the past few years, with almost 600 separate facilities operating or planned as of September, according to analysis by The Texas Tribune.

Work on the Samsung plant is slated to end as construction on the first of Taylor’s three planned data centers, Blueprint Projects, begins later this year. When built, the 135,000-square-foot data storage and AI processing complex would use 60 megawatts at full capacity.

At the same time, Linde PLC will build a $271 million air separation unit and industrial gas facility for chip making on the site of the Samsung campus. The electronics company is also planning a second facility next to the first, with construction starting by the end of the year, according to a July earnings call.

Taylor gave initial approval to the Blueprint Projects data center in 2024. When it first started releasing information online about the project, residents like Samia Brand, a 39-year-old graphic designer, responded to the posts by questioning water sources for the project and asking what could be done to stop the development. But the city’s unclear responses only weakened trust, she said.

“Even when I had that little conversation on Instagram, I tried to ask my questions and they just recopied and pasted what was already in the post, and I was like, ‘That’s not what I asked, though,’” said Brand, who moved to Taylor shortly before the announcement. “I’m actually trying to get an answer here, and it took a few tries before I did.”

In March, Taylor introduced KDC Project Comal, a $2.5 billion, 360-megawatt hyperscale AI data center campus, which would be built near the Samsung facility, though it requires rezoning before any development can progress.

Then, on Oct. 8, the city authorized a development agreement with Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers, co-owners of the third data center project, now named Taylor Technology Campus but formerly called Project Mustang. The City Council approved the 664-acre property’s annexation into city limits, giving the city jurisdiction over regulation and construction as well as opening the door for construction to begin in 2027. The companies had requested annexation before, but withdrew their request two weeks after the city tabled all discussions mid-August for 90 days.

“It’s something different,” said James Brand, Samia’s husband. “I don’t think it’s what we envisioned when we moved here.”

But one data center, on top of the massive Samsung factory, set in motion a full-blown residents’ opposition movement, now known as the HALT Taylor coalition.

The Deed and the Data Center

The Brands live a few miles away from any of the proposed data center developments, but they still have concerns over health and safety. For other residents like Pamela Griffin, the threat is more imminent. A born-and-raised Taylor native, Griffin, a 58-year-old retired learning center director, lives in her recently rebuilt childhood home in the neighborhood around First and Second avenues and Royal Street, less than half a mile from Blueprint Projects site.

She knew nothing about the proposed data center until she found a flyer on her door last year warning of the planned construction out on vacant acreage several hundred feet behind her home. “We didn’t know what a data center was,” Griffin said. “None of us did.”

She started thinking about the land.

After passage of the Fair Housing Act in 1968, which prohibited discrimination on the basis of race, skin color, religion or nationality when purchasing, renting or financing a home, Griffin’s family was one of many that seized the chance to purchase property in the neighborhood. It was the only place people of color could purchase land in Taylor at the time, she said.

Griffin said he father also purchased a vacant lot in back of the family’s home as a safe space for children to play after the closest city park, opened in 1955 as the first recreational space open to people of color—a former landfill—started sickening children.

The vacant lot bordered 87 acres of undeveloped land owned by the descendants of a prominent 19th-century local businessman and lawmaker, Howard Bland, Sr. Because Griffin and her siblings would often chase baseballs out onto the Bland tract, Griffin said members of the Bland family promised her father and the rest of the community that they would preserve the green space for future generations.

As Griffin started researching the Blueprint Projects, she discovered that the Bland family’s promise about preserving the land was not just an offhand remark. In 1999, his descendants sold the property for $10 to the Texas Parks and Recreation Foundation, with this clause in the grantee’s specifications—“to be held in trust for future use as a parkland by Williamson County.”

Members of the Bland family “told my dad and the rest of the community,” Griffin said, that they were going to give the community the tract as parkland. They did so, she said, “but the city did not let us know.”

The Williamson County Park Foundation acquired the land in 2003 for $10, and held onto it for a little over a month before it transferred ownership to the city of Taylor for the same price. The property deeds state that five years later, the city sold the 87-acre property to the Taylor’s Economic Development Corporation for $15,000 and 39 additional acres, which included 16 acres that would become a proposed buffer zone between the data center site and the nearest neighborhood.

The EDC then held onto the land until April 2025, when it sold the property to the Blueprint Project data center’s parent company, NCP Travis TPP Project, LLC, for $10 million.

The company did not respond to a request for comment.

In all ownership deeds written after the initial sale, the original clause stipulating that the land would be used “in trust” as parkland was excluded.

The city informed residents of buildings and homes located within 200 feet of the property of the construction per state law. But because of the 16-acre buffer zone that changed hands as part of the EDC purchase located between the proposed site and Griffin’s neighborhood, no residents received a notice of the data center’s construction, according to a map the city published.

The city says on the project’s website that it recognizes the first deed notes the property was to be set aside for future parkland, but claims it was not a deed restriction. However, it was enough of a gray area for Griffin and four other residents to file a lawsuit in August 2025 on the basis of land misuse.

Judge Ryan D. Larson of the 395th District Court in Williamson County dismissed the lawsuit in October 2025 on the grounds of the plaintiffs not owning the land or having the direct legal standing to enforce the deed, but did not rule on the deed itself. The plaintiffs filed an appeal that same week and are currently awaiting action.

Griffin’s lawyer, Chris Osborn, said that under Texas law, the original landowners who placed the land in trust for specific use stand in a different position from Griffin and the other plaintiffs in a way that might be enforceable in court if they choose to pursue that avenue. The Bland family is exploring their legal options and supports the neighborhood’s opposition, Griffin said.

“They’re not young people, and they want to live out their lives,” Griffin said. “They don’t want to get in a fight, and that’s hard for old people, because it’s hard for me.”

Fighting Blueprint

In late February 2026, dozens of residents began a campaign gathering signatures for their petition calling for the Taylor City Council to add a measure on the November ballot that would impose a moratorium on all data center development until the city developed a new type of zoning for the construction and regulation of digital infrastructure. It would include data centers, cryptocurrency mining and battery energy storage systems as well.

After gathering 1,400 signatures over 130 days, the HALT Taylor coalition submitted the petition to the City Council on June 11, and the council members discussed it during executive session with no action taken on June 25. Two weeks later, it went before the City Council for approval.

Exactly 15 minutes into the meeting and before residents were able to present public comments on the item, the city uploaded its decision to Facebook with no announcement to those in the council chamber—a move denying the measure’s addition to the ballot because state law “does not allow a city to enact or change its zoning by popular vote,” according to the post.

Instead, the city would continue the plan it had announced June 30 to amend its existing land development code to incorporate digital infrastructure construction and regulation requirements. Citizens would be given the opportunity to comment on the new infrastructure before any requirements were codified, with the city’s current timeline placing the code ratification date in 2027. However, under state law, the new amendments would not apply to already-approved data center developments.

“Our approach focuses on establishing permanent regulations that limit the concentration of data centers and provide long-term environmental protections for our community,” wrote Jerrod Kingery, a spokesperson with the city of Taylor, in a September email statement. “Unlike a temporary moratorium, which would take months to put in place, these proposed regulations could be adopted within the next month and would create a lasting framework for where and how future data centers can be developed.”

The city issued an apology the next day for the “untimely online announcement” and said the council had “no prior knowledge that this announcement would be published at that time.”

If data center development had clearly come to dominate public discourse in Taylor, it exploded at summer’s end when Attorney General Ken Paxton announced an investigation on Sept. 17 into the data center development on the former Bland family land and whether the construction can continue based on the clause in the original deed that it be used as parkland.

If that was found to be a restriction on the deed, the state will take steps to ensure it is not “disregarded,” said Paxton, an embattled Republican who was in the midst of a tight Senate race against Democrat James Talarico in which his past support for data center development had become a hot issue.

Kingery said while Taylor is not a part of the Paxton action, it will take all necessary steps to cooperate with the investigation. The city declined to comment further on the pending litigation.

Griffin, along with fellow Taylor resident and coalition member Carrie D’Anna, traveled to Austin Sept. 24 and submitted a petition to the Office of the Attorney General for the state to request an injunction to stop any development from progressing while the investigation is pending.

“Everybody’s very focused on whose fault and who did it, who was the mayor and who gave it away, and I don’t care,” D’Anna said. “What I care about right now is that there’s a community that is about to be disenfranchised. We’re not even fighting for money—we’re fighting just to maintain the status quo.”

The Future of Taylor’s Environment

All three proposed data center developments are major worries across Taylor, given their proximity to neighborhoods and environmental concerns. The unprecedented construction of the centers creates a fear of the unknown, Medina said, as data centers trigger controversies across the country. In Tennessee, there have been reports of potential emissions from unauthorized gas turbines installed at operating data centers. In Oregon, news reports chronicle the contamination of hundreds of potable water wells.

Property values in Taylor, which have already been hurt by the announcement of the developments, could decrease further once construction starts, D’Anna said, making it harder for homeowners to move away from the area.

Under the new proposed digital infrastructure zoning amendments the city is currently discussing, which wouldn’t impact any of the already approved facilities, the permitted noise from data centers between 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. would be 50 decibels, equivalent to the steady buzz of a refrigerator. The allowed noise production would decrease to 45 decibels at night.

For the neighborhood directly bordering Blueprint Projects, the nonstop hum could impact residents’ health, productivity and sleep, Griffin said.

The Samsung chip factory, KDC Project Comal and Taylor Technology Campus data center all occupy prairie land that has historically been used for agriculture, growing acres of corn, cotton and grain sorghum and supporting the rearing of livestock. While homeowners still own farmland surrounding those projects, they fear the impact of potential runoff or contamination.

While Medina said her family has already downsized the number of livestock they tend, she said they run a small-scale side business, named Little Doe Dairy, selling byproducts from their goats. But animal behavior, such as migratory patterns and mating activity, can be disrupted by persistent sounds starting at 40 decibels, which she worries could impact the business.

Residents also raised concerns about how suitable the land is for a data center. A stream running through the Blueprint Projects property, the Mustang Creek Tributary, is marked as a flood risk on FEMA’s flood map.

In 2015, flash floods damaged 280 homes in the city, with many of those impacted living in Griffin’s neighborhood. While many residents have recovered, others are still worried about how the proposed industrial construction could increase the chances of recurring flash floods.

“Taylor’s in a hole, so all that pollution is going to come into the area,” Griffin said. “We’re going to be sick, literally sick, and then the people say, ‘Well, you can turn around and start suing the city,’ but it’d be too late. We’d be sick.”

Taylor’s data center future remains in limbo, but residents have not given up hope, Griffin said. White signs with a giant red “X” and the words “No data center in our neighborhood” stand in yards opposite the empty land sold by the Bland family for the Blueprint Projects data center—a reminder, Griffin said, of promises made decades ago to future generations.

text:
Dominion Energy saw a 15% year-over-year rise in net income, including a $137 million increase associated with the rate increase its subsidiary Virginia utility recieved in 2025, the company announced during its Friday third-quarter earnings call.

Dominion Energy Virginia also saw a $55 million increase associated with weather, and a $112 million boost from rider equity returns.

Bob Blue, the company’s Chairman, President and CEO, said during the call that Dominion’s year-to-date operating earnings per share “benefited from better-than-budgeted sales, better-than-normal weather, and higher-than-expected 45Z credit income, combined with strong overall financial and operational execution.” 45Z is the Inflation Reduction Act’s technology-neutral clean fuel production tax credit.

Dominion installed 44 of 176 turbines at its Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind project, representing more than 640 MW of generating capacity out of CVOW’s total anticipated 2.6 GW of nameplate capacity, Blue said during the call. He noted that installation of the 45th turbine was happening “now,” and that turbine installation “continues to average approximately two days.”

CVOW is around 85% complete, according to Dominion’s presentation slides, and construction is still on track to conclude by the end of 2027. To date, project investment totals $10.1 billion with $1.5 billion remaining in project costs – $800 million of which will be funded by Dominion.

As state and federal regulators weigh NextEra Energy’s proposal to acquire Dominion, Blue said during the call that he is “looking forward” to the Virginia State Corporation Commission’s first evidentiary hearing on the merger, scheduled for Nov. 17th.

In response to an analyst’s question about the 57 conditions that SCC staff proposed Dominion and NextEra commit to before the commission approve the merger, Blue said, “a chunk of them are conditions that we had already voluntarily proposed, so I think it’s important to keep that in mind.”

“But fundamentally, as you heard from [CEO John Ketchum] on NextEra’s call a week or so ago, we’re still focused on the statutory standard, which is ‘no harm’,” he added. “That’s what the judges are going to follow.” Dominion’s rebuttal to staff and respondent testimony is due Monday.

In response to another analyst question about the proposed merger conditions, Blue declined to go into detail, but said, “We’re going to continue to present what we think is a very strong package through that regulatory process.”

text:
Domestic and unobligated: Centrus intends to expand its enrichment capacity to support “large-scale production of LEU for the existing reactor fleet for baseload electricity, HALEU [high-assay low-enriched uranium] for next-generation reactors, and enrichment for national security needs,” the company said.

Uranium used for national security projects must be unobligated, meaning that it must be produced entirely within the United States without use of foreign equipment or material.

Centrus’s Technology and Manufacturing Center in Oak Ridge is the only plant in the United States building gas centrifuges for commercial uranium enrichment, a detail that would contribute to the uranium enriched with those centrifuges being categorized as unobligated. In contrast, the only commercial enrichment facility currently operating in the United States—Louisiana Energy Services’ facility in Eunice, N.M.—does not produce unobligated uranium; the company is a subsidiary of Urenco USA and is a part of the London-headquartered Urenco Group.

In August, the Government Accountability Office issued a report in which it stated that the National Nuclear Security Administration is supplying national security missions through an existing supply of unobligated uranium that it estimates will last until the 2040s. The supply includes both LEU and HEU; the report noted that while unobligated HALEU could be required for future missions, such a need does not exist now.

Centrus’s domestic supply chain efforts appear to be positioning the company to provide unobligated LEU and HALEU should it be needed. Similarly in January, BWX Technologies announced that it had begun manufacturing gas centrifuges at its Centrifuge Manufacturing Development Facility, also in Oak Ridge, with the goal of enriching unobligated uranium. However, unlike Centrus, BWXT does not plan to enrich uranium for the commercial market.

Expansion plans: Centrus initially announced its plans to invest more than $560 million in expanding production capacity at its Oak Ridge manufacturing plant in January. The announcement followed an award of $900 million from the Department of Energy for Centrus to produce HALEU at its American Centrifuge Plant in Ohio.

To support Centrus’s expanded HALEU production as well as continued production of LEU, centrifuges manufactured at Oak Ridge will be assembled in cascades and added to the cascade already operating at the American Centrifuge Plant. Unlike Centrus’s currently operating cascade, which began producing demonstration quantities of HALEU in 2023, the new cascades will feature centrifuges that contain solely U.S.-made parts, including centrifuge casings and other parts sourced through Centrus’s acquisition of Westerman Holdings.

Patrick Brown, senior vice president of field operations and president of American Centrifuge Operating, noted at the October 29 event that the centrifuge being shipped from Oak Ridge represented the first of thousands that Centrus plans to build. “If anyone's been to the Pike[ton] facility, you see the thousands of holes in the ground,” he said. “We’re gonna fill one today. We have 11,519 to go.”

Centrus expects its new centrifuge cascades to come on line in 2029.

text:
Residential solar has long been sold as a simple way to lower utility bills with cheaper power. But as energy demand surges from data centers, electric vehicles, and industrial facilities, the role of residential storage is shifting. Instead of operating primarily as an emergency backup during storms, batteries are becoming vital tools for managing grid capacity and lowering system costs for entire communities.

During a discussion at pv magazine USA Week 2026, Senior Editor Ryan Kennedy sat down with Jigar Shah to examine the rapid evolution of virtual power plants (VPPs), commercial storage hurdles, and why traditional solar installers must adapt to a battery-first market.

Why grid capacity is the new driver for residential batteries

When homeowners install batteries today, they usually think about keeping the lights on during an outage or working remotely through a storm. However, Shah pointed out that the broader energy transition is driven entirely by capacity needs rather than simple kilowatt-hour offsets.

Rapid load growth from artificial intelligence data centers, EV charging stations, and new manufacturing plants requires shared grid capacity. At the same time, utility data shows that existing electrical infrastructure remains heavily underutilized. Shah noted recent utility reports in Virginia showing that Dominion utilized its grid roughly 40% of the time, while Appalachian Power (APCo) utilized its grid just 14% of the time.

Because local distribution networks often force small businesses and developers to wait years for capacity upgrades, distributed batteries offer immediate relief. In Texas, where batteries now supply 19% of peak demand, wholesale prices have stabilized and data centers have connected smoothly. State pilots like the Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) initiative demonstrate that residential batteries can perform the same stabilizing functions as utility-scale assets.

“The game is now all about capacity, and that’s why residential solar folks need to learn how to do this,” Shah explained.

Navigating virtual power plants and complex business models

While virtual power plants are scaling up, navigating the market remains challenging because regulatory frameworks and utility programs differ wildly across the country. Developers currently fund residential installations through a variety of commercial structures.

For example, companies like Base Power provide free batteries paired with low monthly service fees, monetizing the assets by bidding capacity into wholesale markets like ERCOT or partnering with rural electric co-ops to avoid costly feeder upgrades. On the corporate side, Google’s multi-year capacity contract with Voltus in the PJM market values storage at roughly $500 per kilowatt-hour, giving developers a clear financial return.

These stacked revenue streams allow utilities to manage local feeders and flatten peak loads, which ultimately lowers rates for all consumers. Several regional programs illustrate this growth:

Utah: Rocky Mountain Power’s Wattsmart program covers roughly one-third of a battery’s cost while dispatching units 30 to 130 times annually to offset peaking gas plants.

California: The Demand Side Grid Support (DSGS) program has utilized state funds to compensate dispatchable power during grid emergencies, though funding is set to expire.

Illinois: ComEd launched a program featuring upfront rebates ranging from $250 to $300 per kilowatt-hour, targeting thousands of existing solar homes.

New England: Connected Solutions across Massachusetts and Connecticut continues to provide lucrative upfront rebates alongside ongoing capacity payments.

Distributed versus centralized storage

When comparing distributed residential batteries against centralized transmission-level storage, Shah emphasized the unique multi-layered value of distribution-level assets. While transmission-level storage handles bulk congestion and achieves low costs—often falling below $300 or even $200 per kilowatt-hour using utility-scale tech like Tesla Megapacks—distribution-level batteries solve localized overloads.

If multiple homeowners on a single residential circuit adopt electric vehicles simultaneously, local feeders risk overloading. Deploying batteries on the distribution grid manages local circuits while simultaneously freeing up capacity on the transmission grid. This double-duty functionality makes distributed storage exceptionally valuable.

Why traditional solar installers are falling behind

A major friction point in the current market involves customer acquisition and execution costs. Traditional solar companies often rely on legacy marketing and communication frameworks that target a narrow demographic of homeowners who can afford and host rooftop solar. In contrast, battery-first companies target a broader consumer base with dedicated storage marketing campaigns.

According to Shah, traditional solar dealers face severe structural disadvantages:

Customer Acquisition Costs: Battery-first developers operate at a fraction of the customer acquisition cost seen in traditional solar firms.

Installation Overhead: While legacy solar installers often quote high installation expenses and lack dedicated commission structures for standalone storage, battery-first service providers leverage streamlined installation networks (such as Treehouse or Qmerit) to bring installation costs down significantly.

“I would say the vast majority of solar dealers and solar installers are getting left behind, and you have an entirely new group of people who are battery-only, battery-first installers that are leading the charge,” Shah warned.

Commercial storage, plug-in solar, and vehicle-to-grid integration

Commercial and industrial (C&I) storage has historically lagged behind residential and utility segments due to fragmented equipment options and financing hurdles. Last year saw roughly 2.7 GW of residential storage sales compared to just 150 MW in the C&I sector. Overcoming this lag requires scaling standardized commercial equipment volumes and expanding third-party financing structures like 48E tax credit leases.

Addressing emerging trends like plug-in balcony solar micro-storage, Shah noted that consumer demand is bypassing regulatory friction. “Consumers don’t care. They’re going to go on Amazon, they’re going to buy it, they’re going to plug it in,” he remarked, urging utilities and standards bodies to adopt an open, safety-guided approach rather than attempting a futile prohibition.

On the vehicle integration front, momentum is accelerating rapidly. Automakers are expanding bidirectional capabilities: General Motors has unlocked its existing vehicle fleet for vehicle-to-home (V2H) applications, and Tesla has integrated V2H features into new Model 3 and Model Y variants. Because these vehicular batteries boast capacities ranging from 60 to 125 kilowatt-hours, they will increasingly function alongside standard home battery appliances as part of a synchronized home energy ecosystem.

text:
WASHINGTON — Eight fertilizer manufacturing projects will receive funding through the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Fertilizer Investment & Expansion for Long-Term Domestic Supply Program.

The eight selected projects represent more than $1.34 billion in total proposed investment, including approximately $573 million in proposed USDA funding, to strengthen domestic fertilizer manufacturing, reduce America’s dependence on foreign suppliers and increase long-term fertilizer availability for American farmers.

USDA launched the $500 million FIELDS Program to expand domestic fertilizer manufacturing and address one of the most significant supply chain vulnerabilities facing American agriculture.

The Trump administration is also making additional funding available recovered from projects under the Biden administration’s Fertilizer Production Expansion Program, redirecting taxpayer resources toward projects with stronger financial viability, private-sector investment and measurable manufacturing outcomes.

America’s fertilizer industry has become increasingly consolidated, leaving farmers with fewer suppliers and less competition.

Four companies control approximately 77% of North American nitrogen fertilizer production capacity, two companies account for more than 90% of phosphate production capacity and two companies produce approximately 90% of North America’s potash.

The Trump administration is working to reverse decades of consolidation by supporting new domestic manufacturing capacity and expanding competition for American farmers.

The selected FIELDS projects are expected to help reverse this trend by increasing domestic fertilizer production and strengthening competition.

USDA economic analysis estimates that the additional production could reduce nitrogen fertilizer prices by 4.4% and potash prices by 5.3%, while increasing domestic nitrogen production by 3.7% and potash production by nearly 40% once the projects are operational.

The projects will support new and expanded manufacturing capacity for nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and sulfur fertilizers across the United States. These investments are expected to support approximately 1.08 million tons of annual domestic fertilizer production and capacity across the selected projects.

The eight projects selected to move forward in the FIELDS funding process include:

• TalusAg — Iowa, Kentucky, Minnesota, Tennessee, Nebraska, Illinois and South Dakota: Selected for approximately $99.8 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $270.2 million project to deploy 20 modular ammonia manufacturing units across 11 locations in seven states. Using American energy, air and water, the systems are expected to produce approximately 130,000 tons of anhydrous ammonia annually, bringing domestic fertilizer manufacturing closer to the farmers who depend on it.

• Peace Valley — Florida: Selected for approximately $19.9 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $50.6 million project to expand fertilizer manufacturing in Bartow in central Florida. The project is expected to produce approximately 250,000 tons annually of nitrogen, phosphorus-, potassium- and sulfur-containing fertilizer products.

• PCI Nitrogen — Texas and Oregon: Selected for approximately $100 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $200 million project to modernize fertilizer manufacturing facilities in Pasadena in southeast Texas and St. Helens in northwestern Oregon. The improvements are expected to support approximately 148,280 tons of annual fertilizer production, including ammonium sulfate and urea.

• Intrepid Potash — New Mexico: Selected for approximately $139 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $265 million project to construct a sulfate of potash manufacturing facility near Carlsbad in southeastern New Mexico. The proposed facility would produce approximately 220,000 tons annually and establish an additional domestic source of this important specialty fertilizer.

• AdvanSix — Virginia: Selected for approximately $47.4 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $98.1 million project to modernize and expand an existing ammonia manufacturing facility in Hopewell in southeastern Virginia. The project is expected to produce approximately 84,000 tons of anhydrous ammonia annually.

• SUL4R-PLUS Illinois — Illinois: Selected for approximately $34.9 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $69.7 million project to expand an existing sulfur fertilizer manufacturing facility in Marissa in southwestern Illinois. The project will add a manufacturing line and improve storage and transportation infrastructure to support approximately 100,000 tons of annual sulfur fertilizer production.

• True Organic Products — California, Oregon and Arizona: Selected for approximately $15.3 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $30.6 million project to expand fertilizer manufacturing at facilities in Helm in central California, Boardman in north-central Oregon and Arlington in south-central Arizona. The project is expected to support approximately 142,805 tons of annual fertilizer production using agricultural byproducts.

• Agriculture Project Holdco — Kansas and Indiana: Selected for approximately $116.9 million in proposed USDA funding toward a $360 million project to develop two fertilizer manufacturing facilities in Lewis in south-central Kansas and Fair Oaks in northwest Indiana. The facilities would convert dairy manure into approximately 4,100 tons of liquid ammonium nitrate fertilizer annually, creating additional domestic fertilizer production capacity.

These selections represent an important step in the Trump administration’s strategy to restore American fertilizer manufacturing, encourage private-sector investment, strengthen competition and reduce the nation’s reliance on foreign suppliers of critical agricultural inputs.

Unlike previous federal fertilizer investments that struggled to reach construction and operation, FIELDS emphasizes financially viable, implementation-ready projects with committed private investment, demonstrated market demand and measurable production outcomes.

The FIELDS Program is administered by USDA Rural Development’s Rural Business-Cooperative Service using Commodity Credit Corporation authorities.

title: On economic development, Pritzker, Bailey are miles apart | Capitol News Illinois
description:

text:
SPRINGFIELD — The leading candidates for Illinois governor have contrasting views on how to attract economic development to the state.

Incumbent Gov. JB Pritzker has leaned into his business background during his nearly eight years in office while supporting policies that incentivize companies to relocate to or expand their footprint in Illinois. Republican nominee Darren Bailey, on the other hand, favors a laissez-faire approach focusing on less state spending and lower tax rates.

As he prepares to face voters for a third time, Pritzker often touts the scaled-up incentive programs that have helped land some major projects. He also frequently cites balanced budgets and debt retirement during his tenure as the impetus for the dozen credit rating upgrades Illinois has received, and brags that the state’s gross domestic product climbed north of $1 trillion for the first time.

But Illinois still lags in key economic metrics, most notably trailing the country in real GDP growth. Illinois’ unemployment rate exceeds the national rate and that of all but one bordering state. And while there are signs the state has reversed population loss, it still registers among the slowest growth rates in the country. Its credit rating also remains the worst in the nation.

Pritzker’s opponents have criticized the governor and the supermajority Democrats who control the legislature for enacting policies they say have made the state unfriendly to business.

“He can talk about economic growth, but families and businesses are still moving out,” Bailey said in February following Pritzker’s budget address.

Pritzker acknowledges there’s more work to be done but believes they’re “only scratching the surface of what Illinois’ potential really is.”

“We are growing at a faster rate than we were growing before, and it’s very important to me for us to catch up and beat the average in the United States,” Pritzker told CNI in an interview earlier this month. “But when I came into office, it was going the other direction.”

Illinois’ economy

If Illinois were its own country, it would have a top-20 economy comparable to Saudi Arabia and Switzerland. The nation’s sixth-largest state ranks fifth in real GDP and 12th in real GDP per capita, according to the latest statistics from the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis released in June.

It’s also diverse — no industry comprises more than 13% of its GDP. Illinois benefits from Chicago being a hub for financial and professional services and tourism. And its central location makes it a transportation, logistics and distribution powerhouse. It is also home to world-class universities and research institutions, a large, skilled workforce and robust agricultural sector.

“We have the foundational elements to be one of the most powerful economic engines in the entire world, but potential is no guarantee,” Pritzker said at an Illinois Chamber of Commerce event in September. “Just having potential, we have to actualize it.”

Sluggish population growth, a relatively high tax burden and persistent fiscal challenges due to large pension obligations and a structural budget deficit, among other factors, stand as barriers to unlocking the state’s full economic potential, according to an economic forecast prepared for state lawmakers by Moody’s Analytics.

Per a Moody’s Analytics index, business costs in Illinois are about 1% higher than the national average, with labor costs on par with the rest of the country and energy costs about 5.5% lower than the national average. But the Wall Street firm found the state to have the fourth-worst tax burden.

Private-sector job growth has lagged, increasing just 0.3%, or about 17,000, between January 2019 and September 2026, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. This places Illinois 44th in growth rate.

Bailey has frequently blamed the state’s tax burden, especially property tax rates that rank among the highest in the nation. Bailey also highlighted the state’s corporate tax rate, effectively 9.5%, though he wouldn’t state what it should be reduced to at a recent campaign stop, saying “I don’t know those details.”

He also called for rolling back the recent toll hike on the Illinois Tollway and reducing the state’s gas tax, which is among the highest in the nation.

“People need relief,” Bailey said. “We will be able to function for a few years until we get business back here, people back here and get our economy churning.”

Assessing ‘reputational damage’

Pritzker frequently points to the ship he inherited, noting that Illinois’ fiscal problems were decades in the making.

By the late 2000s, the state had racked up one of the largest unfunded pension liabilities in the country. And state budgets balanced via short-term borrowing and gimmicks were commonplace.

Between 2000 and 2018, the state’s GDP grew at about half the rate of the country as a whole and was 39th among U.S. states. Adding to the mess was a budget impasse between 2015 and 2017 that decimated the state’s already shaky finances.

The state’s unpaid bill backlog ballooned to $16.7 billion, and its credit rating dropped to just one notch above junk status.

“That reputational damage, unfortunately, was very real,” said Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity Director Kristin Richards. “My time in government and my time observing government has allowed me to learn that you can break things really quickly, and it takes a while to repair it.”

While running for office, Pritzker focused on achieving what was once regarded as the bare minimum expectation: balancing the budget. He even took his case to Wall Street, telling bondholders in March 2019 that his priorities were “stabilizing our state government, growing the Illinois economy and protecting working families.”

Budget documents show the state’s operating budget in the black every year of the governor’s tenure besides pandemic-impacted 2020. The governor and lawmakers used post-pandemic surpluses to pay down the state’s bill backlog and build up the previously nonexistent rainy-day fund. Wall Street has responded to those efforts with a dozen credit rating upgrades, which lowers the state’s borrowing costs and signals that it’s a stable place to invest.

Illinois nonetheless maintains the highest unfunded pension liability and the worst credit rating of all 50 states.

Bailey, meanwhile, contends Pritzker is too focused on Wall Street elites and has let state spending grow too quickly.

“We need responsible government who’s going to operate Springfield just like I operate my farm: A business cutting where things need to be cut, putting people in charge of these agencies who are responsible and can actually get things done for the people,” Bailey said.

The state’s budget has grown from $40 billion in Pritzker’s first year to nearly $56 billion in the current fiscal year. It’s a 40% nominal increase, but when adjusted for inflation, it amounts to about 7%. Much of the spending has been earmarked for increasing pension payments, additional K-12 education funding and inflationary increases to health care costs for state employees and Medicaid recipients.

During his tenure, Pritzker and lawmakers have generally held the line on broad-based taxes, opting not to raise the state’s flat income tax rate or sales tax rate.

Pritzker in 2019 signed a doubling of the state’s motor fuel tax to fund infrastructure, and the fuel tax was indexed to grow each year with inflation. And last year, he signed legislation authorizing a toll hike on the Illinois Tollway as part of the public transportation funding and reform deal.

“This egregious toll hike is hurting all of Illinois because every one of those products that go across the tollway have now a 30% increase on the tolls,” Bailey said. “The people in Illinois are going to be paying for that.”

Pritzker in recent years has balanced his budgets with tax hikes around the edges, such as on tobacco products and sports betting. And corporations have seen various deductions and write-offs phased out.

Illinois’ property tax rates still rank among the highest in the nation. Though levied at the local level, state funding levels for schools and other services are a key factor in determining the final bill for homeowners and businesses.

Republicans have said those “tax-and-spend” policies make the state an unaffordable place to live and work.

Pritzker has said, however, that the state needs to balance its budget while still investing in key priorities like health and education.

“We’ve increased education funding across the state of Illinois,” Pritzker said in July. “I want to do more, and we’re not yet where we need to be.”

The role of grants and incentives

Pritzker’s answer for economic development has focused on beefing up the state’s tax credits and incentives to attract business, especially in targeted industries like electric vehicles and quantum computing.

It’s a vast difference from Bailey’s campaign, whose indicated he’d take a fine-toothed comb to state grants.

In 2021, Pritzker signed the Reimagining Energy and Vehicles in Illinois, or REV Act, which aims to attract businesses in the clean energy sector.

He also extended and modified the state’s flagship incentive program, Economic Development for a Growing Economy, or EDGE, to attract investment from quantum computing companies as well as making it easier for smaller companies to utilize.

Pritzker has also prioritized capital investments, earmarking $500 million to help develop a quantum computing campus on Chicago’s South Side, $300 million to prepare the sites of former state facilities for new use and $200 million in grants for site readiness. And billions have been invested in the state’s transportation infrastructure via Rebuild Illinois.

Lawmakers in 2023 also authorized a $400 million closing fund that the Pritzker administration can tap to secure large economic development deals when in stiff competition with other states.

This expanded toolbox has helped land some big fish.

In 2023, the state announced it reached an agreement with Chinese electric vehicle battery maker Gotion to build a new plant in Manteno. In 2024, Rivian announced that it would pause construction on a plant in Georgia and instead produce its R2 truck at its existing Normal facility. Both companies tapped into the closing fund and received REV tax credits.

Republicans have criticized the Gotion deal.

“Democrats delivered hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars to companies with ties to the Chinese Communist Party while forcing Illinois businesses to pay more,” Senate Minority Leader John Curran, R-Downers Grove, said at the time.

The state has inked 30 REV agreements providing more than $1.2 billion in tax credits, according to state records. They could result in the creation of more than 5,700 new jobs and the retention of more than 8,800, according to DCEO.

Between 2019 and 2025, the state has inked nearly 200 EDGE agreements with lifetime credits estimated at more than $378 million. These could result in investments into the billions, the creation of more than 11,800 new jobs, and the retention of more than 11,900, according to DCEO.

A few weeks ago, EDGE recipient Hyundai Translead, a subsidiary of Hyundai that manufactures transportation equipment, announced they were expanding their planned investment in Will County, resulting in 3,750 new jobs, which Pritzker claimed to be the largest single announcement of manufacturing jobs in recent state history.

“It’s been important to me to change the trajectory of our state by attracting companies, attracting jobs, getting more investment in the state, giving us a toolbox to go after those businesses and make sure that we’re competitive,” Pritzker said. “Because I want to beat Texas, I want to beat South Carolina, I want to beat Michigan, and we weren’t doing that before I took office. We are now.”

But there have also been high-profile departures, companies like Boeing, Caterpillar and Citadel moving their headquarters out of state, which Bailey blames on the state’s tax and regulatory structure.

Beyond arming DCEO with new tax credits, Pritzker has reorganized the state agency to offer “white glove” service to prospective and existing companies looking to invest in Illinois. Along with Illinois EDC, the public-private business attraction arm that houses the state’s site selection database, they form what Pritzker officials call “Team Illinois.”

The next step in a third term, Pritzker says, would be codifying the somewhat ad hoc Illinois EDC as the state’s permanent economic development corporation.

“I’m on the phone at least several times a week talking to companies across the world about Illinois and why they should come here,” Pritzker said.

Bailey’s plan

Bailey has pledged to root out wasteful government spending, which he said would allow for a reduction in the size of the budget and tax cuts across the board.

“First and foremost, we’ve got to give people, the working families, relief,” Bailey said. “That comes at the gas pump, that comes when they pay their property tax, that comes when they pay their utility bill. Secondly, by doing some of that, that will attract other people. People want to live here in Illinois.”

The Xenia Republican has long expressed skepticism of incentives as a means of attracting and retaining businesses in the state, likening such deals to “corporate welfare.”

He’s argued during the campaign they’re “corrupt” and “bad economics,” though he did vote in 2022 to extend EDGE as part of a broader $1.8 billion election-year tax relief package. Bailey also voted to authorize the REV Act — though he voted against trailer legislation amending and expanding the program’s parameters.

“The sad reality is Pritzker treats Illinois taxpayers like a blank check, ready to pay for whatever project he fancies, forcing businesses and families to vote with their feet,” Bailey wrote in a WTTW candidate questionnaire.

One of the major pillars of Bailey’s plan is an Illinois version of Elon Musk’s federal Department of Government Efficiency to achieve savings and efficiencies to be led by running mate Aaron Del Mar.

DCEO, which runs the state’s tax credit and incentive programs and administers hundreds of grant programs, could be a top target of such an effort.

text:
FirstLight's Canadian business remains under PSP Investments ownership and becomes Caelo Energy

MONTREAL, Nov. 2, 2026 /CNW/ -- The Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) today announced that it has completed the sale of FirstLight's U.S. operations, including the FirstLight brand, to Hull Street Energy, a private equity firm specializing in power infrastructure and energy transition investments. The U.S. portfolio comprises approximately 1.4 GW of installed capacity across hydroelectric generation, energy storage, and other clean energy assets in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Pennsylvania.

PSP Investments retains ownership of FirstLight's Canadian operations – a combination of legacy Hydromega and H2O Power portfolios – which going forward will operate as Caelo Energy ("Caelo"). Caelo operates 18 hydroelectric facilities across Quebec and Ontario totalling 202 MW of installed capacity and a development pipeline of nearly 1 GW of renewable energy and energy storage projects. FirstLight's Canada-based employees will remain with Caelo Energy.

Caelo Energy will continue to be a best-in-class operator of clean power assets while advancing its development pipeline and pursuing new opportunities in the Canadian power sector. This includes the 57.2 MW Fort Frances solar project in Ontario, which is being developed in partnership with the Lac Des Mille Lacs First Nation and was awarded a 20-year power purchase agreement through Ontario's Long-Term 2 (LT2) procurement process.

Patrick Gut has been appointed Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Caelo Energy, bringing nearly a decade of experience at PSP Investments, where his primary focus was on investment and asset management in the power sector in the Americas and Europe. He has extensive knowledge of the business, having served as Interim President of H2O Power and as a board member of both H2O Power and FirstLight. Patrick also brings broader renewable investment experience through his involvement as a board member for Cubico Sustainable Investments, a developer and operator of renewable energy projects across Western Europe, Latin America and the United States.

"Completing this transaction concludes a successful decade of building FirstLight into a leading North American clean energy business, and we thank the U.S. team for everything they accomplished. In Canada, we are retaining a platform with long-term, inflation-linked operating cash flows, an attractive development pipeline and an experienced team positioned to pursue growth opportunities in Canada," said Andrew Alley, Managing Director and Global Head of Infrastructure Investments at PSP Investments. "Patrick has helped shape this portfolio for years as an investor and a board member, and we have every confidence in him to successfully lead Caelo Energy through this next chapter."

"I am honoured to lead Caelo Energy, and to do so alongside such a skilled and dedicated team who I have come to know well over many years," said Patrick Gut, CEO of Caelo Energy. "We start from a strong foundation – hydroelectric facilities that have served their communities for generations – and we are excited to build on that foundation as we shape Caelo's future. I want to thank PSP Investments for its confidence in Caelo and I am thrilled to continue to play a part in it."

About Caelo Energy

Caelo Energy is a Canadian clean energy company wholly owned by PSP Investments, formed from the combination of the legacy Hydromega and H2O Power businesses. Caelo Energy owns and operates 18 hydroelectric facilities in Quebec and Ontario and is advancing a nearly 1 GW development pipeline of wind, solar, hydro, and battery storage projects. Caelo Energy has offices in Montreal and Oshawa. For more information, visit caeloenergy.com and follow us on LinkedIn.

About PSP Investments

The Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) is one of Canada's largest pension investors with $320.6 billion of net assets under management as of March 31, 2026. It manages a diversified global portfolio composed of investments in capital markets, private equity, real estate, infrastructure, natural resources, and credit investments. Established in 1999, PSP Investments manages and invests amounts transferred to it by the Government of Canada for the pension plans of the federal public service, the Canadian Forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Reserve Force. Headquartered in Ottawa, PSP Investments has its principal business office in Montréal and offices in New York, London and Hong Kong. For more information, visit investpsp.com or follow us on LinkedIn.

title: Bipartisan Senate Bill Fractures Climate Movement - ecoRI News
description:
Republicans want to weaken the Clean Water and National Environmental Policy acts to repave the way for fossil fuel projects.
Whitehouse, the ranking member on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, has heard the criticism coming from environmentalists about the bill.
In fact, some provisions push deregulation so far that they read like a fossil fuel industry wish list,” according to Oil Change International.
