text:
On the last day of September, right before the Senate recessed ahead of the midterm elections, leaders of the Environment and Public Works Committee and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee introduced a 417-page bill that has splintered the climate movement.

While the two-party deal — put together by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., Mike Lee, R-Utah, Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., and Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I. — has been applauded by the fossil fuel industry, many environmentalists are alarmed by what the Democrats conceded.

Zack Porter, executive director and co-founder of Standing Trees, found it “really reckless” of Whitehouse and Heinrich to be supporting this legislation.

“It is so shocking to me that someone who has tried to shape an environmental legacy like Senator Whitehouse would, at the tail end of one of the most extreme right-wing sessions of Congress, sign on to co-sponsor legislation that has the support of the fossil fuel industry,” Porter recently told ecoRI News. “Why now, when in possibly just days left-leaning leaders in Congress might actually have a lot more leverage and could actually craft much better, stronger legislation? This seems like incredibly poorly timed and really kind of out of touch with what is actually needed most right now to advance clean energy to protect our environment.”

Standing Trees is a New England-based nonprofit created to advance policy and legal solutions that protect and restore the region’s native forests.

“It would be a terrible thing for this bill to move forward. This bill is just a smokescreen for some really awful giveaways to industrial developers,” Porter said. “The U.S. was already developing wind and solar at an incredible rate. We had lots of projects in the works until the Trump administration started to scuttle those projects very intentionally over the last 18 months. So much of the problem here is not permitting.”

The hefty Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 is designed to hasten the permitting and construction of power plants, renewable energy projects, transmission lines, and gas (methane) pipelines. The bill does this by diminishing some of the country’s bedrock environmental laws, speeding up the timeline for government agencies to issue permits, and making it harder to cancel projects that have already received federal approval.

The proposed legislation has fractured the climate movement: activists and environmentalists focused on drastically reducing fossil fuel use; renewable energy advocates and policy wonks focused on building cleaner energy infrastructure to decarbonize the economy; and the major environmental organizations that are straddling the public opinion fence.

The bill also defines what the two parties seek. Democrats want to boost renewable energy production. Republicans want to weaken the Clean Water and National Environmental Policy acts to repave the way for fossil fuel projects.

U.S. energy mix

During the first eight months of this year, the combination of wind and solar accounted for 21.1% of U.S. electricity production, with wind at 10.6% and solar at 10.5%, according to the Energy Information Administration. Fossil fuels account for about 56% U.S. electricity generation.

From January to August, wind produced 333,367 gigawatt-hours of electricity and utility-scale and small-scale solar combined to produce 329,119 GWh. Hydropower produced 180,940 GWh (5.7%), biomass produced 29,917 GWh (1%), and geothermal produced 10,766 GWh (0.34%). The electrical output of U.S. gas and nuclear power plants grew more slowly — 2.6% and 1.3%, respectively. Electricity produced by U.S. coal plants fell by 8.7%.

Whitehouse, the ranking member on the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, has heard the criticism coming from environmentalists about the bill.

“It’s very fair for them to have those frustrations. There have been a lot of groups that have been working on environmental issues for a long time, and particularly with the way the Trump administration is behaving,” he recently told ecoRI News. “I think feelings are running very hot, and justifiably so. I think part of the answer is what this bill is, and what this bill is is a gateway to a very different clean energy future than looks plausible right now.”

Bill negotiations began in summer 2025. Last December, Whitehouse and Heinrich walkaway from the table after the administration took action against wind projects off the East Coast and solar projects in the West.

Nearly a year later, negotiations on the complicated bill remain tricky. If enacted, the bill would be the most ambitious effort to streamline infrastructure permitting in modern U.S. history, according to the Institute for Progress.

Whitehouse said the bill’s priority is climate change and to reduce carbon emissions. He noted modeling has shown the bill could reduce greenhouse emissions by gigatons. He said the legislation would create construction jobs and would lower electricity costs “by getting cleaner, cheaper energy out of the grid faster.”

Bill proponents, including Big Oil, say energy permitting reform has been on the congressional agenda for decades. They claim there is widespread understanding that the permitting system created some 50 years ago to protect the natural world against industrial pollution is bad for both the economy and the environment. They also claim delays on polluting projects hold up cleaner energy technologies and conservation projects.

The Senate is expected to take a cloture vote on Nov. 9. But as the bill advances through a lame-duck Congress, amendments are sure to be added.

For the moment, however, the bill essentially reduces what industry labels “red tape” when it comes to building electricity transmission lines; enables quicker grid connections; and lessens social and environmental requirements for many energy projects. Bill supporters claim these changes will enable renewable energy to expand faster and, thus, significantly reduce climate-changing emissions.

The fact the largest U.S. fossil fuel industry trade association is a big fan of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would seem to contradict that claim.

“Washington has a generational opportunity to fundamentally transform a broken permitting system and help address the affordability challenges facing American consumers,” American Petroleum Institute president Mike Sommers said. “President Trump and Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse and Heinrich deserve credit for working across party lines to bring durable reform within reach.”

Sommers noted the legislation would modernize the National Environmental Policy Act, reduce duplicative reviews and unnecessary litigation, and provide greater certainty for critical projects. He also claimed the bill would reduce energy costs.

Porter, of Standing Trees, noted the Washington, D.C.-based organization is simply parroting messaging it created.

“Any claim that permitting is the biggest barrier to bringing down the cost of energy in this country is just basically reading from industry talking points,” he said. “The reason that our federal government hasn’t been approving the projects that we need to transition to a clean energy economy are not because of measures that protect our endangered species or protect public participation in government. Our government agencies have been absolutely gutted in the last decade especially, but going back to the Reagan era. State and federal agencies lack the person power to review projects in a timely manner and do the environmental assessments that need to be done to make sure we get good projects, because the government is serving us not just private interests.”

The American Petroleum Institute supports reducing greenhouse gas emissions through industry-led solutions, such as carbon capture, hydrogen, and lower-carbon fuels.

“Over the past two decades, EPA data show that increasing U.S. oil and natural gas production has coincided with measurable declines in carbon emissions and other pollutants,” according to the trade association’s Climate Policy webpage.

The Interstate Natural Gas Association of America, a North American trade organization that represents interstate natural gas transmission pipeline companies, also backs the controversial legislation.

In a press release supporting the bill, the D.C.-based organization noted natural gas is the “backbone of the American energy system,” and meeting projected demand through 2052 will require more than $1 trillion in new capital investment.

“Greater certainty in the permitting process and more efficient reviews are essential to enabling the buildout of the critical gas pipeline infrastructure needed to meet growing demand,” according to the fossil fuel trade group.

Data center power

Oil Change International, an advocacy organization working to expose the true costs of fossil fuels and to facilitate a just transition to renewable energy, noted the bill relies heavily on the idea that the free market will boost renewables more than fossil fuels.

“But the planned project pipeline for the data center boom suggests that fossil fuels will win out,” according to the D.C.-based nonprofit. It noted data center buildout could potentially increase gas consumption in the U.S. power sector by some 40%. Within the next decade, data centers are projected to consume about 20% of U.S. electricity generation.

Whitehouse said there will likely be natural gas that is developed to power data centers, but believes this legislation will actually slow the growth of this fossil fuel for this purpose.

“There will be less of that under this bill, and, frankly, there will also be less data centers because we oblige data centers in the bill to pay their way with respect to infrastructure costs that they put onto the grid,” he said. “It changes the financial equation for data centers because they will have to bear much more cost. So between the hit to the data centers of having to pay their own way, which they presently do not, and the amping up of clean energy availability for data centers, I think this is actually a data center positive. It’s a data center win for for us. It’s a win for the opponents of data centers. Not a complete win, [but] there will likely be fewer data centers because of the added costs they’ll be obliged to bear.”

Last month Forbes reported that 26 senators, including Whitehouse, had at least $7 million in investments tied directly to data center buildout.

Energy projects often trigger a series of obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and other federal laws that protect endangered species and historical artifacts. Under NEPA, federal agencies must carry out an extensive analysis of a project’s environmental impacts before issuing a permit.

This energy review process frequently leads to litigation. Opponents can file lawsuits against a federal agency years after a review is complete, arguing the review wasn’t comprehensive enough. They can ask courts to halt the project until the agency redoes the analysis. A 2023 study found that 64% of solar projects, 38% of wind projects, and 31% of transmission line projects face NEPA lawsuits.

The legislation would make it more difficult to file this kind of lawsuit. Litigation would need to be brought within 150 days of the end of the NEPA review process, rather than six years.

“After years of work in Congress and many months of negotiations, I’m proud we’ve reached a bipartisan agreement to fix this broken process and get America back to building,” Lee said of the act he co-sponsored.

The Utah Republican opposes federal climate change regulations and has argued that the climate crisis is an engineering and technological problem best solved by human ingenuity rather than government mandates.

As a solution to this global emergency he has offered this:

“The solution to so many of our problems, at all times and in all places, is to fall in love, get married, and have some kids. Problems of human imagination are not solved by more laws, they’re solved by more humans. More people mean bigger markets for more innovation. More babies mean forward-looking adults, the sort we need to tackle long-term, large-scale problems.”

The chair of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee has routinely championed efforts to open public land for fossil fuel extraction and mining. He wants the federal government to sell off several million acres of public land in Utah, Colorado, and other western states to corporate interests.

Porter noted Lee’s involvement in the legislation is a clear sign the natural world is in trouble.

“The first hint that this bill is bad for public lands comes in the form of one of the other three leading sponsors of the legislation, Mike Lee of Utah,” the Boston native said. “Senator Lee is the most anti-public lands lawmaker in Congress, and it’s a bad look to be teaming up on legislation that would have impacts on public lands and on a whole lot of other aspects of our environment and energy.”

Beyond the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act, Porter said the bill also targets the Endangered Species Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

“This bill was given a very nice-sounding name of American Affordability and Jobs Act. A classic smokescreen covering up what’s actually going on in the legislation,” he said. “The bill would actually create more barriers to public participation and government decision-making and would impact tribes’ ability to consult on projects.”

Whitehouse said the bill doesn’t gut protections in current environmental laws, nor stifle public participation.

“There’s quite a lot of misunderstanding out there. About the bill and about what it does and about how it compares,” the Rhode Island Democrat said. “One example is people keep telling me that we shut down Section 106 under the Historic Preservation Act. Well, we actually don’t. It continues, and the consultation process we actually bake into law because the old bill really doesn’t have much clarity about the government’s obligations to consult. So, what the Trump administration has been doing is disassembling the consultation process by regulation entirely, and we’ve put in a backstop that prevents that.

“The price of stopping the destruction of the consultation process was that we had to accelerate the timeline of the consultation process. You know, you got to appreciate that there was going to be no consultation process going forward if the Trump administration continued to have its way. That’s what we were negotiating against.”

The bill’s other Republican co-sponsor, Capito, believes it fixes a broken system.

“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth,” she said.

The senator from West Virginia questions the extent of human activity versus natural variation when it comes to climate change and wonders whether specific severe weather events can be directly attributed to global warming.

The chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee has worked with the current administration to “roll back several of the untenable regulations put forth during the Obama administration’s War on Coal that has reemerged under President Biden.” She favors carbon capture technology and supports opening more public land to fossil fuel exploration and extraction.

While the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would limit Clean Water Act Section 401 reviews to water quality impacts associated with discharge, would limit the ability of litigation to halt construction, and would significantly reduce the timeframe for legal challenges, Heinrich believes the bill creates a better energy future.

“We have an enormous opportunity to build big things again to meet this moment — to build more generation, expand our grid, create more jobs, lower energy costs, and make sure we have the energy we need to compete,” the ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee said. “It should not take decades to build the infrastructure our country needs. Our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help us get to ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on energy projects faster, while protecting important environmental safeguards and protecting the ability of Tribes to formally consult during these processes. It will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require — not leave that bill to American families. Our bill puts teeth behind that principle.”

Environmental advocates note the law would remove bureaucratic barriers regardless of energy technology. Given the stranglehold the fossil fuel industry has on U.S. energy production, they believe the law would disproportionately lock in gas-fired power generation, despite what the bill may promise.

“As written, the bill will also cripple federal and state governments’ ability to protect communities and to take important actions to limit climate change in the future. In fact, some provisions push deregulation so far that they read like a fossil fuel industry wish list,” according to Oil Change International. “In short, the bill could end any meaningful regulation of the fossil fuel industry, whether to achieve climate goals or protect air or water quality.”

In a six-page letter to four Democratic leaders, including Heinrich and Whitehouse, 113 organizations expressed their strong opposition to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. They said the legislation “throws aside the massive public lands recreation economy driven by hundreds of millions of people around the United States and the world in favor of a small number of powerful corporations and their profits.”

“This ‘permitting reform’ package will eviscerate public lands protections, prevent the public’s ability to protect themselves from harmful projects, cede management decisions to fossil fuel polluters, restrict Tribal consultation and cultural resource protections, limit judicial review, and further enable foreign-owned mining companies to seize public lands,” they wrote.

Several big-name environmental organizations, including the Sierra Club, the National Audubon Society, The Nature Conservancy, the Environmental Defense Fund, and the Natural Resources Defense Council, didn’t sign the Oct. 22 letter.

The Rhode Island chapter of The Nature Conversancy told ecoRI News TNC’s North America policy team is “actively working on these issues and continuing to review the bill as it evolves.”

The email included a quote from Kameran Onley, TNC’s managing director for North America policy and government relations.

“We appreciate the enormous effort that went into developing the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act. This bill deals with some serious challenges facing America that are important to get right. The Nature Conservancy believes that modernizing our permitting processes can help us move faster in building critical infrastructure and protect people and nature. We can and must do both.

“While we are still analyzing the many details of the bill, we see some promising improvements and hard compromises. We are encouraged to see the bipartisan effort to deliver needed updates to permitting. The Nature Conservancy will continue to work with our partners and members of Congress to see that respect for Tribal sovereignty, local communities and conservation are reflected as the legislative process moves forward.”

The Audubon Society of Rhode Island, which isn’t affiliated with the National Audubon Society, believes the bill has the potential to improve the laws around electricity and transmission. It said important protections for renewable energy projects and improved and connected energy infrastructure “are all real possibilities with this bill.”

The Smithfield-based nonprofit, though, is concerned with the changes the bill makes to the National Environmental Policy Act, Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act, saying the removal of “federal, uniform standards for these protections will be detrimental for historic lands, natural resources, and wildlife.”

“Amid continued attacks on wildlife protections and clean energy progress by this current administration, we acknowledge what our environmental champions in the legislature are trying to put forward,” Maxwell McFarland, Audubon Society of Rhode Island’s director of advocacy, wrote in an email to ecoRI News. “This energy transformation would certainly decrease the nation’s emissions output, combatting negative externalities such as reduced wildlife ranges, public health concerns, and rising sea levels.”

He continued with a caveat.

“However, the bill as currently constructed will prevent this ideal from becoming reality. It does not reinstate the rollbacks already made in environmental protection by this administration. Rather, it creates an opportunity for more ground to be ceded in the wrong direction,” he wrote. “Under this legislation, minimal discernment would be made between renewable or fossil fuel energy projects. Polluting projects will then have the potential to bypass rigorous, science-based review and permitting.”

McFarland noted progress on renewable energy deployment and environmental protection relies on “stringent guardrails and strategic initiatives” and shouldn’t include conceding important environmental protections.

The Citizens’ Climate Lobby noted it “is proud to endorse the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.” The U.S. Chamber of Commerce “strongly supports” the legislation.

“This is a great bill, and it’s a huge step in the right direction,” Ray Long, the president of ACORE, a trade group representing the solar and wind industry, told Grist. “We need to really put this in reality. We need to build a ton of stuff over the next four years, or else we’re gonna have higher [electricity] prices.”

In a two-page document opposing the legislation, the Center for Biological Diversity, which also signed the group letter, wrote that the act “is not meaningful permitting reform, but rather an extensive rollback of environmental laws that prioritizes fossil fuel companies.”

Partnership for Policy Integrity, a Massachusetts-based nonprofit that specializes in energy and climate policy, wants to know why two Democratic senators “would cut a backroom deal that guts environmental protections and silences community voices for the overwhelming benefit of the fossil fuel industry and data center developers?”

“Big Tech is staking its dominance on BAAJA [Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act], and a massive gas- and nuclear-powered build out of data centers for their expansion boom,” according to an Oct. 27 press release from the Pelham, Mass., organization. “They want to dominate the future, and they are willing to sacrifice our climate and public lands for their own pocketbooks.”

In a 2,793-word piece about the bill, Jim Pattiz, co-founder of More Than Just Parks, methodically outlined his concerns about the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

This is his lede:

“For years, the extraction industry has spent fortunes selling Americans a simple lie, that the laws protecting our land and water are the reason this country can’t build anything. It planted that lie in opinion pages across the political spectrum until it hardened into conventional wisdom, and this fall it finally paid off. Two of the Senate’s most prominent Democrats on public lands and climate have bought it whole, and they’re about to hand the results to Donald Trump.”

A few paragraphs further into the piece, Pattiz called the bill “a wholesale assault on the foundation of American environmental law.”

“Today, when an agency breaks the law to approve a pipeline or a mine, a judge can halt the project until the agency does its job,” he wrote. “Under this bill, the judge can no longer stop the project. The bill’s text says the ‘only remedy the court may order’ is to send the paperwork back to the agency ‘without vacatur or issuance of an injunction,’ and the bulldozers keep running while the agency fixes it.”

He said the “rigging starts long before anything reaches a judge.” The National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, which President Nixon signed after it passed the Senate without a single dissenting vote, requires federal agencies to study what a major project will do to the land and water around it and tell the public before any action is taken.

“This bill lets agencies disregard any science published after a review begins,” Pattiz wrote, “and it requires them to throw out any alternative that doesn’t ‘meet the goals’ of the company asking for the permit. In other words, the company decides which options the government is even allowed to consider.”

He reported that once the current administration approves a pipeline, a mine or a gas export terminal, a future president who tries to stop it could force taxpayers to pay the developer a quarter to half of everything it has already spent.

“If a future administration slows approvals for an industry compared with the previous five years, which would be nearly all Trump’s years, developers could collect up to the full expected cost of construction in damages,” Pattiz wrote. “The bill measures what counts as ‘fair treatment’ against the most extraction-friendly administration in history, and then it makes you pay the industry if a future government dares to do better.”

Despite significant environmental opposition to the legislation, the Bipartisan Policy Center has called the bill “a huge step forward.”

“While most stakeholders will find something in it that they do not like, it is also the case that most will find that what they like about the legislation outweighs what they do not,” according to the D.C.-based nonprofit. “The bill is a true compromise, one in which both Democrats and Republicans can claim big wins, and one in which the end result will be reduced costs for Americans, increased quality of life, improved energy security and reliability, better environmental outcomes, and reduced emissions.”

Many environmental advocates don’t agree. They see it as caving to administration threats to undue renewable energy progress.

The Trump administration has sought to halt the development of several offshore wind projects and some three dozen land-based wind projects. It has even resorted to paying companies to relinquish their offshore leases and to instead invest in oil and gas projects.

Last month the administration took action — short of interfering with existing permits or stopping construction — to rescind approval for Revolution Wind, off the coast of Rhode Island, as it nears completion. The project’s 65th and final turbine was installed in September, and developers say the project is on track to begin producing its 704-megawatt output by the end of this year.

The administration has also spent the past two years repealing federal climate policy.

“We say we don’t want to be caught up in these global fossil fuel energy markets anymore, but that’s the opposite of what this administration has done,” Porter said. “They’ve locked us into those markets that are now even more vulnerable.”

He noted a continued transition to renewable energy doesn’t require the gutting of laws that protect endangered species, wildlife habitat, public health, and public involvement.

“This is a bill that is sending us off the cliff at a moment when we should really be pressing pause and being much more careful about how we move forward,” Porter said.

title: Estimating the US Energy System Impacts of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act
description:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is currently under consideration in the US Senate.
Our results reflect the additional impacts of the BAAJA provisions beyond a baseline of current policy without BAAJA.
FAST-41, passed as part of surface transportation reauthorization in 2015, created new streamlined ways of doing federal permitting by creating the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council, project-specific permitting timetables, and a public dashboard to track project changes.
Unpacking the impacts of BAAJA BAAJA is a sprawling, 417-page bill that touches many aspects of federal permitting.
We will also closely monitor the transmission provisions of the bill as they yield the largest system impacts in our modeling.
text:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is currently under consideration in the US Senate. If passed, the bill makes substantial changes to federal environmental permitting laws and how electric power transmission lines are planned, permitted, and paid for. Here we’ve modeled key components of the initial version of BAAJA, introduced on September 30, focused on reducing barriers to building linear infrastructure (i.e., transmission lines and gas pipelines) and on protecting ratepayers from higher grid costs due to AI data center buildout. Our results reflect the additional impacts of the BAAJA provisions beyond a baseline of current policy without BAAJA. We project that the combined impact of these provisions would reduce household electricity bills by $50-78 per year in 2040 compared to without BAAJA, both because easier permitting would allow lower-cost resources to connect to the grid and because the bill explicitly prohibits charging non-data center customers for data center costs. The transmission provisions of the bill enable accelerated average interregional transmission build rates nearly triple that of the last decade or more and drive an additional 17-249 GW of clean resources to be built through 2040. The bill as a whole increases liquefied natural gas (LNG) export levels by 8-15% beyond a 76-145% increase already happening under current policy. Taken together, these provisions uniformly reduce economywide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by 5-148 million metric tons annually in 2040 and as much as 1.5 gigatons cumulatively, compared to without BAAJA.

An opportunity to act on federal permitting

The US Senate is soon scheduled to take up floor action on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a sweeping set of federal permitting reforms negotiated over many months by the Republican chairs and Democratic ranking members of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee (Senators Shelley Moore Capito and Sheldon Whitehouse) and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (Senators Mike Lee and Martin Heinrich). In this note, we provide estimates of the energy system, consumer, and emissions impacts of key components of BAAJA as it was introduced in late September.

A (very) brief history of permitting reform efforts

Historically speaking, Congress rarely acts to change federal permitting rules. The last piece of legislation that made major changes to federal permitting was the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (EPAct 2005), which passed by wide bipartisan margins. EPAct 2005 expanded federal authority over energy permitting by giving the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) greater transmission siting power, increasing federal coordination on energy projects, and shortening National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review timelines for certain projects.

Smaller tweaks since EPAct

Since EPAct 2005, Congress has made marginal additional advances to revise federal permitting frameworks. FAST-41, passed as part of surface transportation reauthorization in 2015, created new streamlined ways of doing federal permitting by creating the Federal Permitting Improvement Steering Council, project-specific permitting timetables, and a public dashboard to track project changes. The Fiscal Responsibility Act (FRA), passed in 2023, streamlined NEPA by narrowing the circumstances that trigger a review, setting time and documentation limits in submissions, and requiring a lead agency in multi-agency reviews.

Recent reform attempts

There are several recent examples of unsuccessful efforts to make major permitting reforms. Senator Joe Manchin (I-WV) introduced his Energy Independence and Security Act of 2022 after Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act. The Senate voted on the bill as an amendment to the annual defense spending bill in December 2022, but it failed to pass. Manchin took another bite at the apple with the Energy Permitting Reform Act of 2024 (EPRA), cosponsored with then Senate Energy and Natural Resources ranking member John Barrasso (R-WY). The bill advanced out of their committee on a bipartisan 15-4 vote but was not taken up on the floor.

Why reform is needed

It takes a long time to build large-scale infrastructure in the United States. A major federally funded water or highway project can take 8-10 years to build on average, while a high-voltage interstate transmission line takes 10 years on average, if it gets built at all. To be sure, these are generally large-scale, complicated, capital-intensive projects, and so planning for and executing on them should be done deliberately. But reform can make a difference—Germany has sharply increased transmission approvals since streamlining its permitting process. In 2025, its federal grid regulator approved 45% more kilometers of high-voltage lines than the year before.

One of the key complaints about the status quo is that the system of federal rules and regulations that the US has put in place over the past 70 years hampers the country’s ability to build infrastructure rapidly. Complex interagency permitting processes, years (or decades) of review without clear timelines, and substantial litigation risk once federal agencies do make a decision all increase the cost of building and dampen developer enthusiasm for large projects.

The need for speed

Over the past few decades in the energy space, the US has been able to muddle through despite these limitations, largely due to the fact that electricity demand growth has been exceptionally low since the 2000s. Put another way, the US power sector hasn’t needed to build much stuff—replace some retiring coal power plants with gas and renewables, struggle to maintain the poles and wires that comprise the backbone of the electric grid, and hold the whole enterprise together with the grid equivalents of duct tape and baling wire.

Today, the US outlook for load growth is fundamentally different. To meet growing electricity demand, whether from AI data centers or electric vehicles, heat pumps, and other electrified end uses, the US needs to build new energy infrastructure at a pace far faster and on a much larger scale than at any time this century. Constraints on building new generators and transmission lines are already slowing energy deployment and will remain a critical bottleneck to meeting future demand with clean power absent reform. As of the end of 2025, more than 2 TW of generation and storage capacity were seeking grid interconnection in the US, and renewable sources and storage represented 85% of this stranded capacity. Clearer interconnection processes and better regional grid planning can unlock this capacity.

The US also has an abysmal recent record of building high-voltage transmission lines, with 2021-2024 representing the four slowest years of construction since at least 2010. Beyond lowering emissions by connecting clean energy to the grid, transmission has the potential to improve grid reliability and lower electricity prices. Despite its benefits, interstate transmission faces barriers to deployment primarily due to a lack of a uniform nationwide permitting process, robust planning requirements, and clear cost allocation rules. Interstate transmission is currently not treated the same way as other interstate infrastructure, like pipelines. Historical data show that Environmental Impact Statements (EIS), the most detailed and time-consuming level of review under NEPA, take more than twice as long for transmission as for pipelines. The median transmission project takes about 34 months to complete EIS review, compared with the median pipeline project taking just 15 months (Figure 1). Furthermore, longer transmission lines (such as those connecting renewable generation) are correlated with even longer EIS reviews.

These challenges are becoming increasingly urgent as load growth intensifies pressure on an already aging, constrained grid and exposes the limitations of the current federal energy infrastructure development process. Without changes to the permitting system, lengthy review timelines risk further delaying the expansion of the energy infrastructure needed to connect new generation and move power across regions.

Unpacking the impacts of BAAJA

BAAJA is a sprawling, 417-page bill that touches many aspects of federal permitting. Describing every change the bill makes is beyond the scope of a short note. The Bipartisan Policy Center has an explainer article that unpacks nearly every section of the bill, and a recent Volts podcast episode with Daniel Palken takes a deeper dive into many of the provisions. We categorize the bill’s changes into five major categories:

Transmission: BAAJA simplifies the federal backstop siting authorities for interstate transmission lines, institutes new interregional planning requirements and codifies existing regional planning requirements, creates new cost allocation rules for transmission, and creates a new consolidated interconnection planning process. The bill also requires deployment of advanced transmission technologies, the use of AI for interconnection queues, and it improves market access for virtual power plants (VPP). Finally, the bill includes an ambitious attempt to require data centers to pay for the costs they impose on the grid and prohibits shifting those costs to other customers.

National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) and judicial review: BAAJA narrows the definition of a “major federal action” to limit what requires NEPA review, establishes deadlines for environmental reviews and decisions beyond what was required in the 2023 FRA, alters standing for who can sue under NEPA and changes the statute of limitations for such suits to 150 days, and reduces the available remedy when finding against the federal government to remand without vacatur.

National Historic Preservation Act (NHPA): In the realm of NHPA, BAAJA narrows what gets reviewed under the statute and excludes non-federal portions of projects from inclusion in the “area of potential effects” that NHPA studies. It also adds deadlines for key steps of the NHPA process and changes how state and tribal consultation is concluded.

Other environmental statutes: BAAJA limits Clean Water Act §401 state review to specific water quality requirements, establishes firm timelines for such reviews, and makes changes to §404 dredge and fill permitting processes. It also shortens Endangered Species Act (ESA) timelines and allows states to assume §7 consultation responsibilities in certain circumstances.

Permit certainty: Sections 1401 and 1402 of the bill take novel approaches to attempt to limit executive branch interference with the federal permitting process. BAAJA limits an agency’s ability to revoke already-issued permits and enables project developers to sue if they can prove that disparate permitting treatment for their class of facilities led to an improper denial or unreasonable delay in permit issuance. The bill also authorizes substantial damage payments if either of these permit-certainty provisions is violated. There is currently a robust debate around the scope of what these provisions would enable and prevent.

This is far from an exhaustive list. The bill also contains a long list of geothermal provisions that will be quite helpful to that burgeoning industry, deals with various staffing and funding issues, and makes a number of other nitty-gritty changes to the way the federal government approaches permitting. In addition, modeled emissions impacts capture only part of the broader range of potential impacts of BAAJA. These provisions have implications for water quality and other environmental metrics and tribal and community consultation that are beyond the scope of this analysis.

How we model the bill

Many of the provisions discussed above are difficult to model in an economy-wide energy system model like RHG-NEMS, the core tool we use for analyzing the US energy system. We’ve narrowed our analysis to focus on the provisions where interpretation of the bill is clear and which are most likely to affect the evolution of the energy system: provisions that enable the build-out of linear infrastructure like transmission lines and gas pipelines. In our modeling, we reduce the cost and speed of the pace of building interregional transmission lines and spur lines that connect generators to the grid, we reduce barriers in the existing interconnection process, and we similarly reduce the cost and accelerate the speed of building interregional natural gas pipelines. We also model the ratepayer protection provisions of the bill by doing separate model runs with and without expected demand growth from data centers and allocate all incremental costs of meeting that load growth to data centers.

Critically, our preliminary modeling does not include an attempt to reflect the permit certainty provisions of the bill. There is currently considerable uncertainty in the interpretation of these sections of the bill, which may be resolved by the amendment process. If so, we will attempt to incorporate those impacts in future rounds of modeling. We also do not currently model the geothermal, advanced transmission technology, or VPP market access provisions of the bill. RHG-NEMS also doesn’t allow us to model local congestion reduction benefits of the transmission title of the bill. Taken together, we would anticipate these non-modeled provisions (apart from permit certainty) to result in more cost reductions in a faster time period and even greater emission reductions; as such, the results we discuss in this note are conservative estimates of impacts.

Capturing future energy market uncertainty

The other source of uncertainty is how future energy market and technology cost trends will evolve over time. Following the approach we use in our Taking Stock reports, we estimate the impact of this bill under three scenarios reflecting different future market and technology conditions. Our low-emissions scenario pairs continued meaningful cost declines for clean technologies with more expensive fossil fuel prices. Our high-emissions scenario assumes the opposite: much less reduction in the cost of clean resources paired with very low prices for fossil fuels. We also present a mid-emissions scenario that is a middle ground between these two extremes. Our deterministic modeling approach doesn’t enable us to put probabilities on the likelihood of any of these outcomes. The low and high-emissions scenarios represent bounding scenarios constructed using our best judgment. We also discuss the impacts of the bill in a scenario with very fast growth in data center electricity demand later in the note. Across all scenarios, we hold all other current policy constant, which includes reflecting clean energy tax credits as modified in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and removing a number of EPA regulations like the GHG standards for power plants and oil and gas methane standards.

BAAJA reduces electricity bills and emissions and enables a more robust grid

The provisions of BAAJA that we modeled deliver consistent results: lower electricity rates and bills, more capacity added to the grid, and lower emissions. The magnitude of those impacts depends on the underlying market and technology conditions, as we illustrate across our low, mid, and high-emissions scenarios.

BAAJA lowers residential electricity prices and reduces household electricity bills

In 2040, BAAJA drives electricity prices down, in inflation-adjusted terms, by 0.5-1.0 cents per kilowatt-hour, a 3-5% reduction compared with prices without BAAJA. This translates into average annual household electricity bills that are $50-78 lower in 2040 than without BAAJA (Figure 2). BAAJA achieves this outcome through two different mechanisms. First, the provisions of the bill that enable more build-out of linear infrastructure, especially electric power transmission, result in lower prices. Second, the ratepayer provisions prevent data center-related costs from being imposed on residential ratepayers. The first mechanism improves access to lower-cost and more efficient generating resources, lowering demand for natural gas as a fuel input, thereby lowering its price, and enabling the sharing of resources across regions for reliability purposes. This effect drives 61%, 4%, and 50% of the price decline in the low, mid, and high emissions scenarios in 2040, respectively. The ratepayer protection provisions require utility regulators to attribute the cost impacts of meeting increased demand from large computational loads (i.e., large AI data centers) only to those customers on the grid, preventing subsidization of those costs by residential ratepayers and other customer classes.

BAAJA provisions may both enable and discourage grid-connected data centers. As discussed above, the transmission and interconnection provisions make it easier and faster to bring more generators onto the grid to meet growing demand from data centers and to get that electricity to sources of load. At the same time, the ratepayer protection provisions of the bill likely increase the cost of that grid-connected power by apportioning all incremental costs incurred in order to meet data center demand to those data centers. If fully implemented in this fashion, we estimate it would result in an 88-102% increase in the retail price for electricity that data centers pay for their grid-connected power. Using EpochAI’s total cost of ownership model, we estimate that translates into a 10-11% increase in total annualized capital and operating costs for a 1 GW data center. There are substantial advantages to data center developers for pursuing on-grid power beyond the emissions impacts, including better reliability, less direct exposure to fuel price fluctuations, potentially lower energy costs than off-grid power depending on the technology and configuration, and potential improvements in social license to operate. Predicting the extent to which this basket of advantages justifies a 10% increase in costs is beyond the scope of this analysis.

The road to reform runs through the lame duck

Capitol Hill watchers expect the Senate to take a cloture vote on or around November 9 upon their return from the election recess. An affirmative vote is required for the bill to move to the Senate floor. Assuming bill sponsors can muster the 60 votes needed to invoke cloture, there will be some period of debate and amendments, including a much-anticipated manager’s amendment that will make technical corrections to the initial draft of the bill that was released on September 30. If the bill passes in the Senate, it will proceed to the House for a vote before landing on President Trump’s desk for signature.

We will be watching a few key issues that could have implications for the energy system, consumer, and emissions impacts of the bill as the legislative text proceeds through this process. Chief among these are any changes to improve the clarity of the permit certainty provisions in sections 1401 and 1402 of the bill. There is currently robust debate around the scope of what these sections will or won’t do. With greater detail, we hope to incorporate permit certainty into our overall modeling. We will also closely monitor the transmission provisions of the bill as they yield the largest system impacts in our modeling. We will also keep an eye on any evolution in the ratepayer protection provisions of the bill, some of which take a pretty novel approach to cost allocation that could carry implementation challenges without changes.

The clock is ticking. There are 16 and 18 legislative days in the House and Senate, respectively, for the lame duck session that lies ahead. If the bill doesn’t pass, then the process begins anew in January with a new Congress and new members in leadership positions—likely with different priorities. We will soon learn the fate of the latest attempt at major federal permitting reform.

This nonpartisan, independent research was conducted with support from CleanEcon. An earlier version of this analysis was conducted with support from the Bipartisan Policy Center. The results presented reflect the views of the authors and not necessarily those of the supporting organization.

About Janus Electric Janus Electric Holdings Limited (ASX: JNS) is a global electrification company focused on converting Class 6–8 heavy diesel trucks to electric using its proprietary modular battery swap and conversion platform.

text:
Janus Electric Holdings Limited (ASX: JNS) (Janus Electric, Janus or the Company) is pleased to announce that California-based King Fio Trucking has placed a repeat order for six Class 8 electric truck conversions and six JBS-650 swappable battery sets, increasing its total commitment to 12 trucks and 14 battery sets.

The Company expects to deliver 18 operational trucks in LA before 31 December which will include the first six King Fio Trucks, four for Ability Tri-Modal, and six for Tradelink. This will bring the operational vehicle total to 46 across the US and Australia. The company is working closely with key supply chain partners to put in place the facilities to convert the previously announced North American order book by early Q4 FY2027.

The additional order has a gross value of approximately A$3.1m, is conditional upon approval of the applicable California incentives and will be fulfilled by Janus' US conversion partner, Electric Vehicle Choice (EVC), in Santa Fe Springs, California.

King Fio operates container transport services associated with the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The six additional trucks will use the charging and battery-swapping infrastructure included in King Fio's original order, comprising a Janus Charge and Change Station (JCCS) with two 250 kW chargers, avoiding the need for an additional charging station.

The additional vehicles are also expected to generate recurring subscription revenue for Janus as they are delivered.

Government incentives and customer economics for King Fio

The additional King Fio order is expected to benefit from several California and regional vehicle electrification incentive programs. Together, these programs could provide King Fio with US$1.6m in funding for the six additional trucks, subject to eligibility, funding availability and approval.

Further incentive programs available to Janus customers

Janus' diesel-to-electric conversion technology enables operators to retain and repower their existing trucks, creating opportunities to access incentive programs that support vehicle repowering as well as broader zero-emission vehicle initiatives.

The company is assessing further conversion-eligible programs in Washington State and Canada, including Canada's Federal Green Freight Program, while new drayage programs announced by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey could support entry to the US East Coast market.

Janus Electric Managing Director and CEO, Ben Hutt said:

"King Fio's decision to double its order is another strong endorsement from our existing customers of our technology and demonstrates continued demand for our electric truck conversion and battery-swapping solution.

"Importantly, the additional trucks will use the charging and battery-swapping infrastructure included in King Fio's original order, demonstrating the scalability of our model and how fleet operators can expand fleets without having to duplicate charging facilities."

This announcement has been authorised for release to ASX by the Board of Janus Electric Holdings Limited.

About Janus Electric

Janus Electric Holdings Limited (ASX: JNS) is a global electrification company focused on converting Class 6–8 heavy diesel trucks to electric using its proprietary modular battery swap and conversion platform. The Company's integrated solution comprises the Janus Conversion Module (JCM), swappable battery systems, and the Janus Charge & Change Station (JCCS), providing fleet operators with an electrification pathway that delivers near-zero downtime and total cost of ownership savings. Janus operates across Australia, the United States, Canada, and other markets, with commercial deployments underway and a growing pipeline of fleet operator, infrastructure, and government partnerships.

About King Fio Trucking

King Fio Trucking is a California-based transport and logistics company headquartered in Long Beach. The company provides local and long-distance container drayage, transloading and warehousing services, operating a fleet of approximately 30 trucks and servicing 30 terminals. King Fio supports freight movements through the Southern California port and logistics network.

For more information, visit: https://kingfiotrucking.com/

title: AI and Responsible Investing: Risks and Opportunities | Davy
description:
As AI becomes increasingly embedded in economic activity and decision-making, effective governance will be essential to maximising its benefits while managing associated risks.
AI is rapidly becoming a core responsible investment theme, requiring investors to assess not only the investment and economic opportunities, but also its environmental footprint, social impact and governance standards.
The need for AI oversight is driven by several well-documented risks, one of which is bias and discrimination.
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) AI Principles and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence both highlight fairness and non-discrimination as key principles for the responsible development of AI.
Ensuring broad and equitable access to the benefits of AI may prove just as important as the technological breakthroughs themselves.
text:
The geopolitical landscape has shifted significantly in recent years as the world has moved from a multilateral, globalised order towards a more multipolar and fragmented regime, where national interests and strategic autonomy have come to the fore. This transition is reshaping trade relationships, supply chains, energy policy and security priorities, while increasing competition for critical resources, technologies and strategic influence. As a result, new responsible investment considerations are emerging, requiring investors to balance traditional sustainability objectives with issues such as energy security, defence, supply-chain resilience, critical minerals and economic sovereignty.

AI has emerged as one of the most significant technological developments of recent years with its rapid adoption. AI presents considerations across each of the Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) pillars. Environmentally, attention is focused on the significant energy demands of AI models and data centres, particularly the source of that energy and its implications for emissions, energy security and climate goals. Socially, AI has the potential to drive productivity, innovation and economic growth, but also raises concerns around job displacement, skills transitions and inequality. Governance considerations include transparency, accountability, data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, intellectual property rights and the development of appropriate regulatory frameworks. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in economic activity and decision-making, effective governance will be essential to maximising its benefits while managing associated risks.

AI is rapidly becoming a core responsible investment theme, requiring investors to assess not only the investment and economic opportunities, but also its environmental footprint, social impact and governance standards.

When innovation outpaces oversight

Much like changing concerns in climate change, AI is evolving from just a technology issue into environmental, social and governance issues. The challenge is now where the responsibility lies.

Companies bear the responsibility for the systems being developed and deployed while the regulators need to establish guardrails and standards. The exceedingly fast pace of development of the technology has raised concerns, which have been echoed by some famous names like Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei, who have backed calls to slow the pace of development. The concerns stem not only from what could happen, but also from what has already occurred, including AI breaches and the use of hallucinated data.

There is no denying that this technology is revolutionary, although it’s important to understand that the pace of development might not be sustainable. Then comes the matter of governance, which brings us back to the question: where does responsibility lie?

Figure 1: Data centre electricity consumption by region, Base Case, 2020-2030

Source: IEA.org. Data Accessed 30th September 2026.

The need for AI oversight is driven by several well-documented risks, one of which is bias and discrimination. AI systems trained on historical datasets may inadvertently replicate or amplify existing biases. The inequality and bias are concerning, with evidence from one of the studies suggesting that the problem is widespread. A study of 133 AI systems found that 44% showed signs of gender bias, while more than a quarter highlighted both gender and racial bias. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) AI Principles and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence both highlight fairness and non-discrimination as key principles for the responsible development of AI.

AI may be both the climate challenge and part of the climate solution

While AI has the potential to deliver sustainability productivity gains and societal benefits, it requires energy-intensive infrastructure. Beyond electricity consumption, data centres depend on significant amounts of steel, concrete, critical minerals and advanced chips, all of which carry environmental costs. As adoption grows, the focus is shifting from whether these technologies are resource-intensive to how their resource demands can be managed sustainably without slowing innovation. Demand for financing is also increasing, with global insurance premiums linked to data centres expected to rise from US$10.6 billion today to US$24.2 billion by 2030.

The central question is not how fast AI should be developed, but how society will manage the trade-off between the environmental costs and societal benefits. This mirrors long-standing debates within climate investing, where investors must weigh the short-term environmental impact of enabling technologies against their long-term contribution to decarbonisation. Renewable energy technologies, electric vehicles and battery manufacturing all require substantial resources yet are widely viewed as essential components of a lower-carbon future. AI may ultimately fall into a similar category.

With the evolution of technology, some modern data centres use closed loop cooling systems which only utilise what is needed to ‘charge’ the system. Additionally, they have a carbon free power utilisation and commitment. While working with local utility companies, the power spikes are not pushed onto local consumers. Utilising such evolved technologies and business practices could potentially minimise the impact on the society while advancing the need and pace of transformation.

For policymakers, investors and businesses, the challenge is ensuring that AI’s environmental footprint remains proportionate to the value it creates. This will require continued improvements in data centre efficiency, cleaner electricity generation, advances in chip design and greater transparency around energy use. If managed effectively, the environmental cost of intelligence may prove to be a worthwhile investment, particularly if AI helps accelerate scientific discovery, improve resource efficiency and support the transition to a more sustainable economy. However, achieving that outcome will depend on intentional governance, responsible deployment and a willingness to confront the trade-offs rather than ignore them.

AI may be both a force for inclusion and a driver of inequality

Artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape labour markets in much the same way that previous technological revolutions transformed manufacturing and communications. However, many observers argue that AI differs from earlier innovations because it has the potential to automate cognitive tasks as well as routine physical work.

The choices we make about AI now are critical. Bill Gates argues that AI may affect professions ranging from customer service and software engineering to legal support and financial analysis, creating a period of significant economic disruption unless societies prepare adequately. Historically, technological progress has created new industries and occupations even as it displaced old ones. The challenge for policymakers, educators and businesses will be ensuring that workers can adapt quickly enough to keep pace with change. Reskilling, lifelong learning and workforce mobility are likely to become increasingly important as AI systems undertake more routine analytical tasks. While AI may boost productivity and economic growth, the benefits will not be evenly distributed unless investment in skills development keeps pace with the technology. According to the World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs research, technological change will simultaneously eliminate and create jobs, with adaptability becoming one of the most valuable workforce attributes in the years ahead.

One of the most important questions surrounding AI is who ultimately benefits from its capabilities. Bill Gates has also warned that AI could become either the ‘greatest equaliser ever invented’ or the ‘worst source of injustice’, depending on how access, ownership and governance evolve. If AI-powered tools increase access to education, healthcare and financial services, they could help narrow opportunity gaps and accelerate development.

Conversely, if the technology remains concentrated among a small group of countries and corporations, existing inequalities may deepen. This concern is echoed in Machines of Loving Grace, where Dario Amodei highlights the enormous benefits that advanced AI could unlock but also recognises the importance of managing the risks that accompany such concentrated technological power.

The companies developing frontier AI models possess unprecedented influence over the infrastructure, data and computational resources that underpin the technology. As a result, debates around transparency, competition, accessibility and regulation are becoming increasingly central to discussions about AI’s social impact. Ensuring broad and equitable access to the benefits of AI may prove just as important as the technological breakthroughs themselves.

The question, therefore, may not be whether AI is inherently good or bad, but whether it can be deployed in a manner that maximises societal value while minimising harm. The choices society makes today will determine whether AI becomes a force that broadens opportunity or one that exacerbates inequality. Like many transformative technologies before it, AI presents a complex trade-off: its long-term value will depend less on the technology itself and more on how responsibly it is governed, distributed and applied.

Figure 2: Total job growth and loss

Source: Davy. Weforum.org. Data accessed 30th September 2026.

The question is not whether to invest in AI, but how?

AI is becoming another test case for responsible investors – a technology with the potential to deliver significant economic and societal benefits while also creating challenges around the environment – energy use, society – labour markets & inequality and governance – ethics and regulation.

According to the IEA, electricity consumption from data centres globally is projected to more than double between 2024 and 2030, reaching around 945 TWh in the base case, equivalent to roughly Japan’s current annual electricity demand. Meanwhile, the World Economic Forum estimates that technological change could create 170 million new jobs globally by 2030 while displacing 92 million, resulting in a net gain of 78 million jobs, albeit with significant disruption and reskilling requirements (Figure 2 above).

The challenge for society is how to adapt to these evolving challenges. For investors, the question is increasingly not whether AI should be part of portfolios, but how capital can be used to influence its development. Responsible investment is moving beyond exclusions towards stewardship, engagement and accountability, with a focus on transparency, safety, energy use and equitable access.

In the age of AI, long-term value creation may depend as much on governance as on innovation itself.

text:
The White House X account (formerly known as Twitter) reposted a message from T1 Energy on October 28. The post from T1 Energy talked up the administration’s visit to Texas, their continued support, and pointed out the company’s two Texas facilities:

“T1 is building G2_Austin, an advanced photovoltaic manufacturing facility in Texas, with an estimated 2.1 GW Phase 1 capital expenditure in excess of $500 million. G2_Austin is expected to create an estimated 1,500 high-paying advanced manufacturing jobs with a $120 million payroll in Milam County, Texas, while helping to reshore a critical industry.”

Breitbart and other media accounts in the White House’s orbit also talked up the T1 Energy post, and the retweet on X.

text:
By Purvi Agarwal and Rashika Singh

Nov 2 (Reuters) – As the US midterm elections approach, Corporate America is bracing for a potential shift in the balance of power in Washington.

In case of a strong Democratic showing, analysts and strategists say clean energy, housing and healthcare stocks could benefit, while AI, data center and defense names may draw greater scrutiny from lawmakers.

The odds of a Democratic sweep stood at 72%, according to Polymarket, the world’s largest prediction market, while that of the Republican Party holding on to the Senate and the Democratic Party winning the House of Representatives stood at 23%.

The chances of Republicans retaining the Senate and the House are a poor 6%, while a Reuters/Ipsos poll showed President Donald Trump’s approval ratings at a career low amid voter concerns over the cost of living and the war with Iran.

Even a divided Congress would give Democrats more control over investigations and funding, but it would still have to overcome any veto from Trump.

Investors are closely watching these sectors:

POTENTIAL BENEFICIARIES OF A BLUE WAVE:

CLEAN ENERGY

A strong Democratic showing could reinforce expectations that federal support for clean-energy development will remain in place, analysts said, benefiting companies such as solar maker First Solar, residential solar installer Sunrun, inverter maker Enphase Energy and clean-power developer NextEra Energy.

The Democratic-controlled Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, devoting hundreds of billions to climate and energy-security measures, including expanded tax credits for renewable energy, nuclear power and EVs.

In case of a divided government, brokerage UBS sees room for bipartisan legislation to speed up energy and infrastructure approvals and expects nuclear power to get backing from both sides.

Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration’s efforts to roll back emissions rules and could use the Congressional Review Act to overturn regulations that make it easier to sell gas-powered trucks and SUVs.

Automakers Ford, General Motors and Stellantis, which have scaled back EV plans and lobbied for looser rules, could face pressure.

HOMEBUILDERS

UBS said the Trump administration would continue to implement the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which Congress passed in late June, to increase the availability of affordable single-family homes.

If Democrats take both chambers, they could add affordability measures, including restrictions on large institutional landlords, though those would still face Trump’s veto, UBS said.

The PHLX Housing Index has slipped close to 5% so far this year as the prospect of higher interest and mortgage rates weighs on the sector.

SECTORS AT RISK FROM A BLUE WAVE:

AI AND DATA CENTERS

Analysts expect a Democratic majority to bring greater scrutiny of AI, potentially pressuring data-storage and memory names such as Micron Technology, Sandisk and Seagate, which have rallied this year.

A slowdown in AI and data-center spending could also weigh on semiconductor-equipment makers, power providers and data-center builders.

A Democratic majority would be more likely to use subpoena powers to compel tech executives to testify under oath or hand over records related to harmful AI-agent behavior.

Also, voters in at least 10 states could consider ballot measures that could impose new restrictions, permitting requirements or pauses on data-center development.

Still, Societe Generale said the AI trade is likely to remain intact as Democrats are unlikely to secure a majority large enough to override a Trump veto and key federal agencies remain under Republican control.

HEALTHCARE

Healthcare faces a mixed outlook under a Democratic sweep, with greater scrutiny of Medicaid and Medicare Advantage plans potentially weighing on insurers, though TD Cowen sees limited risk of major industry changes and broad structural reform.

The S&P 500 healthcare sector has jumped more than 19% this year to record highs, trailing only energy stocks, as investors rotated into defensive sectors amid market volatility.

A Democratic-controlled House would heighten the possibility of raising taxes to fund a fiscal program that includes more health spending.

“A Democratic sweep could create greater momentum behind measures targeting healthcare costs, consumer fees, prescription drug pricing and areas perceived to contribute to affordability concerns,” said Magdalena Ocampo, market strategist at Principal Asset Management.

DEFENSE

Defense stocks rallied in January after Trump called for a $1.5 trillion military budget, above the approved $901 billion, but they have since surrendered most of those gains.

A budget vote is unlikely before 2027. Democratic control of the House could bring military spending back under scruntiny, with analysts noting Congress has yet to appropriate funds for the multibillion-dollar contracts that big defense contractors signed to replenish stockpiles.

However, with the Iran conflict showing no sign of ending, companies such as RTX and Northrop Grumman continue to see robust demand for arms, pushing their backlogs to record levels.

FINANCIALS

Morgan Stanley analysts said additional oversight under a Democratic outcome could slow the pace of regulatory easing, but was unlikely to derail it.

A Democratic Congress last overhauled bank regulations with the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, which tightened capital rules, created a consumer watchdog and imposed new trading restrictions.

A stronger GOP hand would support regulatory clarity and policy continuity. Keeping conditions favorable for mergers and acquisitions and sustaining capital markets activity are a big earnings driver for large banks, Barclays analysts said.

Quarterly results from JPMorgan, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo earlier this month suggested that a dealmaking and trading boom that powered record first-half earnings may be slowing.

CRYPTOCURRENCIES

Analysts say the election is unlikely to have a significant impact on cryptocurrency prices but will likely influence how quickly crypto legislation moves through Congress.

The Senate failed in September to advance the Clarity Act amid Democratic opposition, and analysts say a Democratic-controlled Senate would make it harder for the crypto bill to be revived next year.

Reuters has reported that Democrats in Congress are preparing investigations into crypto companies tied to Trump and his family, arguing the dealings present potential conflicts of interest.

That could generate adverse headlines and legal risks for some publicly listed firms in the crypto and blockchain industries, attorneys told Reuters.

(Reporting by Purvi Agarwal and Rashika Singh in Bengaluru; Additional reporting by Chris Sanders, Mike Stone, Courtney Rozen, Michelle Price and David Shepardson in Washington and Caroline Humer in New York; Editing by Arun Koyyur)

Exelon utilities could spend $3 billion to $7 billion building 1.5 GW to 3.5 GW of regulated energy storage, not including a $1 billion, 500-MW project already proposed for New Jersey, company officials said Friday during an earnings call.

“With regulated storage, we have certainty that projects get built, and control over when and how they’re deployed,” Robert Kleczynski, Exelon’s CFO, said during the call. “We view utility-owned storage as one option alongside competitive development, not a replacement for it.”

Customers would benefit from the projects through lower capacity prices and the flow-through of investment tax credits, which would ease the assets’ effect on electricity rates, he said.

Three states where Exelon utilities operate — New Jersey, Maryland and Delaware — allow them to own energy storage facilities to bolster grid resiliency, Kleczynski noted.

Atlantic City Electric’s 500-MW project, developed with Invenergy, would be the largest battery installation in the PJM Interconnection and is expected to provide more than $700 million in net benefits to customers, he said. Exelon expects the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities to make a decision on the proposal late in the first quarter next year, according to Kleczynski.

PJM isn’t moving fast enough to add generation onto its system, which is the biggest issue facing consumers in the grid operator’s Mid-Atlantic and Midwest footprint, according to Calvin Butler, Exelon president and CEO.

Two key PJM initiatives — its backstop capacity procurement plan and its Interim Resource Adequacy Service proposal — have been delayed by only partial approvals by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

“Neither proposal would have solved the reliability and affordability challenges facing our customers, but both represented important steps forward,” Butler said.

However, adding energy storage and transmission can help address the issue, according to Butler. Exelon’s current capital expenditure plan calls for investing $16.3 billion on transmission through 2029, and the Chicago-based company sees opportunity for $12 billion to $17 billion in transmission spending beyond that plan, including on infrastructure for large loads.

Exelon’s “high-probability” large load additions remained flat at 11 GW — with 9 GW in Commonwealth Edison’s service area in northern Illinois and 2 GW in the Mid-Atlantic region, the company said.

Its future pipeline slipped to 23 GW — 14 GW with ComEd and 9 GW in the Mid-Atlantic — from 25 GW last quarter.

On the financial front, Exelon’s third-quarter income fell to $729 million, down from $875 million in the same period last year, partly due to higher writeoffs related to a rate case, and higher storm and interest expenses. Third-quarter revenue jumped to $7.3 billion from $6.7 billion in the year-ago period.

Not including one-time factors, third-quarter adjusted income increased to 87 cents/share from 86 cents/share in the third quarter in 2025.

In a note, Jefferies equity analyst on Friday said the earnings results and the potential spending on storage and transmission, in addition to Exelon’s $41.7 billion capital expenditure plan, were “favorable.”

However, the analysts warned that regulatory uncertainty in 2027 dampens the outlook and may offset any incremental earnings from new capital expenditures.
