text:
The High-performance Optimised Recycled Nuclear Isotopes for Gen IV reactors (HORNIG) programme is under the US Department of Energy's Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy initiative. Opened for applications in April, HORNIG supports R&D projects that will deliver commercially deployable technologies that recycle transuranic elements found in existing inventories of used nuclear fuel into fissile materials to fuel advanced reactors. HORNIG builds on previous nuclear energy research programmes supported by the Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy's history of support for nuclear energy research programmes, including the CURIE (Converting UNF Radioisotopes Into Energy) programme which was launched in 2022.

TRU fuel includes transuranic elements - these are radioactive elements with an atomic number higher than uranium (the heaviest naturally occurring element) in the periodic table of elements. They are formed artificially by neutron capture (and also possibly subsequent beta decay), so are present in used nuclear fuel. Neptunium, plutonium, americium and curium are all examples of transuranic elements.

The High-performance Optimised Recycled Nuclear Isotopes for Gen IV reactors programme "seeks to overcome key technical and economic barriers that have historically prevented the use of TRU fuels in commercial reactors and to create a path to domestic nuclear fuel security by supporting the design, fabrication, and qualification of TRU fuels", seeking to deliver transformative advances in fuel performance, manufacturability, cost, and regulatory readiness. The projects "will design and test TRU-based fuel systems, improve fuel cost and manufacturability, and shorten qualification timelines from decades to less than 7 years".

The eight awardees are:

• Westinghouse Electric Company: USD7 million for its PowerBlock nuclear fuel technology, an approach which combines new fuel architectures with advanced manufacturing techniques to improve fuel performance and expand operational flexibility.

• Texas A&M University: USD5.4 million to develop and test a liquid, thorium-based nuclear fuel salt incorporating transuranics from used nuclear fuel for use in next-generation molten salt reactors.

• Standard Nuclear: USD7 million for its Mixed Oxycarbide (MCO) TRISO: Fuelling Advanced Reactors with Recycled Transuranic and Uranium Feedstock project, which aims to develop tristructural isotropic (TRISO) particle fuel containing recycled transuranic elements for use in high-temperature gas reactors using advancing fabrication methods. The project will support scalable production of TRISO fuel from recycled nuclear materials.

• Oregon State University: USD7 million for a project to make recycled transuranic-bearing nitride fuel for advanced reactors using an innovative low-temperature fabrication process.

• Oklo Inc: USD6.8 million, for its work to develop transuranic-bearing U-TRU-Zr metallic fuel for use in sodium-cooled reactors by advancing fuel fabrication methods, generating qualification-relevant data, and using fuel performance. The project is known as FORGE (Fabrication of Optimised Recycled fuel for Gen IV reactors from Electrorefiner product).

• Exodys Energy Inc: USD1.3 million for a project to develop a common framework for evaluating transuranic fuel feedstocks, fuel-cycle costs, transportation, and deployment requirements across HORNIG fuel concepts, providing economic and logistical data to support the commercialisation of recycled nuclear fuels.

• Sandia National Laboratories: USD3.4 million to provide an "uncertainty-aware decision support capability" associated with scaling transuranic fuel production across HORNIG fuel concepts, helping fuel developers to identify requirements and constraints affecting commercial-scale manufacturing and deployment.

• Idaho National Laboratory: USD7 million for its Irradiation of Molten Plutonium Actinide Chloride fuels and Testing (IMPACT) project to develop and test a chloride fuel salt containing recycled transuranic elements for use in molten salt reactors.

"President Trump has made clear that America must lead the world in nuclear energy, and that requires a strong domestic nuclear fuel supply chain," Deputy Secretary of Energy James Danly said. "By putting existing nuclear materials to productive use, we can strengthen our domestic fuel supply and reduce our reliance on foreign suppliers. These investments will help lower fuel costs, accelerate the deployment of advanced reactors, and ensure American nuclear innovation translates into more affordable, reliable power for American families and businesses."

Westinghouse's PowerBlock technology is designed to advance the traditional nuclear fuel assembly, targeting 24-month fuel cycles at thermal power levels above 4,200 MW. "As utilities look for new ways to maximise output, extend fuel performance and improve plant economics, innovation in fuel technology has never been more important," the company's President of Nuclear Fuel Ben Solich said. "PowerBlock represents a bold new approach to nuclear fuel design, and Westinghouse is well-positioned to utilize our deep expertise in nuclear fuel technology and manufacturing to further advance fuel innovation."

Standard Nuclear said its MCO TRISO initiative, by establishing an alternative to high-assay low-enriched uranium, aims to diversify the fissile feedstock supply chain for existing and next-generation reactors while actively reducing commercial used fuel stockpiles. It is leading the project, and working in partnership with fusion technology company SHINE Technologies.

"Recycled transuranic material still holds a great deal of usable energy, and TRISO is a fuel form well suited to harness it," Standard Nuclear President and CEO Kurt Terrani said. "With ARPA-E's support, we will work to develop the scalable fabrication methods to turn this valuable feedstock into particle fuel, giving developers of advanced or existing reactors a domestic source of fuel made from recycled feedstock."

State regulators at the New York Energy Research and Development Authority (NYSERDA) announced substantial increases in grants in its EmPower+ program and a relaunch of the NY-Sun program, both of which should deliver meaningful improvements in

energy efficiency and cost savings for low- and moderate-income (LMI) New Yorkers. Additionally, the Public Service Commission (PSC), authorized two utility thermal energy network projects to provide renewable heating and cooling to residents in Buffalo and Haverstraw.

We are grateful to the Governor and the Legislature for ensuring our budget dollars are available for affordable, clean energy. Now, our campaign and partners will work to ensure this funding is spent effectively, projects are completed, and New Yorkers realize the promised benefits,” said Lisa Marshall, Campaign Coordinator for Renewable Heat Now.

This progress demonstrates what sustained advocacy can accomplish. Renewable Heat Now and community, consumer, and energy groups advocated for the state to restore funding to EmPower+ and NY-Sun, while advancing new opportunities for thermal energy networks in the budget. As the global energy crisis continues to hit New Yorkers, advocates are seeking to work with the Governor and the Legislature to bring additional utility bill relief to our communities through the next NY State Budget.

Commenting on a recent article by the Chancellor John Healey in The Times which included comments on Great Britain’s energy policy, RenewableUK’s Executive Director of Policy Ana Musat said:

“The Chancellor is right to focus on value for money for billpayers when deciding which clean energy projects should go ahead. In his article for The Times he highlighted the fact that cheap energy is the foundation of a competitive economy, and that generating clean power is the way to break the grip of international gas prices on our bills. He also warned that those who want to rip up renewables would leave Britain more exposed to volatile markets and hostile international powers.

"As the Chancellor made clear, his approach is not a retreat from clean power - it is the credible route to it, as in his words, cheaper electricity will make it easier for businesses and households to electrify, strengthening our energy security and helping us decarbonise the wider economy.

“As the Chancellor is well aware, our cheapest sources of new power are wind and solar. He also knows that renewables are already reducing bills for hard-pressed consumers by driving the most expensive gas generators off the system. Wind farms cut electricity prices by almost a third in 2025, and wind and solar have saved consumers £5.9 billion so far this year by reducing the need to import gas.

“The Government’s Contracts for Difference which support renewable energy projects offer the best guarantee of clean power at stable and predictable low prices, protecting consumers from the volatility of international gas markets which the Chancellor highlighted in his article.

“He’s also right to recognise the importance of connecting projects to the grid faster. The National Audit Office says households could be £30 a year better off if Britain can accelerate its network rollout, so we need to step up on building new grid as a matter of urgency, both to cut bills and strengthen our energy security”.

text:
The California Public Utilities Commission (PUC) on Oct. 29 directed Pacific Gas and Electric Company, Southern California Edison, and San Diego Gas & Electric to propose a coordinated framework for managing distributed energy resources (DERs).

“Our decision moves the state toward a common framework for the utilities to manage and forecast DERs on our system, and create visibility for the California Independent System Operator,” said PUC Commissioner Darcie Houck, who is assigned to the proceeding. “This integrated approach prioritizes interoperability, and will enable the grid of the 21st century.”

The orchestration framework — which is the coordinated management of DERs by a distribution system operator (DSO), in this case the utilities acting as the DSO — should include customer-sited batteries, electric vehicles, and other technologies that can adjust when and how electricity is used, resulting in a common DER framework that will allow the coordinated management of DERs, the commission said.

The decision aims to help California make better use of such resources to meet local electricity needs, advance electrification and decarbonization, support a reliable grid, and potentially reduce or defer the need for costly infrastructure upgrades, regulators said.

In addition to DER orchestration, the decision also requires utilities to strengthen their distribution planning by evaluating how flexible electricity demand can help address grid constraints and support California’s continued electrification.

“California’s grid is evolving, with investments in resources like batteries, electric vehicles, and distributed solar,” Houck said. “When coordinated effectively, these resources can help support the electric system’s needs, support grid reliability, advance our climate goals, and reduce electric system costs for ratepayers.”

When coordinated, the DERs may help utilities manage periods of high electricity demand, address local grid constraints, support service restoration and outage mitigation, and reduce the need for certain traditional infrastructure investments, said the commission.

The three utilities have been tasked to work with stakeholders to develop a common framework proposal, which regulators said must address open and interoperable communications, data sharing, cybersecurity, customer protections, and clear participation pathways, among other orchestration requirements.

The utilities also must consider input from stakeholders through a working group process, and must address how customers, energy service providers, community choice aggregators, and other resource providers can participate without unnecessary barriers or duplicative compensation, they added.

“I’m pleased to be laying the groundwork for DER orchestration today,” said California PUC President John Reynolds. “There’s more work ahead as we build a future grid that works for everyone, and I will be particularly interested in proposals regarding affordability and competitive neutrality when it comes time to review utility applications.”

The decision also directs the utilities to develop new load flexibility scenarios for their annual distribution planning process, beginning with the 2028–2029 planning cycle, to help utilities evaluate how changes in electricity demand could affect the need, timing, and size of grid upgrades.

“Making better use of the grid we already have can help us connect customers sooner and keep costs down,” said PUC Commissioner Christine Harada. “Our decision gives families and businesses more options to charge a car, electrify a home, or expand operations while reducing the need for costly upgrades. Our responsibility is to make sure they deliver real savings for ratepayers.”

text:
FirstLight's Canadian business remains under PSP Investments ownership and becomes Caelo Energy

MONTREAL, Nov. 2, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Public Sector Pension Investment Board (PSP Investments) today announced that it has completed the sale of FirstLight's U.S. operations, including the FirstLight brand, to Hull Street Energy, a private equity firm specializing in power infrastructure and energy transition investments. The U.S. portfolio comprises approximately 1.4 GW of installed capacity across hydroelectric generation, energy storage, and other clean energy assets in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Pennsylvania.

PSP Investments retains ownership of FirstLight's Canadian operations – a combination of legacy Hydromega and H2O Power portfolios – which going forward will operate as Caelo Energy ("Caelo"). Caelo operates 18 hydroelectric facilities across Quebec and Ontario totalling 202 MW of installed capacity and a development pipeline of nearly 1 GW of renewable energy and energy storage projects. FirstLight's Canada-based employees will remain with Caelo Energy.

Caelo Energy will continue to be a best-in-class operator of clean power assets while advancing its development pipeline and pursuing new opportunities in the Canadian power sector. This includes the 57.2 MW Fort Frances solar project in Ontario, which is being developed in partnership with the Lac Des Mille Lacs First Nation and was awarded a 20-year power purchase agreement through Ontario's Long-Term 2 (LT2) procurement process.

Patrick Gut has been appointed Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Caelo Energy, bringing nearly a decade of experience at PSP Investments, where his primary focus was on investment and asset management in the power sector in the Americas and Europe. He has extensive knowledge of the business, having served as Interim President of H2O Power and as a board member of both H2O Power and FirstLight. Patrick also brings broader renewable investment experience through his involvement as a board member for Cubico Sustainable Investments, a developer and operator of renewable energy projects across Western Europe, Latin America and the United States.

"Completing this transaction concludes a successful decade of building FirstLight into a leading North American clean energy business, and we thank the U.S. team for everything they accomplished. In Canada, we are retaining a platform with long-term, inflation-linked operating cash flows, an attractive development pipeline and an experienced team positioned to pursue growth opportunities in Canada," said Andrew Alley, Managing Director and Global Head of Infrastructure Investments at PSP Investments. "Patrick has helped shape this portfolio for years as an investor and a board member, and we have every confidence in him to successfully lead Caelo Energy through this next chapter."

"I am honoured to lead Caelo Energy, and to do so alongside such a skilled and dedicated team who I have come to know well over many years," said Patrick Gut, CEO of Caelo Energy. "We start from a strong foundation – hydroelectric facilities that have served their communities for generations – and we are excited to build on that foundation as we shape Caelo's future. I want to thank PSP Investments for its confidence in Caelo and I am thrilled to continue to play a part in it."

About Caelo Energy

Caelo Energy is a Canadian clean energy company wholly owned by PSP Investments, formed from the combination of the legacy Hydromega and H2O Power businesses. Caelo Energy owns and operates 18 hydroelectric facilities in Quebec and Ontario and is advancing a nearly 1 GW development pipeline of wind, solar, hydro, and battery storage projects. Caelo Energy has offices in Montreal and Oshawa. For more information, visit caeloenergy.com and follow us on LinkedIn.

title: TWS Opposes S. 5653 over six threats to public lands | The Wilderness Society
description:
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is presented as a false choice between building renewable energy and protecting public lands, cultural resources, and the public’s ability to engage on what impacts shared landscapes.
These tradeoffs are neither necessary nor acceptable—under this administration or any future administration.
The Wilderness Society has grave concerns about the provisions in the bill that threaten public lands below.
Participation in public lands management decisions ensures our shared lands serve the common good rather than private interests.
This bill opens the floodgates to unchecked exploitation of public lands.
text:
The United States can and must reach a clean energy future as soon as possible. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is presented as a false choice between building renewable energy and protecting public lands, cultural resources, and the public’s ability to engage on what impacts shared landscapes. These tradeoffs are neither necessary nor acceptable—under this administration or any future administration. We can move toward a clean energy future while ensuring that America’s public lands, waters, and wildlife habitat are not sacrificed for future generations, and that is the standard elected officials should insist on as well.

This bill would:

Lock in drilling and mining projects making it impossible for future administrations to correct permits, even if they are unlawful;

Weaken public participation in decisions affecting shared lands;

Erode Tribal consultation and Tribal sovereignty while threatening sacred sites and cultural resources;

Limit judicial review and make unlawful projects harder to correct in court; and

Expand industry access to public lands without adequate safeguards.

It is necessary to view this bill in the broader context of escalating threats to public lands and waters, wildlife, Tribes and communities, and the agencies responsible for managing them:

The fossil fuel industry is already benefiting from the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and multiple recent rollbacks and revisions of common-sense reforms that better balanced public lands values with energy development, including the Public Lands Rule and Oil and Gas Leasing Rule.

Counter to the public’s wishes, the Administration has stripped protections from and already granted hardrock mining and fossil fuel industries the green light to mine and drill some of our most iconic public landscapes, including the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, the Arctic, Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and Bears Ears National Monument and the Greater Chaco Region.

Federal agencies that would be responsible for meeting the deadlines in the bill are decimated – recent layoffs and forced early retirements mean there’s limited staff to review permits, consult with Tribes and communities, enforce safeguards, and follow through with the bill’s new requirements. And a provision in the bill would force the government to pay companies for missed deadlines, even if they missed them because of lack of staffing.

The Wilderness Society has grave concerns about the provisions in the bill that threaten public lands below. We call on Congress to oppose this bill because of the threats it poses:

This section bans future administrations from taking any action on permitted projects on public lands, even when permits were approved unlawfully, except under extremely limited circumstances. This means permanently entrenching drilling and mining projects on public landscapes that are currently targeted for shortsighted, corporate control. This includes the Greater Chaco Canyon region, Bears Ears National Monument and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument, the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness, the Arctic, all national public lands in the lower 48 that are currently available to oil and gas leasing, and increasingly, data center construction. Simply put, the “project certainty” provision in this bill would wedge the door open for these cherished landscapes to be permanently developed and exploited.

While entrenching existing sell-outs of treasured landscapes, this section also further emboldens the current administration to make reckless, unlawful decisions over the next two-plus years that hand over even more public lands to drilling and mining, while also restricting access to the courts and limiting the ability of the public and public interest organizations like TWS to challenge unlawful project decisions.

Participation in public lands management decisions ensures our shared lands serve the common good rather than private interests. Since 2025, the administration and Congress have weakened transparency and narrowed the ability of local communities and Tribes to raise concerns about projects that affect their lands, waters, cultural resources and health. Simply put: This bill’s proposed changes to NEPA effectively turn the bedrock environmental law into a dead letter.

The bill provides broad loopholes for actions that would no longer be subject to NEPA and eliminates meaningful judicial review (and therefore government accountability) for communities that seek to challenge agency decisions. If this bill becomes law, most public land management decisions will go under the radar, and communities will be severely limited in their ability to comment on or oppose them. New science and research that could have informed a project will not be considered after the publication of a notice of intent. And communities will have to conform to stricter standards to prove harm from a project and challenge decisions in court.

This bill is not only an affront to Tribal sovereignty, but it would also directly threaten sacred sites and cultural resources across ancestral lands. Places of cultural significance like Chaco Canyon or Bears Ears National Monument would be at risk. For example, under these new standards, negative impacts from oil and gas rigs or mines on the border of protected areas would not be considered a direct harm.

This section proposes to rewrite the provision that is used to identify historic places, consult with Tribal Nations and affected communities, consider alternatives, and seek ways to avoid, minimize, or mitigate harm before federal undertakings move forward.

It would make consultation with Tribes and communities optional, arbitrarily restrict what is considered an important cultural site, allow more projects to skip review and require fewer environmental impacts to be taken into consideration.

Taken together, these changes would restrict the power of Tribal Nations and communities to define the places that matter to them, silencing those who should have a voice in decisions that impact their lands. Congress must heed the call of Tribes and Indigenous groups speaking out against these provisions.

The bill closely reflects the Mining Regulatory and Clarity Act (MRCA) and would reverse over a century of public land law precedent and severely undermine the federal government’s ability to safeguard cultural, environmental, water, and economic resources. Similar to the MRCA, the bill would allow companies to occupy and industrialize vast areas of public land, including waste dumps and infrastructure, without holding valid mineral rights, paying royalties or undergoing rigorous environmental review. It would shut out competing uses such as recreation, renewable energy and cultural preservation.

The bill also would codify a dangerous loophole that prioritizes private mining interests over public good, threatens Indigenous lands and ecosystems and burdens underfunded federal agencies without providing resources or accountability. This bill opens the floodgates to unchecked exploitation of public lands.

This section gives a developer the ability to sue the administration if a project approval is taking too long. The provision could be weaponized against a future administration that might try to deprioritize harmful development like fossil fuel projects or data centers. It would also seemingly make it impossible to put forward a pause or moratorium on an activity, even if the pause would only be to allow time for closer review of potential impacts. For example, it would have prevented the pause on offshore drilling permits and development following the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and the coal leasing moratorium enacted by the Obama administration, and could block a future moratorium on data centers on public lands. At a time when the public and local officials are clamoring for transparency and input into the rapid buildout of data centers across the country, this provision runs counter to the moratorium TWS has called for from the administration.

This section takes this assault to public input a step further by exempting hundreds of thousands potentially millions—of acres of split-estate lands from the federal permitting process, eliminating key public input opportunities that are currently often the only way neighbors and landowners know drilling is imminent. This also eliminates a key federal decision point where BLM can make sure an operator’s bond can fully cover the costs of reclaiming the well when production ends. In short, this provision could grow our national tally of orphaned and abandoned wells that leech into our rivers and streams and leak methane into our atmosphere.

The irreversible destruction these provisions would cause to treasured places like the Arctic, the Boundary Waters, Bears Ears, and Chaco is simply not a reasonable or necessary tradeoff.

Congress must oppose S. 5653.

The Wilderness Society is a national conservation organization dedicated to protecting America’s wild places since 1935. Through science, advocacy and partnerships with communities and policymakers, we champion the protection of wilderness, national monuments, forests, and other public lands that provide clean air and water, wildlife habitat and the freedom to connect with nature. For more information, visit www.wilderness.org.

title: Utilities need to become project developers. Are they ready? - Utility Dive
description:
Load growth is no longer an abstract number in an electricity market report or forecast; it’s a reality.
Rapid load growth changes nearly everything for utilities, from how they plan and invest to how they engage and communicate with customers.
Load growth is also compelling many utilities to do something they haven’t done at this scale and pace before: develop their own generation.
Other utilities have embraced full self-development, choosing to outsource only the capital-intensive step of land acquisition while keeping the rest of project management in-house.
Ultimately, though, what matters is whether a partnership approach allows utilities to function as high-volume generation project developers.
text:
Load growth is no longer an abstract number in an electricity market report or forecast; it’s a reality. According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), U.S. electricity load will increase nearly 2 percent in 2026 and 2.5 percent next year, driven by large loads like data centers and manufacturing as well as increased electrification of transportation and building heating and cooling. To put that number in perspective, annual load growth between 2005 and 2019 was about 0.1 percent, meaning the next two years will see nearly 50 times the growth that the industry experienced in the last 15 years.

Rapid load growth changes nearly everything for utilities, from how they plan and invest to how they engage and communicate with customers. Load growth is also compelling many utilities to do something they haven’t done at this scale and pace before: develop their own generation. “Utilities are used to designing and building a gas plant once every five or 10 years, and then they would contract via PPAs (power purchase agreement) everything else,” said Alex Pope, Manager of Power Development Portfolios 1898 & Co. “But the systems utilities have in place to self-develop generation projects were never built to handle the volume necessary to meet the demand and timelines of today’s customer needs.”

Building from scratch is hard

As PPAs and BTAs (Build-Transfer Agreement) alone become insufficient to close the generation and load gap, many utilities that recognize the need to build more projects themselves face an important question: how do we start? One avenue is to focus inward and develop the internal expertise and resources needed to move projects from concept to commercialization—everything from land acquisition and permitting to financing, regulatory approvals, procurement strategies, and construction.

While this approach gives utilities complete control over the development of new generation, it also has meaningful challenges. One significant hurdle is the need to either augment the teams responsible for each phase of a successful new project or completely build from scratch. “You may have to quadruple your internal team of environmental specialists because you need to be pushing multiple projects forward,” Pope said. “The challenge is that everyone is trying to hire for these project-related roles and competition is stiff.”

Beyond adding personnel, what utilities also find is that the underlying internal processes and coordination needed to efficiently develop a large pipeline of generation projects simply don’t exist. Creating that necessary foundation involves hard choices about responsibilities and collaboration that inevitably take time that utilities don’t have if they are to meet this historic moment of load growth.

A partnership approach

There’s another option, one that leverages existing utility expertise without requiring a vast expansion of staff. That option is to bring in a partner like 1898 & Co. to work alongside utility staff, increase their impact across projects, provide industry lessons and best practices from other utility peers, and act as the connective tissue between departments that need to collaborate for generation projects to move forward efficiently.

The rationale for the partnership is simple: utilities already have exceptionally capable people to handle environmental review, land rights, interconnection, regulatory approvals, and other aspects of project development. What utilities often lack, however, is a foundational infrastructure to ensure their internal teams work together rather than at cross-purposes across a large portfolio of projects in simultaneous development. This is necessary when utilities are trying to expand their self-development capacity from one or two projects per decade to a large and growing portfolio. “Their groups are industry best at what they do,” said Pope, who works directly with major utilities across the country to bolster the utility’s self-development capabilities. “But what they did was suited for one thermal project every five years. It was never set up to handle the throughput of what they’re being asked to do right now.”

The value of a single source of truth

1898 & Co.’s partnership approach is intentionally flexible, designed to supplement a utility’s existing self-development capacity and expand it to align with its goals and strategies. For example, Pope says some utilities start with development transfers, in which a third-party developer brings a shovel-ready project, and the utility completes due diligence before moving forward. This offers a lower-risk way to better understand the demands of self-development before attempting a larger portfolio of self-originated projects.

Other utilities have embraced full self-development, choosing to outsource only the capital-intensive step of land acquisition while keeping the rest of project management in-house. Utilities like Xcel Energy and DTE Energy, with support from 1898 & Co, leverage a blend development-transfer, self-development, PPA, and BTA structures to avoid putting all their eggs in one basket. No matter what model a utility chooses, Pope says 1898 & Co. provides a “single source of truth” across a portfolio of projects. This is possible because 1898 & Co. screens potential sites, manages due diligence, helps steer overall strategy, tracks deliverables, and coordinates across environmental, permitting, interconnection, and land rights teams. That combination of coordination and analysis ensures that a utility’s internal specialists, consulting partners, and selected EPC firms can all work together as one cohesive self-development team.

Real-world results

The financial rationale for pursuing a partnership that enhances a utility’s self-development is also compelling. 1898 & Co.’s services not only help investor-owned utilities keep up with the demands of their customers but also create strong shareholder value in the process.

Ultimately, though, what matters is whether a partnership approach allows utilities to function as high-volume generation project developers. In a recent all-source request for proposals (ASRFP), 1898 & Co. supported over 60 gigawatts of generation projects for its utility clients. Of those, 22 gigawatts were then bid in competitive RFPs. The result: 10 gigawatts won.

text:
Harbinger, a U.S.-based commercial EV manufacturer, has entered into a battery supply agreement with Panasonic Energy, securing a consistent supply of high-performance lithium-ion battery cells for its medium-duty electric vehicle platform. The partnership, announced on April 23, designates Panasonic as Harbinger’s official battery cell provider across its full product lineup.

Harbinger will integrate Panasonic’s 2170 cylindrical battery cells—known for their energy density of over 800Wh/L—into all upcoming vehicle models. This cell technology is set to improve overall range and vehicle efficiency, supporting fleet operators looking for scalable, electrified solutions. For now, production will begin with battery cells sourced from Panasonic’s facilities in Japan, with plans to expand to domestic production in the near future.

U.S. Battery Manufacturing on the Horizon

While the battery cells will initially be produced overseas, Harbinger and Panasonic have signaled intentions to localize manufacturing. Panasonic’s De Soto, Kansas facility is expected to play a future role in the supply chain, supporting efforts to establish a fully U.S.-sourced battery pack system tailored for commercial vehicle applications.

At its Garden Grove, California headquarters, Harbinger handles the design and assembly of its electric drivetrains and high-voltage battery systems in-house. This vertically integrated model has allowed the company to control both cost and quality—key factors in building vehicles that meet the performance and safety needs of commercial customers.

With production now underway, Harbinger is focused on delivering an initial run of approximately 5,000 vehicles to customers including Bimbo Bakeries USA and THOR Industries. These EVs are intended for a range of medium-duty applications, such as walk-in delivery vans, box trucks, and recreational or emergency service vehicles.

Built for Commercial Use, Backed by Experience

Panasonic Energy brings to the table extensive experience in EV battery manufacturing, having delivered nearly 19 billion lithium-ion cells as of March 2025—supporting around 3.7 million EVs globally without battery-related recalls. That established performance record made Panasonic an appealing partner for Harbinger’s growing commercial EV platform.

text:
Just three months after the South Korean government excluded finished electric vehicles from its domestic production tax credit target, the policy is back under review. This renewed discussion is driven by growing concerns that the ‘invasion’ of Chinese electric vehicles could undermine South Korea’s domestic manufacturing foundation.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Lee Hyung-il visited the Hyundai Motor-Kia Technical Center in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, on the 2nd to hold a meeting. Responding to requests from corporations to introduce a production tax credit for electric vehicles, Deputy Prime Minister Lee stated, “The government will actively participate in the National Assembly’s deliberation process and discuss the matter in depth.”

The domestic production tax credit is a system that reduces taxes based on the performance of producing and selling strategic industry products within South Korea. President Lee Jae-myung also visited Hyundai Motor’s Asan plant in February of last year, when he served as party leader, to propose the introduction of this incentive.

In the tax law amendment announced last August, the government included six major sectors—such as semiconductors and secondary batteries—in the tax credit eligibility, but excluded electric vehicles. The initial reasoning was to prioritize support for core parts and materials with vulnerable production bases while simultaneously boosting the competitiveness of finished vehicles through secondary battery support.

The situation shifted as the offensive from Chinese products intensified. According to the Korea Automobile Mobility Association (KAMA), the proportion of Chinese electric vehicles among new registrations (296,801 units) from January to September reached 38.1% (112,968 units), marking a 6.5 percentage point increase compared to the same period last year. For electric passenger cars specifically, Chinese models accounted for 43.5% while domestic models fell below the majority for the first time at 48.7%. This outcome aligns with the expanded sales of Tesla and BYD manufactured at the Shanghai plant in China.

South Korea’s lower trade barriers compared to major nations also played a role. The United States imposes a 127.5% tariff on Chinese electric passenger cars, while the European Union imposes a baseline 10% tariff plus up to an additional 35.3% tariff depending on the manufacturer. In contrast, South Korea only levies a basic 8% tariff without additional duties. In July of this year, the government selected purchase subsidy recipients by evaluating after-sales service (AS) and contributions to the domestic supply chain, successfully excluding BYD from subsidy targets. However, subsidies continue to be paid for Tesla vehicles produced in China.

Cho Chul, a distinguished professor at the Korea Institute for Future Strategy, remarked, “If domestic electric vehicle production declines, battery demand will also decrease, rendering the tax credit meaningless,” adding, “If the current situation persists, one or two domestic plants could face closures upon the complete transition to electric vehicles.”

The National Assembly is also pursuing legislation related to the electric vehicle production tax credit. Ruling and opposition lawmakers, including Lee 언주 (Eon-ju) and Yoon Han-hong, have separately proposed relevant bills. The Ministry of Economy and Finance has yet to finalize its stance, and variables such as trade conflicts remain. A Ministry official stated, “We will actively participate in the National Assembly’s discussions.” The Strategy and Finance Committee of the National Assembly initiated deliberations on the tax law amendment on the same day.

title: Defining and strengthening the built environment workforce - Brookings Institution
authors: James C. Benton, Junjie Ren, Adam Aley
description:
Projected employer demand among built environment occupations is concentrated in a few educational categories: “high school or less,” “bachelor’s degree or more,” and “apprenticeship.” The report’s Discussion section addresses several topics and challenges regarding the built environment workforce: Education requirements and career pathways are remarkably diverse across the 95 built environment occupations.

Discussion Built environment occupations are remarkably diverse in terms of educational requirements and career pathways Many of the 95 built environment occupations are accessible with a high school diploma or less, while others require a four-year degree.
text:
Executive summary

The modern world relies on a range of physical, human-made assets and systems that undergird daily life and make up the built environment. Spanning highways and railways, pipes and power plants, and homes and businesses, the built environment is expansive and foundational to the country’s economy. In turn, these structures rely on an appropriately educated and skilled workforce to design, build, and maintain them. While employers, policymakers, and other leaders widely acknowledge the need for such workers, there has not been a shared understanding of the “built environment workforce,” or the workers who directly create or modify built structures and systems.

This report provides a comprehensive and consistent definition of the built environment workforce, describes its size and characteristics, and identifies common workforce development approaches and challenges. We then provide recommendations for industry and workforce leaders to develop stronger entry points into built environment careers, as well as clearer pathways for incumbent workers. Without more robust built environment career pathways, capital projects are likely to face delays, quality problems, and cost overruns.

In our data analysis, we find:

Ninety-five occupations totaling 15.3 million workers comprise the built environment workforce, which refers to workers who directly create or modify human-made physical structures and systems.

Earnings for the built environment workforce as a whole are competitive with and often higher than those for workers across all occupations, shaped in part by unionization among workers in construction occupations. Nonetheless, there is substantial variation by specific occupation.

The built environment workforce is disproportionately white and male. It also has a smaller share of workers age 24 or under compared to workers across all occupations, and some occupations have high shares of workers over age 55.

Built environment occupations span the educational continuum and require varying levels of on-the-job training and related experience.

Projected employer demand among built environment occupations is concentrated in a few educational categories: “high school or less,” “bachelor’s degree or more,” and “apprenticeship.”

The report’s Discussion section addresses several topics and challenges regarding the built environment workforce:

Education requirements and career pathways are remarkably diverse across the 95 built environment occupations. Many are accessible with a high school diploma, others require a four-year degree, and some value work experience and/or on-the-job training more than formal credentials. Engineers with bachelor’s degrees and apprentices have the clearest pathways from education and training into employment. Occupations with a formal education requirement of a high school diploma or less often rely on work experience or on-the-job training (which can be of varying lengths and formality) for career advancement, but these options for career progression are not always clearly laid out.

Measuring the supply of workers and employer demand for workers is difficult. The prevalence of informal educational and training pathways makes it difficult to estimate the supply of built environment workers. Government-generated employment projections and real-time labor market data from online job postings can provide helpful signals of current and future demand, but both have limitations.

Diversity by race/ethnicity, age, and gender is a real concern. The built environment workforce is disproportionately white (64%) compared to all occupations (60%), especially in higher-paying positions. It is overwhelmingly male (91%). A relatively small share of its workforce is age 24 or under (9%) compared to all occupations (13%). In a demographically changing country, the industry needs to diversify its workforce if it is to remain competitive.

Finally, our Recommendations section proposes the following:

Industry and workforce leaders in the built environment field should focus on interventions at different points in the employment cycle: recruit younger and more diverse workers; improve retention of current workers and apprentices; and develop stronger internal career ladders into supervisory and management positions. Relevant actors include employers, public and private capital asset owners, labor unions, the K-12 and postsecondary education systems, state and local employment agencies, and more.

Capital asset owners should treat labor market forecasting and workforce planning as core to project planning and development. Labor availability is a key input to successful project delivery along with materials and equipment, and should be treated as such.

Introduction

The modern world relies on a range of physical, human-made assets and systems that undergird daily life and make up the built environment—the physical surroundings where people live, work, learn, and interact. More specifically, the built environment encompasses buildings (residential, commercial, industrial, institutional); transportation systems (roads, bridges, rail, airports); utility networks (water, wastewater, electricity, natural gas, telecommunications); and public spaces.

The very existence and ongoing function of these structures depend on a skilled workforce to design, build, and maintain them. Employers, policymakers, and other leaders widely acknowledge the need for such workers, and there are multiple efforts to develop pipelines for a variety of occupational groupings, such as the construction trades, engineers of various disciplines, and workers in the energy and water sectors. But there has not been a shared understanding of the “built environment workforce”—referring to the workers who directly create or modify built structures and systems—as a cohesive and integrated network of shared assets.

This report provides a definition of the built environment workforce based on an analysis of labor market data, literature reviews, and stakeholder engagement, relying heavily on a careful review of industry and occupational definitions. Our goal was to develop a more comprehensive definition to inform workforce development efforts related to the built environment—moving beyond more bespoke groupings of workers based on occupational similarities, academic disciplines, or industry subsectors.

After identifying which occupations belong in the built environment workforce, we describe the size of this workforce, typical wages, and demographic characteristics of its workers—both for the group as a whole and by individual occupation. We identify characteristics of existing workforce development approaches as well as common challenges. Lastly, we close with recommendations to develop stronger career pathways for built environment workers in order to better serve job seekers, incumbent workers, and employers.

Defining the ‘built environment workforce’

To create our definition, we reviewed industry and occupational definitions from the U.S. Census Bureau and the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), and assessed how industries and occupations interact with each other. The Methodology section in the Appendix provides more details on this process, including building off methods from past Brookings research on the “infrastructure workforce”—a closely associated set of workers who are involved in constructing and overseeing large-scale, public-serving infrastructure systems.

We determined that members of the “built environment workforce” perform work that directly creates or modifies built structures and systems, thus capturing a broad range of industrial activities and associated occupations. This includes onsite construction trades (e.g., carpenters, electricians, plumbers), supervisors, managers, and professions such as architects and engineers.

More specifically, built environment workers meet one of the following criteria:

They are employed in construction, architecture, engineering, or design industries.

They are employed in occupations that construct, erect, install, or repair structures and fixtures, or plan and design structures, according to official BLS occupational definitions.

Through this process, we identified 12 detailed industry groups and 95 occupations that make up the built environment workforce. Crucially, this workforce spans many positions traditionally classified in the trades, but also positions involved in management, administration, and other service activities.

Please see the Methodology section in the Appendix for more details about our analytical approach.

Data findings

Ninety-five occupations totaling 15.3 million workers comprise the built environment workforce, referring to workers who directly create or modify human-made physical structures and systems

The 15.3 million workers that make up the built environment workforce account for nearly 8.8% of all workers nationally. These workers design, construct, install, and repair the physical structures in which people live, work, learn, travel, and interact every day, including buildings, transportation systems, utilities, public spaces, and more. The workforce spans multiple occupational categories, with construction-related jobs accounting for the largest share (about half). Other common jobs include those related to installation, maintenance, and repair; architecture and engineering; and management.

Occupations with the largest number of workers include maintenance and repair workers (1.7 million), construction laborers (1.5 million), project management specialists and carpenters (each a little over 1 million), first-line supervisors of construction workers (900,000), and electricians (850,000).

Earnings for built environment workers are competitive with and often higher than workers across all occupations, although there is substantial variation by occupation

Median hourly wages for the built environment workforce as a whole are nearly $30—well above the median for all occupations ($24). As shown in Figure 2, built environment occupations also have a higher floor for workers at the lower end of the earnings spectrum. At both the 10th and 25th percentiles, hourly wages for built environment workers ($17.33 and $22.01, respectively) are considerably higher than for workers in all occupations ($14.21 and $17.59, respectively).

Wages vary considerably by occupation and are correlated with education, experience, and specialization. Some of the largest occupations have relatively low hourly wages, such as maintenance and repair workers ($23.35) and construction laborers ($21.57). Other relatively large occupations pay more, such as project management specialists ($48.38), carpenters ($26.90), first-line supervisors of construction workers ($37.01), and electricians ($29.62). The highest earners are architectural and engineering managers (by a wide margin, at $80.52), followed by electrical engineers ($53.75), and elevator/escalator installers and repairers ($51.24).

Wages are also influenced by unionization rates. A higher share of workers in construction occupations are union members (16%) than among workers across all occupations (10%), and unionized workers earn higher wages than their non-union counterparts—in construction and in other occupations.

The built environment workforce is disproportionately white and male, has a smaller share of workers age 24 or under compared to workers across all occupations, and some occupations have high shares of workers over age 55

Differences by gender in the built environment workforce are stark. Women make up about 10% of these workers, despite accounting for about half of workers across all occupations.

Women are under-represented in the vast majority of built environment occupations—most dramatically in construction occupations typically requiring a high school diploma or less. Women make up about 3% to 4% of HVAC mechanics, plumbers, carpenters, electricians, and operating engineers. Although their shares are sometimes higher, women are also under-represented in occupations typically requiring a bachelor’s degree, such as civil and mechanical engineers (both about 3%), electrical engineers (10%), architectural and engineering managers (11%), and architects (26%).

As Figure 4 shows, the built environment workforce has higher shares of workers who are white or Latino or Hispanic, and lower shares of people who are Black or Asian American compared to workers across all occupations. About 64% of the built environment workforce is white and 22% is Latino or Hispanic; across all occupations, 60% of the workforce is white and 18% is Latino or Hispanic. The share of Black workers in the built environment workforce (7%) is lower than across all occupations (13%). Asian Americans are also under-represented: They account for 4% of the built environment workforce compared to 7% across all occupations.

White workers are concentrated in higher-paying occupations. Of the 10 built environment occupations with the highest median wages, white workers make up between 66% and 81% of the workforce. Among those same 10 occupations, Black workers make up between 3% and 9% of the workforce, and Latino or Hispanic workers make up between 6% and 16%. Black workers make up very low shares of the largest occupations typically reached through apprenticeships, accounting for 4% of carpenters and 6% of electricians and plumbers. Latino or Hispanic workers are disproportionately represented among the lower-paying occupations, such as the “helpers” of various construction trades (brickmasons, pipelayers, painters, roofers, carpenters, and electricians). They account for 33% to 41% of all “helpers,” and 38% of construction laborers. All these positions with high concentrations of Latino or Hispanic workers pay below the median wage for all occupations ($24), and well below the median wage for the built environment workforce ($29.88).

Workers age 24 or younger make up a smaller share of the built environment workforce relative to the workforce as a whole: about 9% compared to nearly 13% across all occupations. Not surprisingly, occupations with the highest concentrations of younger workers typically require lower levels of formal education and little to no related experience. For instance, more than 30% of “helpers” in various construction trades are age 24 or younger. Relatedly, built environment occupations with high shares of younger workers also pay at the lower end of the wage scale for built environment occupations.

However, youth-focused built environment occupations do pay higher median wages ($22.17) than all occupations with above-average shares of young workers ($17.80). Coupled with their relatively low educational requirements, youth-focused built environment occupations could be presented as attractive employment options for young people.

A number of occupations have above-average shares of workers over age 55, pointing to the need for succession planning and strategies to retain existing employees. Across all occupations and within the built environment workforce, about 25% of workers are over 55. Among some positions, the share of workers over age 55 are upward of 30%, including construction and building inspectors (44%), maintenance and repair workers (34%), a variety of managerial and supervisory positions, and more.

Built environment occupations span the educational continuum and require varying levels of on-the-job training and related experience

Built environment workers carry out a diverse variety of tasks and activities. Not surprisingly, their ability to do their jobs is dependent upon varying levels of education, experience, and on-the-job training (OJT). There is clearly not a one-size-fits all workforce development strategy for the built environment workforce.

To develop more tailored approaches to specific occupations or groups of occupations, we adapted a typology from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, as shown in Table 5. The adapted typology allows us to categorize and compare the varying education and training experiences typically required for different occupations—a necessary step in developing workforce development approaches that are responsive to occupations with different characteristics and needs.

The largest group of occupations (50), representing more than 8 million jobs, requires a high school diploma or less in terms of formal education. However, qualification for a number of these occupations involves other learning experiences—OJT and work experience—that are important if not as easily measured.

Work experience is important for front-line supervisors of both construction workers as well as mechanics, installation, and repair workers. Coupled with OJT, work experience is also important for construction and building inspectors, crane operators, earth drillers, and explosives workers.

On-the-job training lasting more than 12 months is important for mobile heavy equipment mechanics, electrical power line installers and repairers, and telecommunications line installers and repairers.

Occupations involving no or minimal OJT and work experience include construction laborers, “helpers” related to a variety of construction trades, insulation workers, pipelayers, and carpet installers.

While we have grouped occupations requiring a high school diploma or less into one category for simplicity, the subgroupings by OJT and work experience have implications for workforce strategies. For instance, approaches for occupations requiring work experience may best target incumbent workers rather than new job entrants.

The next largest set of occupations (17), representing more than 3 million jobs, requires a bachelor’s degree or more. These include engineers (civil, mechanical, electrical, and environmental), project management specialists, and interior designers. Occupations in which experience or some level of OJT are important include construction managers and architectural and engineering managers. Occupations described as requiring internships or residencies include architects and surveyors.

Apprenticeships are a well-known and recognized strategy offering paid, structured work-based learning, typically coupled with classroom-based instruction. Occupations with the largest number of workers in this category include electricians, carpenters, and plumbers. BLS designates a number of other occupations as “typically” requiring apprenticeships, including sheet metal workers, structural iron workers, brickmasons, and glaziers. However, the “apprenticeship” designation is not absolute; workers can also prepare for some of these occupations via informal OJT or community colleges and technical schools.

Occupations typically requiring an associate degree or a postsecondary nondegree award (such as a certificate or industry-recognized credential) account for the smallest number of workers (about 1.1 million combined). The occupations with the largest number of workers in this grouping include telecommunications equipment installers and repairers and HVAC mechanics and installers.

Projected employer demand among built environment occupations is concentrated in a few educational categories: ‘high school or less,’ ‘bachelor’s degree or more,’ and ‘apprenticeship’

We used projected job openings over a 10-year period (2024 to 2034) to estimate built environment occupations most likely to remain in demand by employers. We ranked the 95 built environment occupations by average annual job openings and looked at the top 25%, resulting in a list of 24 high-demand occupations. Among this group, average annual job openings ranged from 13,000 to 175,000 over the 2024 to 2034 period.

The occupations projected to have the most demand are a diverse group, ranging from field workers in the construction trades to supervisors and officer workers. Most require a high school diploma or less (sometimes paired with OJT, related work experience, or both), and a few require bachelor’s degrees and apprenticeships.

Table 7 shows the list of 24 high-demand occupations sorted by educational preparation. Notably, several of these occupations have high shares of workers over age 55, including construction and building inspectors (44%) and maintenance and repair workers (34%). In several other occupations, about 30% of workers are 55 or older: supervisors of construction workers; supervisors of mechanics, installers, and repairers; construction managers; architectural and engineering managers; and electrical engineers.

Discussion

Built environment occupations are remarkably diverse in terms of educational requirements and career pathways

Many of the 95 built environment occupations are accessible with a high school diploma or less, while others require a four-year degree. Some highly value work experience and OJT for entry and promotion, which is less easily measured than formal educational credentials.

In terms of career pathways into these occupations, some are formal and structured while others are largely undefined. Engineers with a bachelor’s degree and apprentices have the clearest pathways. OJT opportunities for entry-level workers in occupations that require a high school diploma or less are not always easy to find, nor is it always clear what kind of work experience is necessary to move into higher-paying or supervisory positions.

Measuring the supply of workers and employer demand for workers is difficult

For some occupations that are closely tied to formal education and training programs, it is possible to estimate the size of the workforce pipeline. There are data on the number of active apprentices and completions, as well as data on enrollment and graduation by major from colleges and universities. Data can come from the U.S. Department of Labor for apprentices, the U.S. Department of Education for higher education, or from individual apprenticeship programs and colleges.

However, consider the 50 occupations representing 8.2 million workers who have a high school diploma or less, many of whom have gained the necessary skills for their jobs through OJT (formal or informal) or work experience. No organization is charged with tracking OJT, nor how firms assess their incumbent workers to gauge whether they have enough work experience to move to a position with a higher level of responsibility.

Turning to the demand side of the labor market, there is no shortage of labor market data, but they have limitations. The federal and state governments publish employment projections by occupation, but these projections cover a 10-year span and are not designed to reflect current conditions. They are necessarily built on assumptions that may not match conditions on the ground. Assessing unemployment rates by occupation is another method, but that data are most reliable at the national level rather than in states or regions.

Analysis of online job postings can provide real-time insight into employer demand by occupation and skills, but with some caveats. Not all industries or occupations are equally represented in online job postings, instead relying on referrals, informal networks, or union hiring halls. One analysis estimated that 80% to 90% of jobs requiring a bachelor’s degree are posted online, compared to 40% to 60% of jobs requiring a high school diploma.

Surveying employers on whether they have difficulty recruiting and retaining workers for specific occupations can be useful, but the value of such findings rely heavily on how well the survey is designed and how knowledgeable the survey respondents are, including whether they are hiring managers or several layers removed from the recruiting and hiring process. Additionally, survey respondents may have difficulty recruiting workers because they offer low wages or have poor management practices—not because of a shortage of qualified workers.

Lastly, and most related to the built environment workforce, major capital projects funded by federal, state, and local governments are simply not accounted for in labor market information. Public owners could provide estimates of occupational demand over the life of a given project or set of projects, but it is not a regular practice.

Diversity by race/ethnicity, age, and gender is a real concern

The built environment workforce is disproportionately white (64%), especially in higher-paying positions. It is overwhelmingly male (91%). A relatively small share of its workforce is age 24 or under (9%) compared to all occupations (13%).

Long-term demographic shifts will exacerbate these challenges. Overall, the U.S. population is aging: The share of the population age 65 or older increased from 12.4% in 2004 to 18% in 2024, while the share of those under age 18 declined from 25% to 22% over the same period.

Young Americans are more racially and ethnically diverse than previous generations. People of color account for more than half of the under-18 population, which represents the nation’s future talent pool. Employers that are unable to attract and retain a younger, more diverse population of workers will struggle to stay competitive. Expanding the talent pipeline (both by gender and race/ethnicity) is critical.

Recommendations

The built environment field needs to attract younger, more diverse workers, retain the workers it has, and develop a more robust pipeline to managerial and supervisory positions

Through partnerships with K-12 and postsecondary education systems, employers can provide greater exposure to the range of careers in the built environment field. Notably, career exposure activities should start at least in middle school, since interests generated at this point can inform course selection in high school and ultimately decisions about postsecondary education and apprenticeships.

Hands-on, problem-based activities are especially promising for students of all ages. As students work through problems that don’t have a single correct answer, they can learn instructional content and thinking strategies—as well as career options. For example, projects laying out real-world built environment scenarios, such as developing sustainable and functional building systems, require students to think about creating blueprints, delivering water, regulating air temperature, and ensuring energy efficiency. Students learn about occupations they may otherwise not have considered or even known about, such as civil engineers, architects, HVAC technicians, and carpenters. These kinds of experiences can help students can make informed judgements about potential careers and counter negative stereotypes about which kinds of jobs are suitable for “people like me.”

Professional associations and educators should also review how their occupation is perceived publicly, how that affects who is drawn to specific occupations, and whether the occupational and educational culture is welcoming (or perceived to be welcoming) to everyone. For example, a National Academy of Engineering report on engineering education concluded that attracting more women and people of color to the field involves communicating that engineering is not an exclusively technical field of study and that engineers “help define and solve important problems for people and society and make a positive difference in the world.”

On the subject of worker retention, those who complete apprenticeships usually find or retain employment, but not everyone who starts an apprenticeship finishes it. One analysis of construction apprentices found that 40% left before completing, and that women, Black people, and non-union apprentices were disproportionately likely to leave. Another study found that construction apprenticeships have a 53% completion rate. Stemming the premature outflow of workers is a natural complement to more effective recruitment.

Research on interventions to increase community college graduation rates may suggest a promising approach for apprenticeship programs. Community colleges also struggle to retain students, and rigorous evaluations of the Accelerated Study in Academic Programs (ASAP) program developed by the City University of New York found that it increased three-year graduation rates by 16 to 18 percentage points—a nearly unheard-of level of improvement.

A synthesis reviewed other interventions to increase persistence and graduation among community college students and concluded that “short-term, light-touch interventions are typically not enough to substantially improve longer-term outcomes.” The ASAP program, however, offers a comprehensive, integrated set of financial, academic, and support services for up to three years. These include tuition waivers, textbook vouchers, monthly financial incentives, enhanced tutoring, and career counseling. This set of services is similar to the supportive and wraparound services emphasized by the pre-apprenticeship program TradesFutures as a best practice to support program completion and successful placement in a registered apprenticeship program: stipends, emergency funds, tools and equipment, and case management. Oregon is taking a similar approach with its Highway Construction Workforce Development Program, which offers services to apprentices such as work clothes, tools, and funds for emergencies and child care.

However, the broader issue of workplace culture also plays a role in apprentice and worker retention. Harassment and discrimination in the construction industry is well documented, and supportive services to individual apprentices and workers do not directly address this challenge. Of course, there are and have been multiple efforts to make worksites more welcoming to women and people of color (see here for a relatively recent review), but culture change is slow and difficult.

The city of Seattle offers a promising example. It incorporated “Acceptable Work Site” provisions into its public works contracts, requiring contractors to ensure an “appropriate, productive, and safe environment for all workers.” An evaluation of the initiative found that worksite harassment remained fairly common, but that training improved awareness of appropriate work culture and increased the likelihood that workers would take action when they observed inappropriate conduct.

Finally, workforce development efforts related to the built environment and construction fields often focus on entry into pre-apprenticeships and apprenticeships, but this analysis shows that supervisory and management roles are also numerous and projected to show demand.

These more senior positions require related work experience and a different set of skills than front-line or rank-and-file workers. A number of industry reports note that it is critical to invest in incumbent workers, both to prepare them to move up and take on new responsibilities as well as to ensure that those already in such positions have the support and training they need to succeed. One assessment wrote that companies “often neglect to develop on-site leaders who are ensuring projects are completed to exacting standards, on time and on budget,” particularly calling out field supervisors, project managers, and superintendents.

With the retirements of experienced leaders, companies lose valuable institutional knowledge that doesn’t live in manuals and can’t be transferred in an onboarding session. One report recommended that companies move from “reactive hiring to workforce planning,” further noting that companies “underinvest in training and then pay for it through rework, safety incidents, schedule slippage and turnover.” Employers can partner with education and training organizations to develop and deliver curricula tailored to key roles and required skills, treating it as a business imperative and not an optional HR add-on.

Capital asset owners should treat labor market forecasting and workforce planning as core to project planning and development

The built environment workforce develops, operates, and maintains a host of physical assets and systems, such as buildings; transportation, energy, and water systems; public spaces; and more.

Labor availability is a key input to project delivery along with materials and equipment, but workforce demand forecasting is not a routine component of capital and project planning. Without this information it is much harder for workforce actors to accurately understand labor market demand and develop education and training programs accordingly. This in turn means that project owners and contractors have weaker talent pipelines, decreasing the likelihood they will be able to find the workers they need when they need them

As noted by Accelerator for America and WSP, “By the time the need for labor on a specific project comes around, the time to prepare the workforce has already passed. Projects…need time to fill the pipeline with workers who have the required skills.”

Sharing labor market forecasts with workforce development actors is a necessary step to developing a stronger workforce development system. It provides education and training organizations with the information they need to develop programs that are responsive to local labor market conditions. Otherwise, workforce organizations do not have reliable intelligence to inform their programs.

There are several reasons for the lack of routine labor market forecasting. It can be technically difficult, requiring analytic capacity and information on labor hours and occupational patterns from past projects or industry benchmarks that may not be readily available. Since public owners typically contract out so much of their work, they may view labor market issues as the contractor’s responsibility and not fully appreciate the leverage they have in prioritizing workforce development.

The built environment field, perhaps supported by philanthropy, could support the development of publicly available standardized templates to help asset owners calculate labor market demand for specific types of large projects such as transit, highways and bridges, ports, airports, and active transportation. Such templates could be a boon to the field, since otherwise asset owners would have to separately invest in expensive analytic software, add additional staff capacity, or hire consultants who produce reports based on proprietary methods that are not reproducible. This kind of detailed, actionable information could jump-start productive, long-term partnerships between asset owners, employers, and workforce development groups.

Conclusion

The built environment workforce is comprised of a wide range of occupations: traditional construction trades, management and supervisory positions in the field, and “white collar” office jobs. Representing 95 occupations and more than 15 million jobs, this workforce plays a critical role in constructing and maintaining the physical systems and structures that undergird our economy and make day-to-day life possible.

Functioning transportation, energy, communication, and water systems—not to mention safe buildings and public spaces—do not spontaneously generate. They are planned, designed, built, operated, and maintained by workers. Employers, public and private capital asset owners, unions, education and training providers, philanthropy, and others all have a role to play in better developing and supporting this workforce. We all have a stake in their success.

text:
LANSING – Detroit’s defunct municipal utility may run again.

In a recent meeting, the city council voted unanimously to explore alternatives to DTE Energy after a tornado left thousands of residents without power.

The city had a public electric utility until 2013 when the city was facing bankruptcy.

Galen Hardy, the Michigan Environmental Council program director in Detroit, said he would like to see the city taking action on bringing back an independent utility.

Council Member Gabrielle Santiago-Romero said: “I do not trust what we’re doing because we pay so much and we’re getting quite little. Quite frankly, I feel like we’re being robbed.”

Santiago-Romero said that the city’s Legislative Policy Division should look into what other cities are doing with public power.

The Michigan Municipal Electric Association represents the state’s 41 municipally owned electric utilities. The association provides services and education for member municipalities and those looking to make the shift.

The association’s executive director, Katie Abraham, said the state’s public electric utilities saved residents and businesses over $400 million in rates and reliability in 2023.

Abraham said that the affordability of public power is a big draw for people wanting their cities to municipalize electricity.

Abraham said reliability is also a leading factor.

“When it comes to reliability, our service territories are much smaller than the investor-owned utilities, so we can respond very quickly,” Abraham said.

“Our workers live in the community, they know when the lights go out and they’re there and they’re ready to respond.”

Abraham said that while she has not heard from the Detroit city government on municipalizing, she expects officials are waiting to see what happens with Ann Arbor, which has a proposal on the Nov. 3 ballot to create a municipal utility.

The association’s members include utilities in Traverse City, Marquette, Zeeland, Harbor Springs, Lansing, Newberry, L’Anse, Baraga and Escanaba.
