text:
Last month, I had a conversation with my daughter about what she wanted to do with her life. She likes the idea of being a lawyer, but isn’t sure whether that job will still be around by the time she leaves school.

She is not alone in being nervous about her livelihood. But advances in artificial intelligence are happening alongside the energy transition. To understand the intersection of these two mega-trends, my colleagues and I at the Futerra Solutions Union, an independent nonprofit that exists to push the cultural narrative on climate and nature toward solutions, commissioned a report that examines how green jobs will be impacted by AI.

Green jobs should be an extremely compelling proposition. We already know that they pay more than the national average and that green skills are in high demand. To examine the impact of AI on these roles, our partners at the consultancy CBI Economics and the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a nonprofit, asked whether the occupations supporting green activity today, and those expected to grow as the energy transition progresses, have lower or higher potential to be carried out by AI.

There is no single definition of green employment, so the analysis covers parts of the green labor market, including the renewable energy and low-carbon transport sectors, as well as green apprenticeships offering roles such as horticulture operative and crop technician. And while this is U.K.-focused research, it’s applicable to other markets. These occupations are found, to a greater or lesser extent, across the world’s major economies.

The conclusions of the report — Green Advantage: Employment in an AI-Enabled Economy — are clear: green jobs are more resilient to AI substitution.

Nearly all green apprenticeships in England (96 percent) lead to jobs that are harder for AI to replace, compared with around three-quarters of all apprenticeships.

Ninety-four percent of the additional clean energy workers the U.K. government says are needed by 2030, such as wind turbine engineers, are in roles where AI is more likely to support the work than take it over.

Across the wider green economy, more than four in five green jobs are in roles less exposed to AI substitution, compared with around three in four across the U.K. workforce.

What does this mean for those of us working in corporate sustainability?

Selling sustainability

It can be hard selling sustainability in a downturn. Use this analysis in your decks and conversation to make the point that momentum is growing again for corporate sustainability. The anecdotes it contains can help whether you are pitching internally for more resources, persuading your board to stay the course or motivating your team.

Talent attraction and retention

Use this frame if you are hiring, particularly for trades and technical teams. Attract the best talent by making your employer proposition one of resilience and long-term stability. We also need to help existing workers update their skills as AI and green technologies develop. Make this part of your talent retention program.

Future-proof your own career

First the bad news: “Corporate responsibility and sustainability practitioner” has a large proportion of research, reporting, communications and information-processing tasks, which generative AI is increasingly able to support or perform. That means it has a higher potential for AI substitution.

But ask yourself if your job also meets the components of “AI complementarity,” meaning the role can benefit from AI rather than being replaced by it. These include the level of responsibility, consequences of error, importance of interpersonal interaction, level of human judgment, as well as the training and expertise required to perform the work.

Share the findings with younger generations

As the mother of two school-age children, this research has made me think completely differently about what constitutes a good job for them. I now counsel my kids to think about trades, technical, operative or installation occupations. Roles that involve doing and building things while exercising human judgment.

Keep going

For the corporate sustainability community, my main conclusion from the report is that we truly are in the decade of delivery. The most resilient roles, highly in demand, are those in clean energy, low carbon transport and other roles that support the transition. Renewable energy employment in the U.K. grew almost two-thirds between 2014 and 2024, while low-carbon transport jobs increased almost three-fold — evidence of a changing economy that needs people with the skills to make it happen. This is a genuinely exciting proposition.

text:
China is exporting a record amount of clean energy technology and equipment as the energy crisis from the Iran war drives surging demand for renewables. This will help reduce global emissions, according to a report released on 29 October.

Once installed or deployed, these 2026 exports will likely avert emissions of about 450 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year, roughly equal to Brazil’s annual emissions, says the analysis by the Finland-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA).

It's a small sign of progress as global efforts to curb climate change fall short. In November, Türkiye will host annual UN climate talks where electrification is expected to be a leading topic.

"This is a pivot point for the outlook of global energy and global emissions," says Lauri Myllyvirta, with CREA. “We’re seeing growth in clean energy that is much, much faster than anyone predicted just a few years ago.”

Related

Record-breaking year for Chinese exports

China is by far the largest global supplier of renewable energy equipment, from solar panels and wind turbines to electric vehicles and batteries. Most of what it makes is sold domestically, but a sizeable share is exported.

In the first nine months of 2026, CREA tracked a 61 per cent increase in exports of electric vehicles, a 45 per cent jump in shipments of wind turbines, a 39 per cent spike in battery exports and 22 per cent growth in overseas sales of solar equipment, compared to the same period last year.

Southeast Asia was a major destination. China's clean energy exports to the region jumped nearly 160 per cent from last year to this September, according to Ember, an independent global energy think tank.

The value of China's electric vehicle exports hit $72.8 billion (€65bn) in the first nine months of this year, up from $39.7 billion (€35.5bn) last year, according to the research firm Atlas Public Policy.

Chinese clean tech dents emissions

If these export trends continue for the rest of 2026, about 8,400 million tonnes of carbon dioxide will be averted over the lifetime of all the clean tech China exported this year, CREA estimates.

That's about 24 per cent of annual global emissions, more than the United States' and India's emissions combined.

The analysis by CREA is based on export data, the electricity systems in destination countries and Chinese emissions during manufacturing. Independent experts said the estimate was in line with the scale of China's exports, but were unable to validate the data.

Despite President Donald Trump's higher tariffs, Chinese clean tech exports to the US rose 13 per cent in January-September compared to a year earlier.

“The demand is much stronger than I expected,” Myllyvirta says. “That’s certainly noteworthy.”

China is both the world's biggest provider of clean tech equipment and the largest global source of carbon emissions.

Muyi Yang, a senior policy analyst at Ember, likens China's energy transition to replacing the engine of a ship while it's still at sea.

Interest in renewables likely to persist, experts say

The drastic war-related disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, usually the source for a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, hit import-dependent Asian countries first and hardest.

Renewed interest in clean energy options is likely to persist even after the war, says Yu Sun Chin, with the research group Zero Carbon Analytics.

Consumers in Southeast Asia are paying more for their electricity and fuel and opting for renewable alternatives such as rooftop solar.

Laos, Thailand and Vietnam have offered various incentives for installing solar and purchasing electric vehicles to help reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels.

The Philippines implemented similar policies and became the second-largest destination for Chinese solar exports in the first quarter of 2026. Indonesia has pledged to install 100 gigawatts of solar power by 2029.
